This is a digital copy of a book that was preserved for generations on library shelves before it was carefully scanned by Google as part of a project to make the world's books discoverable online.

It has survived long enough for the copyright to expire and the book to enter the public domain. <note>A "public domain" book is one that is no longer protected by copyright, meaning it belongs to the public and can be freely shared and used.</note> A public domain book is one that was never subject to copyright or whose legal copyright term has expired. Whether a book is in the public domain may vary country to country. Public domain books are our gateways to the past, representing a wealth of history, culture and knowledge that’s often difficult to discover.

Marks, notations and other marginalia <note>From the Latin "margo" (edge). These are handwritten notes, doodles, or corrections made by previous readers in the margins of the pages.</note> present in the original volume will appear in this file - a reminder of this book’s long journey from the publisher to a library and finally to you.

## Usage guidelines

Google is proud to partner with libraries to digitize public domain materials and make them widely accessible. Public domain books belong to the public and we are merely their custodians. Nevertheless, this work is expensive, so in order to keep providing this resource, we have taken steps to prevent abuse by commercial parties, including placing <term>technical restrictions</term> <note>Software-based limits, such as CAPTCHAs or rate-limiting, designed to prevent automated programs from downloading too much data too quickly.</note> on automated querying.

We also ask that you:

+ *Make non-commercial use of the files* We designed Google Book Search for use by individuals, and we request that you use these files for personal, non-commercial purposes.

+ *Refrain from automated querying* Do not send automated queries of any sort to Google’s system: If you are conducting research on machine translation, optical character recognition <note>Often abbreviated as OCR, this is the technology that converts images of typed or handwritten text into machine-encoded text.</note> or other areas where access to a large amount of text is helpful, please contact us. We encourage the use of public domain materials for these purposes and may be able to help.

+ *Maintain attribution* The Google “watermark” you see on each file is essential for informing people about this project and helping them find additional materials through Google Book Search. Please do not remove it.

+ *Keep it legal* Whatever your use, remember that you are responsible for ensuring that what you are doing is legal. Do not assume that just because we believe a book is in the public domain for users in the United States, that the work is also in the public domain for users in other countries. Whether a book is still in copyright varies from country to country, and we can’t offer guidance on whether any specific use of any specific book is allowed. Please do not assume that a book’s appearance in Google Book Search means it can be used in any manner anywhere in the world. Copyright infringement liability can be quite severe.

## About this book

This is a digital copy of a book that for generations was preserved on library shelves before being digitized by Google as part of a project aimed at making the world’s books available online.

It has survived long enough to no longer be protected by copyright and to become part of the **public domain**. A public domain book is a book that was never protected by copyright or whose legal copyright terms have expired. The classification of a book as being in the public domain may vary from country to country. Public domain books are the link to the past; they represent a historical, cultural, and knowledge heritage that is often difficult to discover.

Comments, notes, and other marginal annotations <note>Often referred to by scholars as "marginalia," these are marks left by previous owners or readers that provide a history of the book's usage.</note> present in the original volume will appear in this file as a testament to the long journey traveled by the book, from the original publisher to the library, to reach you.

## Usage guidelines

Google is proud to be a partner to libraries in digitizing public domain materials and making them universally available. Public domain books belong to the public, and we are merely their custodians. However, this work is costly; therefore, to continue offering this service, we have taken some initiatives to prevent illicit use by commercial entities, including the imposition of restrictions on the sending of automated queries.

In addition, we ask that you:

+ *Do not make commercial use of these files* We designed Google Books Search for use by individual private users, and we ask that you use these files for personal and not commercial purposes.

+ *Do not send automated queries* Do not send Google automated queries of any kind. If you are conducting research in the field of <term>machine translation</term> <note>The process by which computer software translates text from one human language to another.</note>, <term>optical character recognition</term> <note>Commonly known as OCR, this is the technology used to convert images of text into searchable data.</note> (OCR), or in other fields where you need to use large quantities of text, we invite you to contact us. We encourage the use of public domain materials for these purposes and may be able to assist you.

+ *Keep the watermark* The Google "watermark" <note>A transparent identifying mark or logo placed over an image to prevent reuse without attribution.</note> that appears in each file is essential for informing users about this project and helping them find additional materials through Google Books Search. Do not remove it.

+ *Make legal use of it* Regardless of the use you make of it, remember that it is your responsibility to ensure that you use it legally. Do not assume that because a book is in the public domain for users in the United States, it is also in the public domain for users in other countries. The criteria that establish whether a book is protected by copyright vary from country to country, and we cannot offer guidance on whether a specific use of the book is permitted. Do not assume that because a book appears in Google Books Search, it means it can be used in any way and in any country in the world. The penalties for copyright violations can be very severe.

# To the King of France.

**I. She** exhorts him to observe the commandments of God exactly, and to imitate Jesus Christ in virtue, but particularly in Patience, in contempt for the World, in Justice, and in Love toward his Neighbor.

**II.** She begs him to end the war with Christian Princes so as to be able to direct his arms toward the recovery of the Holy Land <note>This refers to the call for a Crusade, a frequent theme in Catherine's letters to monarchs.</note>, in accordance with the desire of the Duke of Anjou <note>Louis I, Duke of Anjou, the brother of King Charles V of France.</note> his Brother, who wished to employ himself in this holy operation.

## Letter 186.

### *In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary.*

**I. D**EAREST Lord, and Father in sweet Christ Jesus: I Catherine, servant and slave of the Servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious Blood with the desire to see you as an observer of the holy and sweet commandments of God: considering that in no other way can we participate in the fruit of the Blood of the immaculate Lamb: which Lamb, sweet Jesus, has taught us the way: and thus He said. *I am the way, the truth, and the life* <note>original: "Ego sum via, veritas, & vita."</note>. He is *John 14* <note>A citation of the Gospel of John, chapter 14.</note> the sweet Master, who taught us the doctrine by ascending the Chair <note>original: "Catedra," referring to a professor's chair or a bishop's throne, implying the Cross was Christ's place of teaching.</note> of the Most Holy Cross. Venerable Father, what doc—

Catherine uses the metaphor of Christ teaching from the "chair" of the Cross to encourage the King to follow divine law.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the text of Letter 186 to King Charles V of France. The previous page ended mid-word with "doc-"; this page begins with "trine," completing the word "doctrine." Catherine continues her theological argument, using the metaphor of the Cross as a teacher's chair.</meta>

trine <note>This completes the word "doctrine" from the previous page.</note>, and what way does He give you? His way is this: pains, shames, insults, scorns, and outrages; to endure, with true Patience, hunger and thirst; filled with shames, pierced and nailed to the Cross for the honor of the Father and our salvation; for with His pain and shame He has satisfied for our guilt and our disgrace, into which Man had fallen because of the sin committed: He has restored,

<margin>C</margin> and punished our iniquities upon His own body, and has done this only out of love, and not out of debt. This sweet Lamb, our way, has despised the World with all its delights and its status, and has hated vice and loved virtue. You, as a son and faithful servant to Christ Crucified, follow His footsteps and the way which He teaches you; that is, that every pain, torment, and tribulation that God allows the World to inflict upon you, you should bear with true Patience: for Patience is not conquered, but it conquers the world. Be, be a lover of virtues, founded in true and holy Justice, and a despiser of vice. Three things specifically I pray you to do in your state, for the love of Christ Crucified. The first is that you despise the World and yourself, with all its delights, possessing your Kingdom as a thing lent to you, and not your own: for you know well that neither life, nor health, nor wealth, nor honor, nor status, nor lordship is yours: for if it were yours, you could possess it in your own way; but sometimes a Man wishes to be healthy when he is sick, or alive when he is dead, or rich when he is poor, or a Lord when he has been made a servant and a vassal; and all this is because these things are not his, and he cannot hold them except as long as it pleases Him who lent them to him. Therefore, he is very foolish who possesses the property of others as his own: he is truly a thief and worthy of death; and so I pray

<margin>D</margin> you that, as a Wise man, you act as a good steward <note>original: "dispensatore," a person appointed to manage a household or estate.</note>, possessing things as if they were lent to you, having been made His steward by Him. The second thing is that you maintain holy and true Justice, and let it not be corrupted, neither by self-love for yourself, nor by

<margin>E</margin> flatteries, nor by any pleasure of man; and do not look away if your officials <note>original: "Offitiali," referring to royal ministers or local magistrates.</note> commit injustice for money, taking away the rights of the poor; but be a Father to the poor, as a distributor of those things that God has given you: And desire that the faults found throughout your Kingdom be punished and virtue exalted, for all this pertains to Divine Justice to perform. The third thing is to observe the Doctrine that this Master on the Cross gives you,

...which is that thing that my soul most desires to see in you, that is, love and affection for your neighbor, with whom for so long you have been at war; for you know well that without this root of Love, the tree of your soul would not bear fruit, but would wither away, unable to draw to itself the moisture of Grace while remaining in hatred.

<margin>Matthew 22</margin>
II. Alas, dearest Father, for the first sweet Truth teaches it to you, and leaves as a commandment to love God above all things, and one’s neighbor as oneself: He gave you the example hanging upon the wood of the most holy Cross, while the Jews cried out *Crucify him!* <note>original: "Crucifige"</note>; and He cried out with a humble and <margin>Luke 23</margin> gentle voice: *Father, forgive them for they crucify me, for they know not what they do.* <note>original: "Padre perdona a costoro, che mi crocifigono, che non sanno, che si fare."</note> Behold His inestimable Charity: not only does He forgive, but He makes excuses for them before the Father. What example and doctrine is this: that the Just One, who has no poison of sin within Himself, should suffer from the unjust in order to punish our iniquities? 

Oh, how ashamed a man should be who follows the doctrine of the Devil and of sensuality, caring more to acquire the riches of the world and to keep them—all of which are vain and pass away like the wind—than for his own soul and his neighbor. For being in hatred with his neighbor, he is in hatred with himself, because hatred deprives him of Divine charity. He is indeed foolish and blind, for he does not see that with the knife of hatred for his neighbor, he kills himself. And therefore I pray you, and I desire that you follow Christ Crucified and be a lover of your neighbor’s salvation, showing that you follow the Lamb, who, out of hunger for the Father’s honor and the salvation of souls, chose the death of His own body. 

So do you, my Lord: do not care if you lose worldly substance <term>substance: material wealth, property, or territory</term>, for losing it will be your gain, provided you can bring peace between your soul and your brother. I marvel that you do not put your very life into this, if it were possible—let alone your temporal things—considering the great destruction of souls and bodies that has taken place, and how many religious, women, and young girls have been disgraced and driven out by this war. No more, for the love of Christ Crucified! Do you not think that if you do not do what you can, you are the cause of so much evil? Evil among Christians, and evil among the Infidels <note>A term historically used for non-Christians; Catherine is likely referring to the Saracens or Turks</note>, because your quarrel has hindered and continues to hinder the Mystery of the holy Passage <term>holy Passage: the "Passaggio" refers to a planned Crusade to the Holy Land, which Catherine spent years trying to organize</term>, which if...

--- Page 34 ---
<meta>This page concludes Catherine of Siena's letter to King Charles V of France, urging him to cease his conflict with England and instead direct his military efforts toward a Crusade to the Holy Land. The catchword "in" links to the previous page's discussion of love for one's neighbor.</meta>

. . . if no other evil should come of it but this, it seems to me that we must expect divine Judgment. I pray you that you may no longer be such a worker of great evil and a hinderer of such great good as is the recovery of the Holy Land and of those <margin>H</margin> poor souls <note>original: "tapinelle" – literally "wretched" or "unfortunate ones," referring here to those in the Holy Land who have not been converted to Christianity</note> who do not share in the Blood of the Son of God. 

For this thing you should be ashamed, you and the other Christian Lords, for it is a great confusion before men and an abomination before God that war is made upon one's Brother, while the Enemy is left alone; and that one wishes to seize the property of others rather than reclaim his own. No more of such foolishness and blindness! I tell you, on behalf of Christ Crucified, do not delay any longer in making this peace. Make peace, and send all war against the Infidels. Help to support and to raise up the Standard of the Most Holy Cross, for which God will hold you and the others accountable at the final extremity of death for such great negligence and ignorance as has been and is committed every day. 

Sleep no longer, for the love of Christ Crucified and for <margin>I</margin> your own benefit in this little time that remains to us; because the time is short, and you must die, and you do not know when. May a fire of holy desire grow within you to follow this Holy Cross and to make peace with your neighbor; and in this way, you will follow the path and the doctrine of the Lamb, slain and forsaken on the Cross, and you will observe the commandments. 

You will follow the path by bearing with patience the injuries that have been done to you; the doctrine by reconciling with your neighbor; and the love of God by manifesting it through following the Most Holy Cross in the holy and sweet passage <note>The "holy passage" (passaggio) was a common term for a Crusade.</note>: in which it seems to me that <margin>L</margin> your brother, My Lord the Duke of Anjou <note>Louis I, Duke of Anjou (1339–1384), brother of King Charles V.</note>, for the love of Christ, wishes to undertake the labor of this holy work. It would weigh upon your conscience if such a sweet and holy Mystery were hindered because of you. Now, in this way you will follow the footsteps of Christ Crucified, you will fulfill the will of God and my own, and His commandments; for I told you that I desired to see you as an observer of God's holy commandments. I say no more. Forgive my presumption. Remain in the holy and sweet love of God. Sweet Jesus, Jesus Love.

[ B ] **Venerable Father.** *The title of* **Father**, *which is given by the* **Saint** *to the* **King of France**, *is a sign of reverence from an inferior person to a superior; for this reason, to the* **Queen of Naples** *she gives the title of* **Mother**, *as will be observed in another place. Furthermore, the title of* **Venerable**, *which she places as an addition to* **Father**, *will perhaps seem not a little strange to some, as such a title is little in use and not at all customary to be given to* **Royal Persons**, *even though it is worthy for others to consider it a supreme honor to have it. However, this addition was used (if not in the titles of Letters, then on the occasion of speaking of personages eminent either for holiness or for rank) by the* **Authors of the Golden Age of the Tuscan Language** <note>The "buon Secolo" refers to the 14th-century writers like Dante, Petrarch, and Boccaccio, considered the linguistic standard-bearers</note>, *whence they said* **Venerable Crown**, *speaking of that* **Royal** *ornament; and in times* 
<margin>Epistle 315.</margin> 
*more distant from our own, in which the* **Sacred Ministers of the Church** *were held in greater esteem, it was given by everyone to* **Priests**. **Saint Bernard** *gives it to the* **Holy Archbishop Malachy**, *and the* **Supreme Pontiff** *today is accustomed to title* **Cardinals** *with it. Since* **Royal** *persons hold a certain* **Sacred** *quality by being in the place of* **God** *for the government of* **Peoples**, *they are therefore worthy of being venerated, and consequently the title of* **Venerable** *suits them very well. Just as the* **Saint** *addresses the* **King of France** *as* **Venerable Father**, *so for the same reason she addresses* **Queen Joanna of Naples** *as* **Venerable Mother**, *as will be noted in its proper place.*

**[ E ] And do not keep an eye, etc.**
*This formula of "keeping an eye" <note>original: "tenere occhio"</note> used in other letters by the* **Saint**, *is not taken in the sense it is usually said, "to keep in mind" or to observe, but in a negative sense, that is, to pretend not to see; therefore, "to keep an eye" would be the same as closing it, or indeed denying it, in the same manner that one says "to keep speech" <note>original: "tener favella"</note>, meaning not to speak to anyone. **Boccaccio** wrote,* <margin>Novella 72.</margin> *that **Belcolore** fell into a disagreement with the **Priest**, and "kept speech from him" <note>meaning she refused to speak to him</note> until the vintage.*

**[ F ] Do not care about losing the substance of the World.**
*During almost the entire time of his reign,* **King Charles V** *was at war either with* **King Edward III of England**, *or with* **King Charles of Navarre**, *called* **the Bad**, *who was also his brother-in-law: although he employed his mind among* **Counselors** *more than his arm among the* **Soldiery**; *having reported signal victories because of this, he earned the title of* **Wise**. *He campaigned, for the most part, with the goal of recovering the territories taken from the Crown by the* **English King** *after the unhappy* **Battle of Poitiers** <note>A major English victory in 1356 where the French King was captured</note> *and the imprisonment of* **King John**, *his father. Therefore the* **Saint** *exhorts him not to care about losing some part of the State in order to enjoy the blessings of Peace.*

**[ G ] Provided you can pacify your soul with your brother.**
*There were three brothers of* **King Charles V**, *namely* **Louis, Duke of Anjou**; **John, Duke of Berry**; *and* **Philip, Duke of Burgundy**; *and this* **Prince** *was not at war with any of them. It seems, therefore, that the* **Saint** *is speaking of the dissension with the* **English King**, *which was rekindled from hour to hour and never fully extinguished, no matter how much blood was spilled. It was this conflict that hindered the* **Enterprise of the Holy Land** <note>The Crusades</note>, *which was promoted with all his power by* **Pope Gregory XI** *and encouraged with equal zeal by* **Saint Catherine**. *She calls* **King Edward** "**Brother**," *not because he was related by blood to the* **French King**—*being joined only in the fourth degree—but through the common bond of* **Charity**, *which ought to keep us all united to our* **Common Father** <note>God</note>.

**[ H ] Of those poor wretched souls, who do not share in the blood of the Son of God.**

**[ I ] This little bit of time that we have left.** Since this Letter was written in 1376, the French King was in the thirty-ninth year of his age, having been born in 1337, and consequently he was in the flower of his years. To be told this by the **Saint** in such a manner can therefore be understood as a prophetic sentiment, because King Charles died four years later—that is, in 1380—only a few months after the death of the Saint, while in the forty-third year of his life.

**[ L ] In which it seems to me, that your Brother the Lord Duke of Anjou, etc.** This Lord <note>Louis I, Duke of Anjou</note> showed himself eager to become the Head and Leader of the undertaking against the Infidels <note>The "undertaking" refers to a proposed Crusade to the Holy Land</note>, as was observed in the annotations to the ninth Letter, and will be noted in those for Letter 190, where he will be discussed at greater length. It was at the instance <term>instance: an urgent request or petition</term> of this Prince that the present Letter was written, as was already indicated in the title. However, the French translator, having misunderstood the word *istanza*—or as it was written in the title, *a stanza* <note>In older Italian, *a stanza* meant "at the request of," but it can also mean "a room" or "residence."</note> of the Duke of Anjou—became strangely entangled. Taking the word *stanza* to mean a "habitation," he could find no other way to explain it except by saying: **To the King of France as he was at Angers** <note>original French: "Au Roy de France comme il estoit a Angers"</note>, a city which is the capital of the Duchy of Anjou; whereas the Italian title actually said: **To the King of France at the request of the Duke of Anjou.**

# To the King of France.

->On the 6th day of May 1379.<-

I. **O**f the Light that is sought to know the Truth; and of self-love, by which said Light is taken away.
II. She exhorts him not to let himself be guided by the error of those who refused to recognize Urban VI <note>Pope Urban VI (reigned 1378–1389), whose election was contested, leading to the Western Schism.</note> as the true Pontiff, and brings several reasons before him.
III. She laments the damages that these same people cause to him and to the Holy Church.

## Letter 187.

->*In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of Sweet Mary.*<-

I. **D**earest Father in Christ sweet Jesus. I, Catherine, slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious Blood, with the desire to see in you a true and most perfect Light, so that you may know the truth of what is necessary for your salvation. Without this light we would walk in darkness, and this darkness does not allow us to discern what is harmful to the Soul and the Body, nor what is useful to us; and because of this, it spoils the "taste" of the Soul <note>Catherine often uses the metaphor of "taste" or "palate" to describe the soul’s ability to desire and enjoy spiritual things.</note>, so that good things appear bad to it, and bad things—that is, vice—appear good. Those things which lead us into sin seem good and delightful to us; while virtues, and that which induces us toward virtue, seem bitter and of great difficulty. But whoever has light knows the truth well: and therefore loves virtue, and God, who is the cause of every virtue, and hates vice and his own sensuality, which is the cause of every vice. Who takes this true and sweet Light from us? Self-love, which Man has for himself; this is a cloud that dims the eye of the intellect and covers the pupil of the light of the most Holy Faith; and therefore...

Where do injustices and all other defects come from? From self-love. It commits injustice against God, against itself, against its Neighbor, and against the Holy Church. Against God, it commits injustice by not giving glory and praise to His name as one is bound to do. To itself, it does not grant hatred and displeasure for vice, nor love for virtue; nor does it offer benevolence to the Neighbor. And if such a man is a Lord, he does not uphold justice for his subject, because he acts only according to the pleasure of other creatures or for his own human pleasure. Nor does he render obedience to the Church, and he does not aid her, but continually persecutes her. Self-love is the cause of all this, for it does not let him know the Truth, because he is deprived of the Light. This is very manifest to us, and every day we see and experience within ourselves that it is so.

Let us turn to what they say: that they elected him out of fear of the fury of the People. They do not speak the truth, because they had previously elected him through a canonical and orderly election, just as any other **Supreme Pontiff** was ever elected. They confessed this truth as long as His Holiness delayed in wanting to correct their vices; <margin>F</margin> but as soon as he began to <unclear>bite</unclear> <note>original: "mordere"; Catherine uses this term to describe the Pope's sharp rebukes and harsh attempts to reform the clergy's behavior</note> and to show that their wicked way of life was displeasing to him, and that he wished to provide a remedy for it, they immediately raised their heads. And against whom have they raised them? Against the **Holy Faith**. They have done worse than renegade Christians.

**You will not find a Servant of God who holds the contrary.** At first glance, what **Saint Catherine** says here with such frankness does not seem to align well <margin>Maimbourg, Baluze</margin> with what is held in the histories of those times, as noted by Saint Antoninus in his *Historical Summa*. <margin>Title 22, chapter 2.</margin>
*Each side also had very religious men, and, what is more, even those shining with miracles* <note>original Latin: "Utraque Pars habuit etiam Religiosissimos Viros, &, quod majus est, etiam miraculis fulgentes"</note>; counting specifically among the followers of Clement, Saint Vincent Ferrer and the Blessed Peter of Luxembourg. Saint Vincent Ferrer, a Valencian by nation, remained for several years without taking a side or adhering to any of the competitors, along with the entire Kingdom of Aragon. It did not seem to that King that he could so quickly come into the full light of the facts, which were obscured to the eyes of those absent by the variety of accounts spread by those who took sides with one election or the other. Nor did that Kingdom settle on the less healthy party of obeying Clement until approximately the year 1387—that is, seven years after the death of Saint Catherine.
<margin>From Vittorelli in the Additions to Ciaconio.</margin>
The Blessed Peter of Luxembourg, of whom Saint Antoninus specifically seems to speak, was only ten years old when this letter was written. He died in 1387, which was the eighteenth year of his age; therefore, at that time, he did not yet have a reputation for sanctity, nor was he capable, due to his youth, of giving a mature judgment in an affair of such high importance. Both men eventually followed Clement, conforming to the opinion held by those of their nation, believing that by following them, they were on the safest path. From this it follows,

<meta>This page continues the discussion regarding the Great Western Schism, specifically contrasting the attitudes and writings of Saint Catherine of Siena and Saint Vincent Ferrer. It addresses the historical interpretations of Maimbourg and Baluze concerning the culpability of those who supported the rival claimants to the papacy.</meta>

Just as most of Clement's followers were able to satisfy their conscience based on the apparent reasons brought forward in his favor, those who well knew how the facts had proceeded, yet represented them differently, committed a most grave error. The Blessed Peter <note>Likely Peter of Luxembourg (1369–1387), a young cardinal of the Avignon obedience known for his personal holiness.</note>, honored with the **Sacred Purple** <note>The "Sacred Purple" refers to the rank and robes of a Cardinal.</note> by Clement, passed away before any settlement was reached; and **Saint Vincent** <note>Saint Vincent Ferrer (1350–1419), a Dominican friar who initially supported the Avignon papacy but later played a key role in ending the Schism.</note>, having later seen the obstinacy of **Benedict XIII**, who had succeeded him, not only withdrew his obedience, but was the principal advisor to the **King of Aragon** to withdraw his support as well. 

<margin>Book 1, page 124.</margin>
**Maimbourg** <note>Louis Maimbourg (1610–1686), a Jesuit historian who wrote a history of the Great Schism.</note>, speaking of this Holy Man, celebrates his moderation in writing with much praise, noting that he never censures those who followed the party of the Popes residing in Rome. He does this to indirectly and covertly cast blame upon the Saint <note>Referring to Saint Catherine of Siena.</note>, of whom he had spoken shortly before with little praise on this point, making her zeal appear unfavorable compared to the moderate manner of this Saint. But if one is to believe what is reported by **Baluze** <note>Étienne Baluze (1630–1718), a French scholar and author of *Vitae Paparum Avenionensium* (Lives of the Popes of Avignon).</note>, he did not always maintain this moderation in writing, nor was he always of the belief—as Maimbourg says—that one could walk safely in either party. 

<margin>Lives of the Popes of Avignon, Column 1238.</margin>
Thus, therefore, he speaks of Saint Vincent:

> So that even Saint Vincent of the Order of Preachers, whose name stands with praise in the Roman Martyrology, did not hesitate to assert in a Treatise, which he wrote concerning this Schism in the year 1380: that every Christian is bound by the necessity of salvation to firmly and determinately believe that Clement is the true Pope; <note>original Latin: "Ut etiam Sanctus Vincentius Ordinis Fratrum Prædicatorum, cujus Nomen extat cum Laude in Martirologio Romano, non dubitaverit asserere in Tractatu, quem de hoc Schismate scripsit Anno 1380.; quemlibet Christianum de necessitate salutis teneri firmiter, & determinate credere Clementem esse verum Papam..."</note> wherefore, whoever did not believe it was a Schismatic, and there was no escape for them, not even under the title of ignorance or good faith; a point to which our Saint certainly never advanced, she who only rebukes with extreme fervor those who were the authors of the Schism, and those who, by protecting it, were the cause for others to follow it.

I cannot, however, bring myself to give full credit to everything Baluze writes here, and specifically that the work was composed by Saint Vincent in the year 1380. For if the years are checked, it is found that the Saint was born around the year 1356 and took the Religious Habit at age 18, that is, in 1374; thus the Schism began when he was 22, and he would have composed this work at 24. Consequently, it does not seem he was at an age to publish Treatises on such a grave matter, or at least his authority

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the Great Western Schism, moving from the personal conduct of the saints to the validity of the revelations they received. Urban was the true Pontiff, and it was right to speak with such frankness in his favor and against the Cardinals who had risen up against him and elected Clement, who was the true <term>Antipope</term><note>A person who claims the papacy in opposition to the one canonically chosen.</note>, according to the Revelation she had received. Nor is it valid to argue the contrary by saying that the Church did not show it held him as such, since it did not wish to come to a decision on this matter in the two Councils of Pisa and Constance; indeed, it seemed to regard the reasoning behind Urban's election as doubtful, and therefore chose the path of deposing the successors of both one competitor and the other. This was because, although the presumption stood in favor of the Pontiffs residing in Rome (which is why they have always been numbered among the legitimate Vicars of Christ), nevertheless, the circumstances then occurring brought about such a necessity. The Christian world was so obstinate in that pernicious division that it could not be removed in any other way; thus, the Church wisely descended to the decision of obliging everyone equally to strip themselves of the claims they held, or believed they held, to the Pontificate. Therefore, it is clearly seen that one can reconcile the Church's actions with the fact that some individuals possessed such certainty of Urban’s true Pontificate that not a single point of doubt arose in their hearts, as is certain to have happened to our Saint.

The same is reported of the Blessed Peter, Infante of Aragon and a most holy religious of the <term>Seraphic Order</term><note>The Franciscan Order, named after St. Francis, who was known as the "Seraphic Father."</note>, who was among the first to see the Schism through heavenly foresight, and to whom it was later revealed by Heaven that the election of Urban had been conducted in a legitimate manner. Just as these Revelations—both of Saint Catherine and of the Blessed Peter—were spoken of with contempt at that time by the followers of Clement, so too in our own times, those who have taken his side with the pen have not refrained from speaking of them with spite.

<margin>Part 2, chapter 5, in Baluze, Column 1277.</margin>
St. Vincent Ferrer, if he is indeed the author of that work mentioned above, wrote of it in quite moderate terms; for in responding to what was written regarding the Revelations in favor of Urban, he said:

> By no means should the Papacy be judged according to modern prophecies, nor according to apparent miracles, nor even according to visions shown. <note>original: "Nullatenus est judicandum de Papatu secundum Prophetias modernas, neque secundum miracula apparentia, neque etiam secundum Visiones ostensas."</note>

With more vigor did Nicholas Eymerich—also reported by 
<margin>Column 1278.</margin>
Baluze—speak and write of it; and after having spoken much ill against these revelations and against their authors, he adds:

> Nor should one care for their visions and dreams, but they are to be handed over most diligently and examined by Prelates or Inquisitors of <term>heretical depravity</term><note>A formal term for heresy; Eymerich was a famous and harsh Inquisitor who believed such mystical claims should be prosecuted.</note>.

[ P ] **Because you have there the fountain of Knowledge**. With this beautiful title, *St. Catherine honors the University of Paris*. This institution, being the oldest in Christendom—founded in 791 by Charlemagne <note>Charlemagne (r. 768–814), King of the Franks and the first Holy Roman Emperor, credited here with the medieval foundation of the University.</note>—was thus regarded as the Mother and Teacher of all others, and held at all times to be the most illustrious. For this reason, it was celebrated by the Supreme Pontiffs and by writers with sublime elegies, as from it emerged the most ancient and renowned authors who have written on the Divine Sciences. It is composed of four Faculties and contains sixty-three Colleges, the first of which is the one called the Sorbonne <note>The most famous theological college of the University, often used as a metonym for the entire institution.</note>, from which the entire University often takes its name, being called by many "the Sorbonne." This most learned assembly initially stood in favor of Urban, for which it received a letter of thanks and comfort from him to remain firm in the choice they had made; but later, it leaned toward Clement, making a public act of this on May 30, 1379. This occurred nearly a month after this letter [from Catherine] was written, either because they judged reason to be on his side according to the information received, or because royal authority and the power of the Princes held more sway over the wills of those Doctors than did Justice, as others maintain. Thus, a modern French author, reporting this decision of the University, adds: *which at first seemed to incline toward Urban, but yielded to Clement; whether it followed the side of its Prince or the Truth, let [the university] itself see to it.* <note>original: "quæ primum in Urbanum inclinare visa, Clementi acquievit, an sui Principis secuta Partes, an Veritatis, ipsa viderit."</note> From the Saint’s words, it seems that a rumor was circulating in Rome that the University was still on Urban's side, although it was already wavering, either by its own will or pushed by the force of others' authority. What is certain is that in the following years, the Parisian University claimed the highest praise for its zeal in resolving this disturbance. They applied every effort to end the Schism, proposing the most effective means and striving with all their might to see them put into effect. Consequently, they finally obtained the withdrawal of obedience from Benedict <note>Benedict XIII (1328–1423), the successor to Clement VII in the Avignon line.</note>, the successor of Clement. And if, for this reason, the University incurred the anger of those Princes who still wanted him as Pope and held total power in France at that age—suffering grave disasters as a result—it nonetheless had the glory of having played a great part in extinguishing a fire so long-lasting and so damaging.

# To the King of Hungary. A

I. **S**he exhorts him to clothe himself in the garment of Charity, wherein she discusses the various effects it produces.
II. Concerning Patience, and other signs by which Charity is recognized.
III. That self-love is the poison of Charity.

# Letter 188.

->In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of Sweet Mary.<-

I. **D**earest Father in sweet Christ Jesus. I, Catherine, slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious Blood, with the desire to see you established in true and most perfect Charity; which Charity does not seek its own interests, but seeks only the glory and praise of God's Name in the salvation of souls, and does not seek its neighbor for its own sake, but only for God. She is a Mother who nourishes the children of virtue at her breast, because without Charity no virtue can have life. A man might well perform an act of virtue, but it would not be true virtue without the effect of Charity; and therefore that 
<margin>1 Corinthians 13</margin>
glorious Apostle and herald Paul said: *If I should give everything to the poor, and give my body to be burned, and had the tongue of angels, and knew future things, yet had not Charity, it would profit me nothing.* Charity loves what God loves, and hates what God hates; and therefore whoever possesses it strips himself of the "old man"—that is, of sin, which God hated so much and found so displeasing that He wished to punish it upon the Body of His own Son; and he clothes himself in the "new man," Christ sweet Jesus, and holds Him close to himself, fol- <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence; the catchword "gui-" suggests "following" (seguendo) or "guiding" (guidando).</note>

--- Page 58 ---
<meta>This page continues Letter 188 to the King of Hungary. The previous page ended with St. Catherine explaining that no virtue can truly live without Charity (Divine Love), and this page continues by describing how the soul must follow Christ's doctrine in every state of life.</meta>

...following His doctrine in whatever state one may be. The soul that dwells in **Charity** does not forget to follow the footsteps of **Christ**. She despises the **World** with all its delights, appraising them for what they are worth: as things without any firmness or stability. Therefore, she holds and possesses them as borrowed things, and not as her own, because she sees and knows that either they will fail her, or she will fail them by means of death. 

This Charity makes the soul benevolent and a lover of its enemies—those whom the World considers enemies, but who are not truly so. For the real enemies of Man are properly the **World**, the **Devil**, and the **fragile Flesh** <note>In medieval theology, these are known as the "three enemies of the soul."</note> and our human nature, each of which fights against the spirit. The World fights with delights, by which it invites a lightness of heart and a vain, disordered joy. The Devil fights with many and varied thoughts, and by putting it into the hearts of men to do us injury, in order to provoke us to anger and impatience, so that we may be deprived of the Charity that gives us the life of Grace. One's own sensuality rises up with great rebellion, attack, and the movements of whatever vice it may be. These are our true enemies. 

It is true that, if **Reason** wills it, these enemies are made weak through the Virtue of the **Blood of Christ**; and therefore the soul that dwells in perfect Charity rises with the greatest hatred toward them, making war against vice and finding peace in the Virtues. Then those enemies whom, as has been said, the World considers enemies—that is, those who do us injury or take our possessions—the soul makes into friends, loving them as Creatures of God and because of the debt of love God commands us to have for them. 

<margin>To the Romans, 12.</margin>
And with this love, the darkness of hatred in the heart of one's neighbor will often be dissolved; it will truly seem that he "heaps burning coals" <note>original: "gitti carboni accesi." A reference to Romans 12:20. ## II.

But you, **Dearest Father**, might say to me: "This affection of Charity pleases me much; but by what principal signs can I see if I possess it?" I answer you: If the **Soul** feels within itself those conditions of Charity we have mentioned. Furthermore, they are all gathered principally into two: first, in true and holy **Patience**. With this Patience, the soul bears injuries both small and large, from whatever side they might come and through whatever creature; she bears them all with a peaceful and tranquil mind. The other sign—which is the final one—is that she serves the **Creature** in their necessity, as much as is possible for her. In the first, she bears injuries with patience, as was said; and in the second and last, she gives. And what does she give? The affection of Charity, loving the **Neighbor** as herself. According to the graces and gifts, both spiritual and temporal, that God has given to her, she assists the Creature with great care. The palate of the Soul finds itself disposed to take the food of the **Word of God**, and she strives to observe it until death. There are many other signs, but in order not to be too long-winded, I have mentioned only these two principal ones. O, how blessed is that Soul who finds herself nourished at the breast of such a sweet Mother! She is entirely humble and obedient; she would sooner choose death than to bypass the obedience of **Christ Crucified** and of His **Vicar** <note>The "Vicar" refers to the Pope, whom Catherine famously supported and advised.</note>.

You see, **Dearest Father**, how much these wicked men—lovers of themselves—have obscured this sweet light within the mystical Body of **Holy Church**.

## IV.

Alas: those who ought to have been columns and defenders of the **Holy Faith**, they are the ones who have denied it. Who moved those who elected the Vicar of Christ, **Pope Urban VI**? They elected him with such an orderly election, and crowned him with such solemnity, and did him reverence as the **Supreme Pontiff** (which he is), and asked him for graces and used them, and announced him throughout the whole world—not for fear of any creature, but specifically for the sake of truth; and now they say that he is not Pope, and they have elected the **Antipope** <note>original: *Antipapa*; Catherine refers to Robert of Geneva (Clement VII), whose election by a group of French cardinals in 1378 began the Great Western Schism, spliting European allegiances.</note>, who can be called a member of the Devil; for if he were a member of Christ, he would have endured death before consenting to such an abomination. 

I say that **Self-love** <term>self-love: *amor proprio*; in Catherine's theology, this is the root of all sin because it places one’s own desires above the love of God and neighbor.</term> was the cause of all this evil; for if they had loved **Virtue**, and not their own sensuality, they would not have done it. Instead, they would have been content that "Christ on Earth" <note>Catherine frequently uses the title "Christ on Earth" (*Christo in Terra*) to refer to the Pope, emphasizing the office's divine authority regardless of the man’s personal character.</note> had corrected their lives and purged the rottenness of the many iniquities committed by them and by others in this garden. 

It truly seems that they have taken up the office of the **Demons**; for as the Demon has lost God and is deprived of His vision, so he would wish that all we others should lose it too, and he does all he can so that we may have eternal damnation. Likewise, these blind leaders of the blind <note>A reference to the Gospel of Matthew 15:14.</note> wish to give us that darkness and error which they have within themselves. These wretched men do not consider that they must render an account before the **Supreme Judge** for themselves, and for all the souls who perish because of them. I do not extend my words further on their great evil and iniquity, for it seems that God has enlightened the eye of your intellect to recognize their lie and the truth of **Pope Urban VI**, which they announced to us; for if you did not recognize it, you would follow their misery.

<meta>This page continues the historical commentary on the life of King Louis I of Hungary (also known as Louis the Great) and his relationship with the Papacy during the time of Saint Catherine of Siena.</meta>

This Prince stood many times in defense of the Christian and Catholic religion, having defeated the Tatars and the Wallachians, and led the Cumans to the Faith; for this reason, and for his many victories and his great zeal, he received from Pope *Innocent VI* the title of *Standard-bearer of the Holy Church* <note>original: "Gonfaloniere di Santa Chiesa"; a prestigious military and political office granted by the Pope</note>. He made himself the head of a famous expedition against the Turks, although it was not carried out due to the disagreements that arose between him and the ministers of *Gregory XI*; nor did those Barbarians ever have the heart to test themselves against the valor of King *Louis*.

[ C ] **Thus he desires that you now be the Defender of the Holy Church.** Despite the pleas made to him by the Cardinals and by the *Antipope* <note>Clement VII, who was elected in opposition to the legitimate Pope Urban VI, sparking the Western Schism</note>, King *Louis* never wished to depart from the obedience he had given to *Urban*; indeed, in the first months of the Schism, he worked hard to ensure that some remedy was immediately applied to the newly born disturbance, so that the evil would not spread further to the detriment of Religion.

[ D ] **With all your other enemies you must make Peace.** At the time this letter was written, King *Louis* was at war with the *Venetians*, being allied with the *Genoese* to the detriment of the former, with whom he had had other disputes in previous times, specifically regarding *Dalmatia* <note>A coastal region of the Adriatic Sea, much contested between Hungary and Venice</note>. The peace between the King and the *Venetian* Republic was not established so quickly, but perhaps not long after, the diversion of Hungarian arms to the defense of the Pope played a significant part: thus, that Republic was able more easily to rise again in strength and conclude an agreement that brought no stain to its ancient glory.

( E ) **That Antichrist, a member of the Devil, and a woman are bringing ruin, etc.** This refers to the *Antipope Clement*, of whom much has been said, as well as the epithet *Antichrist*; and *Queen Joanna of Naples*, who favored him with all her power in Italy, and who will be discussed in another place.

( F ) **But I pray you, that you come, and delay no longer.** He did not come to Italy in person to offer aid to the Pope, but *Charles of Anjou*, called *Charles of Durazzo*, his cousin, went instead; he will be discussed in the *Annotation to the Letter* that follows. The arrival of this *Charles* secured the cause of *Urban*, as will be observed later.

( G ) **Only to wait and see if she corrects herself, and for the sake of your love.** Most authors who have spoken of this expedition against *Queen Joanna*, ordered by King *Louis* and put into action by *Charles*, believe that they were not induced so much...

...driven to wage war against her by the common desire to expand his dominion or glory, or by the invitations of the Pope, as much as by the desire to take revenge for the murder of King Andrew—brother to Louis—which was plotted against him (as rumor would have it) by Joanna, his wife. However, it does not seem that these claims align with the truth. The Saint <note>Saint Catherine of Siena</note> asserts that the Pope, out of love for this King, suspended the impending lightning bolt <note>original: "sopra folgore"; a metaphorical reference to the sentence of excommunication</note> against the Queen, which is a very manifest and clear sign. Furthermore, Louis had already set aside the indignation he felt over his brother's death, since the Queen had cleared herself of all guilt by purging herself of every suspicion as early as the year 1350. At that time, through the mediation of Pope Clement VI, she had returned to the King’s favor. During that period, such correspondence flowed between them as was proper between Princes of the same blood and closely joined; he even showed great kindness by remitting three hundred thousand gold florins that she was obligated to pay him for the expenses of the war he had waged to avenge his brother. 

I would believe, therefore, that Louis was induced to want to cast the Queen from her throne both by a greed for new conquests and, even more so, to secure for his daughter Maria the succession to the Kingdom of Hungary. He yielded to Charles <note>Charles III of Naples, also known as Charles of Durazzo</note> the rights he held—as a descendant of the eldest of King Charles II's sons—over the Kingdom of Naples. He added that the Hungarians were inclined to have him as King, so that by being far away and involved in other wars, it would not be easy for him to contest the rights of that Princess <note>Louis's daughter, Maria</note>.

( **H** ) *That little honor would follow for you and your Kingdom.* Queen Joanna was related by the third degree of kinship to that King, and both were no less of the Royal blood of France than of that of Hungary.

( **I** ) *That she was a public Heretic.* Ever since November 1378, Pope Urban had declared the Antipope <note>Clement VII</note> excommunicated along with some of the Cardinals and their other followers in that error; but he had restrained himself from thundering the excommunication against the Queen for the reasons put forward by the Saint. However, he later took this step of excommunicating her and declaring her to have forfeited the rights she enjoyed over the Kingdom of Naples, as will be noted elsewhere. This happened in the year 1380, and Rinaldi <note>Odoricus Raynaldus, a 17th-century church historian who continued the "Annales Ecclesiastici"</note> estimates that the aforementioned letter from the Saint was written in this same year. He reports much of it in his *Annals* and credits it with the glory of having induced this King to send his troops against the Queen in support of the Pope.

( L ) **Even if it were your son.** In truth, he had no male children, but only two daughters; he speaks in this manner to give the greatest possible weight to his words—unless, by the name of "son," he intended to refer to Charles of Durazzo, the King's cousin. This Elizabeth, in order to preserve the Scepter of Hungary for her daughter against Charles of Durazzo, King of Naples—who, having been acclaimed by the Hungarians, had usurped it—had him killed in the year 138<unclear>5</unclear>, with Nicholas Garai, Palatine of the Realm, lending his arm to the deed. She did not enjoy the fruits of this treachery for more than a few months; for, being suddenly attacked by Horvat, the Governor of Croatia and a great partisan of King Charles, she was thrown into a river to drown at the end of that same year, or as others report the event, she was strangled with a cord in prison in the first month of the following year.

# To Master Charles of Peace.

## Who later became King of Apulia, or rather, of Naples. <note>Charles III of Naples (1345–1386), also known as Charles of Durazzo. He was a key figure in the conflicts surrounding the Great Western Schism.</note>

I. The soul is encouraged to come to the aid of the Holy Church and of Pope Urban VI against the Rebels, and to that end, to first fight *manfully* against the three common Enemies of Man, and against one's own passions, following the example of certain Saints.
II. She detests the iniquity of the said Rebels for refusing to recognize Urban VI as the true Pontiff. <note>The "Rebels" refers to the faction of cardinals who declared Urban VI's election invalid and elected the antipope Clement VII, starting the Western Schism in 1378.</note>

## Letter 189.

## *In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of Sweet Mary.*

I. **D**earest Brother in sweet Christ Jesus, I Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious Blood, with the desire to see you a manful Knight, who fights manfully for the glory and praise of God's Name, and for the exaltation and reformation of the Holy Church. But take heed, dearest brother, that you could not achieve this good—of being courageous and succoring the needs of the Holy Church—if you did not first fight and wage war against our three principal enemies: namely, the World, the Devil, and our fragile Flesh. These are the three principal Tyrants who kill the Soul's life of Grace in whatever state it may be, if the soul, with the hand of <term>free will</term> <note>The human capacity to choose between good and evil, a central concept in Catherine’s theology.</note>, opens the door of the will and lets them inside. The World strikes us with vain and disordered joys, placing before the eye of our intellect status, riches, honors, and greatness with wicked delights; all of these things are vain and corruptible, passing like the wind, and are changeable without any stability. This we see clearly: that Man is alive today and dead tomorrow; from health he falls into infirmity; now he is rich,

This man gives no place to injustice, such that—to gain or acquire status, wealth, or worldly delights—he would do injury to his Neighbor; because he has despised these things, and he does not lift his head in pride, reputing himself greater and wishing to lord over his Neighbor unjustly. They did not act like those who reign today, in whom self-love so abounds that they wish to make themselves gods of this worldly tyrant; and from this are born injustices, murders, and the greatest cruelties, and every other defect. # To the Duke of Anjou.

<margin>I</margin> **S**he prays for him to unite himself to the Cross and to the Passion of Jesus Christ by despising the delights and vanities of the World, and warns that the immoderate pleasures of this life deprive the Soul of the vision of God.
II. She compares eternal Goods to earthly ones by reminding the same Duke of an incident that happened to him during a Banquet he gave the day before, in which a wall collapsed and several people died.
III. She exhorts the Duke to always maintain the memory of such an event in order to amend his life. 
IV. Exhorting him, finally, to take up the cross <note>To "take up the cross" or "cross oneself" here refers to joining a Crusade.</note> against the Infidels.

---

## Letter 190.

->In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of Sweet Mary.<-

**D**earest Lord and Brother in sweet Christ Jesus. I, Catherine, slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious Blood with the desire to see your heart fastened and nailed to the Cross in such a way that your desire may increase, so that you may soon be ready and diligent to raise the Standard <term>Gonfalone: a heraldic banner or flag, here specifically the banner of a Crusade</term> of the Most Holy Cross. I am certain that if you look upon the slaughtered Lamb, consumed on the Cross out of love to take away your death and restore to you the life of Grace, that this will be that holy memory which will kindle the desire in you to do it quickly. It will restrain from your heart and your Soul every disordered delight and vanity of the World—pleasures which pass away like the wind and always leave death in the soul of the one who possesses them. In the end, at death, if one does not correct himself, they lead him to eternal death; so that by his own fault he is deprived of the vision of God, and made worthy of the vision and company of the Demons; and it is a thing...

it is a just and fitting thing that he should suffer infinite punishment who offends God, who is infinite Goodness. I speak of one who spends his entire life in **delights**, and in living **sumptuously**, seeking great honors in grand banquets and many adornments, and who spends all their substance on nothing else while the poor die of hunger; instead, they always seek great and numerous dishes, the cleanliness of vessels, expensive tables, and delicate and ornate garments. ## III.
I tell you on behalf of **Christ Crucified** <note>original: "Cristo Crocifisso"</note>, that you should always carry
the events of yesterday in your memory, so that your affairs may be
conducted in an orderly way, with virtue and the fear of God,

Let it be a holy bridle for you, which restrains every
disordered vanity in you, just as one does to a running Horse, where
the bridle is pulled so that it does not go out of the order of its course.

<meta>This page continues the scholarly commentary on Letter 190 from Catherine of Siena to Louis I, Duke of Anjou. The previous page discussed a tragic accident at a banquet which Catherine interpreted as a divine warning against worldly vanity. This page provides historical context for the figures mentioned and the specific events of 1376.</meta>

<margin>History of Naples, book 6.</margin>
( A ) ***Louis of France, Duke of Anjou, Founder and Multiplier of the second branch of the Royal House of Anjou*** <note>original: "Luigi di Francia Duca d' Angiò Fondatore, e Propagatore della seconda Branca della Casa Reale d' Angiò"</note> was the son of King John of France, and not of John, Duke of Anjou, as Collenuccio <note>Pandolfo Collenuccio (1444–1504) was a famous historian and jurist whose work on the History of Naples was highly influential but sometimes contained errors.</note> wrote with little care. He had traveled in those days to Avignon, driven both by his own interests in the legal case pending between himself and the King of Aragon regarding the Island of Majorca (as noted elsewhere), and by his brother, King Charles V, for the purpose of dissuading Pope Gregory XI from his plan to go to Rome. This design, however, failed due to the firmness of that Pope, and the other objective also met with no success in his favor.

( B ) ***Nor to strong youth.*** Since this Letter was written in 1376 while the Saint was in Avignon, this Lord was in the 37th year of his age, having been born in 1339.

( C ) ***With the greatest fire of Love, you shall take up the Cross.*** Taking up the Cross denoted the resolution to go and fight the Infidels. To this noble Enterprise—which in those days was being managed with great fervor for fear of the Turks, who were threatening the Island of Rhodes with a great display of arms—the Saint awakens and provokes the valor of this Prince. He showed himself most ready for Saint Catherine's invitations and, as we have from the ninth Letter to Gregory XI and the 186th to King Charles, he offered his own person for such a great work, desiring indeed to make himself Head and Leader of it.

( D ) ***And you saw it well yourself yesterday.*** The Saint alludes to the accident that happened the day before to this Prince: namely, the collapse of a wall during a solemn Banquet he had given for many Lords, in which many had died; as was already noted in the title of this Letter in the old printed editions. I find no memory of this event in the Histories, nor is there any remaining in that City; but indeed, a similar and even more disastrous case is told as having happened in the same century—that is, in 1305, in the City of Lyons—at the time when the solemn Coronation of Pope Clement V was to take place. A wall suddenly fell, by which the Duke of Brittany and the Pope's brother were killed along with other personages of high standing, and King Philip the Fair and his brother Charles of Valois (the great-grandfather of this Prince) were wounded, with the Pope himself running a great risk of remaining there.

( E ) ***See to it that before the Holy Father goes away.*** Departed...

In the *Archive of the Dominican Fathers of Siena*, one can read the Brief of *Urban* dated November 21, 1378, addressed to this Lord, in which he mentions having received his letters full of affection toward his person and the *Holy See*; wherefore, following the example of his ancestors—who were faithful above all other princes in the world to the *Holy Church*—he begs him to offer the help required by the current need of the *Schism*. From this, one can gather another argument to deny that the Cardinals in May of that same year wrote to France against the validity of the election of *Urban*. This Prince was adopted as a son and declared heir to the *Kingdom of Naples* by Queen *Joan*, who, frightened by the threats of *Urban* and the war preparations being made against her by *Charles of Durazzo*, hoped to find in this Prince a strong support for her failing greatness. But the Enemy was quicker to oppress her than the Friend was to support her; so he did not move from *France* until after the death of this Princess. With his claims to that Kingdom confirmed and having received the royal insignia from *Clement*, he descended into *Italy* with a powerful army of sixty thousand soldiers with great hope of certain victory. But the army, after suffering much for little gain, eventually dispersed entirely, and he died of a malignant fever in *Bisceglie*, an unremarkable town in *Puglia*, in the year 1384, leaving to his descendants and heirs the claims to that Crown, to be enjoyed for a short time at the cost of much blood.

## To Master Bernabò Visconti, Lord of Milan.

### *Regarding certain Ambassadors sent by said Lord to her.*

I. She exhorts him to the Love of Jesus Christ, demonstrating the obligation we have toward Him.
II. She exhorts him to guard his own Soul with hatred for Vice and Love for Virtue.
III. That in this World there is no true Lordship, except for that which we have over our own Soul.
IV. Concerning the reverence we must have for the Vicar of Christ <note>The Pope</note>, even if he were a wicked man; wherefore she prays the aforementioned lord not to wish to persecute him.
V. She prays him to go with his armies against the Infidels, demonstrating how evil it is to move them against Catholics.

<meta>This page continues the historical and theological commentary on Letter 191, written by Catherine of Siena to Bernabò Visconti. The previous page ended mid-sentence discussing Visconti's political power and the titles used in the 14th century.</meta>

<page-num>59</page-num>
<margin>H</margin>
...was given the title of *Messere* <note>original: "Messere", a title of respect equivalent to "Lord" or "Sir"</note>, or as the Saint says, *Missere*. It was in those times one of the most honorable titles that could be given even to great Lords, such as Kings and Emperors, as is clearly seen in the authors who wrote during that century. Indeed, one finds among these same authors that it was given to the Saints themselves, and to the supreme Lord of the Saints; reading there quite often not only *Lord Charles, King of Sicily*; *Lord Emperor Frederick*, but also *Lord Saint Anthony*, *Lord Saint Jerome*, and *Lord God* <note>original: "Messere Domenedio", an archaic form of "Lord God"</note>; whereas today, people of the lowest condition hardly deign to use it.

( B ) **Reverend Father.** This title, which today is given only to members of religious orders, was in Saint Catherine's age—when human vanity had not yet climbed so high—considered most fitting for great Lords. In truth, both those names of *Father* and *Reverend* possess no small degree of honor in themselves and reveal a humility of spirit in the one who offers them. To Queen Joanna, because she occupied a more sublime position of honor, our Saint gives the title of **Most Reverend Mother**, as will be observed in the annotations to those letters.

( C ) **Because the immaculate Lamb, to restore Liberty to Man, and to make him free, etc.** The Saint does not mean that Christ our Lord, by His death, returned us to Liberty if the word "Liberty" is taken to mean the same as the power to act well or poorly <note>meaning the basic capacity of the human will</note>—as if that power had failed in us due to the sin of the first man. For if such Liberty were taken from us, we would have no mastery over our actions, and neither merit nor sin would be attributed to us. This <term>immaculate Lamb</term> <note>A title for Jesus Christ, referencing his sacrificial role in Christian theology</note> therefore made us free in several ways through His death: namely, by removing us from the servitude of the Old Law <note>The Mosaic Law of the Old Testament</note> through the Liberty of the New; by conquering the Devil, who held most men in slavery; and by giving us the Glory and Bliss of Heaven, through which we will become free from both temporal and eternal calamities. In this same way, one must also understand the Saint’s words that follow—namely, that Christ has restored **free will** to us. This is intended to mean that, having overcome our enemies who held us as slaves, He has returned us to a state of **Grace** and made the use of **Free Will** easier for us to do good works. God Himself, speaking through the mouth of the Saint regarding this liberty, revealed this same sentiment, saying:

# To the Count of Fondi.

I. **D**escribing the qualities of the Vineyard of our Soul, she exhorts the Count to be a good worker of it.
II. On Self-love, with which the Demons render the said Vineyard sterile and wild.
III. That we are bound to cultivate not only the Vineyard of our own Soul, but also that of our Neighbors.
IV. She attempts to persuade him to believe that Urban VI is the true Pope, and therefore he should no longer persecute him, because of the damage that results for him and for the Holy Church.
V. That we must open the door of our Soul to Jesus Christ, the true worker of this Vineyard.

## Letter 192.

->*In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of Sweet Mary.*<-

<margin>1 Corinthians 6</margin>
**I.** **D**earest Father and Brother in sweet Christ Jesus. I, Catherine, slave of the servants of Jesus Christ <note>A signature phrase of Catherine, echoing the humility of the Apostles and the title of the Pope.</note>, write to you in His precious Blood with the desire to see you a true worker in the Vineyard of your Soul, so that you may bring forth much fruit at the time of harvest—that is, at the time of death, when every fault is punished and every good is rewarded. You know that the Eternal Truth created us in His image and likeness; He made of us His Temple <note>Refers to 1 Corinthians 6:19: "Do you not know that your bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit?"</note>, where He wishes to dwell through grace, if it pleases the worker of this Vineyard to work it well and rightly. For if it were not worked, but abounded in thorns and briars, it would no longer be a place for Him to dwell. Now let us see, dearest Father, what worker this Master has placed there. He has placed Free Will <term>Free Will: The human capacity to choose. Catherine views it as the "governor" or "judge" of the soul's internal state.</term>, to whom the entire governance is committed. There is the door of the Will, and there is no one who can open or close it except as Free Will desires! He has placed there the light of Intellect to recognize friends and enemies who might wish to enter and pass through the door; and at this door is placed the Dog of Conscience <note>A classic Catherinian metaphor: conscience acts as a guard dog that "barks" to alert the soul when sin or temptation approaches the "door" of the will.</note>, which barks when

**IV.** Oh, dearest Father, I want you to recognize in what state you find yourself, and look upon your **Vineyard**. I grieve even unto death that the tyrant of **Free Will** <term>Free Will: Libero Arbitrio</term> has turned you from a **Garden**—which cast forth examples of **Virtue** and **Truth**, and the light of **Faith**—and has now perverted it from a garden into a wild forest. This we must hold: that he is the Pope elected through an orderly election, the **Vicar of Christ** on Earth, and him we must obey even unto death. And even if he were a cruel Father to us, to the point of driving us away with reproach from one end of the World to the other with every torment, we must not for that reason forget nor persecute this truth. ->** ( C ) **<-
**He who had been an obedient son and a supporter of the Holy Church.** He had previously made himself known as most faithful to the Church; for this reason, he had assisted it with money, and had been employed by Pope Gregory XI in 1375 to keep the Romans in obedience when they were rioting, showing themselves inclined to rebel following the example of other peoples subject to the Pope.

<margin>Citations: Contr. 4. l. 4. notes 14 and 15.</margin>

->** ( D ) **<-
**This has always been observed, etc.** Just as those who made themselves celebrated by favoring the Church were always prospered by God in this life, so on the contrary, those who persecuted it—either because they were of another religion, or because they wished to interfere in affairs that belong solely to the Church, or because they were adverse in spirit to its <term>Supreme Pastor</term> <note>The Pope</note>—turned out for the most part unhappy, or ended their lives badly. One may see the examples reported by <term>Bellarmine</term> <note>Robert Bellarmine (1542–1621), a Jesuit theologian and Cardinal who wrote extensively on the power of the papacy.</note>, to which many others could be added, such as the prosperity of <term>Charlemagne</term>, <term>Otto the Great</term>, and <term>Saint Henry</term> <note>Holy Roman Emperor Henry II.</note>; in contrast to the misfortune of three <term>Henrys</term> <note>Likely referring to Henry IV, V, and VII, who clashed with various Popes.</note>, and of Louis, and of the two <term>Emperor Fredericks</term> <note>Frederick I (Barbarossa) and Frederick II.</note>, and of <term>Philip the Fair</term>, King of France, whose flourishing lineage withered so quickly without any further sprout.

->** ( E ) **<-
**Therefore I pray you, that you might humbly and with great diligence return to this yoke.** The Count did not benefit from the Saint’s wise advice, remaining immovable in the party he had first embraced; thus he was also among the first to be struck by Urban with <term>Excommunication</term> in 1378, and again in the following years by being stripped of all the rights he had over his County, of which the Pope was the sovereign. Notwithstanding this, he maintained his state and gave all his power to favor <term>Clement</term> and <term>Benedict</term> <note>The Antipopes Clement VII and Benedict XIII of the Avignon line.</note>, who succeeded him in the <term>Cathedra of Avignon</term> <note>The papal throne established in France during the Schism.</note>, against Urban and his successor Boniface, finally passing away in the year 1400.

# To Master Pietro Gambacorti in Pisa.

I. She exhorts him to strip himself of worldly affection.
II. Concerning the effects that sin produces in the Soul.
III. Concerning the knowledge of oneself and of Divine Goodness.
IV. Concerning the virtue of Justice.
V. She states that she does not yet wish to travel to Pisa, as the aforementioned Master Pietro had requested of her in one of his letters, but that she would go there at another time, according as the honor of God and the salvation of souls should require.

## Letter 193.

->In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of Sweet Mary.<-

<margin>Matthew 6</margin>
I. **V**enerable Father in Christ sweet Jesus, your unworthy daughter Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, writes to you; commending herself to you in the precious Blood of the Son of God, with the desire to see your affection and your desire stripped and loosened from the perverse delights and disordered pleasures of the <term>World</term> <note>original: "Mondo"; Catherine often contrasts the "world" or "secular life" with the spiritual life.</note>, which are the cause and the matter that part and divide the Soul from God; because it is necessary that the Soul, which is bound to Christ Crucified—the supreme and eternal Goodness—be loosened and cut off from the <term>Secular World</term> <note>original: "Secolo." Refers to the temporal, worldly life as opposed to the eternal or monastic life.</note>, and he who has his affection bound to the secular world is cut off from Christ; because the world has no conformity with Christ, as the primary Truth said: <note>original: "Niuno può servire a due Signori contrarj..." Catherine is quoting the Gospel of Matthew 6:24.</note> No one can serve two opposing masters, for if he serves the one, he is at odds with the other.

( **B** ) **Venerable Father.** Regarding this title given by the **Saint** to the **Lords of the World**, it was discussed in the *Annotations to Letter 186.* <note>Catherine frequently addressed secular rulers with spiritual titles like 'Father' to remind them of their moral responsibilities.</note>

<margin>Part 2. chap. 8.</margin>
( **C** ) **I received a letter of yours**, which I looked upon with affectionate love. The **Blessed Raymond** <note>Raymond of Capua, Catherine’s biographer and later Master General of the Dominican Order.</note>, writer of the deeds of this **Saint**, narrates how she—requested by many people who were eager to see and hear her and wished for her to travel to **Pisa**—was not inclined to satisfy them in their invitation until she had received an order from the **Lord**. There were many motives that held her back from that journey, and she specifically offers two here as excuses: namely, her being of a frail **Person** <note>original: "Perſona"; here referring to her physical constitution or health.</note>; and her not wishing to provide others an occasion for scandal. This [scandal] could perhaps have arisen from the poor relations that existed in those days between the **Commune of Siena** and **Gambacorti**, while with his favor the **Prior of Pisa of the Knights of Rhodes** had occupied the **Fortress of Albarese**, and then the **Land of Talamone** in the **Sienese State**, and had fortified himself there, holding them in the name of the **Church**, as the **Historians** report. <margin>Malavolti. part 2. book 8.</margin> Notwithstanding this, she went in that year 1375 to **Pisa**, and stayed there for several months, detained there longer than she desired by that **Archbishop**, as was noted in another place. In the **Third Volume of the Antiquities of the Carthusian Monastery of Pisa**, one reads that the **Saint** went in 1375 to that **City** in order to dissolve the **League** <note>An alliance of Tuscan cities against the papacy.</note> that various **Cities of Tuscany** had formed to the detriment of the **Church**, sent there by **Pope Gregory XI.** However, the writer of those memoirs is mistaken in this, as is shown by the **Blessed Raymond** in the cited **Legend** <note>original: "Leggenda"; the standard hagiographical biography of a saint's life.</note>, and the first of the **Letters of the Saint to Gregory**, in which she says nothing of having received such an **Order**. Rather, she mentions to him having been in that **City** to keep it in the faith of the **Pontiff**, not to withdraw it from the **Confederation** with the **Florentines**.
