# To Messer Trinci de' Trinci of Foligno, and to Corrado his Brother

I. She exhorts them to be true servants of God, bound with the bond of Charity.
II. Of the power of this bond, known in the Incarnation and Crucifixion of the Son of God, manifesting to us the Will and the Truth of the Eternal Father.
III. In what manner Christ, exalted upon the Cross, drew all things to himself.
IV. That self-love and love of creatures prevents us from knowing this Truth.
V. She exhorts them to live in the state they are in, and in Marriage with the Holy fear of God, and with the consideration of Jesus Christ.
VI. She exhorts them to be faithful to the Holy Church, whose service is rewarded by God according to the love found within us.
VII. That with hope and faith they should nourish their Family in the Blood of Jesus Christ.

## Letter 194.

### Written while in ecstasy. <note>original: "Fatta in aſtrazione"; this indicates that Catherine dictated the letter while in a state of mystical trance or "abstraction" from her physical senses.</note>

...humiliation of the shameful death of the Cross, I will draw your hearts to the height of the Divinity and uncreated Charity <note>original: "Carità increata"</note>; for once the heart of Man is drawn, it can be said that all the affection and powers of the Soul are drawn, along with all spiritual and temporal exercises. ### IV.
It is well, therefore, to open the eye of the Intellect and gaze upon the affection of one's Creator. I want you to consider, most dear Brothers, that when the eye of the Intellect is clouded by **selfish sensory love** <term>Amore proprio sensitivo: Catherine's term for egoism or an obsessive attachment to one's own desires and physical comforts, which she argues "blinds" the soul's ability to see God.</term> it cannot know this Truth; for just as a diseased eye full of dirt and flesh cannot see the light of the Sun, so the eye of the Soul cannot see if it is covered with the dirt of disordered love and worldly affection—that is, of these transitory things that pass like the wind. And if it is covered with carnal affection by not living honestly, but dishonestly, it becomes entangled in the mud of carnality. This misery makes Man become like a brute beast, and takes away his light and knowledge. These people, I say, cannot know this Truth; and they have also become lovers of lies, following the footsteps of their Father, that is, the **Devil**, who is the Father of lies.

### V.
I desire, therefore, that you lift up the eye of your Intellect and your love from these transitory things and from every carnal Vice, and purify your Soul by means of **Holy Confession**. I do not say, however, that you should leave your social station <note>Catherine frequently advised laypeople, especially those in power, that they did not need to enter a monastery to be holy, but should instead practice "mental" renunciation while fulfilling their duties.</note>, unless the **Holy Spirit** inspires you to do so; but I want you to maintain it with the holy fear of God, standing manfully as virtuous men, and not like fools and animals, governing your subjects with justice and kindness. And as for the state of Holy **Marriage**, uphold it, and do not seek to contaminate it—that is, to break it—through any disordered appetite; rather, restrain your feelings with the memory of the **Blood of Christ** and of the union of the Divine nature joined with Human nature. Your miserable flesh will then be ashamed to fall into such wretchedness, and it will sense the fragrance of purity by having this holy consideration; and with reverence and fear of God, one will remain in holy Marriage; and hav[ing]...

<margin>C.</margin>
...hold in reverence those days that are commanded by the **Holy Church**. He will bind you with that strong bond of **Love** <note>original: "Amore"</note> which held Him fastened and nailed to the Cross. You will be strong and persevering until death; neither the ingratitude of the men you might serve—should they be ungrateful toward you—nor the various and many thoughts of hatred or displeasure toward your neighbor that the Devil might put into your heart will slacken your love or take away your strength, provided you are united and bound in the bond of **Charity** <note>original: "Carità"</note> as has been said. I hope in the goodness of God that you will fulfill His Will and <margin>D</margin> my desire; this will be through His goodness and through the service you provide to His sweet **Spouse** <note>A common title for the Church in Catherine's writings.</note>, because our God is grateful and mindful toward those who serve Him.

### VI. 
Every service we perform for Him is very pleasing to Him, but among others, that which is most pleasing is what is done in service to the **Holy Church**, in whatever way and in whatever state of life we serve her. It is true that the more a man serves her with a pure heart and without any [selfish] regard, the more pleasing he is; nevertheless, everyone is pleasing to Him and is measured according to the measure of their Love. Just as He rewards service, so He punishes offense; and just as he who serves more is more rewarded, so he who offends more is more punished. Why is this? Because one serves the **Blood of Christ**, or does a disservice to the Blood of Christ; therefore, greater reward and greater punishment follows. Therefore, most sweet brothers in sweet Jesus Christ, be faithful servants to Christ Crucified and to His sweet Spouse. Thus you will taste and know the eternal Will of God, which wants nothing other than our **Sanctification**; and as was said <margin>1. ( A ) *This Letter was previously among those addressed to various Doctors of Law and Medicine, and [the editor] Farri, by giving it such a title, had passed off these two gentlemen as such. The Family to which they belonged held the Lordship of the City of Foligno for a long time, and at the time of Saint Catherine, Trincio, the elder of these two brothers, was the one who ruled. He once behaved more like a Tyrant than a just Lord; however, he later adopted a better way of life and remained constantly loyal to the Party of the Church, for which reason he suffered the loss of his State and his death. This death was foretold to him by the Blessed Brother Thomas of Foligno of the <term>Seraphic Order: A common name for the Franciscan Order, referring to the "Seraphic" zeal of St. Francis.</term>, as is read in the Chronicle of this Religion. For when Trincio had sought to have the time of his death revealed to him, he received in response that his life would last as long as the Community Bell remained whole, and he would die at that hour when the <term>Calves: "Vitelli" in Italian; a play on words regarding the heraldic symbols on a banner.</term> flew over the Tower of the City. It was not long before it all came true; for as the Florentine Army advanced toward Foligno after the victory gained near Camerino, the people of Foligno rose up against Trincio, who held the side of the Church. When they began to ring the "alarm bell" to gather the people, the bell fell and broke into pieces. Trincio was killed by the rebels, while others raised above the Tower the banner of Count Lucio di Lando, Commander of the Florentine Army, upon which two calves were painted. This happened in the year 1377. In another Letter, written to the Consort of this Lord, the Saint gives quite good hopes for his salvation.*

## To Benuccio di Piero, and Bernardo di Misser Uberto de Belforti from Volterra

I. She demonstrates how true Peace with God is found in the exercise of Virtues rooted in the love of the same God, and how it is acquired by virtue of the Blood of Jesus Christ.

...[we are at] war with our Creator.

In what way then can we make this peace, since we have fallen into mortal war <note>original: "guerra mortale"; a state of spiritual death caused by sin</note> through our own faults, and are condemned to eternal punishment if peace is not made? I certainly desire that we seek out the way, since we have fallen into such great danger and harm to both Soul and Body; and I see no other way but one: that holy way which God took toward us when, through the sin of Adam, the entire human race fell into war with God. Since God's Mercy wished to make peace with Man, and it was still necessary to take vengeance for the fault committed, He sent us the Word <note>original: "Verbo"; the Second Person of the Trinity, Jesus Christ</note> of His Only-begotten Son as our Peace and Mediator <term>Mediator: "Tramezzatore" in the original, meaning one who stands in the middle to reconcile two parties</term>. The Son of God took our iniquities and punished them upon His own Body, as the Peace and Mediator that He was. And where does He punish them? Upon the sorrowful, painful, and shameful death of the Cross. So you see that God, through His Son, has made peace with Man; and this peace is so perfect and so complete that, even if Man falls back into war through his own sin and defect, He has left the Blood—which Blood we receive in holy Confession, and we can use it and have it every day as much as we please. Since we have received so much grace and mercy from God, I do not want us to be ungrateful or unmindful, but I want you to follow the footsteps of Christ Crucified so that you can be reconciled with Him by following His lead, as has been said; otherwise, you would remain in continual damnation. I have said that God, through His Son, and the Son, through His Blood, has taken away our War and given us Peace: so I say to you, that through Virtue you must remove the war and flee eternal damnation; otherwise, you would be confounded in this life and in the next.

**II.** But I want you to know that neither the love of God nor Virtue can be held in the Soul without the medium of one's Neighbor. How? I will tell you. I cannot show the love that I have for my Creator directly to Him, because no benefit can be done for God <note>Catherine argues that since God is perfect and lacks nothing, our love for Him must be expressed through service to others who actually have needs</note>. It is necessary, therefore, to take the medium of His Creature, and to help that Creature, and to perform for the Creature that service which I cannot do for God.

### III.

<meta>This page transitions from the moral teachings on ingratitude found in the previous page to a historical explanation of the government of Rome during the 14th century, specifically detailing the roles of the Senator, the Reformers, and the Bannerets (Banderesi) during the era of the Avignon Papacy and the return to Rome.</meta>

86

The <term>Senator</term> <note>In the late Middle Ages, the Senator of Rome was the city's chief judicial officer and magistrate, often a foreigner appointed to maintain neutrality among warring Roman factions.</note>, who was elected by the people at their own pleasure, without any intervention from the Authority of the <term>Pope</term>—who merely confirmed the election as a sign of some dominion and power, though in reality the People did not wish him to have a share in it. But because various disturbances had occurred during the election of the <term>Senator</term>, as the highest Lords of Rome aspired to that place of such great honor, it became convenient for <term>Pope Innocent VI</term> <note>Pope from 1352 to 1362, he reigned from Avignon but worked to restore papal authority in Italy.</note> to take the election for himself. An agreement was established that in the future, this official must be a foreigner by nationality and should enjoy the office for one year only; the first to be honored with it was <term>Raimondo Tolomei</term>, a Sienese Noble, in the year 1359.

However, he did not hold any authority in Rome other than the administration of justice according to the law; the government was in the power of seven persons called <term>Reformers</term> <note>original: *Riformatori*; a governing council established to reorganize the city's administration</note>, and those who were called <term>Bannerets</term> <note>original: *Banderesi*; militia leaders who represented the armed power of the Roman people</note>, or by the Tuscans, *Banderari*. These were the Heads of the <term>Districts</term> <note>original: *Rioni* or *Decurie*; the traditional neighborhoods of Rome, which served as administrative and military units</note> of the City, and they took their name from the word <term>Banner</term> <note>original: *Bandiera*</note>, which, having originated in Germany or perhaps in France, had already become Italian through use. Since each of the <term>Districts</term> had its own insignia by which they were distinguished from one another, the one who took care of it was usually called a <term>Banneret</term>, although this name was often applied to all those who, loving the current state of the Government, were enrolled under them.

The Magistracy of the <term>Reformers</term> was suppressed through the industriousness of <term>Hugh IV, King of Cyprus</term> <note>Though the text names Hugh IV, it likely refers to the diplomatic presence of the Lusignan dynasty in Rome during this period.</note>, who was made <term>Senator</term> of Rome by <term>Innocent VI</term> because they had arrogated more authority to themselves than was appropriate. The authority of the <term>Bannerets</term> remained, and as the years went by, they took over the management of affairs and the care of the City; thus, at this time, they were the Heads of that Republic, such as it was.

In addition to these, there were the four <term>Good Men</term> <note>original: *Buoni Uomini*; a term often used for lay committees or boards overseeing charitable or civic duties</note>, who were also Maintainers of the Republic. I am led to believe (since I find no other notice of them among the Authors) that their office must have been specifically employed in works of piety regarding the public good, from which they derived the name <term>Good Men</term>, as those who hold such positions still use that name in Siena and other Cities. The return of the <term>Popes</term> to Rome did not take away this liberty of the Romans; rather, when <term>Pope Gregory XI</term> <note>The Pope who moved the Papal See back to Rome from Avignon in 1377, influenced significantly by Catherine of Siena.</note> wished to return the Apostolic See there and maintain some shadow of Authority, he first had to come to terms with the Romans through lengthy negotiations held by the Cardinals <term>d'Estaing</term>, <term>Tebaldeschi</term>, and <term>Corsini</term>, and satisfy himself with those conditions which at that time seemed...

The name of the Republic was maintained in Rome until the Pontificate of **Boniface IX** <note>Pope from 1389 to 1404</note>, the successor to **Urban VI**. Though young in age, Boniface was old in wisdom and knew how to manage the Roman people in such a way that he brought all the Power to himself, electing the Magistrates <note>original: *Maestrati*; high-ranking civil officials</note> and other administrators of that city's government at his own will. In the year 1378, on the second day of May, those people had made a gift of the city to **Pope Urban VI**, as we learn from a letter written by **Francesco of Siena**, the Pope’s physician, to the <term>Lords Defenders</term> <note>original: *Signori Difensori*; the governing body of the Sienese Republic</note> of the Republic of Siena. However, I am inclined to believe that through this act, the Authority enjoyed by the city's magistrates at that time was preserved, and therefore it held not only the title but also the power of a Republic. The words of the letter are these:

<margin>Volume titled *Memories of Siena and Lucca*, folio 111, which is kept in the Chigi Library.</margin>
I do not send the safe conduct of the Romans, because our Lord [the Pope] does not wish it, since he himself is the most free Lord of the City, both by right and by the donation made to him by the Roman People in a public <term>Parliament</term> <note>original: *Parlamento*; a general assembly of the citizens called to decide on urgent matters of state</note> on the Sunday just past, and since <term>reprisals</term> <note>legal seizures of property or person in retaliation for a debt or injury</note> cannot be taken against the Sienese Ambassadors to the Roman Pontiff. Given in Rome on Thursday, May 6, at the third hour, 1378. The servant and citizen of your Magnificences, Francesco, Physician to the Lord Pope, recommends himself.

( B ) *That you be grateful for the graces that our Creator has granted and continues to grant.* With these words, she alludes to the victory achieved on April 29—eight days before the date of this letter—by the troops of **Pope Urban** against the followers of **Clement** <note>Clement VII, the first "antipope" of the Great Western Schism, who opposed Urban VI</note>, which will be discussed at greater length in the annotations to Letter 219.

<margin>To the Year 1391.</margin>
( C ) *Our Father Pope Urban VI gives us the example, etc.* This action by **Pope Urban VI**, of going barefoot in a procession, was discussed in the annotations to the twentieth letter. **Rinaldi** <note>Odoricus Raynaldus, a 17th-century church historian who continued the *Annales Ecclesiastici*</note>, who records this letter of **Saint Catherine** in his *Annals*, seems to believe that the Saint was moved to write to the Romans because they had taken up arms and rioted against this Pope, and that she scolds them for it in this letter. But in truth, nothing at all is said in this text regarding a riot to the detriment of the Pope, nor does she mention any uprising. Instead, she uses terms of visual reproach toward those governing and toward the Roman People for other excesses being committed, as is easily seen by anyone.

## Letter 197.

### In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of Sweet Mary.

<margin>I.</margin> **D**earest Fathers and Brothers in Christ Jesus. I Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in his precious Blood with the desire to see you as true sons, humble and obedient to your Father <note>referring to the Pope as the spiritual father</note> in such a way and manner that you never turn your head back. ### V.

( C ) *And as a sign that she feels joy, she says <term>Passover</term> <note>original: "Pasqua". In Italian, this word is used for both the Jewish Passover and the Christian Easter.</note>. The word Passover, which is from the Hebrew language, means "Passage," and it refers to the fortunate crossing the Hebrews made through the Red Sea, and to the destroying Angel of the firstborn of the Egyptians, who passed over the houses of the Hebrews without bringing them any harm. Because this solemnity was celebrated by the Hebrews with the greatest joy, the word Passover had become for everyone a term for contentment and happiness.*

Hence, many of the writers of Tuscan history say the war waged against Gregory XI was said to be fought against the Pope's Legates <note>The administrative representatives of the Pope, who were often unpopular in Italian cities.</note>, deceiving themselves into thinking they were not offending the Vicar of Christ or his Church in this. # To the Lords <term>Priors of the Guilds</term> and the <term>Standard-bearer of Justice</term> of the People and the Commune of Florence.
<note>The Priors of the Guilds (Priori dell' Arti) and the Standard-bearer of Justice (Gonfaloniere di Giustizia) were the top governing officials of the Republic of Florence.</note>

**I.** It discusses ingratitude toward God and the self-love with which Adam clothed himself, and through which he lost gratitude toward God along with all the human race.
**II.** It exhorts them to strip off the "old man" and clothe themselves in Jesus Christ.
<note>The "old man" is a biblical reference to the fallen state of humanity before spiritual renewal.</note>
**III.** Concerning the love we must have for our neighbor, and in particular for the <term>Supreme Pontiff</term> and the Holy Church, helping her in her needs to be grateful for God’s blessings.
**IV.** She prays them to be willing to believe in Urban VI as the Supreme Pontiff.

## Letter 199.

-><term>In a state of abstraction</term>.<-
<note>original: "In Aſtrazione fatta". This indicates the letter was dictated by Catherine while she was in a mystical trance or state of ecstasy.</note>

->**In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified and of Sweet Mary.**<-

**I.** **D**earest Brothers in Christ sweet Jesus. I, Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious Blood with the desire to see you grateful and appreciative of the graces that you receive from your Creator; this gratitude nourishes the fountain of Mercy in the soul, just as ingratitude dries it up. Therefore, it is fitting for us, for the honor of God and our own benefit, to be grateful and appreciative. But I cannot see how we can possess it while we remain clothed in the old garment of sensory love; for the man who loves himself with his own sensory love is that "old man" with whom our first father Adam and Eve clothed themselves, to such an extent that not only did the fountain of Mercy dry up within them, but the entire human race felt it; eternal life was locked away, so that with all our righteous acts no one could enter there. Who was the cause of so much evil? Self-love, which

...soul, because **self-love** makes Man ungrateful and gives birth to pride; and because **Adam** was ungrateful for the **Innocence** and **Lordship** <note>In this theological context, "Lordship" refers to the dominion God granted humanity over the natural world before the Fall.</note> that God had given him—having made him Lord over all the Creatures that do not have Reason within them; wherefore whatever animal he might have called would have come to him as his subjects. But then his ingratitude, with which he transgressed the commandment of God, found rebellion in all the animals; and just as he was rebellious toward God, so he was rebellious toward himself, finding rebellion in the perverse law of his fragile **Flesh**, which continually fights against the **Spirit**. So it is that while a person is clothed in the **old man**, <note>A biblical term (Colossians 3:9) referring to the unregenerate human nature prone to sin.</note> he can never be grateful either to God or to the Creatures. 

From what does Ingratitude proceed? From **Self-love**; it takes away the delight of **Charity**, makes Man proud, recognizing whatever good he has as coming from himself and not from God. He does not see that he is **nothingness**, <note>original: "sè non essere." A core theme in Catherine’s mysticism is that God is "He who is" and humanity is "that which is not."</note> because self-love has blinded him; for if he saw, he would recognize that his being, and every grace that is placed upon his spiritual and temporal existence, he has all of it from God, because only God is He who is. 

The ungrateful man is not patient, because he is separated from Charity and the love of his Neighbor; his hope is in vain, because he trusts in himself; he hopes in human help, and not in Divine help. <margin>James 2</margin> His **Faith** is dead, because it is without good works, for Faith without works is dead. If he is a Subject, he is disobedient; if he is a Lord who holds a state of **Sovereignty**, he commits injustice, and does not do justice except by whim—which is not justice, but rather injustice—because he either does it out of hatred and displeasure that he holds toward such a person, or to please (or avoid displeasing) other Creatures, or for his own utility that he might draw from it. Wherefore we see holy **Justice** lacking in every thing. 

Natural Lords are made into **tyrants**. At the breast of the **Commune** <note>The "Comune" refers to the collective corporate body of the Republic of Florence.</note> the Subjects are not nourished with justice or fraternal charity, but each one with falsehoods and lies attends to his own private good, and not to the universal good. Everyone seeks **Lordship** for himself, and not the good state and government of the **City**; but like the blind they do not notice their own woes; for believing they are acquiring and possessing, they lose everything at an hour they do not expect. This we have seen and experienced; God permits it all through Divine Justice to purge our ingratitude, and to make us return to the knowledge...

...to, and with the rod, let us humble ourselves under His powerful hand. Let there be no one so mad that, while remaining in this blindness of ignorance and ingratitude, they believe they can acquire or preserve **Grace**, nor possess **Lordship** over themselves; for with ingratitude, **Reason** is subjected to one's own fragility. There is no evil, dearest Brothers, that does not spring from this vice.

II. Therefore it is necessary for you to strip off the **Old Man**, that is, self-love, from which ingratitude proceeds, and clothe yourselves in the **New Man**, Christ sweet Jesus—that is, in His doctrine, following in His footsteps. Through obedience to the Father and for our salvation, to satisfy for the sin of **Adam**, He did the opposite of what Adam had done. Adam, through disobedience, ran toward delight with pride and ingratitude for the benefit received; but the sweet and loving **Word** <note>original: "Verbo." A theological term for Jesus as the second person of the Trinity.</note> ran like one in love, with obedience, toward the shameful death of the **Cross**. God humbled Himself to Man by taking on our humanity; and as God and Man, He humbled Himself even to the shameful death of the Cross, and thus He satisfied for the guilt of our ingratitude as our **Mediator** <note>original: "tramezzatore." Literally one who stands in the middle; a go-between or bridge-builder.</note>. It is necessary for us, then, to clothe ourselves in the doctrine of this New Man with true and holy diligence, and to clothe ourselves in the affection of His **Charity**, who has shown us so much love; for unless a person is harder than stone, base, and a **hireling** <note>original: "mercenajo." One who serves only for reward or fear, rather than out of love.</note> without light or understanding, they cannot help but love, because it is the nature of love to love when it sees itself being loved. But the cloud of self-love has taken away our light so that we do not see; and those who do not see do not know; those who do not know do not love; and those who do not love are not grateful. Therefore, we need light to recognize how much we are loved by God, as well as our own defects, and to recognize those through whom God wishes us to show the love that we have for Him.

III. We see that our **Neighbor** is placed before us as the means to show the love we have for God; because we cannot be of use to the **Supreme Good** <note>original: "Sommo Bene." A philosophical and theological name for God.</note> directly, He has placed us so that we may be of use to our Neighbor, and in them demonstrate our love by succoring, helping, and counseling them in whatever way possible for each person according to their state of life. This is a debt that everyone is bound to pay, just as it is our debt to be subjects and obedient to the **Holy Church**, and to succor her in whatever way we can.

*[* A *]* This Letter is addressed to the **Priors of the Arts** and to the **Gonfalonier of Justice** <term>Gonfalonier of Justice: The high-ranking executive official in the Florentine Republic, responsible for the city's internal security and the standard-bearer of the community.</term>, who in 1379 sat in government in the City of Florence. Many of the Nobles, in order to have a part in the offices and magistracies, had themselves enrolled in one of the Guilds; for although they were not in fact craftsmen like the commoners, they nonetheless lost that luster which their Nobility provided them by being made equal under that common title of the Arts, shared by both themselves and the common people. Others of the Nobles, however, did not wish to give this mark—as it seemed to them—to their blood, preferring instead to live in private fortune with their ancient splendor, rather than to hold a position of command with that stain <note>This refers to the "Ordinances of Justice" of 1293, which required nobles to renounce their status and join a guild to participate in government; those who refused were "stained" by exclusion from power.</note>. Notwithstanding this, they also obtained the Supreme Honors at certain times, as that City frequently changed its own Laws. But in 1343, they were forced by the People to lay down the Offices they held, and to save their lives, to lose those honors which gave them more Power, but no greater glory. 

The Government in Florence being thus entirely Popular, the Priors of the Guilds, or Trades, into which the People were divided—according to the custom of many Cities Beyond-the-Mountains <note>A term used by Italians to refer to Northern Europe, specifically France, Germany, and England.</note>, and specifically of the City of London, whose People are divided into twelve Guilds, from which the Governor of the City is chosen, whom they call <term>Mayor</term> <note>original: "Maire"</note>, and who acquires the title of <term>Lord</term>, or Master—were the Head of that Government, forming as it were the supreme Magistrate, and they were twelve in total. 

Besides these, there was the <term>Gonfalonier</term> <note>Literally "Standard-bearer," the highest executive office in the Florentine Republic.</note> called "of Justice," to distinguish him from those Gonfaloniers who held the Ensigns of the City's Quarters, of whom there were many, and they were for War, whereas the other was to take care of the upright administration of Justice; hence he was also considered the principal Figure of the Republic, and although from the People, he was nonetheless chosen from the most noteworthy Families. The name of <term>Gonfalonier</term> arises from the word <term>Gonfalone</term>, or as it should rather be said, *Gonfanone*, which signifies an Ensign or Standard cut at the bottom into several pieces that remain hanging, since the word *Fanon* or *Fenon*, from which it draws its origin in the German language <note>original: "linguaggio Alemanno"</note>, signifies a piece of Cloth cut in that manner. Now, it being the custom to raise these Ensigns and carry them before these Personages, they drew from this the name of Gonfaloniers. Saint Catherine makes mention of the *Gonfalone* in many of her Epistles, and by it she usually expresses a Standard with the Cross as a signal of the Holy War <note>Meaning a Crusade or a spiritual struggle for the Church.</note>.

** ( B ) ** *Many are your offenses and iniquities, etc.* Regarding what is mentioned here, we have happened to speak of it several times, and particularly in the Annotations to the first Letter.

*...harm, no one will do what does you good: No warning was so necessary for the City of Florence as that of maintaining <term>Civil Concord</term> <note>The ideal of internal peace and political unity among citizens.</note>, since Discord was the evil that, above all others, had always unhappily troubled her.*
*The Disunity of Minds was born almost at the same birth as the City of Florence, when she was formed of two peoples discordant with one another: the <term>Florentines</term> and the <term>Fiesolans</term> <note>According to legend, Florence was founded by a mix of Roman settlers and the conquered inhabitants of the nearby hill-town, Fiesole; historical writers often blamed this "mixed blood" for the city's fractious nature.</note>; wherefore, as with those evils that are contracted at birth and from which one frees oneself only with great difficulty, it having become like second nature; thus she was almost never able to be entirely free from these internal grudges, so that from time to time she was troubled by such pernicious symptoms that more than once brought her to the point of ruin, as can easily be seen by whoever scans the Histories that speak of the deeds of this illustrious City. To this natural disposition, which led the minds of the Citizens to remain at odds with one another, other causes of new divisions were added, and these were the fatal factions of the <term>Guelphs</term> and <term>Ghibellines</term> <note>The warring medieval factions supporting the Pope and the Holy Roman Emperor, respectively.</note>; of the <term>Whites</term> and the <term>Blacks</term> <note>Sub-factions of the Guelph party in Florence around the year 1300.</note>; of the Nobility and of the People, which, if they were so lamentable to almost all of Italy, led this City to an even more deplorable state. The change of Government from the form of a <term>Republic</term> to that of a <term>Monarchy</term> <note>The transition to the Medici Grand Duchy in the 16th century.</note> brought perfect health to these ancient evils, as the minds of all then conspired toward the greatness and happiness of the reigning **Royal House**, upon whom they clearly see their own greatness and happiness also derive and depend.*

# To the Elders, Consuls, and Gonfaloniers of Bologna.

I. **S**he exhorts them to strip themselves of the <term>Old Man</term> <note>A biblical concept from St. Paul (Ephesians 4:22-24) referring to the sinful human nature inherited from Adam.</note>, that is, from sensual love, and to clothe themselves in the <term>New Man</term>, who is Jesus Christ our Lord, by means of His Holy Charity.
II. She discusses this Charity and its effects, not only toward God, but also toward one’s Neighbor.
III. Regarding self-love and sensual love and their effects, but particularly regarding the Injustice practiced by those who are Governors of Cities.
IV. She responds specifically to a letter of theirs concerning the maintenance of their <term>State</term> <note>In this context, "State" refers to their political standing, authority, and the stability of their government.</note>, saying there is no better means for this than to clothe themselves in the New Man—that is, in the Holy Charity of which she spoke above.

## Letter 200.

->Written while in a state of ecstasy.<- <note>original: "In Astrazione fatta"; this indicates the letter was dictated while Catherine was in a mystical trance.</note>

->*In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of Mary Gentle.*<-

I. **D**earest Brothers in Christ, gentle Jesus: I, Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious Blood with the desire to see you stripped of the <term>Old Man</term> and clothed in the <term>New Man</term>; that is, stripped of the World and of your own sensual love—which is the old sin of Adam—and clothed in the new Christ, gentle Jesus, which is His affectionate Charity.
II. When this Charity is in the Soul, it does not seek its own interests, but is liberal and generous in rendering its debt to God—that is, loving Him above all other things—and in rendering to itself hatred and displeasure for its own sensuality, and loving itself for God’s sake—that is, to give glory and praise to His Name; and to the Neighbor, rendering benevolence with a brotherly charity and with <term>ordered love</term> <note>A theological term (original: "ordinato amore") meaning to love things in their proper priority: God first, then the soul, then others, and finally material things.</note>; because Charity must be ordered, so that the Man...

...[one] should not do oneself the harm of guilt <note>In Catherine’s vocabulary, "guilt" (colpa) specifically refers to the state of being in sin.</note> to save, not just one soul, but if it were possible, to save the whole world, one must not do it; for it is not permitted to commit a small sin to practice a great virtue. And one <margin>B</margin> should not sacrifice our body to save the body of our neighbor, but we ought certainly to sacrifice our physical life for the salvation of souls, and our temporal substance <note>Refers to worldly goods, wealth, or property.</note> for the well-being and life of our neighbor: so you see, that this Charity wants to be ordered, and is ordered within the soul.

**III.** But those who are deprived of Charity and full of self-love do the exact opposite; and as they are disordered in their hearts and in their affections, so they are disordered in all their works. Thus we see that the men of the world, being without virtue, serve and love their neighbor with sin, and for their own pleasure. To serve them, they do not care about serving God; they displease Him and cause harm to their own souls. This is that **perverse love** which often kills both the soul and the body, takes away our light and gives us darkness, takes away our life and gives us death, deprives us of the company of the Blessed and gives us that of Hell. 

And if a man does not correct himself while he has the time, he extinguishes the shining pearl of holy <term>Justice</term> <note>For Catherine, Justice is not just a legal concept but a spiritual virtue of giving God and neighbor what is their due.</note> and loses the warmth of true Charity and obedience. Therefore, whichever way we turn toward any kind of rational creature, we see a lack of every virtue because of this wicked poison of sensual self-love. If we turn to the **Prelates**, they attend so much to themselves and to living in luxury that, seeing their subjects in the hands of the **Demons**, it seems they do not care; and the subjects, neither more nor less, do not care to obey, neither the civil Law nor the divine Law, nor do they care to serve one another except for their own utility. Therefore, this love is not enough, nor is the union of those who are joined by sensual love and not by true Charity; for their friendship lasts only as long as the pleasure, delight, and personal utility they derive from it endure. 

Hence, if he is a **Lord** <note>Meaning a political ruler or magistrate.</note>, he fails in holy Justice; and this is the reason why he fears losing his **State** <note>His political position or the stability of his government.</note>. To avoid causing displeasure, he goes about cloaking and hiding their defects, applying ointment to the wound at the very time it ought to be cauterized and in- <note>The text breaks off; the catchword "cesa" indicates the next word is "incisa" (cut/lanced).</note>

...extinguished with fire. Alas, my wretched soul! When he ought to apply the fire of **Divine Charity** and burn away defects through holy punishment and correction—exercising holy **Justice**—instead, he flatters and pretends not to see them. He does this toward those he sees who could hinder his <term>State</term> <note>In Catherine’s political thought, "State" (Stato) refers both to a person's social standing and the political stability of the government.</note>; but toward the poor, who are of little consequence and whom he does not fear, he shows a zeal for the greatest justice. Without any pity or mercy, they impose the heaviest burdens for the smallest fault. 

What is the cause of such injustice? **Self-love**. But the miserable men of the world, because they are deprived of truth, do not know the truth—neither according to God for their salvation, nor for themselves to preserve the <term>Lordship</term> <note>Italian: *Signoria*. The governing body or the authority of the city-state.</note> of the State. For if they knew the truth, they would see that only living in the fear of God preserves the State and keeps the City in peace. They would see that they must preserve holy Justice, giving each of their subjects their due: showing mercy to those who should receive mercy—not out of personal passion, but out of truth—and administering justice to those who should receive justice, seasoned with a mercy that is not passionate with anger, nor influenced by the words of any creature, but for holy and true justice. They would attend to the common good and not to private benefit. They would appoint <term>Officials</term> <note>Italian: *Officiali*. The various administrative and judicial officers of the Bolognese republic.</note> and those who must rule the city not through greed, nor through favoritism, nor through flattery, nor through bribery, but only by virtue and the way of reason. They would choose men who are mature and good, not "children" <note>Catherine often uses "children" or "boys" (fanciulli) to describe those lacking in moral maturity or wisdom, regardless of their actual age.</note>, and who fear God—lovers of the common good and not of their own private benefit.

Now, in this way, their State is preserved and the city is kept in peace and in union. But injustices, living for greed, and appointing men to rule and govern who do not know how to rule themselves or their families—unjust, wrathful men, filled with anger and lovers of themselves—these are the ways that cause the loss of the spiritual state of **Grace** and the temporal state.

Wherefore, to such as these it can be said: In vain do you weary yourself to guard your city if God does not guard it; that is, if you do not fear God and do not set Him before you in your actions. So you see, dearest brothers and lords, that self-love is the ruin of the City of the Soul, and the ruin and overturning of earthly cities. Therefore, I want you to know that nothing else has set the world in division among every kind of people except self-love, from which are [born...]

## IV.

It seems to me, most dear brothers, that you have a desire to increase and preserve the good <term>State</term> <note>Italian: *Stato*. In Catherine's writing, this refers both to the political stability of the city-state and the social standing of its rulers.</note> of your City, and because of this desire you were moved to write to me—unworthy, miserable, and full of defects. I understood and saw this letter with affectionate love and with a will to satisfy your desires, and to exert myself with that Grace which God will give me to offer you and your City before God with continual prayer. 

If you will be just men, and if your **Government** <note>Italian: *Reggimento*. This refers to the specific administrative body or council governing the Republic of Bologna.</note> is conducted as was said above—not through passion, nor through self-love and private benefit, but for the universal good founded upon the living Stone, Christ sweet Jesus—and if you perform all your works in His fear, then by means of prayers you will preserve the State, the Peace, and the unity of your City. And therefore I pray you for the love of Christ Crucified, since there is no other way: even though you have the help of the prayers of the servants of God, do not fail on your part in what is necessary. For if you were to fail, you would indeed be supported for a little while by prayers, but not so much that you would not soon collapse, because you must help to carry this burden on your part. 

Therefore, considering that with the garment of sensory and particular love you could not assist the servants of God, and that he who does not assist himself through the assistance of Virtue cannot assist his fraternal City with the zeal of **Holy Justice**, I say that it is necessary for you to be clothed in the **New Man**, Christ sweet Jesus—that is, in His inestimable Charity. But we cannot clothe ourselves unless we first strip ourselves, nor could I strip myself if I did not see how harmful it is to keep the old sin, and how useful the new garment of divine Charity is to me. For once a man sees this, he hates it [sin], and out of hatred he strips himself of it; then he loves, and out of love he clothes himself in the garment of the Virtues founded in the love of the **New Man** <note>A reference to the Pauline concept in Ephesians 4:22–24 of putting off the "old self" corrupted by desire and putting on the "new self" created to be like God.</note>. 

Now, this is the way. And therefore I told you that I desired to see you stripped of the **Old Man** and clothed in the **New Man**, Christ Crucified; and in this way you will acquire and preserve the State of Grace and the State of your City. You will never fail in the due reverence toward the **Holy Church**, but in a pleasing manner you will render what is owed and preserve your State. I say no more to you. Remain in the holy and sweet love of God. Sweet Jesus, Jesus love <note>original: "Geſù dolce, Geſù amore." A characteristic closing phrase for Catherine's letters.</note>.

<meta>This page provides historical commentary and annotations for Letter 5 (Letter 200 in other numbering systems) from Saint Catherine of Siena to the government of Bologna. It establishes the political context of Bologna’s relationship with the Papacy and discusses the probable date of the letter based on Catherine’s travels.</meta>

<margin>Annotations of Letter 5.</margin>
( A ) The City of Bologna, during the general revolt that other Italian cities raised against the Pope, also withdrew itself from its required obedience. However, it was not actually the first to rebel, as others have written and has been corrected elsewhere, when it forced *Guglielmo Novellete*, Cardinal of St. Angelo and Legate of *Gregory XI*, to depart. She organized her Government as a Republic, electing twelve *Elders*, *Consuls*, and *Standard-bearers of Justice*, and this new form of Government was called the *State of Liberty*. However, she returned to her duty quite soon; following the arrival of the Pope in Italy—specifically on July 4th of the year 1377—she sought pardon through her Ambassadors from *Gregory*, who was in *Anagni*. Due to his mild nature, she remained in a sort of liberty, with him consenting to her governing herself, but under the obedience of the Church. It was not long, however, before she again shook off this weight of subjection, rebelling against *Urban VI* in 1379, although she remained faithful in wishing to hold him as the legitimate Vicar of Christ. This Letter, which *Saint Catherine* wrote to the Bolognese while in a state of spiritual elevation in response to another she had received from them, is probably from 1377. She speaks to them as free people and masters of themselves, making no mention either of their rebellion from the Church (which was in 1376), nor of the Schism that arose in 1378, nor of their new relapse, which was in 1379. If she had taken the land route on her journey from France, she would undoubtedly have passed through *Bologna*, where she would have made herself illustrious through her holy and wondrous works, as happened to her in other cities; those Lords, as eyewitnesses of her holiness, could then have requested her advice on how to govern themselves well. But of this there is no certainty at all, even though it seems to be asserted quite openly by Pope *Pius II* in the <term>Bull of her Canonization</term> <note>The official papal document issued in 1461 that formally declared Catherine a saint.</note> in these words:

-> For the peace of the Florentines, who were at odds with the Church and were placed under an ecclesiastical interdict, she did not hesitate to cross the Apennines and the Alps, and to travel as far as Avignon to *Gregory XI*. <note>original: "Pro pace Florentinorum, qui cum Ecclesia dissidebant, & Interdicto suppositi erant Ecclesiastico, Appenninum, & Alpes transire, atque usque in Avenionem ad Gregorium XI. proficisci non dubitavit."</note> <-

These words, however, can still be true if the Saint went by sea to *Genoa*, from where she then traveled by land, crossing the Apennines and the Alps without touching *Bologna*, reaching *Provence* by very arduous roads. It is also probable that she traveled there by the sea route, according to the very constant tradition in *Genoa* that the Saint was in that city more than once.

<meta>This page transitions from the historical commentary on Letter 5 (addressed to Bologna) to the text and summary of Letter 201, addressed to the government of Siena. <margin>( B )</margin> One should not offer up our own body to save the body of our neighbor. It is not ordinarily permissible to put the life of another before one's own, since, *according to the rule of well-ordered Charity, one must love one's own life more than another's, as St. Augustine teaches us.* If anyone loses their own temporal life for the temporal life of another, it is no longer loving that person as oneself, but more than oneself, which is contrary to sound rule. <note>original Latin: "Si quis pro alterius temporali vita, suam ipsam temporalem perdit, non est jam diligere illum sicuti se ipsum, sed plusquam se ipsum, quod sanae regulae repugnat." St. Augustine’s "well-ordered charity" suggests a hierarchy of love starting with one's own soul, then one's life, then the neighbor's soul, and finally the neighbor's life.</note>

# To the Lords Defenders and the Captain of the <margin>A</margin> People of the City of Siena, while it was at St. Antimo. <note>Sant'Antimo is a famous Benedictine abbey near Montalcino where Catherine stayed in 1377. The "Lords Defenders" and "Captain of the People" were the primary governing bodies of the Republic of Siena.</note>

I. That we must rule over ourselves and our passions, since we cannot rule over others in any other way.
II. She prays that the said Lords do not trust wicked and ignorant men, but only the servants of God.
III. Furthermore, that they should not suspect—as was suggested to them by others—the Archpriest of Montalcino, but value and assist him as a perfect man and servant of God.
IV. She says that her coming to Siena is not permitted. <note>Catherine was often restricted in her movements by her spiritual directors or political circumstances.</note>
V. She informs them of the prayers and all that she does for the salvation of their souls, and of the benefit she has brought to souls in the place where she was staying.

<meta>This page continues Letter 201, addressed to the governing bodies of the Republic of Siena. Having just finished the introductory points, Catherine now begins the body of her letter, focusing on the spiritual requirements of leadership.</meta>

The man who is to rule over others and govern must first rule and govern himself. How could the blind see and guide others? How can the dead bury the dead? The sick cannot govern the sick, nor could the poor help the poor. Truly, dearest Lords, he who is blind and has obscured the eye of his <term>Intellect</term><note>The "Intellect" in Catherinian thought is the faculty of the soul that perceives truth through the light of faith.</note> through <term>mortal sin</term><note>A grave sin that separates the soul from God's grace.</note> knows neither himself nor God. He will, therefore, be poorly able to see or correct the fault of his subject; and even if he does correct it, he corrects it with that darkness and imperfection that he has within himself. Often, due to his lack of insight, I have seen and still see faults punished where they do not exist, while those who are iniquitous and wicked—deserving of a thousand deaths—are not punished. 

The lack of light does not allow one to discern the truth; it places slander where there is none and generates suspicion toward those in whom one could be secure and trust—namely, the servants of God. These are the ones who give birth to the rulers <note>This "giving birth" is a frequent metaphor for Catherine, referring to the spiritual labor of prayer and sacrifice offered for the sake of others.</note> with tears and sweat, through constant and holy prayer, exposing themselves to every danger, pain, and torment for the honor of God and the salvation of the rulers and the whole world. Instead, rulers trust those who are rooted in self-love, who turn with every wind. All of this proceeds from a lack of light and the darkness of sin; there is a need, then, to have the light. 

I say that the dead cannot bury the dead; that is, he who is dead to <term>Grace</term> has neither the courage nor the strength to bury the "dead" fault of his <term>Neighbor</term>, because he feels himself to be in that same state of death, and therefore he does not want to, nor does he, provide correction. Seeing himself in that same infirmity, he does not care for it. He does not care for his subject even if he sees him to be sick; furthermore, the weight of the infirmity of mortal sin is so great that he cannot apply a remedy unless he first heals himself. Once it happens that he exists in mortal sin, he has fallen into poverty and lost the wealth of the true and real <term>Virtues</term>, by not following the footsteps of <term>Christ Crucified</term>. Therefore, he cannot help the poor man, being deprived—as I said—of the wealth of Divine Grace through the darkness. He has lost the light and cannot see the fault where it actually lies, and thus injustices are committed rather than justice. Through this infirmity, he loses the vigor of holy and true desire to seek the honor of God and the salvation of his neighbor; and there always grows...

<summary>Catherine explains that a ruler must first govern their own soul, as a leader blinded by sin cannot discern truth or execute justice. She warns the Sienese leaders that without spiritual "light," they will punish the innocent and trust self-interested flatterers over the true servants of God.</summary>

( A ) *This Letter is addressed to the <term>Supreme Magistrate</term><note>original: "Supremo Magistrato"</note>, who at that time governed the <term>Sienese Republic</term><note>original: "Repubblica Sanese"</note>. Those who ruled in Siena in that age belonged to the Order called the <term>Reformers</term><note>original: "Riformatori"</note>, of whom mention has been made elsewhere, and who are discussed at length in the supplement to the Life of the Saint by Mr. <term>Girolamo Gigli</term><note>An 18th-century Sienese scholar and editor of Catherine’s works</note>. This Magistrate was formed by the People and elected from them, called the <term>Lords Defenders of the People and Commune of Siena</term><note>original: "Signori Difensori del Popolo, e Comune di Siena"</note>, composed of fifteen persons who resided in the Palace of the Signoria. Of these fifteen, one held the title of <term>Captain of the People</term><note>original: "Capitano di Popolo"</note>, who served as the Head of all. Formerly, these were chosen from foreign lands and changed every six months; but by an ordinance established in 1355, it was settled that in the future the Captain of the People would be elected every two months, and he should not be a foreigner, but a Sienese. After various changes of government in this City regarding the manner of ruling, the name of the "Defenders" fell away, as it was too greatly hated by the Nobility, though the name of the Captain of the People remained, who even at present is the principal figure of the Excelled Senate of Siena, and is elected every two months by the Royal Highness of the Most Serene Patron. To these rulers, then, the Saint wrote while she was staying at the <term>Abbey of Sant' Antimo</term><note>original: "Abadia di Sant' Antimo"</note>, which, as mentioned elsewhere, is five miles distant from <term>Montalcino</term>.*

centuries, without interruption until the Years of **Saint Catherine**, maintaining from that beginning a certain dependence on the **Emperors**, and on those who had charge of the **Affairs of Tuscany** for them. From this Liberty, and from the Faith that always looked toward the <term>Imperial party</term><note>original: "partito Cesareo"; referring to the Ghibelline faction which supported the Holy Roman Emperor</note>, she <note>Siena</note> profited to her great advantage, extending her Dominion to the most remote borders and receiving from time to time new graces and exemptions. In the times that were so disastrous for **Tuscany** due to divisions, when other Cities fell into the power of others, this city was never a servant; hence if in 1286 many of them redeemed themselves with money from that very light servitude which they held more in appearance than in substance with the **Empire**, it was not necessary for **Siena** to remove any bond from herself, however thin, because she was already completely free. Rightly, therefore, the Saint says to these Rulers, who represented the **Republic**, that God had granted them <term>temporal Lordship</term><note>original: "Signoria temporale"; political authority over earthly matters as opposed to spiritual authority</note>, enjoying it for such a long time and with such legitimate possession.

[ C ] *That for the Archpriest of Montalcino etc.* The territory of **Montalcino**, which today is a City by ancient concession of **Charlemagne**, or **Louis the Pious**, was in large part subject to the **Abbot of the Monastery of Sant’ Antimo**, who held Jurisdiction there in both spiritual and temporal matters. Dominion was ceded by the Abbots to the **Republic of Siena**, and although such a cession was declared null by the Popes, nevertheless in the end, after many <note>struggles</note>, the Sienese established themselves in Lordship after the famous victory achieved over the <term>Guelphs</term><note>The political faction supporting the Pope against the Emperor</note> at **Montaperti**. As in the times of **Saint Catherine** the Abbots had lost almost entirely their temporal Dominion, so too had they suffered a great loss of their spiritual Authority; hence it is that the **Archpriest** of this land was in conflict with the **Abbot**, a very clear sign that the latter's rights were no longer in their former bloom. The Archpriest was the Priest of the principal Church, titled the <term>Parish Church</term><note>original: "Pieve"</note> of **San Salvadore**, and it was in 그hat part which belonged to the Dominion of the Abbots, now changed into a Cathedral. From the Year 1370 until 1380, three Archpriests are found there named **Guido**, **Mino**, and **Battista**; thus the Abbot was in contention with one of these, and perhaps with the second.

# To the Lords Defenders of the City of Siena.

I. She exhorts them to be strong governors of their own City, and of their own Souls.
II. Concerning servile fear, which proceeds from self-love, and does not allow a Man to act as a Man, nor to know the truth.
III. That we must not judge the Servants of God, but let them act according as the Holy Spirit guides them, and how ready God is to punish such judgments.
IV. Concerning holy fear, with which we must govern our Soul, in order to be able then to govern the City.
V. She thanks them for the desire they have for her return, for which, however, she excuses herself due to certain affairs that occupy her in the place where she finds herself.
VI. She grieves for her fellow Citizens, who were murmuring about her and her Company.

## Letter 202.

### In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of Sweet Mary.

I. **D**earest Brothers, and temporal Lords in sweet Christ Jesus. I, Catherine, servant and slave of the Servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious Blood with the desire to see you as strong <note>original: "virili"; Catherine frequently uses this term to denote spiritual strength, courage, and maturity as opposed to the "effeminacy" of indecision or fear.</note> men, and not fearful Governors of your own City and of the lent City <note>The "own city" refers to the soul, while the "lent city" refers to the earthly city of Siena, which Catherine viewed as a temporary stewardship granted by God.</note>, considering that servile fear <term>servile fear</term><note>A theological concept referring to a fear of God based only on the dread of punishment, rather than the "filial fear" based on love.</note> hinders and debases the Heart, and does not allow one to live or act as a reasonable Man, but as an animal without any reason; because servile fear issues and proceeds from self-love. And how dangerous this self-love is, we see in Lords and in Subjects, in Religious and in Seculars, and in every manner of People; for they attend to nothing other than themselves. Hence, if he is a secular Subject, he never obeys, nor observes that which is imposed upon him by his Lord; and if he is a Lord—

You make a Man unbearable to himself, because he desires that which he cannot have, and that which he possesses, he possesses with pain, because he has fear of losing it; whence, not having what he wants and always fearing with pain because his Will is not fulfilled, he rightly tastes **Hell** in this life.

III. O blindness of self-love, and disordered fear, you reach such blindness that you do not only condemn the common people and the wicked men—who could justly be condemned, and whose falsehood should be feared—but you leave behind the fear of the wicked and condemn the just, treating with contempt the poor Servants of God. These servants seek the honor of God, the salvation of Souls, and the Peace and quiet of Cities, never ceasing to offer sweet desires and continual prayer, tears, and sweats before the **Divine Goodness**. How then can self-love and servile fear allow you to fear and judge those who dispose themselves to death for your health <note>Here, "health" (salute) implies both spiritual salvation and physical well-being.</note>, and to preserve and increase your State in peace and in quiet? 

But truly, Dearest Brothers, this is 그 perverse fear and love that killed **Christ**; because **Pilate**, fearing to lose his Lordship, was blinded and did not know the truth, and for this reason he killed Christ. And nevertheless, that which he feared came upon him, because later, at the time that pleased God—not that his fault pleased Him—he lost Soul, Body, and Lordship. <margin>A</margin> Whence it seems to me that the whole World is full of these Pilates, who out of blind fear do not care if they persecute the Servants of God, throwing at them stones of words, infamies, and persecutions, and so...

blindness is theirs; for they look neither at how nor at whom, but like beasts they let themselves be led by their own sensuality, applying those standards <note>original: "colori," literally "colors," used here to mean pretenses or appearances</note> and that law to them which is applied to men who attend to nothing but the world. Wherefore it seems to me that Christ was more patient regarding His own injury than that of His Apostle **St. Thomas**; because He did not wish to avenge His own, but benignly replied to the one who struck Him on the cheek, saying:

The private City <note>original: "Città propria," referring here to the internal state of the soul as a domain to be governed</note> is the City of our Soul, which is possessed through holy fear founded upon fraternal Charity, Peace, and unity with God and one’s Neighbor, and with true and real Virtues. **Borrowed Lordship** <term>Lordship: in this context, "Signorìa" refers to political authority or the right to govern a city-state</term> refers to the rule of Cities or other temporal powers, which are lent to us and to other men of the world for a time, according to what pleases the Divine Goodness and the customs of the lands. Whether through death or during the course of life, these powers pass away; so, in whatever way it happens, they are truly "borrowed." 

He who rules himself will possess his authority with holy fear and with an ordered love <note>original: "amore ordinato," the theological idea of loving things in their proper priority, with God first</note>, rather than a disordered one. He will treat it as something borrowed and not as his own property; he will look upon the gift of the Lordship given to him with fear and reverence for the One who gave it. You have received it from God alone, so that when the borrowed thing is requested back by the Lord, it can be rendered unto Him without the danger of eternal Death. # To the Lords Defenders of the People and the Commune of Siena.

I. On Justice, through which we must pay our debt to God—that is, love and honor; to the Holy Church, reverence and love; to ourselves, hatred and displeasure for our own faults.
II. On the contrary ways that we employ.
III. That one must revere and help the Sovereign Pontiff; even if he were a perverse and wicked man, much more so being a holy and just man. <note>Catherine frequently argued that the office of the Papacy required obedience regardless of the personal character of the Pope, though she staunchly defended the legitimacy of Urban VI.</note>
IV. That Pope Urban VI is the true Sovereign Pontiff, and that one must remain united to him. <note>This letter was written during the Western Schism, a period when there were rival claimants to the papacy.</note>

## Letter 203.

->Written while in a state of ecstasy.<- <note>original: "In Astrazione fatta." Catherine often dictated her letters while in a deep state of prayer or trance.</note>

->In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of Sweet Mary,<-

<margin>I,</margin>**D**earest brothers in sweet Jesus Christ. I, Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious Blood with the desire to see the pearl of Holy Justice shine within you, so that you may justly render to everyone their due. To whom are we debtors? To God, and to the Holy Church, and to our neighbor by the commandment of God, and to ourselves. Let us see what this debt is. It is such that to God we must render glory and praise to His Name through love. Love is given to us, because He loved us before we existed; and honor was done for us, removing the shame into which we fell through the sin of Adam, through the Blood of His Son, in which we received the fruit of Grace <term>Grace: "Gratia," the free and unmerited favor of God, which Catherine views as the primary "utility" or benefit given to humanity.</term>. This was the greatest benefit we could receive, because it took away death from us and gave us life. Therefore, we must render honor and love to Him, but we can do Him no service <note>original: "utilità." Catherine explains that while we owe God everything, we cannot actually "benefit" Him since He is already perfect; our "utility" is instead directed toward our neighbor.</note>,

so that we must do it to our **Neighbor**, helping them according to our ability and rendering them the debt of love, just <margin>Matthew 22.</margin> as it is commanded of us by the Eternal Truth, who says: "Love God above all things, and your **Neighbor** as yourself." Toward ourselves, we ought to render hatred and displeasure for **Vice** and for our own sensuality (which is the cause of vice), and love for the **Virtues**, loving them within ourselves for the sake of God with an affectionate love.

II. But it appears we do the contrary, acting like thieves and wicked debtors, taking what belongs to others with great injustice—that is, the honor and love that we should give to God and to our **Neighbor**, we instead give to ourselves. To ourselves we give honor, seeking like proud men the ranks, delights, and greatness of the world while offending God; we attribute and repute what we have to our own wisdom, and thus, like ignorant people, we bring shame upon God. To ourselves we give love, and to Him we give hatred—not a reasonable love, but a sensory love <note>In Catherine’s theology, "sensory love" (amore sensitivo) refers to selfish, physical, or worldly desire, whereas "reasonable love" is aligned with the soul and God's will.</note>. To Him we give a stench, and to ourselves the fragrance, seeking human delights and pleasures; but like blind men, we do not see the harm, the stench, and the stones of our iniquities, which fall back upon us. For our evil does not harm Him, nor does our good benefit Him, because He has no need of us, but we indeed have need of Him. To our **Neighbor** we return hatred and resentment, committing many injustices. Thus, if a man is a Lord <note>Referring to the "Lords Defenders" of Siena to whom the letter is addressed.</note>, he does not grant his neighbor reason or justice except for his own utility, or to please other creatures, or himself, and not by the light of Reason. He does not care if he takes away the neighbor's honor, reputation, worldly substance, or even their life. With such injustice does he govern his **Subjects**, as if he had no Lord over himself; he does not consider that the rod of the **Supreme Judge** <note>God.</note> can repay him with the same measure he gives to others. He does not attend to the universal common good, but only to his own private good, being blinded by self-love. These people do not pay the fourth debt to the **Holy Church** and to the **Vicar of Christ** <note>The Pope, whom Catherine viewed as the earthly representative of Christ.</note>. What debt must we render to him? A due reverence and a filial love, not only in word, but as true children, helping the Father in his time of need; regarding any injury done to him as if it were done to us, and doing all we can to remove his enemies from before him.

Truly we act like mercenaries, who consider every grace they receive to be something they are owed; and they often wish to cover their own defects with the defects of others. But they reveal themselves even more by showing such ingratitude. We can also receive discipline <margin>B</margin> from all created things, because we see the time of the Lord's coming. It is better for us, then, to stay united with our Father and Mother—that is, Pope Urban VI and the **Holy Church**—than with tyrants. It is better for us <margin>C</margin> to stay leaning against the firm Column, which, even if it is struck by many persecutions, is nevertheless not broken, rather than leaning on the straw, which we are certain will fail us, as every little wind blows it to the ground.

For you can no longer say that he asks your help to acquire the temporal goods of the **Holy Church** which have been lost, but rather for our Faith: to confound the lie and exalt the truth, to draw souls from the hands of the devils, and so that our Faith is not contaminated by the hands of the wicked.

And therefore I told you that I desired to see the Pearl of Holy Justice shining in you. I say no more to you. Remain in the holy and sweet love of God.

Regarding the <term>Censures</term> <note>Ecclesiastical punishments, such as excommunication or interdict, used by the Church to enforce discipline.</note> of the **Church**, nothing at all is mentioned by **Malavolti**, an accurate writer of the events of his homeland, nor by **Angelo di Tura di Grasso** in his handwritten Chronicle, though he lived during those times. However, **Tommasi**, in his manuscript History, speaks of it in this manner:

<margin>*Part 3, Book 2:*</margin>
**Messere Jacomo Tolomei**, Bishop of **Narni**, by order of His Holiness <note>original: "Sua Beatitudine," a title of respect for the Pope.</note>, absolved the City of **Siena** from the <term>Interdict</term> <note>A decree that prohibits individuals or a whole territory from participating in most sacraments and religious services.</note>, as is found recorded in the public acts of 1379. I have not read for what occasion, or at what time it had fallen under <term>Censures</term>, unless perhaps **Pope Gregory** <note>Pope Gregory XI, the last of the Avignon Popes.</note> interdicted all those allied against the French Clergy when he excommunicated the **Florentines**.

<margin>*Letter 125:*</margin>
But outside of the public acts, **Saint Catherine** speaks of this <term>Absolution</term> in this Letter, and in another she also makes mention of this <term>Censure</term>. Thus, one may observe how much weight arguments taken from the silence of authors often have—arguments which are held in such high value today—seeing that both that Historian and this Chronicler, who is so detailed in reporting the facts that happened in his time, pass over this event without a word. It is certain, however, that the City incurred the <term>Interdict</term>, if not directly, at least indirectly, for being in league with the **Florentines**, and for having given them aid and refuge in the City against the Pope's prohibition; for this reason alone, the Pope had also interdicted both **Pisa** and **Genoa**. If the Sienese historians did not speak of it, this perhaps happened because such a punishment was not unique to this city alone, nor was it published in such a sensational form as had been done for others. We see also that ancient writers do not keep silent about other similar penalties of the Ecclesiastical Power into which the City had deservedly fallen, as was observed by **Don Bartolomeo Scala** in the *Life of **Blessed Pietro Petroni***; they were content to have remembered the most famous ones, such as that launched against it by **Clement IV.**

Having reduced it to a fortress in the name of the Church, he held a garrison there. Requests were made by the **Republic of Siena** to the Pope so that the place might be returned to them, a possession to which the **Pisans** also aspired. And although the requests were renewed many times, they never succeeded in returning it to [Sienese] sovereignty during the time of **Gregory XI**. <page-num>135</page-num>

# To the Magnificent Lords Defenders of the People and Commune of Siena.

**I.** She exhorts them to be faithful to Holy Mother Church, to have zeal for Justice, and to strip themselves of self-love, showing the disorders that proceed from it.
**II.** She stimulates them to be obedient to **Urban VI**, recognizing him as the true and Supreme Pontiff and Vicar of Christ, and to help him in the turmoils of the Schism <note>The Western Schism began in 1378, shortly before this letter, creating deep political divisions in Italy.</note>.
**III.** She reproaches them because in the past they favored his Rebels, and she effectively exhorts them to a resolute and prompt amendment of such a great error.

---

## Letter 204.

->In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified and of sweet Mary.<-

**I.** **D**earest Brothers and Fathers in sweet Jesus Christ. ### III.
No Sacrifice can you give to your Creator that is as pleasing to Him as this; and let it not seem hard to you, for it did not seem hard or difficult for all the time that has passed to have served against God and against all reason those who were then foul members, rebels against the Holy Church. From that service you have not had, nor did you ever have, anything but harm to the Soul, the Body, and your temporal substance, along with much shame, confusion of mind, and disgrace, leaving behind the <term>worm of Conscience</term> <note>A common medieval metaphor for the persistent gnawing of guilt or remorse.</note>. However, such "faith" should not have been observed, because it could not be kept without sin, and sin should never be committed in any way. And if so much was done in the service of the Devil, how much more must you now exert all your power? You must serve for the sake of <term>Christ Crucified</term> and out of duty to his <term>Vicar</term> <note>The Pope, considered the representative or "Christ on Earth."</note>, Christ on Earth, Pope Urban VI. You must hold him as the <term>Supreme Pontiff</term>, and whoever holds the contrary is a heretic, rejected by God and a member of the Devil.

Do not act thus, for the love of God, but with heartfelt love hold affirmatively that our Father is Pope Urban VI, despite anyone who says the contrary; you must obey and help him, and if necessary, die for this Truth. By the fruit of the aid you provide, I will recognize that the flower of the Most Holy Faith is within you, and that you are faithful servants to the Holy Church and to your sweet and just Father. I confess, and will confess before the whole World until death, that Pope Urban VI is truly the true Pope and Supreme Pontiff. * ( A ) *This Letter, which was missing from the older printed editions, was obtained from a Copy provided by Signor Cornelio Guidini, a Sienese Knight. At the end of this Copy is the testimony that it was taken from a book of memoirs belonging to Monsignor Deifebo Mancini, and drawn from his Original, which was kept in the public Archive of the City, and later passed into the hands of Signor Balì Agostini, Lord of Caldana. Since the Letter is dated the ninth of December 1379, it was written from Rome, where the Saint had been staying for more than a year. The title she gives to the Defenders of the People and Commune of Siena is that of "Lords" and "Magnificent ones," whereas in other letters addressed to them, she honors them with no other title than that of "Lords"; therefore, if it was not placed there by others—as I am not far from believing—one can clearly see how little care She took in applying these titles of honor. Little attention was paid to them in that Age by others as well, not even by Royal Personages, as was noted on another occasion. The title of "Magnificent" was used quite frequently in that century, and* <margin>Memoirs of the Carthusian Monastery of Pontignano <note>The Certosa di Pontignano was a monastery near Siena; these memoirs likely refer to records kept by Stefano Maconi.</note></margin> *it was often offered to Lords of higher affairs. This addition remained in a place of honor until the sixteenth century, in which it is also found to be given to Lords of great Power; since at that time, as Italy changed its State in great part, it also made a change in titles—consoling the loss of Authority and Power (which passed in great part into the sway of foreign nations) with the acquisition of specious words of honor. Hence, no one now deigns to use "Magnificent," and "Most Illustrious"—which is taken from the greatest Kings that the Christian World ever had—is now desired today by anyone who is Noble, or has pretension of being so, who in times past would not even have reached the level of being called Master.*
