[ **D** ] **And** *therefore God allowed, and allows, that we receive so many disciplines and scourges.* And very many, and most grave, were the calamities that the City of Siena had to suffer in the times in which Saint Catherine lived. For, if one begins to run through the years from 1348—which was the year of the Saint's birth <note>Modern scholarship generally places Catherine's birth in 1347, but the editor here cites 1348.</note>—one will find that almost no year passed without a heavy scourge. In that year, the city was so badly afflicted by the plague, common to the entire world, that it killed eighty thousand people, leaving more than one hundred Noble Families entirely extinct; nor from that time could the City ever again recover its ancient greatness and power. Then came the changes of Government, which from 1355 until 1368 was changed three times, passing from the Order of the Nine to that of the Twelve, from that to the Order of the Nobles, and in 1368 to that of the Reformers <note>These "Orders" (Monti) were political factions representing different social classes in the Sienese Republic.</note>; for this reason, riots and seditions broke out from hour to hour with much bloodshed both in the City and in the Countryside. The Plague returned anew in the year 1374, and with it was joined Famine, both of them bringing death to a great number of people. The free Mercenary Bands <note>original: "Masnade"</note> of soldiers, who were plundering Italy, came from time to time to bring new affliction to this Republic, which was forced to extract itself from such a most troublesome whirlwind—which brought everything to ruin—sometimes by the sword, and more often with gold.

<margin>*Memoirs, Annotations 1375.*</margin>
( **E** ) *To have served against God. That is, against the Church; since not only the Florentines, but the Sienese as well took up arms against the Legates of the Pope at the time of Gregory XI, they having sent their Brigades in favor of Perugia and Bologna, which had rebelled against the Church.*

[ **F** ] *For wanting to be found faithful to that which you had promised.* The Republic of Siena had already for some years been allied with the Commune of Florence along with other cities of Tuscany; therefore, under the title of "given faith" <note>meaning their sworn oath of alliance</note>, they wished to be excused for the War they had waged against the Church.

# To the Lords Priors of the People and the Commune of Perugia. <note>The "Priors" were the chief magistrates of the city-state of Perugia.</note>

1. **S**he begs them to be willing to aid the Holy Church and Pope Urban VI <note>Urban VI was the Pope whose election in 1378 triggered the Great Western Schism; Catherine was one of his most fervent supporters.</note> for the benefits that come to us from him, both spiritual and temporal; and for the punishments that they might expect from God by neglecting to do so.

## Letter 205.

->***In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified and of Sweet Mary.***<-

I. **D**earest Brothers in Christ Jesus. I, Catherine, slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious Blood with the desire to see you as helpers in the necessity of your Father, and in your own necessity as well; because to aid him is to aid your own salvation, both spiritually and temporally. Spiritually, insofar as by aiding this sweet Bride of the Holy Church and Pope Urban VI, you pay your debt, which we are all obliged to pay; by paying it, we show ourselves to be grateful and mindful toward God and toward him for the graces he has granted us, and continues to grant us—graces that we could never compare to anything we might return to him in respect of what he gives to us. For what he gives us is a good that grants us eternal life: these are the Sacraments of the Holy Church and other spiritual gifts, all of which have life and are effective for us by virtue of the Blood, provided we receive them with a true and holy disposition and with the Light of Holy Faith. Otherwise, they would bring us death, not through any defect in the gifts, nor in him who gives them, but through our own evil disposition in receiving them. And all these are administered by him <note>Referring to the Pope as the steward of the sacraments.</note>, and without him we cannot receive them, because he holds the keys to the Blood of the humble Lamb shed for us with such fire of Love. Thus, he gives to us an infinite good, provided we dispose ourselves as has been said.

## Letter 206.

->*In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of Sweet Mary.*<-

**T**o you, most beloved and dearest Brothers in Christ sweet Jesus, I Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, write in his precious Blood with the desire to see you full of divine Grace and the Light of the Holy Spirit; considering that without this Light we cannot walk. You know, dearest Brothers, that we are pilgrims and travelers on the way in this dark life; we are blind by ourselves. Our sweet God is powerful in willing and being able to preserve us, and to pull us from the hands of our enemies, provided that you attend to his honor and to the exaltation of the Holy Church, which is our own exaltation, because the Soul receives life in no other thing except in the Church herself.

## V.

You know well that God is He who is strong, and all strength and virtue proceed from Him; this strength is not taken away from the Spouse, nor do I believe she is without this strong help. But her enemies, who act against her, have lost this strength and help; for like putrid members they are cut off from her body. As soon as the member is cut off, it is weakened. Foolish, therefore, and mad is he who is but a small member and wishes to act against a great Head, especially when he sees that Heaven and Earth would sooner fail than the virtue of this Head would fail. And if you should say:

<margin>C</margin> I do not know, I only see the members who prosper and move forward. Wait a little, for it must not go, nor can it go this way; <margin>Psalm 126:</margin> <note>original: "Pfal. 126". A translation/paraphrase of Psalm 127:1.</note> Therefore, it cannot last; she cannot help but fail, and Soul and Body be destroyed; because they are deprived of God through grace, who guards it, because they have acted against His Spouse, where God rests, who is the supreme strength. Therefore, let no servile fear <term>servile fear: a fear of punishment or loss of status, rather than "filial fear" which is driven by love of God</term> deceive you, for servile fear was that which Pilate had, who for fear of losing his dominion, killed Christ, and through his ignorance lost the state of his Soul.

## VI.

Therefore, I pray you for the love of Christ Crucified, my dearest brothers and children of the Holy Church, that you always stand firm and persevering in that which you have begun. Let neither the Devil nor any Creature <note>In Catherine’s writing, "Creature" refers to any created being—human or otherwise—contrasted with the Creator.</note> move you—for such people are worse than Devils. They have directly taken up the Devil's office: it is not enough for them to be evil themselves, but they go about inviting and pulling back those who wish to be, and have been, children of the Church. <margin>D</margin> Do not be moved by any fear of losing peace or your status <term>Stato: referring both to their political standing and the stability of their city-state</term>, nor by threats that these Devils might make against you. You have no need for such fear; instead, comfort yourselves with a sweet and holy thanksgiving that God has shown you grace and mercy. For you are not untied from the Head <note>The "Head" refers to Christ and, by extension, the Pope in Rome during the Great Schism.</note> and from Him who is strong, and you are not bound to that weak and putrid member which is cut off from His strength. <margin>E</margin> Look, look, that you do not form this bond with them! Rather, choose every pain, and let the fear of God and the offense against Him always come before any other pain; then you will have no need to fear. I rejoice and exult within myself for the good strength <term>fortezza: a term meaning both a physical fortress and the spiritual virtue of fortitude or courage</term> that you have had until now, in being strong, persevering, and obedient to the Holy Church. <margin>F</margin> Now, hearing the contrary, I was greatly saddened. Therefore, I came here on behalf of Christ Crucified to tell you that you must not do this for anything in the world. Know that if you did this to preserve yourselves and have peace, you would fall into the greatest war and ruin that the soul and body ever had. Do not, therefore, fall into such ignorance, but be true and persevering children. You know well that if a Father has many children, and only one remains faithful to him, he will give the inheritance to that one. I say this because even if you were to remain alone, stay firm in this field and do not turn your head back; for by the grace of God, <margin>G</margin> there is still another left to us. These are the Pisans <note>The people of Pisa, who at this historical moment remained allied with Catherine's cause.</note>, your neighbors, who—so long as you wish to stand firm and persevering—will never fail you, but will always help and defend you even unto death against anyone who would do you wrong. Oh, my sweetest brothers, what Devil could impede these two members who are bound together to avoid offending God, supported by the bond of Charity and held tight within His Body? Not a single one.

* ( A ) The Supreme Magistracy of the City and Republic of Lucca, both in the time of Saint Catherine and in those times that followed until our own present day, is composed of ten persons. * ( C ) *I see indeed the members who prosper and move forward.* The Florentine armies, with a prosperous course of good fortune, had defended the cities of Bologna and Perugia from the Pope's troops and had achieved various other victories in every encounter.

*At the beginning of the year 1375, a league was formed for common defense against the ambition of the Pope's Legates* <note>The Pope's Legates were often French administrators whose heavy-handed rule in Italy triggered widespread resentment.</note> *between Queen Joanna of Naples, Bernabò Visconti, Lord of Milan, and the peoples of Florence, Siena, Lucca, Pisa, and Arezzo, according to what is mentioned by Malevolti* <note>Orlando Malavolti, a 16th-century historian of Siena.</note>, *although there is no absolute certainty regarding this, and he himself speaks of it with incomplete assurance. Indeed, this seems contrary to what is reported by the majority of authors: namely, that the Florentines were still in league with the Church, and if not in open discord, certainly not in good understanding with the Lord of Milan, whom they did not approach until after the peace with the Pope was broken. Whatever the case may be, it is beyond doubt that those of Florence were striving with all their power to draw the other peoples of Tuscany into a new confederation to the detriment of the Church. The Lucchesi at first kept their distance from this League, not listening to the requests of that Republic, but later they showed an inclination to follow its desires, as is hinted at by the Saint.*

[ F ] 
-> And therefore I came here on behalf of Christ Crucified, to say to you etc. <-

*The Saint traveled to Lucca for the purpose of keeping that Republic firm in the party of the Church in the year 1375, and she informed Pope Gregory XI of this journey, as appears from her first letter; upon arrival there, she wrote the present Epistle to those who were in the Signoria* <term>Signoria: the governing council of the city-state</term> *in those days. She stayed in Lucca for several days and, as tradition holds, resided in the house of the Balbani lords, forging holy friendships with many people of singular virtue, to whom she later wrote several letters. During her stay, various unique miracles occurred, such as remaining dry during a pouring rain while walking on business for the spiritual benefit of souls; and discovering through celestial light that a host brought to her by an ill-advised priest had not been consecrated at all, as he had pretended; and other wonders reported by the Blessed Thomas Caffarini in the "Supplement," which he left to the "Legend" written by the Blessed Raymond.* <note>Blessed Raymond of Capua was Catherine’s confessor and primary biographer; Caffarini later expanded on his work.</note> *In the "Process"* <note>The "Process of Venice," a legal inquiry into Catherine's sanctity held several decades after her death.</note> *he speaks thus of the Saint’s stay in Lucca:*

During the time that the Virgin <note>original: "Virgo"; a title for Catherine as a consecrated virgin.</note> was in the City of Lucca, she performed many deeds there; and there still remain very many persons of both sexes of that city who have reported things as numerous as they are miraculous and commendable concerning her.

[ G ] *These are the Pisans, your neighbors. Pisa is ten miles from Lucca. The Saint also went there in the same year.*

<meta>This page contains historical and biographical commentary regarding Pietro, Marquess of Monte Santa Maria, the recipient of Saint Catherine of Siena's letter. The text clarifies his lineage and his role as the Senator of Siena, correcting errors found in previous historical accounts by authors like Sansovino.</meta>

<page-num>152</page-num>

<margin>Manuscript Chronicle of Angelo di Tura di Graffo</margin>
( **A** ) Pietro, Marquess of the Mount at Saint Mary <note>original: "Pietro Marchese del Monte a' Santa Maria"</note> was the Senator of Siena from February of the year 1375 until August 18, 1376. A certain Pietro, Marquess del Monte—who is likely this very same man of whom we speak—along with his other kinsmen <note>term: Consorti — members of the same noble house sharing hereditary rights and titles</note>, obtained very extensive privileges and various exemptions from Emperor Charles IV in the City of Pisa in the year 1355. By order of the same Emperor, both he and others of his illustrious family took the surname "of the Mount" <note>del Monte</note>, having previously been called "of Bourbon" <note>di Borbone</note>.

<margin>Sansovino, *Illustrious Families of Italy*</margin>
If such a surname was brought by them from France when they came to Italy—which, according to what is said, occurred in the ninth century—they certainly did not receive it from the Royal House of those monarchs. This is because the surname of Bourbon did not pass to that Great House before the thirteenth century, when Robert of France (the sixth of the sons of King Saint Louis) married Beatrice of Burgundy, who was the Lady of Bourbon because of her mother, Agnes. It is from them that all the royals of France descend. Therefore, if the surname of Bourbon came to Italy with the first lords of this House, it could not have been from the royal line. [In this, Sansovino makes a very great blunder, as he claims this family is descended from the Royal House of France and the Dukes of Bourbon and came to Italy in the ninth century. At that time, not only was the branch called "Bourbon" not yet royal, but not even the Capetian stock <note>term: Capeti — the dynasty of French kings founded by Hugh Capet</note> from which it derives was yet crowned, as the descendants of Charlemagne were still flourishing on the French throne]. Instead, they were either of those more ancient people called the Archimbolds <note>Arcimbaldi</note>, who were also well-known in history, or of others from a more aged memory, of whom the records are very poor. From very ancient times, the lords of this House, which is among the most illustrious in Italy, have held the Marquessate of the Mount called "at Saint Mary" <note>Monte Santa Maria Tiberina</note>, located in the province of Umbria in the vicinity of Città di Castello <note>City of the Castle</note>, but not in the province of the Marches, as was read in old printings. It is a small but sovereign state, with various other noble fiefs. It is found in the Chronicle of Angelo di Tura di Graffo <note>A 14th-century Sienese chronicler</note> that in 1379, this lord having begun to harass the Lord of Cortona (of the Casale family) with weapons, the Sienese sent Pietro Tolomei and Niccolò Meucci to inform him that he should cease from further troubling that lord, who was under the protection of the Republic of Siena.

<meta>This page continues the historical discussion of Sienese governance, specifically detailing the evolution of the office of the Senator, which was held by Pietro, Marquess of Monte Santa Maria, as mentioned on the previous page. It traces the transition of power from the nobility to the people through various administrative titles.</meta>

<page-num>153</page-num>

<margin>Malavolti, part 2, book 6, page 115.</margin>
...had already been practiced for a very long time in this City. That official, who was later called the *Senator*, was first called the ***Captain of War***, because the primary responsibility entrusted to him was the command of the military for the defense of the Republic. Later, around the year 1355, the title of *Captain of War* was changed to that of *Conservator* <note>term: Conservatore — an official tasked with "conserving" or protecting the state and its constitution</note>, and his primary duty concerned criminal cases, specifically those that pertained in any way to the preservation of the Government. However, they still maintained the management of the military; for this reason, they always elected persons of high standing and extreme skill in the art of warfare.

<margin>Malavolti, at those years</margin>
Thus, we find in the office of the *Conservator* of Siena in 1360, *Niccolò, son of Lord Roberto, Marquess Pallavicino of Parma*, and in 1362, *Francesco di Giordano Orsini*, and not a few others of great quality.

<margin>Malavolti, part 2, book 8, page 136.</margin>
The *Senator* succeeded the *Conservator* around the year 1368, at the time when the Government of Siena had fallen from the hands of the Nobility into those of the People, from which the *Order called the Reformers* <note>term: Ordine de' Riformatori — a political faction of middle-class citizens who ruled Siena in the late 14th century</note> was formed. In addition to the *Senator*, there was the *Podestà* <note>term: Podestà — a high-ranking magistrate, usually a foreigner invited to rule for a fixed term to ensure impartiality in local disputes</note> for Civil Cases, who no longer held that place of honor that he once had when this office was first established. Previously, in Siena as in other free Cities, the *Podestà* dealt not only with Civil and Criminal cases, but also with affairs of War, acting as the Commander of the Armies; therefore, he was always a great Master of both the Laws and of Arms.

<margin>Malavolti, part 1, book 4, page 40.</margin>
Siena obtained the faculty to elect its own *Podestà* in 1186 from the Emperor *Frederick I* <note>Frederick Barbarossa</note>, though the first election for it did not occur before the year 1199. The *Podestà* also had to be a foreigner, just like the *Senator*, although on occasion, from time to time, Sienese citizens were still elected. But as the management of War had already passed to the *Senator*, as was mentioned, the dignity of the *Podestà* fell significantly in prestige, as nothing more was required of him from then on but to be skilled in the Law; thus, the office eventually disappeared entirely from the City of Siena. Because by a new Decree in 1374 made by this Republic, it was ordered that the *Podestà* should be removed, and that in the future, the *Senator* should exercise both offices, as Pope *Pius III* has left us a record of in his memoirs.

<margin>Pius III, Annals, book 10, Seneca, page 6.</margin>
> In the month of August it was decreed that the Senator must perform the duties of the Praetor <note>original: "Senatorem Prætoris Officium gerere oportere" — here 'Praetor' refers to the office of the Podestà</note>, and that Praetors should no longer be appointed <note>original: "neque ultrà Prætores creandos"</note>.

The *Senator* therefore remained in possession of all that authority which the *Podestà* had already held in his original institution, and which previously...

# To Pietro, Marquess del Monte, Podestà of Siena,

I. **T**he soul must fight manfully against sins, but especially against those of Incontinence <term>Incontinence: In Catherine’s vocabulary, this refers to lust and the lack of self-restraint over physical desires.</term>.
II. She exhorts him to judge justly, yet without forgetting Mercy.
III. She recounts an abominable case to him, so that he might remedy it by punishing the guilty party as he deems most appropriate, provided that he spares his life.

## Letter 208.

->*In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary.*<-

I. **T**o you, Dearest Father in Christ sweet Jesus, I Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, commend myself to you in the precious Blood of the Son of God, with the desire to see you as a true servant and Knight of Christ <note>original: "Cavaliere di Cristo"; likely an allusion to the *miles Christi* or soldier of Christ, a common medieval metaphor for spiritual struggle</note>, always fighting manfully against vices and sins—not with negligence, but with true and holy diligence. Thus, when that sweet moment of death arrives, we may return with Victory to the true City of Jerusalem, the vision of peace <note>original: "Gerusalem visione di pace"; a traditional medieval etymology for the name Jerusalem</note>, where we shall not find the Flesh which wishes to rebel against the Spirit. But take heed, Father: if we desire lasting life, we have need to leave the Flesh behind before death arrives and the Flesh abandons us; that is, we must leave behind the appetites, the desires, and the carnal feelings. Alas, do not wait to be invited to leave them, for there is no time; and there is nothing that makes a Man more beastly than this perverse vice. It is a great folly for a Creature to strip themselves of such dignity and, for such a wretched thing, become a brute animal.
II. Therefore, let us uproot and fight against this vice, and against every other, with the fragrance of holy Continence and Honesty <note>original: "Onestà"; in this context, it implies moral purity or chastity</note>, using the shield of the most holy Cross to ward off the blows.

*(A) Podestà of Siena <term>Podestà: The high-ranking official, often from another city, who served as the chief magistrate and administrator of a medieval Italian commune.</term>. He is called Podestà even though he was a Senator, for the reason provided in the Annotations to the previous Letter.*

*(B) The Monastery of Saint Michael the Archangel of Vico. The Monastery of Saint Michael the Archangel of Vico was about a mile from Siena, and is called "of Vico" because it was located in the municipality of that name. It belonged to the holy Virgins of the Order of Saint Benedict and was suppressed in the year 1480, when Cardinal Francesco Piccolomini—who was later Pope Pius III—was Archbishop of Siena. Because the Abbess and all the nuns had passed away, he used the revenues of that monastery to found two canonries <term>Canonries: Benefices or positions within a cathedral or collegiate church, providing an income to the priest (canon) holding them.</term> in the Metropolitan Church, to be granted by certain Lords of the House of Piccolomini; and this foundation was approved and confirmed in every part by Pope Sixtus IV. The place where the Monastery stood, being on an elevated site, is called today Vico Alto.*

*[C] I would not, however, want him to lose his life. Since the crime was enormous, the Saint truly feared that the guilty man might lose his life for it, having a very fresh example in three other young men, who had dared to commit an assault upon the modesty of the nuns of the Monastery of Saint Emilian <note>original: "Sant' Emiliano"</note>.*

# To Pietro Marchese del Monte,

I. **S**he recommends Justice to him, which we must all maintain against ourselves, for without it we cannot exercise it against others.

## Letter 209.

### In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary.

I **T**o you, Lord Senator, I Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, write to you, greeting you in the Precious Blood of the Son of God, with the desire to see you a true Ruler of Justice, first within yourself and then in others, so that you may appear before the most just Judge with a confident face; for he who does not maintain justice over himself cannot, with a good face, exercise it over others; because a work is only as just as it proceeds from Justice and a pure will. O most sweet brother in Christ Jesus, take your example from the precious Lamb, who performed justice for the sins of others upon Himself; how much more, then, must we take vengeance for our own sins upon ourselves. Now, therefore, ascend to the throne of Reason, and see to it that Memory accuses your evil deeds, and your evil words, and your evil thoughts, and that the Will grieves for the injury done to its Creator and demands justice, and then let the Intellect judge the penalty that the heart and body must endure, and give it with great impetus and great fervor. Then the just Judge will be appeased, and not only will He forgive the offense, but He will cause the one who has justly judged himself to become a just judge of others; and in this way, we become true Rulers. <note>Catherine uses the faculties of the soul—Memory, Will, and Intellect—as a "courtroom" where one must judge oneself before judging the citizens of the state.</note>

[ B ] *Otherwise you might be forced to put your hand to the bar, and you would pay before you could remove it. This manner of speaking used by the Saint was common in those times, and shows it was the custom that the debtor of some sum was forced to place his hand upon a bar, unable to remove it except by payment; if the payment was delayed, the hand was to be cut off. In the handwritten Chronicle of Angelo di Tura di Grasso, who lived during this age, this custom is noted. He reports how the Senator Francesco of Padua (who was the successor in office to the Marquis Pietro) made a certain Antonio di Pietro Chinazzoni from Montalcino, guilty of some crime, come to Siena; and once he had him in Siena, he made him put his hand on the bar, and said, "before twenty-four hours have rung, have eighteen hundred florins paid"; whereby he was forced within the term...*

...assigned to him to pay that sum: If I am not mistaken, such a custom originates from an ancient Law of this City which, having fallen into disuse, was returned to practice on February 22, the Year 1446. By this law, anyone condemned to pay a sum of one thousand lire who did not pay within a month's time would, three days later, have a foot or another limb cut off. This was to be carried out upon a <term>Bar</term> <note>original: *Stanga*</note> designated for such use: thus, making one "put their hand to the Bar" was like a final notice, either to pay the due sum immediately or to have the hand soon cut off, according to the Law.

[ C ] **My companions, who used to write for me.** The Saint usually made use of the work of her female companions for writing when the Letters were more informal, and to more close friends and people of less social standing, whereas for others she used the hand of her Disciples and Secretaries, who were Pagliaresi, Cangiani, and Maconi, as was noted on another occasion. At this time, she had not yet learned to write, as was stated in the annotations to Letter 90, having acquired the gift in a miraculous manner while she was at the Fortress of the Salimbeni <note>original: *Rocca de' Salimbeni*</note> in the Year 1377, so far as I am led to believe, as was observed there.

[ D ] **If Neri wants to come here.** That is, Ranieri di Landoccio de’ Pagliaresi, one of her disciples. Since Siena was perhaps in some suspicion of the Pisans because of the hostilities committed in Sienese territory by the Prior of Pesa, it was not permitted for a Nobleman—such as Pagliaresi was—to go to Pisa at his own whim without casting a shadow of suspicion upon himself; therefore, it was necessary for him to have permission from the Senator.

( E ) **Written in Pisa on the second day of September.** That is, of the Year 1375, a good part of which she spent in that City; since she was there in April and received the sacred Stigmata, and in September, as seen here, showing further that she was not to depart from there so soon.

# To Pietro, Marquis del Monte.

I. **O**f the strong armor with which God has armed us to resist the temptations of our enemies—namely, His help and our free will.
II. **Encouraging the soul not to fear**, by demonstrating the victory achieved by the Son of God over all our enemies through His death.
III. **That we must conceive a hatred for our own selves** to avenge the death of the Redeemer caused by our sins; we shall achieve this by remembering the great benefit of the Redemption.
IV. **She thanks him for the alms given** to a certain Friar James <note>original: "Frate Jacopo"</note>.

## Letter 210.

->In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary.<-

**T**o you, Most Reverend and Dearest Father and Son in Christ Jesus: I, Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, write to you with the desire to see you as a manly knight, and not a fearful one. For a man should not fear when he sees he possesses strong armor. O most dear son, we see that God has armed Man with armor of such strength that neither the Devil nor any created thing can harm him. This is the free Will of Man; and because of
<margin>A</margin>
this freedom, God says: "I created you without you, but I will not save you without you" <note>This famous theological maxim is traditionally attributed to Saint Augustine, emphasizing that while life is a gift, salvation requires human cooperation.</note>. God wills, therefore, that we use the armor given to us, and that we use it to resist the blows we receive from our enemies. We have three singular Enemies: the World, the Flesh, and the Devil. But let us not fear, because Divine Providence has armed us so well that we have no need for fear. The armor is good, and the Helper is the best—that is, God. He is such that there is no one who can resist Him. Thus, as long as the Soul looks upon such a sweet and strong Helper, it cannot fall into weakness regardless of any fragility it might feel.

## II.

Let us therefore follow in His footsteps, driving out vice with virtue: pride with humility, impatience with patience, injustice with justice, impurity with perfect purity and continence, and vainglory with the glory and honor of God. ### III.
We see that sin alone is the cause of Christ's death, and Man is the one who commits sin. Therefore, it can be said that we are the ones who have killed the Son of God; and every hour that we sin mortally, we can say it. We must, therefore, take vengeance upon ourselves—that is, upon our perverse thoughts, vices, and sins—for the greatest enemy a man has is himself. When the Soul looks at its Father and at its own <term>sensuality</term> <note>Catherine uses "sensuality" to refer to the lower, selfish impulses of human nature that rebel against the spirit.</note> which killed Him, it cannot be satisfied until it has taken vengeance in such a way that it is content to see that sensuality suffer every pain and torment, as its mortal enemy.

It would be too great an ignorance if we were negligent in feeding ourselves upon this sweet Food.

# To Master Andreasso Cavalcabuoi, then Senator of Siena, <note>Andreasso Cavalcabuoi was a Florentine nobleman who served as the Senator of Siena, the city's highest judicial and administrative officer, around 1378.</note>

I. **O**f the virtue of Justice, and the way to acquire it, and of self-love, which holds us back from such an acquisition.

II. To this virtue she exhorts the aforementioned Master Andreasso, and furthermore she urges him to come to Rome, sparing no effort, to be released by Pope Urban VI from the censures <note>Ecclesiastical censures were spiritual penalties, such as excommunication or interdict, which could have severe political and social consequences for a ruler.</note> with which he was bound, stating that such is the sentiment of the Pope himself.

## Letter 211..

### In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary.

**D**earest Brother in sweet Jesus Christ. I, Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious Blood with the desire to see you a just Lord; that is, that in your office of the Signoria <note>The *Signoria* refers to the governing council of the Republic of Siena.</note> where you are, you may be just and an upholder of holy Justice, always acting with reason. Do not be unjust by committing injustice, wishing to please men rather than God; for I do not see how a man can ever possess this virtue of holy Justice if he does not first justly strip himself of self-love and every human pleasure. Indeed, all vices proceed from these: we only offend God when we seek to fulfill our disordered desires, longing through self-love for those things that are outside the will of God with a disordered pleasure that a man has in himself. And because this pleases himself, he therefore strives to please the men of the world and does not care to please God. In such a man there can be no Justice, because he is not just; he is, as has been said, even cruel, for unjustly—either through greed and the desire for money, or through the entreaties of men—he will become a devourer of the flesh of his neighbor. Hence we often see that such people maintain Justice...

# To Master Andrea di Vanni, Painter, while he was Captain of the People of Siena. <note>Andrea di Vanni (c. 1332–1414) was a celebrated Sienese artist and a devoted follower of Saint Catherine. In 1373, he held the high political office of "Captain of the People."</note>

I. It teaches how we cannot govern others, if we do not first know how to govern ourselves with justice.
II. That to exercise this justice upon ourselves, we must first put in order all three Powers of the Soul, and the method of correcting them. <term>Powers of the Soul: According to medieval theology, these are Memory, Intellect, and Will.</term>
III. Concerning self-knowledge: of Confession and Communion, from which we must not fear to draw near; these things are necessary to order our Powers, as has been said.
IV. That Justice must not be contaminated by the desire for riches, or by servile fear, and other similar vices.

## Letter 212.

->*In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary.*<-

I. **D**earest Son in Christ sweet Jesus: I, Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious Blood with the desire to see you as a just and good Ruler, so that the honor of God may be fulfilled in you, along with your own desire. I know that God, in His mercy, has given you good desires, but I do not see how we can rightly govern others if we do not first govern ourselves. When the Soul governs itself, it governs others in that same manner; because it loves its Neighbor with the same love with which it loves itself. Just as the perfect Charity of God generates perfect Charity for the Neighbor, so too, with that same perfection by which a Man governs himself, he governs his Subjects. In what way does he who fears God govern himself? And with what justice? His method is this:
II. That with the light of Reason he orders the three Powers of the Soul, and with that order, he regulates his entire life spiritually.

<meta>This page continues Letter 212 to the painter Andrea di Vanni. It moves from the theoretical definition of the Three Powers of the Soul (Memory, Intellect, Will) introduced on the previous page to the practical administration of internal justice through what Catherine calls the "seat of Conscience."</meta>

...mind and body in every place, state, and time, as is just. It orders the **Memory** to retain the benefits of God and the offenses that the person has committed against the **Supreme Good**. It orders the **Intellect** to see the love with which God has granted His graces and to know the Doctrine of His **Truth**; likewise, it orders the **Will** to love the infinite goodness of God, which it has seen and known through the light of the Intellect. And because it has recognized that God must be loved by His creatures with all our heart, all our affection, and all our strength, the soul then ascends to the seat of **Conscience** to administer justice <note>original: "per tenervi ragione", a legal metaphor for holding court or rendering an account</note>, whenever it sees that sensuality seeks to ruin this sweet and glorious order. And if, through the illusions of the **Devil** or through one’s own fragility, the perfection given by this holy order is ruined or hindered, the soul carries out **Justice**: like an enlightened person who gives to each their due. 

Wherefore, if sensuality strikes a mortal blow, it receives death in return, cutting off the head of one's own perverse will with the knife of the hatred of **Vice** and the love of **Virtue**. Then **Justice**, according to the gravity of the fault, disciplines the disordered affection of the **Soul**, making it pay the penalty <note>original: "condennagione", referring to a judicial sentence or fine</note> imposed by **Divine Justice**. What penalty is this, and in what way is it given? I will tell you: To the sensitive appetite <note>The "sensitive appetite" refers to our physical desires and animal nature, often contrasted with the "rational" part of the soul.</note> which seeks status, honors, and the riches of the world, just reason wills that it desire and embrace shame, despise high rank, and seek lowliness; it wills that it voluntarily abandon wealth and marry poverty, trusting in God and not in itself nor in the states of the world, which possess no firmness or stability at all.

And if this perverse appetite seeks the stench of impurity, **Justice** binds it and constrains it to seek and take delight in purity. If it desires pride, it gives it humility; for faithlessness, it gives faith; for avarice, the abundance of **Charity**; for hatred and resentment toward one's Neighbor, benevolence; to the imprudent, prudence. And thus all the **Virtues** are those edicts and condemnations that the Judge, seated upon the throne of **Conscience**, decrees should be applied to the soul's affection to punish the sensitive appetite and destroy the inclination toward **Vice**, decapitating one's own will, as has been said. Now, in this way, the soul is held to account, rendering to it the debt of **Virtue**, and it is placed in authority as a Mistress, while sensuality is held—

### III.
The place where one should dwell is the house of self-knowledge and of the goodness of God within oneself, measuring others with that same measure by which one wishes to be measured. One should frequently wash the face of the **Soul** from every stain of sin in the **Blood of Christ** by means of pure and holy **Confession**, nourishing it with the **Food of Angels** <note>original: "Cibo degli Angioli", a traditional term for the Eucharist</note>, which is the sweet **Sacrament** of the **Body** and **Blood** of **Jesus Christ**, who is fully God and fully Man. Every faithful Christian is required to take this <margin>C</margin> at least once a year; whoever wants it more, let them take it more, but not less. No one should skip it for any reason, neither the righteous person nor the sinner; for if the sinner is not prepared, they <margin>D</margin> ought to prepare themselves; if one is righteous, they should not skip it out of humility, saying: *I am not worthy of so great a mystery; when I feel more worthy, I will receive communion.* One should not do this, but should instead think that through one's own righteousness one would never be worthy; and if one *did* make oneself worthy, then one would actually be unworthy, for one would be cloaking **Pride** with the mantle of **Humility**. But God is worthy of making us worthy, and therefore we must receive Him in His own dignity. 

We must receive Him <margin>E</margin> in two ways: actually <note>physically receiving the consecrated host</note> and mentally—that is, with a holy, true, and burning desire. This desire should not only exist at the moment of **Communion**, but at all times and in all places, as a food that is taken to give the life of **Grace** to the **Soul**. All of this, which holy **Justice** dictates, proceeds from the order that [Justice] established and observed with right **Reason** within the **Three Powers** <term>The Memory, Intellect, and Will, which Catherine believes must be ordered toward God</term> of one's soul. 

Once a person has this order within themselves, they administer it to their **Neighbor** through prayer, through the word, and through a good and holy life. And if he is a man who must govern—just as he is an observer of the **Law** within himself—so he desires it to be observed by his **Subjects**. In order that it be observed with the zeal of **Justice**, he punishes those who transgress. Just as he has punished his own sensuality, which rebelled against the **Divine Law**, so—when he must govern the bodies of his **Subjects**—he desires to punish them when they do not observe the **Civil Law** and other good statutes and ordinances made by those who have had to rule and govern. And according to what the order of **Justice** requires, he gives little or much, according to what **Reason** demands.

### IV.
This **Justice** must not be contaminated; it should not be diminished by fear of punishment or bodily death, nor by threats or flattery, nor for the pleasure of Creatures <note>This refers to people or created things as opposed to the Creator</note>, or for temporal wealth. One must not sell out the honor or the lives of men for money, as do those who live unjustly without any order or light of **Reason**. Rather, the just man abandons it for no reason; instead, according to his power, he observes it, seeking in everything he must do the honor of **God**, the salvation of his **Soul**, and the universal good of every person, advising honestly and showing the truth as much as possible. 

One must do this if they wish to maintain themselves and the **City** in peace, and to preserve **Holy Justice**; for it is only because of Justice—which has been lacking—that so many evils have come and continue to come. And therefore, with a desire to see it in you and to maintain it in our **City**, to rule it and govern it with order, I said that I desired to see you as a just and true governor. If this **Justice** does not first begin with oneself, as has been said, it can never be observed toward one's **Neighbor** in whatever state one might be. 

Therefore, I invite you and I wish for you to always order yourself with all diligence, as has been said, so that you may completely fulfill that purpose for which **Divine Goodness** has now placed you. Always place **God** before your eyes in all things you have to do with true **Humility**, so that **God** may be glorified in you. Remain in the holy and sweet love of **God**. Sweet **Jesus**. **Jesus Love**.

## Letter 213.

### In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary.

**D**earest son in Christ sweet Jesus. I, Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious blood with the desire to see you constant and persevering in virtue; not like a leaf that turns with the wind, but like a tree you must be planted in the depths of the earth of true humility, so that the wind of pride cannot harm the tree of your soul. All these winds harm the tree, making the fruit fall and the branches break; and if the tree does not fortify itself by applying remedies, it is cast to the ground. ### II. What remedy is there then, so that this Tree may be transplanted into the valley and into the soil of Humility? I tell it to you.

With a true knowledge of ourselves, and with a hatred and displeasure for our own sensuality; for in no other way could we be humble. But then the soul will find itself between two strong mountains—that is, between the Virtue of fortitude and of true patience—which receive the blows of whatever contrary wind there may be. Indeed, the more contrary it is, the more the Soul is fortified and the more it is proven to be strong, as the Virtue of patience is tested. Then the Virtues are preserved, and these fruits ripen, giving doctrine with the word and edification to the Neighbor, with fragrant flowers of holy thoughts of right judgment. 

The Soul takes this up by judging the Will of God in itself and in its Neighbor—who wills nothing other than our good and not that of Men <note>Catherine suggests that God focuses on our eternal spiritual good, which often contradicts worldly success or human opinion.</note>—mortifying its every opinion and killing its own Will, and maintaining and nourishing the Tree of Charity for its Neighbor with an anxious desire for the salvation of Souls, delighting in this Food for the honor of God. 

Oh, how glorious is the Tree of our Soul when it is planted so sweetly, for it conforms to the humility of the immaculate Lamb, from whom we have received life and a Sun of Grace and mercy. This mercy could not be had through all our own Just deeds; <margin>B</margin> but since God humbled Himself for Man, giving us this sweet and loving Word <term>Word: Referring to the "Verbo" or Logos, the Second Person of the Trinity, Jesus Christ, who expresses God's will to humanity.</term>, and the Word of the Son of God with true patience humbled Himself to the shameful death of the Cross, our Just deeds and every Virtue have value through His humility and through the...

<meta>This page continues Letter 214 to Master Andrea di Vanni. The text begins mid-sentence, concluding the first point regarding the inheritance of eternal life and the necessity of stripping away self-love.</meta>

...[all] your life you may have the inheritance of Eternal Life. But I want you to know that the Law of God cannot be observed as long as a person lies in self-love; for he who loves himself with a disordered love cannot love or serve his neighbor purely, as he ought. The commandments of the Law consist solely in the Charity of God and of one's neighbor—that is, to love God above all things, and one's neighbor as oneself. Therefore, he who loves himself disordered-ly cannot observe them until he strips himself of the <term>Old Man</term><note>A biblical reference (Romans 6:6) to the unregenerate, sinful nature of humanity before spiritual renewal.</note>, which is to say, his own sensuality, and clothes himself in the new Christ, sweet Jesus, following His doctrine. Thus, it is necessary for us, dearest son, to come to a holy hatred of ourselves, so that we may truly love and fear God. And if you should say to me: "What method can I hold to have this hatred, so that I may have this love, and where do I find it?"

II. I answer you: the method is this: that you open the eye of your Intellect with the light of the Most Holy Faith; for without that light you could not see the place. The place where it is found is the <term>House of self-knowledge</term><note>A central metaphor in Catherine’s spirituality, referring to the internal space of reflection where the soul recognizes its own nothingness and its total dependence on God.</note>; and in no other place can we know ourselves. And by not knowing the good thing from the bad, one cannot hate or love; but with the eye of the Intellect, with the light of Faith, look into this House of self-knowledge. There, the soul sees that it is nothing, and recognizes that its very being is received from God. From this, when the soul sees and knows such great abundance and fire of Charity—that is, having been created in the image and likeness of God, and recreated in the Blood of His Son—and further sees that it is that very stone and earth which holds upright the <term>Banner of the Most Holy Cross</term><note>An image of the soul as the foundation or "socket" that allows the Cross to stand; Catherine often argues that it was not nails, but love, that held Christ to the Cross.</note>. It sees that the Cross was not sufficient, nor the earth, to hold Him upright, nor the nails to keep Him fastened and bolted to the Cross, if Love had not held Him there. Then the Soul grows in Love with anxieties and sweet desires, observing His commandments—that is, to love Him above all things and the neighbor as oneself. And seeing that it can be of no utility to God, it provides utility to its neighbor, loving and serving him in whatever way it can. In this way, the soul demonstrates the perfect love that it has for its Creator, because by no other means can it show the love and virtue that is within the soul, except through the neighbor.

<summary>Catherine explains that the Law of God is fulfilled through Charity, which requires "stripping off the old man" of self-love. She directs Andrea to the "House of Self-Knowledge," where the soul realizes its existence depends entirely on God's love.</summary>
<keywords>self-love, Charity, Old Man, House of Self-Knowledge, Intellect, Light of Faith, Passion of Christ, service to neighbor</keywords>

...because every Virtue is tested by this means.

III. And since the Soul has found love through the knowledge it has had of God, it finds the nurse of <term>Humility</term><note>In Catherine’s teaching, humility is the "nurse" because it protects and feeds Charity (Love), preventing it from being killed by the "wind" of pride.</note>, who is the nurse and nourisher of Charity. Where did it find her? In the House of self-knowledge, there where it found Charity, as was said; because he who knows himself has no reason to become proud; for that which is nothing cannot come to pride. It is necessary then, that he who is not proud be humble; and therefore, since he has known himself and the Goodness of God in himself, he loves and is humble. From humility he recognizes his defects, and sees himself always attacked by the <term>perverse law</term><note>A reference to St. Paul's description of the conflict between the spirit and the flesh (Romans 7:23).</note> of his body against the great Goodness of God, which he has known in himself.

IV. And therefore the Soul rises up with hatred and displeasure for its own <term>sensuality</term><note>In this context, "sensuality" refers to the lower, physical impulses and self-centered desires that distract from spiritual growth.</note>, and because of the hatred it has, it wants to take vengeance. And with what does it take it? By giving it the opposite of what the sensitive love wants. Sensuality wants to take delight in Vice, and Reason gives it the opposite, because it delights in Virtue. It delights in honor, and status, and disordered pleasures, and in doing injustice to the Neighbor; but the Soul, which with the light of Reason has known God, takes vengeance on it by despising the World with all its delights—either actually, meaning that it departs entirely from the World <note>By entering a monastery or religious life.</note>, or while remaining in it actually, it rises above it with holy desire. 

And this every creature who possesses reason must do, and do justice; because it justly renders to God the glory and the honor, and to itself renders hatred and displeasure for its own sensuality, and love for Virtue. To the Neighbor, it renders the affection of Charity and labor, toiling for their salvation. For this reason the Soul offers prayers, and the Body assists with temporal substance if the neighbor has none, or with whatever other thing it can provide. And if he is in a state of <term>Authority</term><note>The original Italian "Signoria" refers to holding political office or being a ruler.</note>, he does justice and right to the great and the small, to the poor as to the rich; he does not fear to displease any creature, but only fears God. For he lost <term>servile fear</term><note>Fearing God only out of fear of punishment, like a slave (servus) fears a master, rather than out of love.</note> in Divine Love and in the holy hatred of himself; and this is the principal vengeance that the soul takes on its own sensuality. Another vengeance it takes is that it punishes its body when it attacks the Spirit, and yet it does not call itself content with this, but whatever it does...

it seems to do little, and he desires that others do it for him when he thinks of the offenses he has committed against his <term>Creator</term>. Therefore, he is not scandalized by injuries, nor by any other <term>tribulation</term><note>A term used by Catherine to describe any form of suffering, trial, or hardship intended to test the soul's virtue.</note> or pain that he might sustain, whether from <term>Creatures</term><note>Catherine uses "creatures" to mean all created beings, including other people, who might cause us grief or suffering.</note> or from God—that is, if God should give him some discipline, or if He should withdraw from his mind the consolation of the soul and allow the <term>Devil</term> to bring him many temptations and battles. And thus he draws out patience, which is the <term>marrow</term><note>Catherine often uses this metaphor: just as marrow is protected inside the bone, patience is the inner strength that proves the existence of Charity (Divine Love) within the soul.</note> of **Charity**; and in this way, he has fulfilled the whole Law—that is, to love God above all things and his Neighbor as himself.

With what, then, did he see and know this? With the eye of the **Intellect** and with the light of the **Most Holy Faith**. Where did he find it? In the knowledge of himself; in which knowledge he found the Goodness of God, and therefore he loved Him; and he found his own misery, and therefore he humbled himself and conceived hatred for Vice and for his own <term>sensuality</term><note>In Catherine’s writings, "sensuality" refers to the lower, self-centered nature that rebels against the spirit.</note>. Without this knowledge, therefore, he could not observe the Law; and by not observing it, a person is deprived of **Grace** and of the Kingdom of God. This Kingdom is the inheritance that the Supreme Father gives to His legitimate children who manfully fight on the battlefield against their enemies, without turning their heads back.

And therefore I told you that I desired to see you as an observer of the holy and sweet Commandments of God, so that you might have the life of **Grace** here, and eternal Life in the other world. I pray you, then, for the love of Christ Crucified, that you strive to observe them even unto death. I say no more. Remain in the holy and sweet love of God.

# To Buonaccorso di Lapo in Florence, while the Saint was in Avignon.

## Letter 215.

->*In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary.*<-

<margin>1.</margin> **D**earest Brother in Christ sweet Jesus. I, Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious Blood, with the desire to see you and your other Lords <note>The "Lords" (Signori) refers to the members of the Signoria, the governing body of the Republic of Florence.</note> pacify your heart and your Soul in His sweetest Blood, in which Blood all hatred and war are extinguished, and every pride of Man is brought low; for in the Blood, Man sees God humbled for him, taking on our humanity—which humanity is opened, and pierced, and nailed to the Cross, so that through the wounds <note>original: "forami" - literally "openings" or "holes," referring to the stigmata or wounds of the crucifixion.</note> of the Body of Christ Crucified, the Blood issues and pours out over us, and is administered to us by the Ministers of the <term>Holy Church</term><note>Catherine views the Church not just as an institution, but as the "Spouse of Christ" who holds the "keys" to the Blood (the Sacraments).</note>. I pray you for the Love of Christ Crucified, that you receive the Treasure of the Blood which is given to you by the Spouse of Christ; be reconciled, be reconciled with her in the Blood. Acknowledge your faults and the offenses you have committed against her: for he who acknowledges his fault, and shows by his actions that he knows it and is humbled, always receives mercy; but he who shows it only with words, and goes no further with his deeds, never finds it. I say this not so much for you, as for the others who might fall into this defect.

All this is because there is not yet a true knowledge of our own defects; and I perceive that the humble words proceeded more out of fear and necessity than out of a feeling of love or virtue. For if there had truly been a recognition of the fault committed, the actions would have responded to the sound of the word; and your needs, and that which you wanted from the Holy Father, you would have placed in the hands of the true Servants of God. They would have been the means who would have so directed your mandates and those of the Holy Father that you would have had a good concord. You have not done so, for which thing I have felt great bitterness because of the offense against God and our own loss; but you do not see how much...

Sweet Jesus. Jesus Love.

# To Niccolò Soderini in Florence.

I. **S**he exhorts him to live with the holy fear necessary for the true servants of God.
II. She shows him how it is fitting that he live not only as a true servant of God, but as a son, and how it is therefore necessary to employ time well in the acquisition of virtue and the increase of Grace.
III. ## Letter 216.

->In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified and of gentle Mary.<-

I. **M**ost reverend and beloved brother in Christ Jesus. I, Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, comfort and bless you in His precious Blood, with the desire to see you a true son and servant of Jesus Christ Crucified—you and your entire family—as a servant ransomed by the Son of God. This I wish you to do always: to see that the Blood, which we are obligated to serve, has its eye always upon us; wherefore we must always fear to offend so sweet and dear a Lord. This is that holy fear which enters the soul as a servant and draws out every vice, sin, and action that might be contrary to the will of its Lord.

II. <meta>This page continues Catherine’s instruction to Niccolò Soderini regarding the spiritual "merchandise" of life, continuing the metaphor of the Father as a provider of capital (time and will).</meta>

...gives the treasure of time, and the <term>free choice</term> <note>original: "libero arbitrio"</note> of the Will, so that he may grow rich. Thus you see how it is; because we are foreigners and pilgrims in this life, and with this treasure of time and with free choice, we earn our way. It is true that during this time the creature <note>In Catherine’s writing, "creature" refers to any created human being.</note> can drown the Will and his own free choice, and with it he can drown perverse vanity, pleasure and displeasure, anxieties, and the delights of the world—which is that merchandise that always impoverishes a person, because it has no stability or firmness within itself, and has nothing but an outward show, while inside it is spoiled and left to the stench of many sins; and this show causes a person to agree to a bargain with it.

Therefore, most dear and venerable brother in Christ Jesus, I do not intend, nor do I want, that this treasure given to us by the Father through Divine Grace and Mercy should be spent on such vile merchandise, for we would justly be rejected by the Father. Therefore, as true children, and with perfect diligence, let us spend this sweet treasure on a perfect merchandise, which is the opposite of that other one; for it has a pale, poor, and lowly color; but inside there is a treasure that nourishes and enriches here through Grace, and then leads one into the lasting life of the Father to enjoy his inheritance.

Now let us see, then, what treasure he who has grown rich has bought. The treasure is this: contempt for honor, for delights, for riches, and for every consolation, recreation, or the pleasing of men; and he has desired those true and real virtues which seem small and of little account in the eyes of the world, but inside there is the treasure of Grace. It truly seems a small thing to the world to choose suffering, mockery, insults, and reproaches, and to choose voluntary poverty—which casts down human pride, greatness, and worldly status—which appears so high and yet becomes humble, lowering itself through Virtue. And he does not wish to follow any other footsteps than those of his Master, who entrusted to him the treasure of free choice, with which he can gain or lose according to what he wants and according to the merchandise he buys.

O sweet and holy treasure of the Virtues, you who go safely in every place, on sea and on land, and in the midst of enemies fear nothing, because within you is hidden God, who is Eternal Security. Perfect patience is not taken away by men nor by insult, because it does not <note>The text cuts off here, continuing the thought that patience is not lost through external trials.</note>

...finds in the world those who desire injuries, and patience proves them through injury and labors. Thus, the most burning and loving <term>Charity</term> <note>In Catherine’s theology, Charity is the supreme love of God that displaces self-love.</note>—because self-love always seeks the opposite of itself—but the heart, expanded and humbled by the wealth of Charity, desires joy and gladness and every security. And it does not regard or seek itself for its own sake, but itself for God, and the Neighbor for God. Briefly, its every action is directed toward Him, not for personal profit, but for the honor of the Father, when one returns to His House. Come then, let us sleep no longer in the bed of negligence, for it is time to invest this treasure in a sweet trade; and do you know which? In paying with our life for our God, where all our iniquities find their end.

And he says that if he finds willing hearts, he will give every help and will use his power with diligence. So says the <term>Bull</term> <note>A "Bolla" or Papal Bull is an official decree issued by the Pope.</note> which he has sent to our Provincial, and to the Minister of the <term>Friars Minor</term> <note>The Franciscans.</note>, and to <term>Brother Raymond</term> <note>Raymond of Capua, Catherine’s confessor, disciple, and future biographer.</note>, commanding them to be diligent in investigating good will throughout <term>Tuscany</term> and every other land; he wants it in writing to see their desire and how many they are, to then give orders and put it into effect. Therefore, I invite you to the wedding of eternal life, and ask that you be kindled by the desire to pay blood for blood—and invite as many as you can; for one should not go to the wedding alone, and you cannot afterward turn back. I say no more to you.

<margin>D</margin> IV. I thank you with the affectionate love of Charity that you have shown, as I have understood from the Letter and from the Master; I am not sufficient to reward your affection, but I pray and will continually pray to the supreme Eternal Goodness that He may reward you with Himself. Recommend me [to God] and bless me a hundred thousand times in Christ Jesus. Remain in the holy and sweet love of God. Sweet Jesus. Jesus Love.

# To Niccolò Soderini of Florence
## *While he was one of the Priors <note>The "Priori" were the executive magistrates of the Florentine Republic.</note> of Florence at the time the League <note>The "League" refers to the alliance of Italian cities against the Pope during the War of the Eight Saints (1375–1378).</note> was formed.*

I. She exhorts him to bind himself with his fellow citizens by means of holy Charity.
II. That there can be no good league between Cities or between Men if they are not bound with Jesus Christ by means of Holy Charity. Here she strongly reproves the league made by the Florentines against the Pontiff, and begs them to humbly ask him for Peace.
III. That by offending the Supreme Pontiff, one offends the Blood of Jesus Christ.
IV. Concerning the benefit of Peace.
V. She begs Niccolò to establish it with all haste.

It is He who gives and administers the Sacraments to us, which give us life because of the life they have received from the Blood of Christ; for before that Blood was given to us, neither Virtue nor anything else was sufficient to give us Eternal Life. How, then, are we so bold that we despise this Blood?

# To Niccolò Soderini in Florence,

<margin>I.</margin> **O**n the Virtue of Patience and the Love of Jesus Christ, from which this Virtue is born; and to this she exhorts the aforementioned Niccolò Soderini.

## Letter 218.

### *In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of Mary, Sweetness.*

<margin>1.</margin> **D**earest Father in Christ, sweet Jesus. I, Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious Blood with the desire to see you founded in true and holy patience <term>patientia: In Catherine’s theology, patience is not just waiting, but the active endurance of suffering out of love for God.</term>, because without patience we would not be pleasing to God, nor could we remain in a state of Grace, for patience is the marrow of Charity. Since it is so necessary to us, we have need to find it. But where shall we find it? Do you know where, sweetest and dearest Father? In that same manner and place where we would find love. And where is Love acquired? We find love in the Blood of Christ Crucified, who for love shed it upon the wood of the Most Holy Cross; and from the ineffable Love that we see He has for us, we draw and acquire love; because he who sees himself loved cannot help but love in return. Loving, he immediately clothes himself in the patience of Christ Crucified, resting with this sweet and glorious Virtue in the tempestuous sea of many labors. This is that Virtue which does not forget the Will of God; she is strong, because she is never defeated, but alway— <note>original catchword: "sem-" for "sempre" (always).</note>

<meta>This page continues Letter 218 to Niccolò Soderini. The previous page defined patience as the "marrow of Charity" and directed the reader to find it through the love of God. This page elaborates on the victory of patience and the necessity of detachment from worldly things.</meta>

...always wins, because she has with her fortitude and long perseverance; and therefore she receives the fruit of all her labor. She is a **Queen** <note>Catherine frequently personifies virtues as royalty to emphasize their power over the chaotic emotions of the human soul.</note> who rules over impatience; she does not let herself be conquered by anger, nor does she regret the good she has done—even if she often receives toil and tribulations for it. Instead, she rejoices, and it nourishes the Soul to see herself enduring without fault. We should only feel distress for our faults (sins), and for nothing else, because through fault we lose that which is truly ours. And what is lost? **Grace**, which is the **Blood of Christ** <note>In Catherine’s theology, the "Blood of Christ" and "Grace" are often used interchangeably to represent the life-giving gift of salvation.</note>, which is ours, and which cannot be taken from us by any Devil or any Creature unless we ourselves wish it. But these other things—wealth, honor, status, delights, health, and life, and every other thing—because they are not ours, but have been given to us for our use as long as it pleases the **Divine Goodness**, they can be taken from us. And therefore we must not be troubled, nor fall into impatience, but return them without pain, for it is necessary to return and to leave behind that which is not our own. Thus we see that there is no one who can hold onto these things as he pleases; rather, it is necessary to leave them, for either they leave us, or we leave them by means of death.

<margin>II.</margin> Since it is so, he is truly a madman and a fool who places disordered and miserable affection upon them; but it is fitting, like a courageous man, to strip our heart and our affection of every transitory thing and of our own self-love, and to embrace ourselves with the **Most Holy Cross**. There we shall find ineffable love, tasting the **Blood of Christ**, and there we shall find the patience of the humble and immaculate **Lamb**. We shall see that with that sweet Love with which He gave His life for us, He gives, and has permitted, and permits all our labor, tribulation, and consolation. It seems to me that the sweet **Divine Goodness** of God has now shown you once again a most singular love, having made you hold fast to the doctrine and life of the Saints, making you worthy to suffer for the glory and praise of His Name, so as to give you the fruit in the life that lasts, and not in this life. Now is our time, dearest Father, to do some good for our salvation, to place before us the **Blood of Christ** to hearten ourselves for the battle, so that we do not turn our heads back through impatience, nor falter under the powerful hand of God; but with patience let us endure, making a mockery of our own *sensuality* <term>sensuallità: In this context, it refers to the "lower nature" or the physical impulses and self-centered desires that distract from spiritual goals.</term> and of the World with all its delights, recogniz...

# To Count Alberico da Barbiano, Captain General of the Company of Saint George, and other Captains.

I. She exhorts them to be faithful to the Holy Church and to the Supreme Pontiff Urban VI, fighting for no other purpose than for the honor of God and of Jesus Christ, reflecting also on the rewards that He has prepared for us.
II. She further advises them to prepare themselves for battle by means of Holy Confession.
III. Regarding Self-love, which prevents us from being faithful to God and to His creatures.
IV. She exhorts the Count to provide them with good officers and to guard as much as possible against betrayals, and to this end, to frequently offer himself to the Virgin Mary.
V. She provides him with other motives to fight manfully.
VI. That prayer must be used to aid those who fight.

## Letter 219.

-> On the 6th day of May, while in a state of ecstasy. <- <note>The original phrase "in Astrazione fatta" refers to Catherine’s habit of dictating her letters while in a state of mystical trance or religious ecstasy.</note>

By this Light we see the dignity and goodness of Him whom we serve, and it makes us know the fruit that follows; and knowing Him, one loves Him;

### III.
She also said: what takes away our faithfulness, making us unfaithful to God and to his creatures? It is **self-love** <note>original: "Amore proprio"; Catherine views this as the root of all sin</note>, which is a poison that has poisoned the whole world; it is a cloud that shadows the eye of our **Intellect** <note>The faculty of the soul that perceives truth</note> so that it does not allow us to know or discern the truth. Therefore, it sees nothing other than its own pleasure, by which it delights in pleasing creatures more than the Creator, placing before itself only the **transitory goods** of this dark life, seeking the statuses, delights, and riches of the world—all of which pass away like the wind. This disordered affection, upon which they have placed their efforts, is fit to make a man disloyal or unfaithful except in cases where he sees his own utility being drawn from it. And they also carry the greatest danger that a man might perish himself, and cause others to perish, by wishing to attend in these cases solely to the acquisition of property; for the understanding cannot attend to two things at once: the physical exercise of stealing and that of fighting. You know that many have been losers because of this, and therefore Truth wishes that, so that this case does not happen to you, you...

Stand in the field with the banner of the **Most Holy Cross**; consider that the blood of these **Glorious Martyrs** <note>The early Christian martyrs whose blood was shed in Rome, the site of the current conflict</note> always cries out in the presence of God, asking for His help upon you. Consider that this land <note>Rome</note> is the garden of blessed Christ and is the beginning of our Faith; therefore, everyone should be encouraged within themselves. Now our defects are being paid for, if we are willing to sincerely serve God and the Holy Church. I have nothing more to say to you. Remain in the holy and sweet love of God. Be grateful, you and the others, and recognize the benefit you have received from God and from that **Glorious Knight Saint George** <margin>c</margin> <note>St. George was the patron saint of Alberico’s military company, the "Company of St. George"</note>, whose name you bear; may he defend you and be your guard until death.

( A ) *Alberico da Barbiano, Count of Cunio, was a Captain of great renown in arms, and the one to whom, above all others, Italy owes its return to the ancient glory of its military. He was the architect of his own fortune, owing nothing to his birth in the land of Barbiano in Romagna (from which he took his surname); by valor alone, he rose through the lower ranks to the supreme position of Captain General. Serving in the pay of various Italian Princes during the wars of his era as a **soldier of fortune** <term>Soldato di ventura: a professional mercenary commander</term>, he gathered a small army composed of four thousand men-at-arms and as many light horses, made up of seasoned and brave Italian soldiers. He gave them the name and the banner of St. George, and thus it was called the Company of St. George. Biondo <note>Flavio Biondo (1392–1463), a famous Renaissance humanist and historian.</note>, followed by other more recent writers, maintains that he formed this brave Company at the time when Bernabò Visconti was imprisoned by his nephew Giovanni Galeazzo—that is to say, in the year 1385. But they are proven wrong by this very Letter, which not only in its title (where an error might occur) but also in its content clearly shows that these troops were already serving under the banner and name of the Martyr Saint George <note>Catherine died in 1380, so her writing to the "Company of St. George" proves the unit existed at least five years before the date cited by earlier historians.</note>. With this valiant Company, Count Alberico performed great feats, specifically that of liberating Italy from the **transalpine** <note>original: "Oltramonti"; refers to foreign mercenary groups from across the Alps (French, German, etc.)</note> troops, who had arrived in great numbers, causing no less damage than disgrace to this region, as if Italian cavalry were of no value in warfare. He first drove out those from Germany, then those of Brittany, and finally the English; from then on, every Prince in Italy enrolled Italian knights in his service, who became famous for the valor they learned under the military discipline of such a brave Warrior. One of the most notable enterprises successfully completed by Count Alberico was the liberation of Rome from the insults and injuries continually inflicted upon it by the bands of soldiers who followed the party of Clement VII <note>The Antipope during the Western Schism.</note>, securing with his victory the true Pope in Rome and for Italy.
