...titled *The Propylaeum* <note>Referring to the *Propylaeum ad Acta Sanctorum*, a scholarly work by the Bollandists used to provide historical context for the lives of saints.</note>, in two ways: namely, that there might be an error by the **Printer** in putting the **6th of May** instead of the **6th of March**; or truly, that the date was placed there arbitrarily by whoever took the care to organize them, and certainly with no accuracy, since for the most part the **Saint** did not follow the custom of adding to her Letters neither the day nor the Year in which she wrote them. This is clearly seen from the **Originals** themselves of these Letters, some of which are kept here in **Siena**, nor is it outside the custom of those times, as observed by the **Authors** cited. Hence it is that the **Edition** by **Farri**, which is later than that of **Aldo** <note>Aldus Manutius (c. 1449–1515), the famous Venetian printer who published the first collection of Catherine's letters in 1500.</note>, rejected those few Dates that were present, as if they had no certainty. But aside from this, I cannot see for what reason this Letter should be considered written before the battle, rather than after, while from the words of the **Saint**, if I am not mistaken, she seems to speak of a **Battle** already happened, and a **Victory** already acquired. Let us hear her words:

> You are the first who have given blood. <note>original: "Voi siate i primi, che avete dato il sangue."</note> And further on: Be grateful, you and the others, and cognizant of the benefit you received, to God and to that glorious Knight **Saint George**, etc. <note>original: "Siate grato voi, e gli altri, e cognoscenti del beneficio, che ricevesti, a Dio, e a quello glorioso Cavaliere San Giorgio."</note>

All of which denotes that the Company <note>The Company of Saint George, a celebrated band of mercenary soldiers (condottieri) led by Alberico da Barbiano, who fought for the Pope.</note> had already both fought and won. **Rinaldi** <note>Odoricus Raynaldus (1595–1671), a church historian who continued the *Annales Ecclesiastici*.</note>, cited above, in reporting this Letter, alters the sense of this last passage by changing one word regarding the tense, so that according to the words he presents, the error is not apparent, since he conveys it using the present tense:

> Be grateful, you and the others, and cognizant of the benefit that you *now* receive from God, etc. <note>original: "che ora ricevete"</note>

But that it must be read in the past tense, namely ***received*** <note>original: "ricevesti"</note>, we are assured by both the Text of **Aldo** and of **Farri**, as well as the manuscript in **St. Dominic** <note>The Basilica of San Domenico in Siena, which houses major relics and original manuscripts of the Saint.</note>; therefore even the **French Translator** has said:

> the favor that you have received from it, <note>original French: "la faveur, que vous en avez receüe"</note>

and it becomes clear she speaks of a **Benefit already received**, that is, of the **Victory obtained**. She indeed exhorts them to fight with valor and give their blood in defense of **Urban VI**, but this does nothing to contradict what was said, since the war was not ended by that defeat. The losers had near them the powerful support of **Queen Joanna of Naples**, hence she exhorts them to new battles, there being a need to keep them encouraged and faithful to the **Faction** already chosen. For this reason, also in the Letter she wrote to the people of **Rome** on the same day, she reminds them of gratitude toward these victorious Squads, also as a way to reaffirm them to their side, since they being of mercenary folk—

## Letter 220.

# To Tommaso d’Alviano. <note>Tommaso d'Alviano was an Italian nobleman and military leader. Saint Catherine frequently wrote to such men to encourage them to use their power in service of the Church rather than for private warfare.</note>

I. **T**Hat all the Faithful are bound to serve the Holy Church faithfully.
II. Concerning the three types of Workers whom God has placed in the Holy Church; the first of which is common to all the Faithful, the other two only to some.
III. She exhorts <note>The Italian rubric uses the third person; this summary was likely added by a later editor to describe Catherine's message.</note> the aforementioned Tommaso, as a worker in the Holy Church, to serve her with his possessions and his person, demonstrating how pleasing this is to God, fulfilling this with a right intention and with thanksgiving to the same God.

## Letter 221.

->In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary.<-

**D**earest Brother in sweet Jesus Christ. I, Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious Blood with the desire to see you a faithful servant to the Holy Church, even as a pillar and defender of this sweet Bride of Christ; for he who is found faithful at the moment of his death shall not see eternal punishment. Every faithful Christian is bound to be faithful and to serve the Holy Church, and each according to his state of life. God places His workers in this glorious Garden, and we are those workers who must serve in three ways...

II. The first way pertains generally to all faithful Christians, who must work with humble and holy prayers and with true obedience—that is, being obedient and reverent to the Holy Church, which is the Garden of Christians, where they take delight and from whence they draw the life of Grace, provided they are not despisers of the Blood <note>Catherine often refers to the "Blood of Christ" as the source of the Church's power and the sacraments; to "despise the blood" means to live in a state of serious sin or to rebel against the Church's authority.</note>. That is, that they do not despise it through mortal sin, nor through irreverence and disobedience toward the Holy Church, but remain as workers, as has been said. The second way concerns those who are placed to work in this Garden as Ministers, who have the duty to administer the Holy Sacra-

This is so pleasing to God that even if there were many who did not have that right and holy intention which they ought to have, they will still be rewarded for every service done for this sweet Bride; for God will act for those who labor for her, and if God is for them, no one shall be against them.

(C.) *And after the Peace let us all go in a fine company against the Infidels.* <note>The "Infidels" refers to the Saracen forces in the Holy Land; Catherine was a vocal proponent of a new Crusade.</note> It never entered the mind of Saint Catherine to go herself in person on the Expedition against the Infidels, as some have imagined; the Blessed Raymond, her Confessor and the sincere and faithful Guardian of all the secrets of her Heart, being a witness to the contrary, and who speaks of this specifically in his *Legend* <note>original: *Leggenda*; referring to the *Legenda Maior*, the primary biography of Catherine written by Raymond of Capua</note>; hence the phrasing in this Letter, and in others, "let us all go in a fine company," is a manner of speaking commonly used to express the desire that others prepare themselves to put into effect some highly longed-for Undertaking. From this manner of writing, and perhaps also of speaking, several devout Women took motive to want to go beyond the Sea <note>The "Overseas" or "Beyond the Sea" was the standard term for the Crusader states in the Levant</note>, and to write of it to Don Giovanni delle Celle, a Vallombrosan Monk and Disciple of the Saint, of whom we have spoken elsewhere. ->To the Venerable and most honest Virgin Domitilla, health full of Wisdom and the Science of the Saints.<-

<margin>Manuscript at the Penitentiary in the Abbey of Santa Trinita.</margin>
The Letter says:
> I have heard how you, with many Virgins and honest Women and other Youths, wish to go beyond the Sea, etc. It is a pious desire in the bark <note>The "bark" refers to the outward appearance or superficial layer of an idea</note>, but in the pith <note>The "pith" or "marrow" refers to the inner reality or spiritual essence</note> it is more cruel than any cruelty, an enemy of all honesty; a Gate of perdition, and dispersion of all Virtues, the perdition of all Innocence and purity. The Enemy of the Human Race <note>A common title for the Devil</note>, just as he drove Eve out of Paradise under the guise of good, so every day he transfigures himself into an Angel of light, and wishes to drive you and many others from the Paradise of Innocence and Purity. Perhaps you will answer me that the Saint Catherine preaches that one should go beyond the Sea. I will answer you that if she encourages you in this so that you may find Christ, I deny this along with all the Saints who speak of it. Do you then have Christ, or do you go hunting for stones? <note>Giovanni is arguing that Christ is found through internal prayer, not by visiting physical ruins or "stones" in the Holy Land</note> And if indeed you would give more faith to your Saint Catherine than to the Holy Doctors; go to her once more and ask her by what means she came to such perfection, and you will find clearly that it was through silence and prayer, for she kept silence for eight Years, as it is said, and always stayed in her Room and prayed. Do this first, and when you have reached her perfection, I will give you permission to go beyond the Sea.

<summary>This page discusses the historical context of Catherine's letters regarding the Crusade and clarifies that her calls to go "beyond the sea" were often interpreted as spiritual or symbolic exhortations. <meta>This page continues the discussion of a letter from Giovanni delle Celle to the virgin Domitilla, which clarifies Saint Catherine’s views on women participating in the Crusades. It also addresses historical rumors that Giovanni had criticized the Saint.</meta>

...you. But if you were to go there now, being so imperfect, you would lose the little that you have. Just as one cannot draw the argument from these words that she intended to go in person with other Crusaders against the Infidels, so too it cannot be directly concluded that she exhorted these, or other women, to go there without those regards appropriate to their sex or age. The Saint did have a desire to go there to venerate the sacred memories of our Redemption, and she made a petition to Pope Gregory XI for permission, as is found in Letter 117; but this must be understood as her going in the manner of a Pilgrim, as was very much the custom in that Age, and with the due precautions.

Because of this letter by the Blessed Giovanni, a rumor was spread that he had cast blame upon our Saint, even writing a letter of little praise regarding her work; hence the report went to Lecceto <note>A famous Augustinian forest hermitage located near Siena</note> and reached the ears of the Blessed William of England, who lived in the solitude of that sacred Hermitage. The latter made a complaint to the Blessed Giovanni, who wrote a most beautiful letter in response, which is entirely in praise of Saint Catherine, speaking at length of her great merits, even though she was still alive and yet unknown to him, except by the report of others. This letter, together with two others—all three of which are meant to offer praise to the Saint—I received from the Charterhouse of Pavia through the most courteous efforts of the Questor Francesco Stoppani, who at my request had them transcribed with exact diligence by a person knowledgeable in the Ancient Script <note>original: *Carattere Antico*; referring to the medieval paleography that can be difficult for modern readers to decipher</note> in which they are written, and they were left there, it is believed, by the Blessed Stefano Maconi, the beloved Disciple of this Holy Virgin. It pleases me to provide a few lines here, as they will be given in their entirety in the supplement that will be added to her *Life*. If he therefore says:

*I never wrote any letter to the Venerable Catherine of Siena; nor have I become so senseless as to dare to chatter with a rash mouth against the most faithful Spouse of Christ <note>original: *Sponsam Christi*; a title reflecting Catherine’s mystical marriage to Jesus</note>. But, being asked, I wrote to a certain young girl who lives in Florence, fearing lest, while she wished to win over the Saracens <note>original: *Saracenos*; the Muslim forces in the Holy Land</note>, she might lose her own innocence, etc.*

Then I add: *Wherefore I wrote to the girl herself, saying: Go, and ask Saint Catherine if she attained Christ by praying, or by traveling as a pilgrim, etc.*

# To Tommaso d’ Alviano

I. She exhorts him to be a faithful servant of God, demonstrating how the Light of Holy Faith is necessary for this; through this light we know with how much love we were created by God in His image and likeness, and with what inestimable Charity we were Redeemed by His Only-begotten Son.
II. How, in ascending the Cross, Christ drew to Himself all three of our powers, both spiritually and temporally. <note>The "three powers" refer to the faculties of the soul: memory, intellect, and will.</note>
III. Regarding the words spoken by Jesus Christ: *If two or three are gathered in my Name, I will be in their midst.* <note>original: "Se faranno due, o tre congregati nel Nome mio, Io sarò nel mezzo di loro." A paraphrase of Matthew 18:20.</note>
IV. That the Soul cannot bleed <note>The original "sagnare" likely implies "to be wounded" or "to bleed," suggesting the soul only suffers harm through its own rebellion.</note> except from itself, when it rebels against God.
V. Regarding the Love and the holy fear with which we must resist vices.
VI. That to be faithful to God we must employ ourselves in the service of our Neighbor.

The movement was love, because He gave it for the love of God, so that Man might have a restraint on his evil actions. Then the sweet and loving Word came with the Law of Love, not to dissolve the Law given <note>The "Law given" refers to the Old Testament Law of Moses, often characterized by Catherine as the "Law of Fear."</note>, but to fulfill it; because fear did not give us life. He then harmonized the Law of Love with the Law of fear, and this was of such perfection that it made the imperfect thing perfect. It is therefore necessary to hold to both, because they are united in such perfection that whoever does not wish to be separated from God cannot have the one without having the other, because they are bound together (speaking always with regard to the ten Commandments). Together they give the life of Grace; if someone wished to separate them, it would be impossible for them to have God through Grace in the center of their Soul.

And therefore He said, "if there are two," and He did not say, "if there is one," because one cannot make more than one, and thus one cannot reach three without two. Instead, it is necessary that the Soul first has two; and gradually it possesses two: that is, the love and the fear of God. From there, one finds the three <term>Potentie dell’Anima</term> <note>The "Powers of the Soul": Memory, Intellect, and Will.</note>, which are nothing other than one Soul, in which that unity, adorned with the perfection of Charity, is so perfect that it holds both two, and three, and more. 

And why does He say, "where two or three or more are gathered in My Name"? These are the holy and good works of the Creature who possesses Reason; because every work that they might do—even let us suppose they had the appearance of being "of the World," such as holding great Status and Lordship, or being with a Wife or children, which seems like a worldly thing, or in whatever other situation—all are directed toward God, once the Soul has made its beginning by regulating and gathering all its Virtues in the Name of God. Then it knows its truth well—that is, that God has not given it anything in this life that must be an impediment to its salvation; rather, if the soul so wills, these things are instruments to make it practice Virtue and to give it greater knowledge of its own misery and of the Divine Goodness.

### VI.

It is true that you can be of no utility or service to Him, because He has no need of our service, but He has established the means, and considers done to Himself that which we do for our **Neighbor** for the glory and praise of His Name. And singularly among the other services we can show that please Him well, is to serve His **sweet Bride** <note>The "Bride of God" or "Sweet Bride" is Catherine’s standard term for the Holy Mother Church.</note>, to whose service it seems He has called you. Serve her, therefore, freely, for in whatever spiritual or temporal service you serve her, it is all pleasing to Him, provided it be done with a right and good intention. In doing so, God is grateful and mindful, and will render to you the fruit of your **labor** in this life through Grace, and in the enduring life you shall receive the eternal **Vision of God**. There, you shall see with clear and perfect light, and without any darkness, the love and truth of the Eternal Father; for down here we see Him imperfectly, but up there without any imperfection. I say no more. I pray His Goodness that He may give you perfect light to serve Him perfectly.

## To the Count of Monna Agnola, and Companions in Florence.

I. She exhorts them to fight manfully against our three Enemies, and demonstrates the way in which they attack us, and how they were overcome by Jesus Christ.

The Devil attacks us with many temptations, causing us to do injury, and often to seize what is ours, only to withdraw us from the Charity of our Neighbor; for having lost Love, we have lost life. Our Enemies never sleep, but are always intent on persecuting us; and for this reason God permits it, to give us always the material through which we may merit, and to rouse us from the sleep of negligence. The delights and riches of the world He defeated through lowliness and voluntary poverty, enduring hunger, thirst, and persecutions. He defeated the Devil and his malice with His Wisdom, catching him with the bait and hook of our humanity <note>This "hook and bait" imagery was a common medieval theological concept: Christ’s humanity was the "bait" that the Devil snapped at, only to be caught by the "hook" of His hidden divinity.</note> through the union of the Divine Nature with the human nature. Our flesh is defeated by His Flesh, which was scourged, macerated, and overwhelmed with insults upon the wood of the most holy Cross, and finally raised above all the choirs of angels in the Resurrection of the Son of God. There is no body nor mind so corrupt that, looking upon our humanity united with the Divine Nature in such excellence, would not be purified, and would not rather give itself up to death than defile its mind and body. 

Since we have found the remedy—our Captain Christ has defeated them for us, making them weak and binding them in such a way that they cannot conquer us unless we so will it—we must not fear, but fight manfully. We must sign ourselves with the sign of the most holy Cross, setting before us the Blood of the Immaculate Lamb, taking up the knife of hatred and love, and with it striking our enemies. This is the common battle that every person who is born and reaches the age of reason must face on this field of battle. It seems to me that the inestimable goodness of God has chosen us as Knights <term>Knights: *Cavalieri*; referring to both the social status of her addressees and their spiritual calling</term> to fight truly against vices and sins, to acquire the wealth and treasure of Virtue. Now it seems to me that He invites you to grow...

<meta>This page provides scholarly commentary and historical annotations for Letter 223, which was introduced on the previous page. <margin>Testimony from the Pen of the Carthusian Monastery of Pavia.</margin>
Regarding the address to the Count, it should be read as **To Conte, son of Lady Agnola**; in this case, the word *Conte* would be a personal first name, as it was for many people in that era and still is for some in **Tuscany**, rather than a title for any **Fief**. This is further supported by the addition of **Lady Agnola**, which seems to name his **Mother**, rather than any location referred to in that manner. This **conjecture** is confirmed by **Letter 237**, also addressed to **Florence** to one of her **disciples** called **Conte di Conte** <note>literally "Conte, son of Conte"</note>. In the early **printed editions**, this was also listed as **To the Count of Conte**, but it is quite certain that the word *Conte* is a name, not a title; just as there is a mistake in one title, it is easy to believe the same occurred in the other. Further proof can be taken from seeing that this **Conte, son of Lady Agnola**, was a subordinate of **Don Giovanni delle Celle**, a **Vallombrosian Monk** <note>An order of monks following the Rule of St. Benedict, named after their founding monastery in Vallombrosa, Italy</note>, as will be noted further on. Furthermore, **Conte di Conte** was also a **spiritual son** of his, as seen from the two **letters** that the **religious man** <note>Don Giovanni delle Celle</note> later wrote to him in **praise** of this, their common **Mother** and **Teacher** <note>Referring to Catherine of Siena</note>. I therefore believe it should be read as **to Conte, son of Lady Agnola**, which was the name of his **mother**, just as in the other he is called **Conte di Conte**, that being the name of the **father**.

[ B ] **And it seems that He wishes you to be the first Strikers.** From this, we see that he was the **leader** of others who were preparing themselves to make the **Passage** <term>Passage: *Passaggio*; a common medieval term for a Crusade to the Holy Land</term> against the **infidels**.

( C ) **The Holy Father sends the Krieri**, that is, the **Knights of Rhodes** <note>The Knights Hospitaller, who were based in Rhodes at this time</note>, who were in these parts of **Europe** to bring aid to that island, which was threatened by the **Turks** in 1376, as was noted in the annotations to Letter 42.

( D ) **That you join together with Don Giovanni.** This **Don Giovanni** was probably **Don Giovanni delle Celle**, a monk of **Vallombrosa**, of whom we spoke in the annotations to Letters 70 and 71, and whom we will speak of again in those for Letter 309. It could also be argued that this **Don Giovanni** was **Don Juan Fernández de Heredia**, Castellan of Emposta in the Kingdom of Valencia and a Knight of Rhodes, who had been the **Head of the Assembly** held in **Avignon** by order of **Gregory XI** to provide aid to the Island of Rhodes. He had come to **Italy** to provide an escort with the **galleys** of his **Order** to the **Pope** on his journey to **Rome**, and was preparing for the **Voyage to the Levant** <note>The East, specifically the Holy Land and surrounding areas</note>, having been elected **Grand Master** in that very year, which was 1377.

( E ) **And Leonardo along with them.** Who this **Leonardo** might be...

> [ 'F ] "As much as I believe, our Savior is now making this beginning in order to later carry out the General Passage <term>General Passage: A historical term for a Crusade to the Holy Land</term> in effect." This general passage was never actually carried out. By the Saint saying "as much as I believe," she clearly demonstrates to others that she was speaking from her own personal motivation and did not wish to peddle her words as divine revelations, as others falsely claimed. Critics used this as an argument to cast a negative light on the Saint’s prophetic spirit, but she was defended from such slander by the *Blessed Raymond* <note>Raymond of Capua, Catherine’s confessor and first biographer</note> in his *Life* of her.

# To Master Lorenzo del Pino of Bologna, Doctor of the Decretals <term>Decretals: Letters or decrees of the Pope that form part of Canon Law</term>

I. Of Eternal Life, which is manifested to us by Jesus Christ through our redemption from sins, and in Him we know it; wherefore she exhorts the named Master Lorenzo to love it, hating lies.
II. Of the difference between the one who hates the truth and the one who loves it.
III. How we can live in the Grace of God even among the goods of this Earth, and in every state, by loving Creatures not apart from God, but only in Him.
IV. Of the brevity of earthly Goods.
V. That Charity, when it is in the Soul, is not content with the common state, but desires to go further, detaching itself perfectly from the World.
VI. She begs him to immerse himself in the Blood of Jesus Christ in order to know the truth.

## Letter 224.

->Written while in a state of ecstasy.<- <note>original: "In Astrazione fatta"; this indicates the letter was dictated while Catherine was in a mystical trance</note>

->*In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary.*<-

Who is truth? God is the supreme and eternal Truth. In whom shall we know it? In sweet Jesus Christ; for through His Blood He manifests to us the truth of the Eternal Father. His truth toward us is this: that He created us in His Image and likeness to give us Eternal Life, so that we might participate in and enjoy His Good; but because of the sin of Man, this truth was not fulfilled in him, and therefore God gave us the Word of His

...might have part in Him, and taste His sweetness. This truth the Father showed us through His Son, and imposed this obedience upon Him: that He should restore Man to Grace <term>Grace: the divine influence which operates in humans to regenerate and sanctify</term> through much suffering, purging the guilt of Man upon Himself, and that in His Blood He might manifest His truth. Hence, through the ineffable love that Man finds shown to himself by God, through this means of the Blood of Christ, he knows that God seeks and wants nothing else but our Sanctification; and for this end we were created. Whatever God gives or permits to us in this life, He gives so that we may be sanctified in Him. 

Whoever knows this truth does not forget it, but always follows and loves it, keeping to the footsteps of Christ Crucified. And just as this sweet and loving Word <note>original: "Verbo"; referring to Jesus as the Word of God (Logos)</note>, for our example and teaching, despised the World and all its delights, and willed to endure hunger and thirst, insults and reproaches, even to the shameful death of the Cross for the honor of the Father and our salvation, so does the lover of truth follow these ways and footsteps. He knows this truth by the Light of Most Holy Faith; for without this Light it could not be known, but having it, he knows it, and knowing it, he loves it, and becomes a lover of what God loves and hates what God hates.

II. This is the difference between the one who loves the truth and the one who hates it: The one who hates the truth is he who lies in the darkness of mortal sin <term>mortal sin: a grave action that leads to a total break in a person's relationship with God</term>. This man hates what God loves, and loves what God hates. God hates sin and the disordered delight and pleasure of the World, yet this man loves them, nourishing himself in the misery of the World, and in every state he becomes corrupt. Hence, if he holds an office by which he must minister anything to his Neighbor <note>original: "Prossimo"; here referring to any fellow human being according to the Christian commandment</note>, he does not serve him except in so far as he sees himself drawing profit from it, and no more; he is made a lover of himself. 

Blessed Christ gave His life for us, yet this man does not want to give a single word in service of his Neighbor unless he sees himself paid and overpaid. And if it is a poor person who cannot pay, he makes him suffer before he tells him the truth, and often he does not tell it at all, but makes fun of him. Where he ought to be merciful and a Father to the poor, he is instead made cruel to his own Soul, because he offends the poor ones. But the wretched Man does not see that the Supreme Judge will return to him nothing else but what He receives from him; because justly every sin is punished, and every good is rewarded. Christ ab-

<meta>This page continues Letter 224 to Lorenzo del Pino. The previous page contrasted the lover of truth, who follows Christ’s example, with the lover of "the lie" (sin), who dwells in darkness.</meta>

...embraced voluntary poverty, and was a lover of continence <term>continence: self-restraint, especially regarding physical or worldly pleasures</term>; but the wretched man, who has become a follower and lover of the lie, does the exact opposite. It is not merely that he is dissatisfied with what he has, or that he refuses things for the love of Virtue, but he steals the goods of others. Nor is he content with the state of Marriage—in which, if one observes it as they ought, they can live with a good Conscience—but instead, like a disordered and brute animal, he wallows in every misery. Just as a pig wallows in the mud, so does he wallow in the mud of impurity. 

But one might say: "What shall I do, I who possess riches and am in the state of Marriage, if these things are the damnation of my soul?"

### III.

O dearest Brother, in whatever state a man finds himself, he can save his soul and receive within himself the life of Grace <term>Grace: the divine influence which operates in humans to regenerate and sanctify</term>, provided he does not remain in the guilt of mortal sin. For every state of life is pleasing to God; He is not a respecter of social states, but of Holy Desire! Therefore, we may hold onto these things when they are held with a well-ordered will. Because everything that God has made is good and perfect—except for sin, which was not made by Him and is therefore unworthy of love. 

Riches and the worldly state: if a man wishes to keep them, he may, and he does not offend God or his own soul. However, if he were to leave them, he would achieve greater perfection, for it is a greater perfection to leave than to keep. But if he does not wish to leave them in actual fact, he must leave and reject them with holy desire, not placing his primary affection in them, but only in God. He should hold them for the use of his needs and those of his family, and treat them as something borrowed <note>This is a central theme in Catherine's teaching: "mental detachment" allows a person to use worldly goods without being enslaved by them.</note>, and not as his own. 

By doing this, he never receives pain from any created thing; for a thing that is not possessed with 
<margin>Augustine in the *Enchiridion* <note>The *Enchiridion on Faith, Hope, and Love* is a handbook on Christian piety written by St. Augustine around 420 AD.</note></margin>
disordered love is never lost with grief. Thus we see that the servants of the world, those lovers of the lie, endure the greatest pains in their lives, and in the end, are tormented by excruciating pangs. What is the cause of this? It is the disordered love they have for themselves and for created things, loving them apart from God. For the Divine Goodness has permitted that every disordered affection becomes unbearable to itself. Such a man always believes the lie, because there is no knowledge of truth in him. He believes he holds the World and lives in delights, making a god of his body and of the other things he loves inordinately—a god that he will eventually be forced to leave behind.

<meta>This page continues the counsel from Letter 224 to Lorenzo del Pino. Catherine continues the theme of how one's internal will, rather than their external circumstances, determines their relationship with God.</meta>

### IV.

Therefore we see that either a person leaves these things by dying, or God permits that they be taken away from us; we see this every day. For at one moment a man is rich, and at another poor; today he has risen in the status of the world, and tomorrow he has fallen; now he is healthy, and now he is sick. Thus every thing is changeable, and things are taken from us just when we think we have a firm grip on them, or we are taken from them by means of Death. 

So you see that every thing passes away. Since we see that they pass, they must be possessed with moderation and the light of Reason <term>Reason: the faculty of the soul that allows one to distinguish right from wrong</term>, loving them in the way they ought to be loved. By holding them in this way, one will not hold them with the stain of guilt, but with Grace <term>Grace: divine favor and help from God</term>, with a generous heart rather than greed; with mercy for the poor rather than cruelty; with humility rather than pride; with gratitude rather than ingratitude. Such a person will recognize these gifts as coming from his Creator and not from himself. 

With this same ordered Love, he will love his children, his friends, his relatives, and every other creature that possesses Reason. He will maintain the state of Marriage in an ordered way—ordered because it is a Sacrament <term>Sacrament: a religious ceremony or act regarded as an outward sign of inward spiritual grace</term>—and he will hold in reverence the days commanded by the Holy Church. He will be and will live as a man, not as an animal. Even if he is not naturally continent <term>continent: practicing self-restraint, particularly in a sexual context</term>, he will become continent and will bring his Will into order. 

Such a man will be a fruitful tree that produces the fruits of Virtue. He will be fragrant, because even while standing in the midst of the stench <note>Catherine often uses "stench" or "filth" to describe the corruptions of the world or the flesh</note>, he will give off a sweet odor, and the seed that comes from him will be good and virtuous. 

So you see that in every state of life you can have God; for it is not your state of life that takes Him from us, but only an evil Will. When the Will is set on the love of the lie, it is disordered, and with that Will a person corrupts every action. But if he loves the truth, he follows the footsteps of the truth; thus he hates what the truth hates, and loves what the truth loves, and then every one of his actions is good and perfect. In any other way, it would be impossible for him to participate in the life of Grace, nor would any of his actions bear the fruit of life.

### V.

Therefore, knowing no other way, I said that I desired to see you as a lover and follower of the truth, and a despiser of the lie—that is, that you hate the Devil, who is the Father of Lies, and your own sensuality which follows such a Father. I desire that you love Christ Crucified, who is the Way, the Truth, and the Life. For whoever walks through Him reaches the Light, and clothes himself in the shining...

<meta>This page continues the spiritual counsel of Saint Catherine of Siena to the Bolognese jurist Lorenzo del Pino. ...the garment of Charity <term>Charity: in this context, "Carità" refers to the highest form of Christian love—selfless, divine love for God and neighbor</term>, upon which all the Virtues are founded. When this Charity and ineffable love is within the Soul, it is not content to remain in a common state, but desires to go further. Thus, from poverty of the mind, it desires to move toward actual poverty; and from continence of the mind, it wishes to move toward actual continence, in order to observe both the commandments and the counsels of Christ. Such a person begins to feel a weariness for the corruption of the World; because it seems so difficult to live in the midst of worldly things and not be defiled, the soul desires—with anxious longing and burning charity—to be released from the World all at once, as far as it is possible. And if it is not possible to leave the world physically, the soul strives to be perfect within its own current state; at the very least, the desire for perfection is not lacking.

### VI.

Therefore, dearest Brother, let us sleep no longer, but wake from our slumber. Open the eye of the Intellect with the Light of Faith to know, love, and follow this truth, which you will recognize in the Blood of the humble and loving Word <note>Word: "Verbo," referring to Jesus Christ as the Word of God</note>. You will come to know the Blood through the knowledge of yourself, for the face of the Soul is washed with the blood. This blood is ours, and no one can take it from us unless we ourselves will it. Do not be negligent, then, but like a vessel, fill yourself with the Blood of Christ Crucified. I say no more. Remain in the holy and sweet love of God. Sweet Jesus. Jesus Love.

<margin>(A) This Lorenzo dal Pino—a Bolognese Noble and Master of Decretals <term>Decretals: letters of the Pope that formulate decisions on points of canon law</term> to whom Saint Catherine sent this Letter—was the son of Matteo, known as Mattiolo Uguccione dal Pino. He was a distinguished Lecturer at the University of Bologna from the year 1365 until the year 1391. He served among the Elders of that Republic in the year 1367, and in 1370 he was one of those who formed the Council of the Four Hundred in that City. In the following year, he was one of the four men chosen to negotiate the peace treaty between Pope Gregory XI and the people of Bologna regarding the Rebellion they had raised against the Church, a task he brought to a successful conclusion. He was later Deputed in the year 1380 to provide a response to the Ambassadors of the Antipope Clement <note>original: "Antipapa Clemente." This refers to Clement VII, the first antipope of the Great Western Schism who reigned from Avignon</note>, who was attempting to win this powerful Italian city to his side. Lorenzo stripped them of all hope of succeeding, as the city wished to remain firm in recognizing Urban as the Vicar of Christ <term>Vicar of Christ: a title for the Pope, signifying his role as the representative of Christ on Earth</term>, even though, having regained their liberty, they did not wish to have him as their political Lord. This man left behind several legal opinions which are currently in the press...</note></margin>

# To Master Francesco da Montalcino, Doctor of Civil Law

I. **O**n the virtue of patience, exhorting the aforementioned Master Francesco to embrace it.
II. That impatience belongs to Hell, Peace to the Blessed, and that we are deprived of Peace by our own poorly regulated Will.
III. That this Will is taken from us by stripping ourselves of our own selves and clothing ourselves in the Will of God.
IV. On the reward granted to patience, as a motive to embrace it.
V. On the knowledge of oneself as a means to acquire it.
VI. On the consideration of the sufferings of Christ to acquire said virtue.
VII. On the evil that tribulations prevent.

## Letter 225.

->In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of Mary sweet.<-

I. **D**earest Brother in Christ, Sweet Jesus: I, Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious Blood, with the desire to see you founded in true and holy patience. Considering myself, I see that without patience we could not please God; rather, we would even taste the earnest money <note>original: "arra"—referring to a down payment or foretaste of what is to come</note> of Hell in this life, for through impatience we begin to taste the experience of Hell in this world.

## Letter 227.

->In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary.<-

I. Dearest Brother in sweet Christ Jesus: I, Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious Blood, with the desire to see you a despiser of **mortal sin** <term>peccato mortale: in Catholic theology, a grave sin that destroys charity in the heart and turns the soul away from God</term>, because in no other way could you have Divine Grace in your soul. But I do not see how you, or anyone else, can have this grace if a person does not have the light—the light by which one can see and recognize the gravity of sin and the goodness of **Virtue**. For a thing that is not known cannot be loved (that is, if it is worthy of love), nor can a thing be hated if it is worthy of hatred, nor can it even be recognized without the light. We have need, then, of the light; and we possess this light in the eye of the **Intellect** by means of the pupil of Most Holy Faith, provided that the cloud of **self-love** <term>amor proprio: a central concept for Catherine, referring to the selfish ego that blinds the soul to God's truth</term> has not obscured it.

II. And if self-love were present, we must cast it away so that our vision is not hindered, and with holy love we must drive out the perverse love of our own sensuality, which—

--- Page 273 ---
<meta>This page continues Letter 227 to Master Francesco, a physician of Siena. The previous page established the need for spiritual light to recognize the gravity of sin and the goodness of virtue.</meta>

...self-love consumes and takes away the **Divine Grace** <term>Divina Gratia: the supernatural gift of God's life and favor within the soul</term> of the **Soul** <note>original: "Anima"</note>, and it corrupts every one of its actions. Just as from a bad tree all its fruits are corrupt, so are the fruits of a man who remains in sensory love <note>meaning love focused only on physical or worldly pleasures</note>, from which he is drawn into the weight of **mortal sin**. And therefore every one of his actions is corrupt; the light is taken from him and darkness is given, in such a way that he neither knows nor discerns the truth. Furthermore, the taste and the appetites of the soul are spoiled, so that good things seem bad to him, and bad things seem good. He despises true **Virtue**, flees from the love of God and the affection for his **Neighbor** <note>original: "Prossimo"; referring to one's fellow human beings</note>, and takes all his delight in the pleasures and delights of the world. And if he loves his neighbor, he does not love him for God's sake, but for his own advantage.

But he who is truly stripped of sensory love loves his **Creator** above all things, and his neighbor as himself. This love he cannot have unless, through the light of the **Intellect**, he first recognizes that he is nothing of himself, and acknowledges that his very being comes from God, along with every grace that is added to that being. Then, when he so sweetly knows himself and his own defect, and the goodness of God, he hates his defect and the self-love that causes it, and he loves virtue. And for the love of virtue—which he loves for the love of his Creator—he disposes himself to suffer any pain rather than offend God and contaminate virtue. All his actions are directed toward God, whether spiritual or temporal; and in whatever state he is in, he loves and fears his Creator. 

Therefore, if he has riches, worldly status, children, relatives, and friends, he possesses everything as a thing on loan, and not as his own; and he uses them appropriately, and not immoderately. And if he is in the state of **Marriage**, he lives in it orderly, as in a Sacrament, holding in reverence the days that are commanded by Holy Church. If he has to interact with other **Creatures** <note>meaning other people or created beings</note> and serve them, he serves them sincerely, not with a deceitful heart, but a free one, having respect only for God.

### III.
He orders the **Powers of his Soul** <term>Potentie dell'Anima: the three faculties of the soul—Memory, Intellect, and Will—which medieval thinkers believed mirrored the Holy Trinity</term> and all the senses of the body. Thus he orders Memory to retain the benefits of God, the Intellect to understand His Will—which desires nothing other than our **Sanctification** <term>Santificatione: the process of being made holy or consecrated to God</term>—and the Will he disposes to love his Creator above all things. He orders—

...ordered, which are the **Powers of the Soul** <term>Potentie dell' Anima: traditionally the memory, intellect, and will</term>, all the senses of the body are also ordered. By doing so, in whatever state you may be, you will be pleasing to God; you will be a **fruitful Tree** and will produce fruits of life—that is, true and holy **Virtues**—and in this life you will begin to taste the earnest money <note>original: "l' arra"; a down payment or foretaste given as a guarantee of more to come</note> of **eternal Life**.

* ( A ) This Master Francesco, son of Master Bartolomeo, was of the noble family of the Casini of Siena, which has already been extinct for several years. Because of his great skill in medicine, he rose to high esteem in his day; having already taught medicine publicly at the University of Siena, he went to the papal court in **Avignon** <note>The city in France that served as the seat of the papacy from 1309 to 1376</note>. He arrived there in the year 1376, when the Saint <note>Saint Catherine of Siena</note> was also present, as we learn from the letter of the Blessed Stefano. In Rome, he was the physician to **Pope Urban VI**. A testimony by this man in favor of that Pope is cited by Oldoino, the beginning of which follows this tenor: *I, Francesco of Siena, Doctor of Medicine, etc.* <note>original Latin: "Ego Franciscus de Senis Medicinae Doctor &c."</note> This was also cited by Baluze and refuted as noted in the annotations to Letter 29. He wrote several letters to the Republic of Siena, keeping them informed of daily occurrences in Rome; he also wrote others to this community in the name of Urban VI regarding various public affairs. However, these were written in such a barbaric style <note>likely referring to "vulgar" or non-classical Latin/Italian</note> that they move one to pity to read them; from them, one can see how much confidence and power he held with the Pontiff. After the death of Urban, he returned to his homeland and served in the Supreme Magistracy in the year 1390, dying that same year. From what has been said, and from much more that could be said to show that this Francesco was truly a Sienese citizen (such as the testimony of the title of this letter), and the words spoken by Blessed Ste-* <margin>fano...</margin> <note>The text cuts off mid-name, referring to Stefano Maconi, Catherine’s disciple and secretary.</note>

therefore, if one of the brothers was Sienese, the other must have been as well, and consequently the son also. In the public records of Siena, there is authentic memory of this family,

which belonged to the **Order of the Reformers** <term>One of the political factions or "Monti" that governed the Republic of Siena</term>, and among those families who sat in the **Signoria** <term>The supreme executive council of the Republic</term>, and not among those enrolled as foreigners to this citizenship, as *Ughelli* believes. It is true that in
<margin>Ammirato, book 8, chapter 9.</margin>
Florence, there was also a *Casini* family in that same century; it is recorded that in 1336 *Rinaldo* was a **Gonfaloniere** <term>A high-ranking municipal official, literally a "standard-bearer"</term> there, and in 1340, *Naddo Casini* held office, but these were not related at all to the *Casini* of Siena. The Sienese family perhaps later obtained Florentine citizenship as well, as the Cardinal's father lived there for some time, where he obtained the Provostship of Segni and a Canonry, and his sisters took the religious habit there. However, none of this serves to prove him Florentine, as there are too many clear proofs to the contrary that make him Sienese, such as the inscription on his tomb in the Church of **Santa Maria Maggiore** in Rome, which reads:
> The tomb of Antonio Casini of Siena, Cardinal-Priest of the Title of Saint Mark, who died on February 4, 1439. <note>original Latin: "Sepulcrum Antonii Casini de Senis Titul. S. Marc. Presbit. Cardinal. qui obiit IV Februarii MCCCCXXXIX."</note>

and his will, in which he is called several times "of Siena" (*de Senis*), a term that always denotes one’s homeland, as observed by
<margin>In the Life of Martin V.</margin>
*Oldoino*, cited above. *Oldoino*, however, is in doubt as to whether he should be called the son of *Francesco* or of *Giovanni Casini*. It is certain, based on reliable records from this city, that he was the son not of *Francesco*—regardless of what the inscription at his altar in the **Siena Cathedral** says, which should be corrected—but of *Giovanni* and a Roman lady of the
<margin>Oldoino, in the place cited, and Ugurgieri, Title 2.</margin>
*Capocci* family, who was the niece on her sister’s side to **Pope Martin V**.

# To Master Ristoro di Pietro Canigiani in Florence.

I. On the virtue of perseverance, exhorting him to the same.
II. Rejoicing in the resolution he made to forgive those who offended him, and how harmful a thing is revenge, and how useful and joyful it is to forgive.
III. On conducting one's business with justice, which is permitted to everyone with a good conscience.
IV. Exhorting him to a life of solitude.
V. Exhorting him to help the poor with the virtue given to him by God, following the example of **St. Ivo** <note>St. Ivo of Kermartin, known as the "Advocate of the Poor," 1253–1303</note>.
VI. That one must have God before one's eyes in every action.
VII. On the stripping away of superfluous things and various luxuries.
VIII. How he ought to maintain the fear of God within the state of marriage.
IX. On refusing public offices.
X. On frequent Confession and Communion.
XI. On Prayer and other exercises of piety, to which he is exhorted to ensure the health of the Soul.

This delight the **Soul** then receives, and joy and rest in **Conscience**—no tongue could narrate how great it is. And even according to the World, it is a very great honor to him who, for love of **Virtue** and through magnanimity, does not lust for nor wish to take revenge on his **Enemy**. **[ B ]** *Like Saint Ives, who was in his time the Advocate of the Poor.* This Lord <note>Ristoro Canigiani</note> was a Lawyer by profession, and for this reason the Saint offers him Saint Ives as an example. This man <note>Saint Ives of Kermartin (1253–1303), the patron saint of lawyers.</note> was of the French nation from the Province of Brittany, illustrious for both his profound doctrine and sublime holiness; he made it his custom to take up the defense of the causes of the poor, widows, and orphans without seeking any personal gain.

**( C )** *You will do very well to refuse the Offices.* To withdraw from public offices to attend only to oneself is not worthy of praise in a citizen, except in cases where the Republic is so poorly regulated that one cannot otherwise hope to be able to rightly fulfill one’s duty, or where it is so abundant with people able to sustain them that, even if one does not lend a hand, no harm can come to the public good. Outside of these cases, the citizen is under a strict obligation to offer his labor to the needs of the Fatherland. This second case was precisely that of the City of Florence, which was always rich in men of consummate prudence and subtle wit, able therefore to exercise public magistracies not only in their own Republic but in other cities and regions, as they have made clear at all times to their greatest glory. Therefore, the saying of Dante was reputed to be full of vain self-belief and envy of others' merit when, upon being proposed by his Republic to go as head of a famous Embassy to the Pope, he withdrew into himself, and after some thought, 
<margin>Life of Dante by Boccaccio.</margin> 
said: "If I go, who remains? And if I remain, who goes?" <note>A famous anecdote from Giovanni Boccaccio’s biography of Dante Alighieri, suggesting Dante felt himself indispensable to Florence.</note> It was as if he alone comprised the Republic of Florence, and he alone were fit for the ministry of ruling it from within and managing its interests abroad. Perhaps she <note>Saint Catherine</note> also discouraged him from meddling in public affairs because the Republic was in a quarrel with the Pope and bound by an Interdict <note>A "censura ecclesiastica" or Interdict was a punishment that prohibited residents of a city from receiving the sacraments or having Christian burials; Florence was under such a ban during the War of the Eight Saints (1375–1378).</note>, and thus by having a part in the Government, he could be held in greater guilt for the excesses being committed.

**( E )** *That we are pacified with our Father.* From these words, it is evident that the Letter was written at the time when Florence had been placed under interdict by Gregory XI. <note>An interdict was a collective punishment by the Pope that suspended church services and most sacraments in a city. <margin>Dictionary of the Crusca <note>The authoritative dictionary for the Tuscan/Italian language.</note></margin>
**( F )** *See to it, that the solemn Easters.* To speak with propriety, there is only one Easter, and no more, which is that of the Resurrection. Yet the name of "Easter" <note>original: "Pasqua"</note> among various Nations, and particularly in Italy, is given to several of the major Feasts celebrated by the Holy Church. Thus, the name of Easter is given to the solemnity of the resurrection of Christ our Lord, but also to the Nativity <note>Christmas</note>, the Epiphany, the Ascension, Pentecost, and the Feast of the Body of Christ <note>Corpus Christi</note>, being found referred to by the name "Easters" <note>original: "Pasque"</note> by the authors of good Tuscan speech.

Canon *Omnis utriusque* regarding Penance. <note>A decree from the Fourth Lateran Council (1215) requiring all Christians to confess and receive communion at least once a year.</note>

Part 2, ch. 14.
</margin>
**[ G ]** *Or at least once a year you receive Communion.* The piety of the first Christians led them to feed their Souls with the Eucharistic Bread every day. That fervor having later cooled, so that the use of this Sacrament would not fall into disuse for many, the Precept was made by Innocent III that at least once a Year the Soul should be restored with the Celestial Bread. Although the Saint was accustomed to partaking of it very often—for which she also endured significant criticism—it was not common in her days, even among people who lived a more exemplary life, to receive communion more than very rarely. The frequency of this Sacrament was renewed in the sixteenth century through the work of the new Religious Orders <note>Specifically the Jesuits and other Counter-Reformation orders who promoted frequent communion.</note> who began to flourish in the Church during that century, and was later encouraged by the holy diligence of all.

<meta>This page continues the scholarly annotations or "notes" on the works of Saint Catherine of Siena, specifically focusing on devotional practices mentioned or implied in her writings. While the previous page provided (216) discussed the Sacrament of Penance and the interdict on Florence, this page (257) focuses on the history of the Little Office of the Blessed Virgin Mary and the tradition of Saturday devotions.</meta>

<page-num>257</page-num>
<sig>Kk</sig>

The Office of Our Lady <note>The "Little Office of the Blessed Virgin Mary," a shorter version of the daily cycle of prayers (Liturgy of the Hours) recited by clergy and religious orders.</note> is older in the Church than the eleventh century. The first to undertake its recitation were the monks of Monte Cassino before the year 752, by order of Gregory III and Zachary, as Paul the Deacon <note>An 8th-century Benedictine monk and historian.</note> testifies in his *Exposition of the Rule of Saint Benedict*. Saint Peter Damian, who flourished in the eleventh century, introduced its use into other Benedictine monasteries and restored it in those from which it had departed; for this reason, he was considered by some to be its primary founder. <margin>Theophilus Raynaud, Volume 17, page 352.</margin> In the Council of Clermont held in the year 1095, the custom of reciting it in other churches was introduced by the Pope <note>Pope Urban II.</note> in order to obtain, through the work of the Great Virgin, a successful outcome for the First Crusade, which was proclaimed there against the Infidels. It was thereafter embraced with great fervor by the Faithful, and today it is the practice of almost everyone to give this small tribute of praise to Our Lady every day.

**( L )** *Fasting on Saturday out of reverence for Mary.* The day of Saturday has been consecrated to the honor of the Mother of God since very ancient times. The reason for this is reported by Saint Peter Damian, and is as follows. This name "Sabbath" (which is Hebrew) signifies "rest," because on it God ceased from the Creation of the Universe, and—according to our limited understanding—as if he were weary from the labor, he rested. Now, the Virgin was that Building which Divine Wisdom built for itself, and in her, as if in a bed of holiness, He came to take His rest in the mysterious union He made with human lowliness. The words of the Saint are these: <margin>Work 33, chapter 4.</margin> *The Sabbath, which is interpreted as rest, the day on which God is said to have rested, is quite suitably dedicated to the Most Blessed Virgin. For Wisdom indeed built for herself a house, and in her, through the mystery of the humility she assumed, he rested as if in a most sacred bed.* <note>original Latin: "Sabbatum, quod requies interpretatur, quo videlicet die Deus requieviſſe dicitur, satis congruè Beatiſſimæ Virgini dedicatur. Quam nimirum sibi Sapientia Domum ædificavit, atque in ea, per humilitatis assumptæ mysterium, veluti in ſacratiſſimo lectulo requievit."</note> <margin>Raynaud, book 4, chapter 1, from number 31 to 36. Raynaud, Volume 17, page 452.</margin> Other reasons are brought forward by William Durand <note>A 13th-century French canonist and liturgical writer.</note>, though not all of them are approved as sound by Raynaud. That it was the will of Heaven, for this or some other fitting reason, that such a day be consecrated to Our Lady, was revealed through a Miracle. In Constantinople, an Image of the Virgin was venerated and kept covered by a veil. Every Friday, once Vespers <note>The traditional evening prayer service.</note> were finished, this veil would lift by itself and disappear, allowing the Sacred Image to be seen without any hindrance until the Vespers of Saturday were finished, at which hour the veil would return, without human aid, to hide the features of the Great Virgin. Whether from this miraculous sign the Church took the custom of celebrating the...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the historical origins of Saturday devotions to the Virgin Mary. <page-num>258</page-num>
<sig>A</sig>

<margin>Rainaud, in the place cited. <note>original: "Rain. loc. cit." Referring to the theologian Theophilus Raynaud mentioned on the previous page.</note></margin>
...the day of Saturday, as sacred to Mary, it must be said that the event occurred before the year 600; since in the times of Saint Ildefonsus <note>Saint Ildefonsus of Toledo (607–667 AD), a prominent scholar and bishop famous for his writings on the Virgin Mary.</note>, who flourished in that age, this custom was already introduced, it being false that this was established by the Council of Clermont <note>A church council held in 1095 where Pope Urban II called for the First Crusade.</note> of 1095.

<margin>Bellarmine, *Controversies*, final part, book 2, chapter 18. <note>original: "Bell. Contr. ult. l. 2. c. 18." Referring to Robert Bellarmine, a central figure of the Counter-Reformation.</note></margin>
Regarding the practice of abstaining from meat on such a day, there was anciently some difference within the Church. The very ancient custom of its first years was not to avoid it, as there was even an express order in Canon 65 of those which are called the Canons of the Apostles <note>A collection of ancient ecclesiastical decrees, once thought to be written by the Apostles but now dated to the 4th century.</note>. The reason for such a prohibition was to oppose the Simonian <note>Followers of Simon Magus, often cited as the first heretics.</note> and Marcionite heretics <note>Followers of Marcion, a 2nd-century figure who believed the God of the Old Testament was different from and inferior to the God of the New Testament.</note>, who had the audacity to assert that the true God was not the one who built the world and rested on the seventh day; they wanted that day to be spent in fasting out of spite for Him, so as not to show any sign of joy for His rest. Therefore, to oppose those perfidious men, Catholics were forbidden from fasting.

Once the danger of conforming to these impious people ceased because their errors had been extinguished, the Roman Church desired the abstinence from meat on such a day, and this specifically for four reasons. Namely: to show a sign of sorrow on that day when the Savior lay dead; to further distance themselves from the Jews, who make that day solemn; to keep company in some way with the sorrow of the Blessed Virgin and the Apostles; and to dispose oneself with greater preparation to celebrate the upcoming solemnity of Sunday. The piety of the faithful has since advanced even further, with many now abstaining not only from meat on such a day, according to the Precept <term>Precept: A formal command or rule of the Church that carries the weight of law for the faithful.</term> of the Church, but also from other foods not prohibited, in honor of the Virgin; and to this very thing the Saint <note>Likely referring to Saint Catherine of Siena.</note> here exhorts this Lord.

# To Master Ristoro Canigiani. <note>Ristoro Canigiani was a prominent Florentine lawyer and politician who became a devoted "spiritual son" of Catherine of Siena.</note>

1. **O**f self-love, by which the necessary light to know Divine Goodness and our own misery is taken from us, and we are also deprived of Charity. <note>Catherine uses "light" as a metaphor for spiritual discernment.</note>
II. That in the knowledge of oneself, one acquires contrition for sins.
III. That the benefits of God exceed our requests.

## Letter 229.

1. **D**earest Son in Christ sweet Jesus: I, Catherine, servant and slave of the Servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious Blood, with the desire to see you deprived of all self-love of yourself, so that you do not lose the light and the knowledge to see the ineffable love that God has for you. And because light is that which makes it known to us, and self-love is that thing which takes the light from us, I therefore have a very great desire to see it extinguished in you. Oh, how dangerous to our salvation is this self-love! It deprives the Soul of Grace, because it takes away the Charity of God,

### IV. Therefore, since He gives so much without our asking, how much more will He fulfill our desires when we desire something righteous? Furthermore, who is it that makes us desire and ask? It is He alone. Therefore, if He makes us ask, it is a sign that He wishes to fulfill it and give that which we ask for.

<margin>Matthew 7.</margin>
### V. But you will say to me: "I confess that what you say is true; but how does it happen that many times I ask for contrition and other things, and it does not seem they are given to me?" I answer you: either it is through the fault of the one who asks, asking imprudently only with words and not with the heart's affection; and of such as these our Savior spoke, who call Him Lord, Lord <note>original: "Signore, Signore"</note>, saying that they will not be known by Him—not because He does not know them, but because of their faults they will not be recognized by His Mercy. Or, he asks for something that, if he had it, would be harmful to his salvation; whereby, not having what he asks for, he actually *has* it <note>Catherine suggests that not receiving a harmful request is itself an answered prayer</note>, because he asks for it believing it to be for his good, and having it would harm him, while not having it benefits him; and thus God has fulfilled the intention with which he asked. So, on God’s part, we always have it; but it is certainly this: that God sees the hidden and the manifest and knows our imperfection. Therefore He sees that if He immediately gave us the grace as we ask for it, we would act like the unclean animal <note>This is likely a reference to a fly or a scavenger; Catherine often uses animal metaphors to describe human fickleness</note> which, having been lifted from the honey, which is most sweet, does not then care to avoid placing itself upon something foul. Thus God sees that we often do: receiving His graces and benefits, and participating in the sweetness of His Charity, we do not care to avoid falling back into miseries, returning to the vomit of the rot of the World <note>A reference to the proverb "a dog returns to its vomit," signifying a return to sinful habits</note>; and therefore God sometimes does not give us what we ask for as quickly as we would like, to make us grow in hunger and desire, because He delights—that is, it pleases Him—to see before Him the hunger of His creature.

He uses this way with providence, because He knows that if a person felt they had it, they would either loosen the rope of desire or would fall into presumption; and therefore He withdraws the feeling, but not the grace. ## VII.
It seems to me that the first sweet Truth <note>Catherine's frequent title for Jesus Christ</note> teaches us what we should ask for when, in the Holy Gospel, He rebukes man for his disordered anxiety—the kind he puts into acquiring and keeping the status and riches of the world. He said: "Do not worry about tomorrow, for today's own anxiety is enough for the day" <note>Matthew 6:34</note>. Here He shows us that we should prudently consider the shortness of time; then He adds: "Seek first the Kingdom of Heaven <note>original: 'Reame del Cielo'</note>, rather than these minor things; the Heavenly Father knows well that you have need of them" <note>Matthew 6:33</note>.

## VIII.
What is this Kingdom? And how is it asked for? It is the Kingdom of Eternal Life, and the Kingdom of our soul; and this Kingdom of the soul, if it is not possessed by Reason, never enters the Kingdom of God. With what is it asked for? Not only with words (for we have already said that such people are not known by God) but with the affection of true and real virtues. It is Virtue that asks for and possesses this Kingdom of Heaven. Virtue makes a person prudent, so that they act with prudence and maturity for the honor of God, their own salvation, and that of their neighbor. With prudence, one bears and tolerates their own defects; with prudence, one orders the affection of charity <note>original: 'Carità' - in Catherine’s writing, this refers to the highest form of divine love</note>, loving God above all things, and their neighbor as themselves. The proper order is this: that one is prepared to give up physical life for the salvation of souls, and temporal goods to save the body of one's neighbor. Prudent charity establishes this order; if it were imprudent, it would be the exact opposite—as many do, who practice a foolish and mad charity. Often, to save their neighbor—and I do not mean the neighbor's soul, but the body—they put their own soul at risk by spreading lies and giving false testimony. These people lose charity because it is not "seasoned" with prudence. We have seen that we must ask for the Kingdom of Heaven prudently; now I will answer you regarding the manner we must maintain concerning Holy Communion, and how we ought to receive it.

## IX.
And we must not practice a foolish humility, as the secular men of the world do; I say that it is right for us to receive this sweet Sacrament <term>the Eucharist</term>, because it is the food of the Soul, and without this food we cannot live in Grace; for no bond is so great that it cannot and should not be cut in order to come to this sweet Sacrament. A person must do everything on their part that they can, and that must suffice for them. How should we receive it? With the Light of the Most Holy Faith, and with the mouth of holy desire; by the Light of Faith, you will behold the whole God and the whole Man in that Host <term>the consecrated bread of the Eucharist</term>. Then the affection, which follows the Intellect, receives Him with an affectionate love and with a holy consideration of one’s own faults and sins, from which comes contrition <term>sincere remorse for one's sins</term>; and one considers the abundance of the inestimable Charity of God, who with such love has given Himself as food. And even if it does not seem that one has that perfect contrition and disposition that they themselves would wish for, they must not abandon it, because the good Will alone is sufficient, as is the disposition that has been made on their part.

## X.
I also say that it is right for us to receive it just as it was prefigured in the Old Testament, when it was commanded that the Lamb be eaten roasted and not boiled, whole and not in part, girded and standing upright, with staff in hand, and that they should place the blood of the Lamb upon the lintel of the door. In this same way, it is right for us to receive this Sacrament: to eat it roasted and not boiled. For when it is boiled, there is Earth and Water in between—that is, earthly affection and the water of self-love—and therefore it must be roasted, so that there is no intermediary at all. It is received "roasted" when we receive it with the fire of Divine, sweet Charity <note>Catherine uses the imagery of fire to represent the direct, transformative power of God's love</note>. And we must be girded with the belt of Conscience, for it would be a most unseemly thing to approach such cleanliness and purity with an impure mind and body. We must stand upright; that is, our heart and our mind must be entirely faithful and directed toward God. With the staff of the Most Holy Cross, from which we draw the Doctrine of Christ Crucified—that is, that staff upon which we lean, and which defends us from our Enemies: namely, the World, the Devil, and the Flesh. ### XI.
I said that it is not fitting for us to act—nor do I want you to act—like many imprudent secular people who transgress what is commanded by the Holy Church, saying: "I

"...[What] then am I? Am I not a stone, or a tree, or some beast? [I am not,] because your Goodness so ordained it; and my merits did not precede your ordaining this." <note>This quote is from a popular medieval devotional text. The speaker marvels that God chose to create them as a rational human being rather than an inanimate object or a mindless animal, purely out of divine grace.</note> *If, however, we take this thought for what it appears to be, it possesses more piety than the soundness required to withstand the examination of rigorous philosophy, since it is impossible for things to be anything other than what they are. Nor is this sentiment, as many scholars believe, the work of Saint Augustine, but rather of Saint Anselm—though he wished the author of the book of* Soliloquies <note>The *Soliloquies* mentioned here are a collection of medieval meditations. While long attributed to St. Augustine, they were actually compiled in the 12th century, likely drawing on the tradition of St. Anselm of Canterbury.</note> *to bear the name of Saint Augustine. But from whoever it may be, it can receive an explanation that is not contrary to the truth and is equally favorable to piety. That is to say: God, by His pure Goodness—while having the power to cause a brute animal to be born, or something else entirely void of not only reason but even feeling—willed instead that this human individual should be born, who otherwise could have remained in his nothingness for all eternity. This could also be interpreted in another way: that the author, in order to kindle more warmth in the heart of man toward his Creator, reviews all the gifts given to him by Him. This is not to say that God could have brought man into being without these essential qualities, but so that by considering them distinctly, man might better know how much he is indebted to Him who gave them. In whatever manner one chooses to understand it, the words of the Saint will always breathe piety; and if they do not align perfectly with the laws of natural philosophy, they will never discord with those of Christian philosophy. See Theophilus Raynaud* <note>Theophilus Raynaud (1583–1663) was a prolific Jesuit theologian known for his vast and often eccentric writings on a wide range of ecclesiastical subjects.</note>*, who speaks at length of this sentiment and brings forward various expositions of it.*

<margin>Book 3 on the Faith, chapter 6.</margin>

# To Master Ristoro Canigiani. <note>original: "Misser." A title of respect in 14th-century Italy, typically used for knights, judges, or men of high social standing like Ristoro, who was a Florentine lawyer.</note>

I. On true and perfect Charity, and the sweetness that it brings; which Virtue is acquired in the knowledge of oneself, and of Divine Love.
II. On Charity toward one's Neighbor, which proceeds from Charity toward God.
III. On the vices and temptations that are conquered by Charity.
IV. On the Virtue of Purity in particular, which is called the Sister of Charity.

## Letter 230.

-> In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary. <-

**D**earest Son in sweet Jesus Christ. I, Catherine <note>Saint Catherine of Siena (1347–1380), a mystic, activist, and Doctor of the Church.</note>, servant and slave of the Servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious Blood, with the desire to see you established in true and most perfect Charity, which Charity is the Mother and Nurse of all the Virtues. It makes a person constant and persevering in Virtue, so much so that neither the Devil nor any creature can separate him from it, if he does not so will. She <note>Catherine personifies Charity as a motherly figure.</note> is of such sweetness that no bitterness that might afflict the Soul falls within her; rather, she generates a "sweet bitterness" <note>A key concept in Catherine's theology: the holy sorrow for one's sins which is simultaneously joyful because it is rooted in the awareness of God's mercy.</note> that nourishes the Soul in a true knowledge of itself. In this state, the Soul knows its past and present faults committed against its Creator; through this knowledge, it feels bitterness, grieving for having offended such Supreme and Eternal Good, and for having defiled the face and beauty of its soul, which was washed in the Blood of the humble and Immaculate Lamb. In this Blood, the soul recognizes the fire and the abyss of His Charity; through this knowledge, the Soul comes to love, for it could come to it in no other way; because the creature loves its Creator as much as it perceives itself to be loved by Him. Thus, all the coldness of our heart proceeds from nothing else but this: that we do not look upon how much we are loved by God. And why do we not see it? Because the cloud of self-[love...]

<summary>A letter from Saint Catherine of Siena to Ristoro Canigiani outlining the four effects of Charity and the importance of self-knowledge in experiencing God's love. She emphasizes that knowing one's sins through the lens of Christ's sacrifice leads to a "sweet bitterness" that fuels spiritual growth.</summary>
<keywords>Catherine of Siena, Charity, self-knowledge, Blood of Christ, Ristoro Canigiani, virtue, spiritual growth, divine love</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Letter 230 to Ristoro Canigiani. The previous page discussed how the soul must move beyond self-love to find the "Light" of faith. <page-num>200</page-num>

...self-love has obscured the eye of the **Intellect** <note>The "Eye of the Intellect" is a frequent metaphor in Catherine's writing, referring to the soul's capacity to perceive divine truth through reason and faith.</note>, where the pupil of the Light of the most holy **Faith** resides.

II. With this Light we come to the most perfect **Charity of God**, and with this we come to the Charity of our Neighbor; for the Soul that loves its **Creator** wishes to love that which He loves dearly. And therefore, seeing that He loves the **Creature** <note>In this context, "Creature" refers to any created human being.</note> dearly, it is constrained by the fire of His Charity to love them, and to serve them with great diligence and solicitude. That benefit which it cannot do for God—because He has no need of us—it wishes to do for the neighbor, ministering to them those graces and gifts, both spiritual and temporal, which it has received from God within itself. Whatever it ministers, it does so with a spiritual intention; for pure and liberal Charity does not seek its own interest <note>An allusion to 1 Corinthians 13:5: "Charity... seeketh not her own."</note>, because it does not love itself, nor the Creator, nor Creatures for its own sake, but loves every thing for God.

III. Charity is not feigned, nor double-minded, such that she shows one thing outwardly and carries another within. She is humble and not proud; indeed, **Humility** nourishes Charity in the Soul. She is not unfaithful, but faithful, serving God and her Neighbor faithfully, hoping in Him and not in herself. She is not imprudent, and therefore she conducts all things with great prudence. She is just, rendering to everyone their due: to God she renders glory and praise to His Name through holy **Virtues**; to the Neighbor, benevolence; and to herself, she renders hatred for the fault committed and displeasure toward her own fragility. She is strong, such that neither adversity can weaken her through impatience, nor prosperity through disordered joy. She pacifies those in discord, restrains anger, and tramples down sloth and envy, because she loves and enjoys the good of the Neighbor as if it were her own. She clothes the Soul with the garment of **Grace** with such strength that no blow can pierce the flesh; rather, it returns upon the one who throws it. Hence we see that if the Neighbor strikes us with injury and we bear it patiently, the poisoned blow of the fault returns to the one who threw it; and if the World strikes us with pleasure, delights, and its Statuses, and we receive it with displeasure, the blow returns to it with hatred; and if the Devil strikes with many and various and diverse temptations, we strike him with the strength of the **Will**, standing firm, constant, and persevering.

<summary>Saint Catherine explains how the "Light of Faith" leads to a perfect Charity that extends from God to one's neighbor. She describes Charity as a protective spiritual armor that deflects the "blows" of injury, worldly temptation, and demonic influence back upon their source.</summary>

I am certain that if you have this sweet Mother **Charity** within you, you will do it according to your power; you will fight your own frailty when it wishes to kick against **Reason**—otherwise, no. VII. Regarding the moderation of those who follow **Jesus Christ**.
VIII. Regarding the restlessness caused by **Self-love**.

## Letter 231.
