Hence we see that one moment a man is rich, and the next he is poor; now he is in great height, and now in great lowliness; and from health we come to infirmity, and from life to death. If they were his, he would keep them as long as he wished; but they have been given to him so that he may use them for his needs, but not so that he holds them with disordered love, loving them apart from God. When this is not done, his obedience is bypassed, and once he has become disobedient, he is deprived of the life of **Grace** and made worthy of eternal death.

Then, when the **Soul** regards this, it immediately conceives a hatred for its own **sensuality**, and for all the **World**—not that it does not love created things or **Man** (for one who has children loves his children, and his wife, and others who are joined to him), but he loves them with an **ordered love** <note>In medieval theology, *ordered love* (caritas) means loving things in their proper priority: God first, then others for God's sake. *Disordered love* (cupiditas) puts the self or the object above God.</note>, and not a disordered one. That is to say, for their sake he does not wish to set aside his **Soul** by offending God. Thus he loves with order, and not without order; for God does not forbid us to love, but rather He commands us to love our **Neighbor** as ourselves, but He forbids our disordered ways of loving. And this is what the **Soul** hates, because it sees that it is forbidden by God and is to its own harm. Then, since it has conceived a hatred toward that which it ought to hate—because the **Soul** cannot live without love—it immediately loves itself, and its **Neighbor**, and created things with an ordered love and with an affection for **Virtue**, placing before the eye of the **Intellect**, by the Light of the **Most Holy Faith**, the object of **Christ Crucified**; and in Him, the soul sees and knows what it ought to love.

<margin>Psalm 15 <note>original: "Pfal. 15." In the Vulgate Bible used by Catherine, this is Psalm 15 (Psalm 16 in modern numbering), which says, "I have said to the Lord: Thou art my God, for thou hast no need of my goods."</note></margin>
V. And because in the **Blood of Christ** the soul sees the ineffable love that God has for it—for the **Blood** has manifested the love and **Charity** of God to us more clearly than anything else—it immediately extends itself to love Him with all its heart, all its affection, and all its strength. For it is the nature of love to love as much as one feels oneself loved, and to love all the things that the beloved loves. And so, step by step, as the **Soul** has known the love of its **Creator** toward it, it loves Him, and in loving Him, it loves all those things that God loves. And because the soul sees that God supremely loves His **Creature** who possesses **Reason**—loving us so much that He gave us the **Word** of His Son so that He might give His life for us and wash away the leprosy of **mortal sin** in His **Blood**—therefore **Man** extends and shares his affection and **Charity** with his **Neighbor**. To the **Neighbor**, he wishes to return that which he cannot return to God: that is, to be of use to them. For He is our God, who has no need of us; and therefore, that usefulness which one cannot provide to Him, one provides to the **Neighbor**, who is the means that God has placed before us.

in which way we manifest the love that we have for Him. Because of this love, **Man** does not conceive hatred toward his **Neighbor** for any injury that might be done to him, but with **patience** he carries and supports his defects, grieving more for the offense against God and the damage to the other’s **Soul** than for his own injury or loss. This is **ordered love**, for it does not leave the order of **Charity**, and it clothes itself in the **New Man** <note>A reference to the Pauline concept in Ephesians 4:24 and Colossians 3:10 of putting off the old, sinful nature and putting on the nature of Christ.</note>, the sweet **Jesus Christ**, following His footsteps and His **Doctrine**, returning good to those who do him evil. He hates that which blessed Christ hates, and loves that which He loves. What did blessed Christ hate? He hated **Vice** and sin, honors, delights, and the statuses of the **World**. Sin displeased Him so much that, although there was no poison of sin in Him, He willed to take vengeance for our guilt and punish it upon His own **Body** with such torment and pain that our tongue would not be sufficient to narrate it. Honors and delights He despised; hence, when <margin>John 6</margin> they wished to make Him King, He vanished from their midst. Instead, He embraced **poverty**, injuries, scorns, and insults, enduring hunger, thirst, and many persecutions until the shameful death of the **Most Holy Cross**. He did not flee from this, but went to meet the Jews when they wished to take Him, saying: "Whom do you seek?" ### VI.

And thus the **Sweet Truth** <note>Catherine's characteristic name for Christ.</note> gave us the doctrine of **Charity** for our **Neighbor**—how much we ought to love him—and of **patience**, how we must bear everything that God permits to happen to us for the glory and praise of His **Name**. We must not avoid any fatigue or labor, nor ever turn our head back to look at the plow <note>original: "mirare l’ aratro". And truly we must bear this, and we have good reason to do so: first, because the fatigue is small; second, because it yields great fruit; and third, for the love of Him who gives it. How small is it? Do you know how much? As small as the point of a needle, because the fatigue lasts only as long as time; and you will see well that time is so small that **Man** cannot even imagine it. <page-num>278</page-num>

[ B ] **The liberty which was returned to him, etc.** This was discussed in the Annotations to Letter 191.

<margin>Part 3, final chapter.</margin>
[ C ] **I am he; take me, and let these others go.** <note>original: "Io ſon eſſo, pigliatemi, e laſciate ſtare coſtoro." This is a paraphrase of Christ’s words in the Garden of Gethsemane (John 18:8).</note> How well the Saint imitated her Divine Spouse in this example—which He left for us—is recounted by the Blessed Raymond <note>Raymond of Capua, Catherine’s confessor and biographer.</note> in his *Life of the Saint*, and was also reported in the Annotations to Letter 15.

[ D ] **And if he has sons, etc.** He had two sons, namely Pietro and Carlo, who married Francesca Strozzi.

<margin>Book 14. Book 9.</margin>
[ E ] **Rejoice in the event that has occurred, for it is the life of your Soul.** In the tumult raised by the People in Florence in the year 1378 <note>This refers to the Revolt of the Ciompi, a period of violent social and political upheaval in the Florentine Republic.</note>—of which we spoke in the Annotations to Letters 15 and 218—this Lord <note>Ristoro Canigiani.</note> suffered no small amount. This was because he had taken part in the *admonishing* <term>admonishing: "ammonire," a political tactic where citizens were accused of being Ghibellines (enemies of the Papacy) to bar them from public office</term> and was most devoted to Saint Catherine. He was, along with several other Lords of "Popular" families who therefore participated in the Government, declared "incapable" of ever holding any Office or Magistrate in the Republic again. This is confirmed by Ammirati <note>Scipione Ammirati (1531–1601), a famous historian of Florence.</note>, who states that the <insert>Balìa</insert> <note>A temporary committee with extraordinary powers in the Florentine government.</note> published a decree that Pietro degli Albizi, Carlo degli Strozzi, Buonajuto de' Serragli, Ristoro de' Canigiani, and Iengo de' Buondelmonti were to be numbered among the <term>Grandi: "the Great Ones," the old nobility who were legally excluded from government to prevent them from seizing power from the middle-class guilds</term> in the future. Because the Republic of Florence was governed by "the People," only those of the Popular class were eligible for public charges and to take part in affairs; thus, being "made a Grandee" was the same as losing all Authority and power in the Fatherland. That man called himself "blessed" who, through some merit, could obtain being received into the Popular Order, since being placed among the number of the *Grandi* had become a sort of punishment and condemnation. So says the same Author <note>Ammirati.</note>. The "event that occurred," therefore, can be nothing other than the aforementioned punishment of being made a Grandee, whereby in truth he was obliged to stay away from the Offices. Just as he had been exhorted by the Saint in another letter to do this of his own will, so that he might better attend to his Soul, she here adds that this was the "life of his soul." Perhaps she also speaks of the burning of his house, as will be mentioned in the Annotations to Letter 233.

# To Master Ristoro Canigiani of Florence, in Pistoia.

I. It demonstrates the necessity we have for the perfect light, in order to know the vanity of the world and our own sensuality, and to embrace virtue.
II. That the natural light given to us by God is insufficient, being obscured by self-love.
III. She rejoices with him for having been enlightened to know the perfect state, and how the state of marriage is imperfect, and she seeks to encourage him in the acquisition and exercise of virtue.
IV. Of four things necessary to grow in the aforementioned light.
V. Finally, she exhorts him to live with holy fear and frequency of the Sacraments.

## Letter 232.

->In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary.<-

**D**earest son in sweet Christ Jesus. I, Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ <note>This was Catherine’s standard greeting, mirroring the papal title "Servant of the servants of God."</note>, write to you in His precious Blood, with the desire to see you stir up the light that God has given you, so that it may grow continually in you. For without the perfect light <note>The "perfect light" refers to spiritual discernment or "the eye of the intellect" illuminated by faith.</note>, we could not know, nor love, nor clothe ourselves in the truth; and if we did not clothe ourselves in it, that light would turn into darkness for us. Therefore, it is necessary for everyone to have it perfectly, in whatever state of life they are. How is its perfection demonstrated? In this: that one sees perfectly, and through that seeing, knows and discerns the truth from the lie, and the vanity of the world. In this way, one holds fast to and embraces with the affection of love that truth which they have known, making themselves a lover of Virtue and hating Vice and their own sensuality <term>sensuality: "sensualità," in Catherine’s writings, refers not just to physical desires but to the self-centered ego that opposes the spirit</term>, which is the cause of every vice. This is because sensuality is a perverse law that always fights against the Spirit. Then, in truth, one shows that their [light] is perfect...

his vision, and that the cloud of unbelief <note>original: *Infedeltà*. II. But in what way, dearest son, can we attain this perfect light? I tell you: through light, in this manner. We have within us a natural light <note>The "natural light" refers to human reason and the innate conscience given to all people to distinguish basic right from wrong.</note> which God has given us, so that we may discern good from evil, the perfect thing from the imperfect, the pure from the impure, light from darkness, and the finite thing from the infinite. This is a knowledge that God has given us by nature, and we experience it continuously as a proven fact. 

But you might ask me: "If this knowledge is within us, why is it that we still cling to the side that is contrary to our salvation?" I answer you that this proceeds from self-love, which has covered this light just as a cloud sometimes covers the light of the sun; thus our error is not due to a defect in the light, but to the cloud. Then, free will <term>libero arbitrio: the human capacity to choose between different courses of action, which Catherine views as the gatekeeper of the soul</term> blindly takes those things that are harmful to the soul, and not those that are useful. 

The soul, by its nature, always desires what is good and a good thing, but its error lies in this: because the darkness of self-love has taken away its light, it does not seek the good where it actually is. And so such people wander like madmen <note>original: *Frenetichi*. Catherine often uses this term to describe those who have lost their spiritual senses and frantically pursue worldly vanities that cannot satisfy them.</note>, placing their hearts and their affection on transitory things that pass away like the wind. O man, foolish beyond all foolishness, who seeks the good where there is ultimate evil, and light where there is darkness! You seek life where there is death, wealth where there is ultimate poverty, and the infinite in finite things. 

Such a person could never find the good by searching where it is not. It is necessary to seek it in God, who is the Supreme and Eternal Good; and seeking it in Him, we shall find it, for our God has no evil in Himself, but only perfect good. Therefore, He would give us nothing other than what He has in Himself, just as the sun—because it has light within it—cannot give darkness. Hence we see that if we wish to see with this light, every thing that God...

<meta>This page continues Catherine of Siena’s letter to Ristoro Canigiani. In the previous section, she explained that while humans have a "natural light" (reason) to discern good from evil, it is often clouded by self-love. Here, she explains that God uses the trials of life to clear away these clouds and lead us toward "supernatural light" (faith).</meta>

God gives to us, and permits in this life, whatever labor, tribulation, and anguish there may be; he does it all to lead us to the Supreme Good. He does this so that we might seek our well-being in him and not in the world, for it cannot be found there—neither in riches, nor status, nor worldly delights. Instead, one finds only bitterness, sadness, and the loss of Grace in any soul that possesses these things outside the Will of God. So, for our own good and perfection—that is, so that we may seek him in truth—he allows these trials. Yet a person blinded by their own passion judges as "bad" that which is actually for their own good. Such a person does not seem to see the sin that deprives them of God and the life of Grace as an evil, and thus they deceive themselves. 

It is necessary, then, to stir up this natural light <note>The "natural light" refers to the human capacity for reason and conscience, which Catherine believes everyone possesses by birth.</note> by despising all worldly things and embracing Virtue. With this light, we must seek the "good" where it truly is; by seeking it, we shall find it in God. We will see the ineffable love he has shown us through his Son, and the Son's love shown through the Blood shed for us with such a fire of love.

<margin>1 Thessalonians 4</margin>
With this first natural light, which is imperfect, we will acquire a perfect, supernatural Light infused by Grace into our soul. This light will bind us to Virtue, confirming our resolve in every place, every time, and every state to which God may lead us. It keeps us always in accord with his sweet Will, which we will see desires nothing other than our sanctification <note>original: *Santificatione*. In this context, it refers to the process of being made holy or being set apart for God's purposes.</note>. While the first light, when stirred up as I said, "cuts" <note>Catherine uses the metaphor of "cutting" to describe how reason helps us detach from worldly vices.</note> us away from sin, the second light "binds" us and unites us with Virtue.

II. Oh, what greatest joy and heartfelt gladness I feel for your salvation! For it seems to me—as far as I can see in the presence of God and from the letter I received later—that the natural light in you is not clouded by the darkness of unbelief <note>original: *Infedeltà*. This refers to a lack of trust in God or a rejection of spiritual truth.</note>. If it were, you would not recognize so well the "stinking" world, its inconstancy, and the blows it deals to those who want to make a god out of it. Nor would you hold yourself to account with such self-reproach, nor would you cut yourself off from Vice, nor desire Virtue and the "perfect state"—that is, moving from the imperfect state of Marriage to the angelic state of Continence <term>angelic Continence: A medieval term for a life of celibacy or chastity, considered "angelic" because angels were thought to have no physical bodies or sexual impulses.</term>, which is perfect. 

Since God, through his infinite Mercy, has restored this light to you—of which you were deprived for so long through your own ignorance and fault—I want you to exercise it diligently. Cut yourself off from Vices and from selfish, sensory love <note>original: *amore sensitivo*. This refers to love based purely on physical feelings or selfish desires rather than spiritual principles.</note> with the knife of hate and love <note>A favorite metaphor of Catherine’s: "hatred" for one's own selfish ego and "love" for God's goodness.</note>, and with the light...

...to bind you to the **Virtues** with a true and perfect **Charity**, loving **God** above all things, and your Neighbor as yourself. But with this sweet light, you will trample all these battles and troubles under the feet of your holy affection.

### IV.

I want you, therefore, so that you may grow in light, to set four things before the eye of your **Intellect** as objects of meditation, so that light and **Virtue** may increase in your **Soul**. The first is that you consider how much you are loved by God. It is this love that created you in his Image and likeness, and "recreated" <note>Catherine uses the term "recreated" to describe the act of redemption; if the first creation was birth, the second is being "born again" into a state of grace through Christ’s sacrifice.</note> you in Grace through the **Blood of his Son**. Out of love, he has preserved time for you, so that you might have the space to correct your life, and he has given you all the other graces and spiritual and temporal gifts which I will not list here; all these are given to you out of the affection of love, by grace, and not because they are owed. 

If you consider and reflect on them carefully, you will be compelled to love, because the soul is naturally drawn to love that by which it sees itself loved. Thus, seeing itself so ineffably loved, the soul runs after love, loving him and that which he loves most; it is pleased by what pleases him and displeased by what displeases him. And because the soul sees that the **Creator** supremely loves his Creature who possesses Reason, the soul loves that creature too. The service and utility that it cannot perform for God, it performs for the Creature for the sake of his love. 

The second thing is that we consider how much we are bound and obligated to love God sincerely, as free people and not as slaves—meaning we should not show one thing in our actions while holding another in our heart. We cannot hide from the eye of God, and therefore it is necessary for us to serve him with great sincerity.

**Virtue** is pleasing and useful to the **Soul**. Sin was so displeasing to Him that He made the body of the humble and Immaculate Lamb into an anvil, forging our iniquities upon it <note>This "anvil" metaphor is a hallmark of Catherine's writing, suggesting that Christ’s body took the "hammer blows" of human sin during the Passion to reshape humanity.</note>. It is so harmful to us that it takes away our light, deprives us of the life of **Grace**, and gives us eternal damnation. **Virtue** is so pleasing to Him that, out of the sweet affection of love, He makes the virtuous Man into another Himself, and in this life He makes him taste the earnest <note>original: "arra" — a down payment or security deposit; Catherine means that the peace felt by the virtuous is a "deposit" or foretaste of Heaven's joy</note> of eternal Life; for while standing in the tempestuous sea of many labors and bitternesses, he tastes Peace and sweetness. The fourth and last [point] is that we consider how every fault is punished and every good is rewarded, because God knows how to, is able to, and wants to punish the fault and reward the pains that we sustain in this life for the glory and praise of His Name. Of this reward the glorious Apostle Paul speaks, saying: the sufferings of this life are not <margin>To the Romans 8 <note>original: "Ad Rom. 8."</note></margin> worthy of that future glory which God has prepared for His servants. 

This object, divided into four parts, will regulate and order your life in love and in the holy fear of God; you will follow and improve the order that you have begun to keep in your living. Let the fire of holy desire grow in you, and it will give you what you lack in perfection; and God, like a just and good Physician, will apply a remedy to whatever you feel is hindering you. Give, give a kick to the World <note>original: "Date di calcio al Mondo" — a strong idiomatic expression meaning to reject or spurn worldly values</note>; cast it out of your heart and your affection just as it casts you out. Bind yourself to Christ Crucified so that you may receive the fruit of His precious Blood with the supernatural Light. In that Light, you will see the natural [light] excited <note>Catherine often discusses the "natural light" of human reason being elevated or "excited" by the "supernatural light" of faith.</note>, as was said; you will fulfill all the aforementioned things, and in no other way. And therefore I said that I desired to see you excite the light that God has given you, so that it may continually grow in you; for without the light, we would walk in darkness. With this light, I want you to raise your family with the holy and true fear of God. In the state of **Marriage**, live as an orderly Man and not like an animal, holding in due reverence the days that are commanded by the Holy Church, so that your Tree may produce good fruit.

### V.

I want you to use **Confession** often, and **Communion** during the Easter seasons, as a person who fears God ought to do. Then you will be my joy and my gladness, when I see you walking in light and not in darkness. Being at a distance...

# To Pietro Canigiani in Florence.

I. She desires to see him clothed in the wedding garment of Charity, so as not to be excluded from the Wedding of Heaven.
II. Of the confusion of the Soul at death, which finds itself without Charity.
III. That self-love and sensory love is what deprives us of Charity, as it is contrary to it, and of the difference that exists between the two.
IV. Of the pains and labors borne by the lovers of the World.
V. Of the sweetness that Charity brings, and how it separates us from the World and unites us to God.
VI. How through it, Man orders his Powers and his senses.
VII. She exhorts him to leave behind the anxieties of the World and embrace the Virtues, frequenting the Most Holy Sacraments and raising his Family in the fear of God:

## Letter 233.

->In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified and of sweet Mary.<-

...she made herself a servant, serving them—the World and her own sensuality; the reward she receives for it is confusion and reproach with much suffering and torment. ## III. Who has deprived us of it?

Self-love; for he who loves himself with sensory love <note>sensory love: *amore sensitivo*, referring to love driven by the physical senses, ego, and worldly desires rather than spiritual logic</note> cannot love God, nor even himself with reasonable love, because the one love is contrary to the other, so much so that they have no conformity together. O dearest Father, look how different they are, and how dangerous and painful sensory love is, and how sweet Divine Love is. The difference is this: he who has placed his affection in the World loves and seeks all those things in which he can take sensory delight; he seeks honors, high positions <note>original: *Stati*, referring to social status, rank, or political offices</note>, and worldly riches, whereas the Servant of God flees them like poison. For the Servant has removed his affection and love, pulling his heart away and placing it only in his Creator, considering it a glory to be deprived of his positions and riches, delights and pleasures, and to receive great persecutions and reproach from the World and its followers. 

He bears everything with true and holy patience, because he has trampled <note>original: *conculcato*; meaning to tread underfoot, subdue, or master through discipline</note> everything with the feet of his affection. He is made Lord of the World because he has left it fully—not halfway, but entirely—and if not in actual practice, at least with holy and true desire, valuing the World for what it is worth and nothing more, and despising his own fragility, holding it as a servant subjected to the Lady of Reason. 

In contrast, the lover of himself makes himself a god of the World, its pleasures, and himself. That is, the time he should spend serving his Creator, he spends on vain and transitory works and on his fragile body, which is here today and gone tomorrow; for it is food for worms, food for death, and a sack full of dung <note>A common medieval ascetic trope used to remind the reader of physical mortality and the corruption of the flesh compared to the eternal soul</note>. He loves pride, and God loves humility; he is impatient, and God wants patience; he has a narrow heart, where neither God nor Neighbor can fit through love, whereas God is vast and generous. And therefore the Servants of God, followers of Divine Charity, who truly walk by the Doctrine of Christ Crucified, dispose themselves to give their lives for the honor of God and for the salvation of...

...neighbor, and the wretched man, the **Servant of the World**, gnaws him with the teeth of envy and hatred; with anger and displeasure, he devours his own flesh with an appetite for revenge. This one delights in the mire of impurity <note>original: *loto dell’immonditia*; referring to the "mud" or "filth" of moral corruption</note>, while the **Servant of God** delights in the scent of Purity and Continence; even while remaining in the legitimate state of Marriage, he strives for the love of Virtue to sense and taste the fragrance of Continence <note>The text suggests that even within marriage, a "Servant of God" maintains a spiritual self-control and purity of intent</note>. In all things we find that these two are contrary to one another, and therefore they cannot remain together; rather, the one drives out the other. 

Hence we see that when a man turns to recognize his own misery, and the little firmness and stability of the World—and its inconstancy—he immediately hates it, and with that hatred, he drives out [worldly] love. And because the Soul cannot live without love, he immediately loves that which he has seen and known through the light of the Intellect in the affection of Divine Charity. He finds within himself the great Goodness of God, and the firmness and stability that he receives from Him, seeing himself recreated in Grace in the Blood of the humble and Immaculate Lamb, who for love has washed the face of his Soul with His own Blood. Seeing himself loved so much, he cannot help but love in return. Therefore, the light [of the intellect] is very necessary for us to recognize the love that God has for us, and the graces and gifts we receive continually from Him. 

This Love makes a man grateful and mindful toward God and his Neighbor, just as self-love makes him ungrateful and unmindful, because he attributes what he has to his own wisdom. And what proves this is so? His ingratitude; this ingratitude shows itself through the faults he commits every day, just as gratitude demonstrates that the Soul attributes only to God that which she possesses—except for sin, which is nothingness <note>In medieval theology, sin was often defined as a "non-thing" or a privation of being, rather than a created substance</note>; and Virtue demonstrates this gratitude. It is indeed true, then, that in every thing they are different.

## IV.

I say that the **Servant of the World**, a lover of self, bears very great and intolerable burdens; for, as **Saint Augustine** says, the Lord has permitted that the man who loves inordinately <note>To love "inordinately" means to love things out of their proper order, such as loving the creature more than the Creator</note> shall be a burden to himself. This person carries the Cross of the Devil; for if he acquires delights, he acquires them with pain; and having them, he holds them with anxiety for fear of losing them; or if he loses them, he is tortured with the greatest impatience; and if he cannot have them,

...with difficulty, because he would desire them. He is so blind that he loses his liberty, making himself a servant and **slave to sin**, to the world with its delights, and to his own fragility. These are the general pains for the lovers of the world: but how many are the particular ones? Every day we see the labors that men endure in the service of the Devil. Alas, to acquire Hell they do not care for bodily death, nor do they refuse any labor; and I, wretched as I am, to have God and to acquire God, never sustained even a small thing! My own shadow has made me afraid. Truly I confess that the **children of darkness** put the **children of the Light** to shame and confusion <note>original: *fanno vergogna, e confusione*; likely referencing Luke 16:8, where the "children of this world" are described as more shrewd than the "children of light."</note>, because they go with more diligence, practice, and with greater labor to Hell than the children of the Light go to **Eternal Life**; so that the labor is great, and the bitterness is much, which this perverse and miserable love provides.

**V.** But true and most perfect love is of such delight, sweetness, and gentleness, that no bitterness can take away its sweetness, nor can bitterness disturb it; rather, it greatly strengthens the mind, because it draws the soul closer to its Creator, and in Him, the soul tastes the sweetness of His **Charity**, holding with living faith that whatever God gives and permits, He does for its own good and for its **Sanctification**. Who has shown this to the soul? The **Blood of Christ**, in which it saw with the light of faith that if He had wanted anything other than our good, God would not have given us such a **Redeemer** <note>original: *Ricomperatore*</note> as was the Word of His Son; and the Son would not have given His life, which He gave with such a fire of love, laying our iniquities upon His own Body. He fills the soul with strength and long perseverance, not wanting the head to turn back to look at the plow <note>A reference to Luke 9:62: "No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for service in the kingdom of God."</note>. He is not scandalized, neither in himself nor in his neighbor, but with benevolence and fraternal Charity he bears and supports his neighbor's defects. He feels no pain for the loss of status, nor, if he has it, does he possess it with anxiety; and if he does not have it, he does not seek it, nor does he labor to have it, because his affection is ordered and directed according to the **Will of God**, in which he has slain his own self-will <note>original: *Volontà propria*; in this mystical tradition, "slaying" the self-will is the key to spiritual peace.</note>, which is the very thing that gives us pain and labor.

**VI.** This love cuts him off from the world and unites him to God through the affection of love; it orders the memory to retain Your benefits; it—

And so it finds itself clothed in Charity, for in no other way could it reach its end.

### VII.
Wherefore, considering that there is no other way, I said that I desired to see you founded in true and most perfect love. And so I wish for you to do in this moment of time, which God has preserved for us by mercy: that you now begin anew to strip yourself of yourself and clothe yourself in **Christ Crucified**. Let the dead bury their dead from now on <note>A reference to Matthew 8:22, advising the recipient to leave behind worldly or spiritually "dead" concerns</note>, and you follow Him in all truth. Let go of the worries of the world from this day forward; leave anxiety where it belongs, and steal time for holy exercises with true and real virtues. Do not wait for more time, for we are not certain of having it. Love, love, for you are ineffably loved! Take delight and enjoyment with the servants of God, keeping their company. Go to confession very often, though I do not believe I need to say it; and receive Communion on all the solemn Easters <note>original: *Pasque solenni*; referring to the major feast days of the Church year</note>, so that you may more perfectly acquire this sweet garment; and study so that the family may be raised in the holy fear of God. I say no more to you. Remain in the holy and sweet love of God. Sweet Jesus. Jesus Love.

# To Matteo di Giovanni Colombini of Siena.

I. **O**f the truth revealed to us by God, namely, that we are created in His Image and likeness, to later possess God Himself as the supreme Good.

## Letter 234.

->In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary.<-

I. **D**earest Brother and Son in sweet Christ Jesus, I, Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, write to you with the desire to see you with true and most perfect light, in which light you may know and see the truth; which truth is that thing which sets us free—that is, that by knowing it, we love it, and by loving it, it frees us from the servitude of mortal sin. What truth is this, which it behooves us to know? It is a truth birthed by the ineffable love of God,

...to which truth we must render the debt of love and of hatred. <note>In Catherine’s theology, "loving the truth" usually involves a corresponding "holy hatred" for one's own selfish or sinful inclinations.</note> In what way? In this: that we know the supreme and Eternal Good, and the ineffable Love with which God created us in His Image and likeness; and He created us for this truth, so that we might taste His supreme and Eternal Good, and so that we might give glory and praise to His Name. And to fulfill this truth in us, He gave us the Word of His Son, <note>The "Word" (Verbo) refers to Jesus Christ as the eternal expression of God the Father.</note> and in His Blood, He recreated us in Grace.

**II.** We must come to this knowledge, practicing it with the greatest care; but to this we cannot come without the light, and the light we cannot have while under the cloud of self-love. This self-love clouds the eye of the Intellect, so that it does not let it know or discern the truth; instead, it sees a lie as truth, and truth as a lie. It considers transitory things to be firm and of great consolation, yet they all fade away just like a flower which, once picked, immediately loses its beauty. Honor, riches, status, and pleasures all pass like the wind. Everything is changeable, whereby from health we come to infirmity, from wealth to poverty, and from life to death. And the foolish man, a lover of himself, being blind, judges everything to the contrary and holds it so. And what demonstrates that he holds it so? The disordered love and affection that he has for himself and for the world.

**III.** All this happens to him because he has lost the light; for if he had light in truth, he would hold that God is supremely Good—an incomprehensible and inestimable Good that no one can estimate, but only He Himself understands and values. He is the supreme and Eternal Wealth; He is the just and merciful Physician who gives us the medicines necessary for our infirmities. Thus says the glorious Paul: <margin>Romans 5</margin> <note>original: "Ad Rom. 5." Catherine frequently paraphrases St. Paul's teachings on God's grace and intervention.</note> When the human race lay sick, the great Physician of the world came and healed our infirmities. So He gives to everyone according to what our wounds need with the fire of Divine Charity; sometimes He draws blood from us—that is, by taking away those things that are harmful to our salvation and which stand in the way between God and us. Hence, from some He takes away children, from others temporal substance, from others health, and from some worldly status, striking us with many tribulations; and this He does not do...

...out of hatred, but out of singular love; He deprives us of the vain delights of the Earth, to give us fully the Goods of Heaven. He is a benign and Eternal Judge, and, as a just Lord, He renders to everyone their due; wherefore every good is rewarded, and every fault punished. And with the holy force that we shall use against our perverse **Will**, and with violence <note>Catherine frequently references Matthew 11:12, suggesting that the "violent" or those who use spiritual force against their own selfish nature take the kingdom of heaven by force.</note> we shall acquire the true and real **Virtues**, and our labor shall be rewarded with immortal Goods. With this light, one knows the truth regarding the **World**, which has in itself no firmness nor any stability. In vain does he labor who has spent and spends all his time in the **World**, making a God of his **Children** <note>original: "Figliuoli". Catherine warns against an attachment to family that replaces one's devotion to God.</note> and of riches, and does not realize that all these things give him death, depriving him of the life of **Grace**. Nor does he seem to know that God has permitted disordered love to be unbearable to itself; whereby in this life he tastes the earnest-money <term>arra: a pledge or down payment; here, a foretaste of future suffering.</term> of **Hell**, only because he has not known the truth due to the loss of light.

**IV.** Therefore I desire, Dearest **Son**, that we sleep no longer, but with great solicitude let us wake from sleep, lifting the cloud of self-love from the eye of our **Intellect**; and by doing so, you will fulfill in yourself the **Will** of God and my desire. For considering that without light we cannot know the truth, I have a desire to see true light in you, so that you may perfectly know the truth, which light and truth will make you constant and persevering in that which you have begun with a holy and true desire. Do not delay for any space of time, for you are not certain of having any; but in everything, without servile fear <note>Fear based on the threat of punishment rather than love for God.</note>, with true and perfect hope, trusting in your **Creator**, order your life and regulate yourself in all things, satisfying **Conscience**, putting an end and limit to every disordered way of living with true perseverance. Take away the sadness from your heart, and with the greatest joy recognize the ineffable Love and the fullness of Divine **Mercy**, which has overflowed upon you. ## To Pietro di Giovanni Venture of Siena.

I. She exhorts him to perseverance in Virtue.
II. That this is obtained by reflecting on the love that God bears for us, and on His benefits, with which He moves us to love Him in return.
III. That beyond this, the knowledge of oneself and of one's own faults is necessary, depriving ourselves of self-love.
IV. That we must not trust in ourselves, but withdraw into the Side of Christ Crucified.
V. She exhorts him to conform himself to the Infant Jesus at His Holy Nativity, and discourses on the love shown to us in this holy Mystery and in His other works.

## Letter 235.

### In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified and of sweet Mary.

I. **D**earest son in Christ sweet Jesus. I, Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious Blood, with the desire to see you persevering in every virtue; for without perseverance you would not receive the Crown of Glory, which is given to true combatants. But you will say to me: "How can I acquire this perseverance?" I answer you: That a person serves a creature only as much as he loves it, and no more; and he fails in service as much as he lacks love, and he loves as much as he ought to love.

## II. You see, then, that love is born from seeing yourself loved, and this love makes you persevere. To the extent that you open the eye of your <term>Intellect</term> <note>The faculty of the soul responsible for spiritual understanding and perceiving divine truths.</note> to gaze upon the fire and the abyss of God's inestimable Charity toward you—which love He has shown you through the <term>Word of the Son</term> <note>A reference to Jesus Christ as the "Logos" or Eternal Word, through whom God’s love is communicated to humanity.</note>—to that same extent you will be compelled by love to love Him in truth with all your heart, all your affection, and all your strength. You will do so freely, sincerely, and purely, without any regard for your own self-interest. You see that God loves you for your own good and not for His own, because He is our God and has no need of us. In the same way, you and every rational creature ought to love God for God’s sake, insofar as He is the supreme and eternal Good, and not for your own profit; and you should love your neighbor for His sake. Once you have established this beginning and foundation in the affection of Charity, you immediately begin to serve Him with the instrument of the Virtues.

## III. Thus, with light and with love you will acquire Virtue and persevere in it. But take heed: in seeing yourself loved by God, it is necessary that you also see your own guilt and ingratitude. You must weigh your faults within the holy knowledge of yourself, so that you do not forget the "little virtue" of true Humility, and so that you do not become local or fall into self-pleasing. Do you know how necessary it is for us to acknowledge and weigh our faults in order to preserve and increase the life of <term>Grace</term> in the soul? It is as necessary as bodily food is for preserving life in the body. Therefore, take away the cloud of self-love so that it does not block the light. From this light you will gain perfect self-knowledge, and with that knowledge comes love and hatred <note>In Catherinian spirituality, this refers to a "holy hatred" of one's own selfish sensuality or ego, which stands in the way of God.</note>. In that love you will find the virtue of perseverance, and thus you will fulfill the Will of God and my desire for you—which Will and desire is to see you grow and persevere until death in true and real Virtues.

## IV. And take care that you do not trust in yourself. Such trust is a "subtle wind of reputation" <note>An inflated or vain opinion of oneself.</note> that rises from self-love. If you trust yourself, you would immediately fail and turn your head back to look at the plow <note>A reference to Luke 9:62: "No one who puts a hand to the plow and looks back is fit for service in the kingdom of God."</note>. Just as the love of God, acquired through self-knowledge with true humility, makes you persevere in Virtue, so self-love—with the self-esteem that makes you trust in yourself, as was said—takes Virtue away from you,

## V.
I want you to begin now—you and those other negligent sons—to conform yourselves to this Child, whom Holy Church now presents to us: the <term>Word Incarnate</term>. And what more can we see to the confusion of our Pride than to see God humbled for Man? The height of the Deity descended to such lowliness as is our humanity? Who is the cause of it? Love. Love makes Him dwell in the stable in the midst of animals; Love makes Him enveloped in reproaches <note>original: "fatollare d'obbrobrij." An archaic expression suggesting being swaddled or surrounded by shame/insults.</note>; [Love] clothes Him in pains, and makes Him endure hunger and thirst. Love makes Him run with prompt obedience even unto the shameful death of the Cross. Love makes Him go to Hell and strip <term>Limbo</term> <note>In medieval theology, the "Harrowing of Hell" where Christ rescued the souls of the righteous who died before His resurrection.</note> to give full reward to those who had served Him in truth and had waited a long time for their Redemption. Love made Him leave Himself to us as food. Love, after the Ascension, sent the fire of the Holy Spirit, which enlightened us with His doctrine—which is that way founded in truth that gives us life, draws us out of darkness, and gives us light in the eternal Vision of God. 

Everything, then, has been done by Love. Well, then, should man be ashamed and confused within himself, he who does not love nor respond to such an abyss of love. Truly wretched is he who, being able to have the fire, lets himself die of cold, or having the food before him, lets himself die of hunger. Take, take your Food, Christ sweet Jesus Crucified, and in no other way; for if you wanted Him in any other way, you would not be constant nor persevering, and perseverance is that which is crown- <note>The text breaks mid-word here; the catchword indicates the word "coronata" (crowned).</note>

[ A ] Pietro di Giovanni Venture is found numbered among the disciples of our Saint; and besides this letter, he received another from her along with Stefano di Corrado Maconi <note>Stefano Maconi was Catherine's primary secretary and later became a Carthusian monk.</note>. He was a Sienese Noble, and in 1395, he was sent by his country to the Mountain Regions as an Ambassador for affairs regarding public service. The name "Venture" was originally a personal name, not a Family name, although in the long run—as the descendants of Venture kept that name as an addition to distinguish themselves from others—it later became a Surname, as has happened to other families. There were several houses of the "Venturi" of old standing in <term>Siena</term>, some of which are called the Venturi, one the Venturi Gallerani, another the Venturi Guelfi, and another simply of Venture. The two which, besides their own surname, have that of either the Gallerani or the Guelfi, are probably of the same <term>Consorteria</term> <note>A "consorteria" was a family alliance or clan in medieval Italy, often sharing a coat of arms and political interests.</note>, displaying the same <term>Device</term> <note>original: "Divisa" — a heraldic symbol.</note> of three red roses cut by a blue <term>Fess</term> <note>original: "Fascia" — a horizontal band across a heraldic shield.</note> in the first and fourth partitions of the shield; they belong to one of the four <term>Orders</term> <note>original: "Ordine" — likely referring to the *Monti*, the political factions or "orders" that governed Siena (such as the Monte dei Nove or Monte dei Gentiluomini).</note> into which this flourishing and numerous Nobility is distributed. They hold that additional name because they were grafted into those houses that were already noble but are now extinct. That of the Venturi is in the same Order, but the <term>Coat of Arms</term> <note>original: "Arma".</note> is somewhat different, being of silver, whereas that of the other two is of gold, without any other variety in the Arms. That this Pietro was not of any of these, but of another of a completely different Order and Shield, is shown to us (if other proofs were lacking) by his being called "of Venture" and not "of the Venturi," just as he is still called today. In truth, he is spoken of as one of the Borgognoni, but his lords always used the surname of Venture, placing it after the other name of Borgognoni. This is believed to have been brought from France into this house by one of their ancestors who lived for a long age in Burgundy <note>original: "Borgogna".</note>, from which he took the nickname of "Borgognino," which remained with his descendants; from there, perhaps, he also brought the insignia of the **Golden Lilies** on the blue <term>Bend</term> <note>original: "Banda" — a diagonal heraldic stripe.</note> upon the **Golden Shield**.

## To Rainaldo da Capua <note>Rainaldo da Capua was a Dominican friar and a close associate of Catherine. He later became the Master General of the Dominican Order.</note> of subtle intellect in Naples, Investigator of the Mysteries of God, and of the Holy Scripture.

II. Which things they may be that take this Light from us.
III. Which things they may be that restore it to us, and especially of keeping the love of Christ Crucified before our eyes.
IV. That which the Soul does when it possesses this Light within itself.
V. Of the effects that this Light produces in the Soul.
VI. That there are many who go about investigating Divine Mysteries without study and without Humility, and how presumptuous a thing this is.
VII. That the humble Believer frankly confesses his defects.
VIII. Of the fruit of Faith, that is, Eternal Life.
IX. Of Hope, and its effects.
X. The Temptation which the Devil is accustomed to make regarding the full Confession of sins.

### Letter 236.

->In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary.<-

I. **D**earest Brother in sweet Jesus Christ. I Catherine, servant and slave of the Servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious Blood, with the desire to see in you a true and most perfect light, that is, the <term>Light of Most Holy Faith</term> <note>In Catherine’s theology, "Light" (lume) is not just knowledge, but a supernatural clarity granted by God that allows the soul to see the truth of its own sinfulness and God’s infinite love.</note>, because without the light we would walk in darkness, and by the darkness we would be harmed. It is necessary for us, therefore, to have the light. Now let us see what it is that takes it from us, and what gives it to us, and what the Soul does that has this light within itself, and what fruit it receives from it.

<margin>B</margin>
II. If we consider closely why the physical <note>original: "temporale," literally "temporal" or "worldly" as opposed to the eternal/spiritual eye.</note> eye is lost, we see that it is lost either by a knife that strikes the eye, or by a stone, or by dirt, or by some other thing that hits it, or by excessive heat—as in the case of those who have been <term>blinded by the basin</term> <note>original: "abbacinati." This refers to a medieval method of blinding where a red-hot metal basin was held before a prisoner's eyes to dry the pupils and destroy sight through intense heat and glare.</note>, where the heat and the glare of the basin dry up the pupil and sight is lost. In many other and diverse ways the physical light is lost; in the same way, the eye of the **Intellect** is blinded by heat and glare—that is, by the heat of self-love and the glare of human opinion and pleasure. What is the knife? It is the hatred of Virtue; and the stones are Vices, with which the hand of **free will** strikes the eye, making it unfaithful to God and faithful to the World. With this hand, it throws dirt into the eye—that is, the eye of the Intellect—and as soon as this Intellect has placed the Earth <note>“Earth” here symbolizes worldly, material desires and concerns that obstruct spiritual vision.</note> before itself, night appears, and thus the Soul is continually harmed by darkness. Many are the causes that deprive us of light, but these are the primary ones.

III. What way is there to flee the darkness and acquire the light? I say that Man can regain it in the same way he lost it; not with the same affection, but with the same act and with that same hand of **free will**. No Demon nor any creature can bind this will unless we wish it, by binding it with our own Will. What is that "heated basin" which we ought to place before the eyes of our Intellect? It is **Christ Crucified**, who, within the basin of our Humanity, holds a great heat, manifesting to us the fire and the abyss of the inestimable Charity of God through the glare of the said Divine Nature, which is steeped and kneaded with the fire and with our own Nature. This object of this sweet **Word** <note>original: "Verbo," referring to Christ as the Logos.</note> Christ Crucified casts out such heat and light that it dries up the moisture of self-love, and with His Light, He dissolves the darkness, and the Soul receives a **supernatural Light** infused into the Intellect.

IV. As soon as the Light is within the Soul, it begins to remove from itself that thing which takes away the light, and places within itself that which gives it light. Then it takes up the knife of the hatred of Vice and the stones of the love of the Virtues, and with them, it strikes its own eye; that is, the eye focuses upon the Virtues to look upon their excellence and how pleasing they are to God.

<summary>Catherine explains how the spiritual "eye" is blinded by self-love and vice, much like physical eyes are blinded by heat or injury. She proposes that looking upon Christ Crucified acts as a restorative "heat" that burns away self-love and restores supernatural sight through free will.</summary>

Here, she explains how the soul can regain its spiritual vision through prayer and the "wind" of the Holy Spirit.</meta>

and useful to oneself. And immediately, once he has seen them, there comes a subtle wind of a hunger for the honor of God and the salvation of Souls, with a desire to follow the **Doctrine of Truth**. This desire is a subtle wind that draws the earth <note>As established on the previous page, "earth" represents worldly distractions and material desires that clog the spiritual eye.</note> out of the eye, purifying it continually with humble, continual, and faithful **Prayer**, in which Prayer it draws to itself the Clemency of the Holy Spirit, who directs the affection into an **ordered Love** <note>original: "Amore ordinato." In medieval theology, this refers to the proper "order of charity," where one loves God above all else, and neighbors and oneself correctly for God's sake.</note>. This affection draws to itself Heaven and Earth—that is, the vessel of the Body of one's Neighbor, who should be placed within the pupil of Faith; and in his affection, he must be faithful for the honor of God, in seeking the salvation of Souls and aiding the Body in its necessity, as much as possible. Now, by this way, as **free will** changes the affection, it will regain its light.

V. There are many other ways, but these are the principal ones.
<margin>C</margin> Let us see now what this **Light of Faith** does in the Soul; it does this: it gives birth to a **Son of Love**. Once it has given birth to him in the Doctrine of Christ Crucified, it nourishes him in the delight of **Charity for the Neighbor**; for without it, this Son would fail, because the Love of the Creator cannot exist, nor be preserved, without the love of the Creature for God’s sake. Why did I say that it gave birth to a Son of love? Because a thing is loved only as much as it is known, and it is known only as much as it is seen, and the seeing is as perfect as the light is perfect. One nourishes the other, just as a Mother does, who gives birth to the Son and nourishes him at her breast; then, when the Son is grown, he nourishes the Mother with his labor, and thus each aids the other. 

In this way, the Son of Divine Charity nourishes the light, giving to the Soul sweet, loving, and painful desires in the sweet presence of God, following the footsteps of Christ Crucified girded with true Humility, glorying in the shames <note>original: "obrobrij," meaning the insults or reproaches Christ suffered during the Passion.</note> of Christ Crucified and in His pains, delighting in bearing the pains of Body and mind; in whatever way God grants them, he is patient in everything. Who has done this? **Faith**; because with that light, he knew in the Blood of Christ that God wants nothing other than our **sanctification**, and whatever He gives—tribulation, consolations, and temptations—He gives only for this end, so that we may be sanctified in Him. Therefore, the Believer is patient, for he cannot, nor should he, complain about his own good.

<meta>This page continues Catherine of Siena’s discourse on the spiritual life. While the previous page discussed the "ordered love" required to see clearly through the eye of the intellect, this section warns against the spiritual pride of trying to intellectually master God's mysteries without first practicing self-knowledge and humility.</meta>

<page-num>301</page-num>
<margin>D</margin>
<margin>E</margin>
<meta>catchword: fear (timore)</meta>

**VI. The humble faithful person does not wish to investigate the hidden Mysteries of God within themselves, nor in others, nor in things visible or invisible; instead, they only seek to know themselves, and in everything to know and see the eternal Will of God, tasting the fire of His Charity within. They do not wish to lift themselves up like the proud or the presumptuous who—before they have known themselves and entered the valley of Humility—wish to set themselves to investigating the deeds of God, thinking and saying: "Why has God done this? And why has He not done it in such a way? And why has He given this to me, and not to that person?" This presumptuous person wants to impose laws there, where they ought instead to recognize and consider His greatness and Goodness in the diverse things they see—just as the humble faithful person does, who sees and considers everything within His Greatness, Power, and infinite Goodness.**

**There are many who, without Humility and without the study of knowing their own defects, will sharpen their Intellect, and with a darkened eye will want to understand the Holy Scripture and its depths, wanting to explain and understand it in their own way. They will study the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation, often considered the most difficult and mysterious book of the Bible to interpret.</note> not with humility, nor with the light of Faith, but with Unbelief; they will entangle themselves in things they do not know how to escape, and thus from life they draw death, and from light, darkness. The Mind, which should remain full of God, is then full of fantasies; the fruit they acquire is confusion and darkness of the mind. This happens to them because before they descended, they wanted to ascend.**

**Oh, how shameful is our life, for we do not yet know even ourselves! I do not even observe the Law that is set for me, yet I want to impose laws on God to know His secret things! If we want to be able to see these Stars of His Mysteries, let us enter into the depths of the Well of true Humility <note>This refers to the ancient observation that one can see the stars during the daylight if one is at the bottom of a deep, dark well; Catherine uses this as a metaphor for how only the humblest soul can see divine truths.</note>. This is what the faithful person does: they cast themselves to the earth, seeking lowliness. Then God makes them very high. They do not go seeking reasons for how things can be, because holy Faith makes clear to them whatever the Devil or their own passion might put into doubt. They mirror themselves in the mirror of continual Prayer—that is, they continually see themselves in the truth, and from the truth they draw holy and true desire, with which desire they offer up the incense of humble Prayer.**

**VII. This faith makes the heart sincere, which sincerely confesses its defects and does not hide them out of shame, nor for [fear]**

<summary>Catherine warns against the intellectual pride of trying to scrutinize God's mysteries, arguing that true spiritual vision is only achieved through the "well of humility" and self-knowledge. She criticizes those who try to interpret complex scriptures like the Apocalypse without a humble heart.</summary>

...fear of punishment, but with hatred of the fault. Through holy Confession, the soul throws out all its foulness; it does not hide its sins out of fear of being reproached, nor does it omit anything for any reason. This is the work of Faith.

VIII. Now let us see what fruit Faith gives us. In this life, it gives us the fullness of Grace, and in the next, Eternal Life. Whom has God appointed to administer this to us? **Hope**. By what power? By the power of the Blood of the humble Lamb <note>For Catherine, the "Blood of the Lamb" (Christ) is the ultimate evidence of God's love and the source of all spiritual strength.</note>. This is that humble Hope which does not rely on its own strength, nor does it fall into despair over any sin that has entered the soul. Instead, it hopes in the Blood and casts out despair, judging the **Mercy of God**—which it finds in the Blood—to be far greater than its own misery.

IX. O Hope, sweet sister of Faith! You are the one who, with the keys of the Blood, unlocks Eternal Life. You guard the City of the Soul from the Enemy of confusion <note>In this context, "confusion" refers to a spiritual state of overwhelming shame and anxiety that makes a person doubt God's forgiveness.</note>. You do not slow your steps even when the Devil tries to weigh the soul down with the gravity of committed sins to drive it into despair. Instead, you persevere manfully in virtue, placing the price of the Blood in the balance. You place the Crown of Victory upon the head of perseverance, because you hoped to receive it through the power of the Blood. You are she who binds the Devil of confusion with the rope of living Faith. You respond to a subtle deception that he uses against the soul to keep it in continuous darkness and affliction.

X. This deception is this: sometimes, after the soul has confessed its defects honestly—leaving nothing out through malice <note>original: "covelle," an old Sienese dialect term meaning "anything at all."</note>—the Devil then tries to hinder the Mind. To prevent the soul from receiving the fruit of Confession with a burning heart, he wants to make it feel as though it has not confessed its defects well, saying: "You have not told them all, and those you did tell, you did not reveal in the way you should have." He sends many other such thoughts and passions into the soul. If the soul does not then rise up with prudence and hope, it remains in a state of lukewarmness, in trembling, and in distress of mind. It stays in darkness, binding the arms of its own holy desire and tangling itself in the snare of confusion; as has been said, the soul is then deprived of joy and becomes unbearable to itself.

XI. **What means is there to guard against falling into despair?** There is no other way except that, with the **Light of Faith**, you look upon your **Conscience**. It shows you that you have not willfully or with malice left any poison of sin in your soul that you have not already spat out through **Confession**. <note>Catherine frequently uses the visceral image of "spitting out" (sputato) sin to describe the purging and honest nature of oral confession.</note> However, do confess with humility that you have spoken of these sins imperfectly, perhaps not having fully weighed the fault as much as you could; but let this Confession be seasoned with the hope of the **Blood of Christ**, trusting that what is lacking on your part, He Himself will complete. The other remedy is that, through the **Light**, you observe how ineffably you are loved by God. This love does not despise the testimony of a good conscience, nor would God allow anything to remain in the soul that would offend Him. With this Faith, Love, and Hope, drown yourself in the **Mercy of God**. Speak to your own soul and confess with simplicity of heart, and do not burden yourself any further; let go of thoughts of yourself and think instead of the Mercy of God, which you have received and receive continually. And if the struggle and distress return, cast them behind your back as an affliction, and place them before you for humiliation and self-knowledge—yielding the fruit of true and perfect Hope. Hope that to endure and travel the way of the **Cross** is more pleasing to God than any other way, and that you will more abundantly receive the fruit of the Blood. This is the remedy, dearest brother, that the **Eternal Truth** <note>original: "Eterna Verità" — Catherine’s standard title for God, emphasizing His constancy and reliability.</note> gives you against your infirmity. Now we have seen what it is that takes away our light and what it is that restores it; we have seen what Faith does—how it strikes down **Pride**, removes presumption, and provides the fruit of Faith, which is **Hope**.

XII. **Since we have seen this,** though it be less than a tiny drop <note>original: "sprizarella" — a splash or a very small amount, highlighting the vastness of the subject compared to her brief words.</note>, I pray and urge both you and myself, for the love of **Christ Jesus**, that we cross this stormy sea with this glorious **Light**, with firm hope and true self-knowledge. Let us cast to the ground our every will, opinion, and pleasure through true **Humility**, seeking to clothe ourselves in true and real virtues in the teaching of **Christ Crucified**. I am certain that if you have the **Light of Faith** within you, you will do this; otherwise, you will not. And therefore I told you that I desired to see in you this sweet

( D ) They shall study the **Apocalypse** <note>Also known as the Book of Revelation.</note> not with humility, nor with the Light of Faith. This is the last of the Books of Sacred Scripture, but perhaps it is the first in the depth and obscurity of its Mysteries. The name is Greek, and in our Language it means **Revelation**, wherein the Apostle Saint John set forth in twenty-two Chapters—while he was in Exile on the Island of Patmos, currently called **Palmosa**—all that God revealed to him regarding the State of His Church, from then until the end of the World. To trace the truths veiled in other Likenesses that are found in all the Sacred Books, one requires great Light from Heaven and a low estimation of one’s own strength; this is singularly required of anyone who undertakes to read this Divine Prophecy, so as not to stumble into those faults into which those have miserably fallen who, with pride of Spirit, have pretended to fully comprehend those Secrets that God willed to be hidden from us, reserving to Himself their discovery from time to time, according to what His Divine Providence has ordained for His greater glory and for the salvation of His Faithful. However, this sacred book has not lacked its **Commentators**, <note>The original term is "Spositori," referring to those who explain or expound upon scripture.</note> who, with the humility that the Saint here requires of this Man, have unveiled for us many of those Secrets that are hidden there. <margin>In the Preface.</margin> More than a hundred of them are numbered by **Lodovico Alcazar**, <note>Luis del Alcázar (1554–1613), a Spanish Jesuit theologian who wrote a famous commentary on the Book of Revelation.</note> who is one of them, and one of those who emerged with success; hence, if he has not manifested all those truths that lie covered there, he has at least shown that he has discovered them.

# To Conte di Conte of Florence, a Spiritual Man.

I. **O**n the Light of Holy Faith, without which no work can be perfect, and of its effects.
II. That perfection is attained by way of Humility, and other Virtues, and through many battles with the Devil, and troubles from Creatures <term>Creatures: In Catherine’s theology, this refers to all created things, particularly other people who may cause us difficulty or distraction</term>.
III. For what reason God allows these troubles to come upon us.
IV. The properties of Faith; why God permits our falls.
V. That the Light of the Most Holy Faith is very useful and delightful.
VI. An exhortation to him not to depart from his Brothers in Christ, and to humble himself to them.

## Letter 237.

->In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary.<-

I. **D**earest Son in Christ sweet Jesus: I Catherine, servant and slave of the Servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious Blood, with the desire to see in you the Light of the Most Holy Faith. This Light shows us the way of truth, and without it, no exercise, desire, or work of ours would come to fruit, nor to perfection, nor to that end for which we might have begun; rather, everything would become imperfect, and we would be slow in the Charity of God and of our Neighbor. The reason is this: it appears that Faith is as great as Love, and Love is as great as Faith. He who loves is always faithful to the one whom he loves, and faithfully serves him until death. O dearest Son, this is that Light which conducts the Soul to the port of salvation, draws it from the mire <note>original: "loto"</note> of misery, and dissolves within it every darkness of self-love; because in this Light the soul knows how displeasing self-love is to God, and how harmful to its own salvation; and therefore it rises up with hatred and casts it out of itself.
II. With living faith the soul knows that every fault is punished, and every good is rewarded, and therefore it embraces Virtue, and despises

...from vice, with great diligence one becomes constant and persevering until death, so much so that neither the Devil, nor any creature, nor the fragile flesh can make one turn their head back, when this Light is perfectly in the Soul. One arrives at this perfection with much exercise, with anxious desire, and with deep Humility. The Soul acquires this Humility in the <term>House of self-knowledge: A central metaphor in Catherine’s spirituality, representing the internal "cell" where the soul discovers its own nothingness and God’s infinite love</term> by means of continual, humble, and faithful Prayer, with many battles against the Devil, and troubles from Creatures <note>In this context, "creatures" refers to other human beings or worldly distractions that test one's patience</note>, and from oneself—that is, from the perverse will and the fragile flesh, which always fights against the Spirit. One resists all these with the Light of the Most Holy Faith. With this Light, through the Doctrine of the Word, the soul fell in love with enduring pain and labor in whatever way God might permit, not choosing time, nor place, nor labors in its own way, but according to what the <term>Eternal Truth: Catherine’s frequent title for God, emphasizing His unchanging nature</term> wills, who seeks and wants nothing other than our Sanctification.

III. But why does He permit these labors and so many rebellions in us? So that Virtue may be tested in us, and so that through the Light we may know our own imperfection and the help that the Soul receives from God in battle and labors; and also so that we may know the fire of His Charity in the good Will that He has preserved in the Soul during times of darkness, troubles, and many labors.

IV. Through this knowledge, gained in times of struggle, the soul puts aside the imperfection of Faith and comes to a most perfect Faith through the great experience it has had and proven while still on the path of imperfection. This Light takes away all confusion of the Mind; not only in times of battle, but even if a Man had actually fallen into the guilt of mortal sin—whatever sin it might be—Faith raises him up. This is because with the Light he gazes upon the Mercy, the fire, and the abyss of the Charity of God, stretching out the arms of Hope. With these arms he receives and clutches the fruit of the Blood <note>original: "Sangue" — Catherine focuses intensely on the Blood of Christ as the physical manifestation of God's love and the price of human redemption</note>, in which he has found this sweet and loving fire with a perfect Contrition, humbling himself before God and his Neighbor for His sake. He considers himself the least and the most vile of all others, and thus he extinguishes the guilt within his Soul through Contrition and hope in the Blood, which Blood...

...<note>original: "gue," likely the end of "sangue" (blood) or "prosegue" (it follows)</note> was introduced by the **Light of Faith**; in this way, one reaches such perfection and such love for the **Divine and loving Fire**, that one can say along with the sweet Gregory: <margin>B</margin>
-> O happy and fortunate fault, which merited such a **Redeemer**. <-
<note>original: "O felice, & avventurata colpa, che meritasti avere così fatto Redentore." This is a reference to the "O felix culpa" from the Exultet, a hymn sung during the Easter Vigil, often attributed to Saint Gregory the Great or Saint Ambrose.</note>

Was Adam's fault happy? No, but the fruit we received because of it was happy, as God clothed His Son in our humanity and placed upon Him that great obedience which restores the human race to Grace; and He, like one in love, ran to pay the price with His own **Blood**. So I say of the Soul: its fault is not happy, but the fruit it receives in the affection of **Charity** is—because of the great and perfect amendment it has made with the Light of Faith, as was said. And because the soul grows in self-knowledge and **Humility**, it goes along quite joyfully in obedience to God’s commandments, receiving this yoke upon its shoulders with both hatred <note>In Catherine’s writings, "hatred" usually refers to a holy "hatred" of one's own selfish will or sin</note> and love. It immediately runs, like one in love, to give its life if necessary for the salvation of souls. For through the light, the soul has seen that it cannot return to God the love and the graces it has found in Him; it can certainly return love, but it cannot perform any service of utility for Him, since He has no need of us. However, the soul can certainly render this to its **Neighbor**, being of use to them since it cannot be so for God. And truly it is so: by serving the Neighbor charitably, we demonstrate in them the love we have for the **Supreme Eternal Truth**. In this Charity, it is proven whether the Virtues are truly in the Soul or not. Thus the Soul runs, as an obedient servant, and has bound its will to fulfill the Will of God in its Neighbor, not abandoning this for any pain, nor for any thing, even unto death.

V. With this Light, the soul tastes the <term>earnest-money: "Arra" in the original, referring to a down-payment or pledge that guarantees a future full payment</term> of **Eternal Life**, nourishing itself through the affection of Love at the breast of **Christ Crucified**. It delights in <note>original: "furare le Virtù," literally "stealing the virtues." This is a Catherinian metaphor for imitating the saints so intensely that one "claims" their virtues as their own</note> "stealing" the virtues, the life, and the maturity that the true tasters and Citizens of the blessed life possessed while they were Pilgrims and Wayfarers in this life. With this **Faith**, one carries the **key of the Blood**, with which **Eternal Life** is unlocked. Faith does not presume of itself, but of its Creator, because the Wind of Pride is not found there with its own self-regard. For such self-regard, pride, impurity, and every other defect and misery are the fruits of **unfaithfulness**.

...[the gratitude] <note>original: "tà", the suffix of "gratuità" or "umiltà," continuing from the previous page</note> that we have toward **God**, and from the presumption of trusting in ourselves; which is a **worm** that stays hidden under the root of the **Tree of our Soul**; and if **Man** does not kill it with the **knife of hatred** <note>In Catherine’s theology, the "knife of hatred" refers to a holy rejection of one's own selfish will and sinful pride.</note>; it gnaws so much that it either makes the **Tree** twist, or it sends it to the ground, unless the **Soul** procures help with great diligence and **humility**. Often a **Man** will be so ignorant through his own **self-love** that he will not realize this worm is hidden there; and therefore **God** permits many battles and persecutions, and allows the **Tree** to twist, and sometimes to fall. He does not permit the evil will, but He permits the time and lets it be guided by its **free will**, only so that it might return to itself, and with this humbled light, seek out this worm, put its hand to the **knife of hatred**, and kill it. And does that **Soul** not have cause to rejoice and recognize the grace that **God** has given it by seeing and finding within itself that which it did not know? Yes, indeed. So in every way, **dearest Son**, in every state a **Man** is in—whether just, or a sinner, or one who has fallen and then rises again—this light is necessary. How many are the inconveniences that come from not having it? I will not set myself to narrate them, nor to say more of them, for it would be too long; let what I have said suffice for now. How useful and delightful it is to give it to you, I cannot express with tongue nor with ink; but may **God** make you experience it through His infinite mercy. Thus I wish it to be. And therefore I said that I desired to see in you the **Light of the Most Holy Faith**.

<margin>C</margin>
VI. I am very much marveled at the **Letters** you sent to **Barduccio** <note>Barduccio Canigiani was one of Catherine’s most devoted secretaries and disciples.</note>. For no reason do I want you to depart <margin>D</margin> from the **Congregation** of your Brothers; <margin>E</margin> see to it that you do not go looking for the "perfect place" of **Religion** <note>Catherine often cautioned against the temptation to leave one's current duties in search of a supposedly "more perfect" or quieter religious setting, viewing it as a trick of spiritual pride or restlessness.</note>, nor that you ever come to confusion of mind, but entirely humbled, make yourself a subject to the very least among them. Nor for this reason should you stop offering them that truth which **God** makes known to you. Now let us begin once more to take the aforementioned remedies, so that the **Demon of sadness** and confusion does not assail our **Soul**, for the last state would be worse than the first and would be a great offense to **God**. Remain in the **Holy and sweet delight** of **God**. **Sweet Jesus. Jesus Love.**

**( A )** The name **Conte** is not a title of honor, but a personal name, as was noted above; therefore both this man and his father were called Conte. He was most devoted to **Saint Catherine** and her disciples, as can be seen from this letter, and testimony is given of him by the **Blessed Thomas Caffarini** in the Process <note>The "Process of Venice" (1411–1416) was a legal inquiry into Catherine's sanctity.</note>, as he was still alive when it was formed in the year 1411.
