The title of those letters is this: *To a certain son in Christ who was called Conte, to him was directed the same, and the same letter that follows* <note>original Latin: "Cuidam Filio in Christo qui dicebatur Conte, eidem directa fuit, & idem que sequitur Epistola."</note>. From these repeated names of "Conte," the **Conti** family in Florence has derived its surname.

**( B )** He can say, with the sweet **Gregory**, "O happy and fortunate fault" <note>original: "o Felice, & aventurata colpa." This refers to the *Felix Culpa*, a theological concept attributed to St. Gregory the Great, suggesting that the fall of man was "happy" because it brought about an even greater redeemer.</note>. See concerning this matter that which was observed in the annotations to Letter 87.

**( C )** *Of the letter that you sent to Barduccio.* **Barduccio Canigiani** was a Florentine nobleman and one of the Saint's most faithful followers, of whom mention is made in the annotations to Letter 228.

**( D )** *That you departed from the congregation of your brothers in Christ.* He must have belonged to some devout assembly of laypeople who employed themselves in works of piety. Perhaps the **Blessed Giovanni delle Celle** had formed a kind of company in Florence for this purpose, as there is a letter from the Saint addressed to certain Florentine youths, adoptive sons of **Don Giovanni**, since this man, as was said, was one of them.

**( E )** *Take care, now, that you do not go to the perfect place of Religion.* <note>In this context, "Religion" refers to a formal religious order or monastery.</note> According to what is said in the annotations to Letter 83, the Saint uses the verb "to take care" <note>original: "guardare"</note> to mean the same as "to except." ## To Luigi, son of Messer Luigi Gallerani of Siena, in Asciano.

I. She seeks to encourage him toward fortitude and perseverance, leaning on and trusting in the Holy Cross of Jesus Christ; there she takes the opportunity to show the immense Charity of God, which was shown to us in this Mystery, and the good that flows into us from it.

### Letter 238.

->In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary.<-

And I do not wonder at this; for the strength of Love held Him bound and nailed upon the wood of the Holy Cross. Now here, then, I pray you to bind yourself; and thus you will not be able to turn back. There you will find all the virtues founded. <meta>This page continues the editorial commentary and biographical notes regarding Ser Cristofano di Gano Guidini, the recipient of the preceding letter from Saint Catherine of Siena. Siena twice held him among the **Lords Defenders** <note>The "Signori Difensori," a high-ranking governing body in the Republic of Siena during the 14th century.</note>, namely in the years 1383 and 1384. He had formed a friendship with the Saint through the efforts of Ranieri de’ Pagliaresi and Dionisio di Boccio, and was so captivated by the words of this Virgin <note>Saint Catherine</note> that he had firmly intended to abandon the world and give himself entirely to God in a Religious Order, had he not been dissuaded by the pleas of his mother, as will be mentioned further below. The title he holds, **Ser Cristofano**, is shortened from *Sere*, just as that is shortened from the other, *Messere* <note>original: "Messere"; a title of respect similar to "Master" or "Sir."</note>. Both in the time of Saint Catherine and in our own times, it is customary in Tuscany to grant this title to Notaries.

<margin>
Acts of the Saints
April 30th, in
Notes on the Life
of St. Catherine.
</margin>
The continuators of the work of Father Bollando <note>The Bollandists, a Jesuit scholarly society that compiled the "Acta Sanctorum" or Lives of the Saints.</note> observe that the word *Sere* or *Sire* is in use among many nations of Europe, being employed in all those countries that speak not only languages derived from Latin—such as France and Italy—but also those where Germanic tongues are used, such as Germany and Flanders. From this word, surnames have even been formed for many illustrious families, as has also happened in Italy, and particularly in Tuscany, where many families begin their names with the word *Ser*. Indeed, other nations outside of Europe use the same word with slight variation, as noted by the authors just cited; thus the word *Sara* <note>original: "Sara"</note> means the same as "Lady" in the Hebrew language; *Ser* was the same as "Lord" in ancient Egypt, from which was formed the name of the mythical *Serapis*. And the Muscovites give their Sovereign the title of **Czar**, that is, "Lord," if indeed that word does not come from that of **Caesar**, as others believe. In France, the name *Sire* is reserved for the King alone, and this usage has also passed into Italy, where in older times it was not so restricted to the Royal Person that it was not also given by Tuscan authors to figures who were quite far below such exalted dignity.

Dictionary of the
Crusca

*(A) The name Sano is a shortened form of Ansano <note>St. Ansanus the Baptizer is the patron saint of Siena.</note>, which is widely used in Siena in memory of the Holy Martyr Ansano, Protector of the City, and the one by whom it was led to the light of the Gospel; and the name Maco is a corruption of Giacomo <note>James</note> according to Tuscan usage. The Saint wrote eight letters to this man, who was one of her disciples, as we learn from Ser Cristofano di Gano; however, they were so disordered in their sequence that it has been necessary to arrange them differently than they were previously. To which family he belonged cannot be known from the addition of "Maco," as this was his father's name, which according to the custom of Tuscany at those times was a very frequent way of naming people; indeed, most families took their surnames from such names, which is why they mostly have the ending corresponding to the second case of the Latin noun <note>This refers to the genitive case, often ending in "i" in Italian, indicating "son of."</note>. In some records of the Public Books, he is said to be of the Mezzocorno family, which is now extinct. Memory of him is found in the public books of the Declarations of Contracts.*

**battle**, surrounded by our Enemies, who always fight against us. Thus, hope and believe firmly that the Soul that hopes in Him is always provided for by Him, and the Devil can use no force against it; for the Virtue of the sweetest and Most Holy Cross takes it away from him, whereby he loses his power against us. Wealth desires voluntary poverty, and uncleanness acquires Continence and Purity; every disordered delight and appetite is despised there, and one remains clothed only in true and royal Virtues. One delights in nothing other than Christ, and neither considers nor wishes to know anything other than Christ Crucified; <margin>Galatians 6</margin> as it also says: I delight and wish to glory in my Lord Jesus Christ, for whose love the World is in contempt to me, and I to it. <note>original: "mi diletto, e vuomi gloriare nel mio Signore Gesù Cristo..." ...[foundatio]nal <note>This continues the word from the previous page, likely "spiritual" or "original."</note>, even when the flood is great, it cannot cast down this Soul, because it is established and fixed upon that Stone, in which there was no softness of delights or bodily comforts, but only firmness in pains and sorrows. Therefore, the Soul enamored of him can desire nothing else but to always suffer with him: reproaches, scorns, hunger and thirst, heat, insults, and slanders; and at the last, even to lay down and give up one's bodily life with great delight for the love of him. Even then, the Soul thrives and <term>grows fat<note>original: "ingrassa"; Catherine uses this culinary metaphor to describe the soul finding spiritual nourishment and abundance through suffering.</note></term> when it sees itself made worthy to endure torments, derisions, and mockery from the World for the love of the sweet and good Jesus. <margin>Acts 4</margin> Thus we read of the Holy Apostles, that they rejoiced even then, when they began to be despised and vilified for the Name of Jesus. In this way, my Soul desires to see us founded in Christ Crucified—so much so, and in such a manner, that neither the water of tribulations, nor the wind of temptations, nor even the Devil with his cunning, nor the World with its flatteries, nor the Flesh with its impurities can ever separate us from the Charity of Christ and from that of our Neighbor.

And do not let words sown by the Devil through other creatures move you to disturb your mind, or the minds of my other sweet sons and daughters in Christ Jesus; for this is his ancient art: to make his instrument of the tongues of the wicked. And sometimes, by God’s permission, he makes his instrument of the tongues of God’s own servants, in order to disturb other servants of God.

...of the Letter, and since this was written twenty-six days after her arrival, it would have been written on the twelfth or thirteenth of the month of July. In that City, the Saint was provided lodging in the house of one Giovanni de Regio, as we have from a testimony by Tommaso Buonconti, who, speaking of one of the spiritual ecstasies of this Virgin, adds: *These things took place in Avignon in the House of Lord Giovanni de Regio, before the Altar of the Chapel, etc.* <note>original Latin: "Acta sunt hæc Avenione in Domo Domini Joannis de Regio, ante Altare Cappellæ &c."</note> This house was built in the manner of a very wide Tower, and it is still preserved today, as there is still a memory of the room she inhabited; the entire structure is joined to the College of the Fathers of the Society of Jesus <note>The Jesuits</note>, the illustrious Brancacci gentlemen—no less famous in Italy than in France—having purchased it for this purpose and donated it to them for the expansion of the College. Saint Catherine had twenty-three people in her company, all of whom were provided for by the Pope’s Palace. Among the others who were with her, the aforementioned Buonconti names the Blessed Raymond <note>Raymond of Capua, her biographer and confessor</note> her Confessor with his companion, Brother Giovanni Tantucci, and Brother Felice da Marta, Hermits of Saint Augustine, a certain Brother Guidone, Tommaso, Gherardo, and Francesco Buonconti, brothers and Pisan nobles, Neri de’ Pagliaresi, Niccolò di Mino Cicerchi, Stefano di Corrado Maconi, a Sienese noble, and three of her female companions.

( B ) *In the matters for which we came here, etc.* Saint Catherine went to the Court of Avignon <note>The "Avignon Papacy" period, when the Popes resided in France rather than Rome</note> specifically to bring some resolution to the grave disturbance that had arisen between the Pope and the Republic of Florence; in addition to this affair, she also managed there with all her fervor the expedition against the Infidels <note>A proposed Crusade</note> and the return of the Pope to Italy, and she was only able to bring this last matter to perfection. If the present Letter were available in its entirety, some other light might be shed on these dealings, but the person who transcribed it for printing, with little foresight, neglected to include what pertained to business matters—as he has done with many others—being content to give us only those documents that aim toward the perfection of Souls.

# To Sano di Maco, and to all the other Children in Siena.

I. On the Virtue of perseverance, and the fortitude that is necessary for us to obtain it.
II. That we are besieged by our Enemies, and the manner in which we must respond to the deceptions of the World.
III. In what way one must respond to the Devil, namely with living Faith.
IV. That one should not judge God’s servants rashly.
V. Concerning the imperfect love of those who judge the will of others.
VI. In what way one should respond to the allurements of the Flesh.
VII. She commends the Monastery of Santa Maria degli Angeli to them, and encourages them to love one another, and to pray for the salvation of Souls.

## Letter 245.

->In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of Sweet Mary.<-

I. **D**earest Children in sweet Jesus Christ. I, Catherine, servant and slave of the Servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious Blood, with the desire to see you strong and persevering until the very end of your lives; considering that without perseverance no one can please God, and does not receive the Crown of the Prize <note>A reference to the biblical "incorruptible crown" promised to those who finish the race of faith</note>. He who perseveres is always strong, and fortitude causes him to persevere. We have a great need and necessity for the gift of Fortitude, because we are besieged by many Enemies.

The Flesh rises up with its own sensuality, wishing to fight against the Spirit. So then, all these our...

Enemies have besieged us; but we must not fear with a servile fear <note>servile fear — a fear of punishment or harm, rather than a "filial fear" rooted in love for God</note>, for they are defeated by the Blood of the Immaculate Lamb <note>original: "Agnello"</note>.

III. We must boldly respond to and resist the World by despising its delights and its status, judging that it has no firmness or stability within itself. It shows us a long life with flourishing youth and with much wealth, yet these are all seen to be vain; for from life we come to death, from youth to old age, from wealth to poverty, and thus we always run toward the boundary of Death. Therefore, we have need to open the eye of the Intellect <term>Intellect — the faculty of the soul that perceives spiritual truth and God’s light</term> to see how miserable is he who trusts in these things. In this way, he will come to feel displeasure for, and will hate, what he previously loved. To the deception of the Devil <note>original: "Dimonio"</note> let him respond manfully, seeing his weakness; for he cannot conquer anyone except the one who wishes to be conquered. Let him respond, then, with living Faith <note>original: "Fede"</note> and hope, and with a holy hatred of himself; because in this hatred he will become patient in every temptation, trouble, and tribulation of the World. From whatever side they come, he will bear them all with true patience <note>original: "patientia"</note>, if he is a hater of his own sensuality <term>sensuality — the selfish part of human nature that seeks pleasure and avoids suffering</term>, and if he loves to stay on the Cross <note>original: "Croce"</note> with Christ Crucified.

IV. From living Faith he will draw a Will in accord with that of God, and he will extinguish from his heart and mind every human judgment; he will judge only the Will of God, which seeks and desires nothing other than our Sanctification <note>original: "Santificatione"</note>. In this way, he is not scandalized by his Neighbor <note>original: "Prossimo"</note>, and he does not murmur <note>murmuring — a common term in Catherine's writing for the sin of gossip or complaining against God's will</note> about them, nor does he judge the one who speaks against him. He condemns only himself, seeing the Will of God which permits those people to trouble him for his own good. O how blessed is that Soul who clothes itself in such sweet judgment! He does not condemn

### V. 
But if he opens his eye, he will find the worm of presumption with a perverse opinion; this opinion acts as a Judge, judging according to its own way and not according to the mysteries and the holy and diverse ways that God employs with His creatures. Let human Pride be ashamed, and let it desire to see that in the House 
<margin>John 14</margin> 
of the Eternal Father there are many mansions <term>mansions — referring to John 14:2, suggesting many paths and levels of spiritual life</term>; let it not wish to impose a rule upon the Holy Spirit, who is Himself the Rule and the giver of the rule; nor let it measure Him who cannot be measured. The true Servant of God, clothed in His supreme Eternal Will, will not act this way; rather, he will hold in reverence the ways, the acts, and the customs of His servants, because he does not judge them as things done by man, but by God. Even if things do not please us, and do not go according to our own customs, I must presuppose and believe that they are pleasing to God. We neither should nor can judge anything, except that which is seen to be manifest and express sin. And even this, the Soul enamored of God—who has lost herself <note>To "lose oneself" in Catherine’s theology is to set aside self-will and ego to be filled with God's love</note>—does not take as a judgment, but as a displeasure for the sin and the offense against God, and with great compassion for the soul of the one who offends, being willing to give herself to every torment for the salvation of that soul. 

Now, I invite you to this perfection, most dear Children; study with every true and holy diligence to acquire it. Consider that every perfection, without any scandal or pain, will give you this holy and true judgment. Conversely, false judgment gives every pain, blame, and murmuring <term>murmuring — a term for sinful gossip or complaining against God’s providence</term>, and the ruin of unfaithfulness toward the Servants of God. All of this proceeds from one's own passion and rooted pride, which moves one to judge the Will of Man. Therefore, such a person always turns his head backward and does not persevere in the love of his Neighbor; his love is never strong or persevering. Rather, it is like the imperfect love of Christ's disciples which they had before the Passion; because they delighted much in His presence, they loved Him, but because their love was not founded in truth, but rather in their own pleasure and delight, it failed when His presence was taken away. They did not know how to bear the pain with Christ, but fled out of fear. 

Look, look, that this does not happen to you! You delight much in presence, but in absence you become a straw fire <note>original: "fuoco di paglia" — an idiom for a passion that flares up brightly but lacks substance and dies out quickly</note>; for when presence is taken away, every little wind and rain extinguishes it, and nothing remains—

<summary>Catherine warns her followers against the "worm of presumption" and judging others' spiritual paths, urging them to love with a "straw fire" passion that fails during absence or trial.</summary>

...nothing else but the black smoke of darkness and of conscience. And all this happens because we have made ourselves Judges of the Will of Men, and of the customs, ways, and paths of the Servants of God, and not of His sweet Will. Now, do so no more for the love of Christ Crucified, but be faithful children, strong and persevering in sweet Jesus Christ; in this way you will defeat the temptations of the Devil and his words, which he speaks by placing himself upon the tongues of Creatures <note>Catherine frequently warns that the devil uses the criticisms and gossip of other people to disrupt the peace of the soul</note>.

### VI. 
Our last Enemy—that is, the miserable <term>Flesh — in Catherine’s writing, the "flesh" refers to the lower, sensual nature that must be disciplined to serve the spirit</term>, along with the sensual appetite—is defeated with the Flesh of Christ, scourged and nailed upon the Wood of the Most Holy Cross, by subduing it with fasting, vigils, and continuous Prayer <note>original: "Oratione"</note> with burning, sweet, and loving desire. Now, in this way, we shall sweetly conquer and defeat our Enemies with the Virtue of the Blood of Christ. Thus you will fulfill His Will and my desire, which grieves when it looks upon your imperfection. I hope by His infinite Goodness that He will console my desire for you; therefore I pray that you be not negligent, but diligent, nor be like a leaf that turns with the wind, but firm, stable, and constant, loving one another with true fraternal Charity, bearing and supporting one another's defects. By this I will know if you love God and me—for I desire nothing else but to see you in true unity. Drown yourselves in the <term>Blood of Christ — Catherine’s primary theological symbol for the transformative power of divine love and grace</term> Crucified, and hide yourselves in His most sweet Wounds. I say no more.

<margin>A</margin> 
### VII. 
Let the Monastery of Santa Maria degli Angeli <note>A Benedictine monastery in Siena with which Catherine had close ties</note> be recommended to you. Do not be concerned because I am not there; for good children do more when the Mother is absent than when she is present, wishing to show the love they have for their Mother and to come further into her grace. I pray you, <unclear>Siano</unclear> <note>Likely referring to Sano di Maco, one of Catherine’s most devoted disciples and frequent correspondents</note>, that you read this Letter to all the children, and all of you pray to God 
<margin>B</margin> for us, that He may grant us to complete His honor, which has begun, and the salvation of Souls—for we have no other desire, 
<margin>C</margin> nor do we wish to work for anything else, despite those who wished and wish to impede it. Remain in the holy and sweet love of God. May God fill you with His most sweet Grace. Sweet Jesus. Jesus Love.

...as, by the authority obtained from Pope Gregory XI <note>Gregory XI was the last of the Avignon popes; Catherine famously traveled to France to persuade him to return the Papacy to Rome</note>, she had converted a villa—given to her by Nanni di Ser Vanni of the noble Savini family of Siena—into a Monastery of Holy Virgins. # To Sano di Maco, and to the other Sons in Christ, she being in Florence.

**I.** She exhorts them to be true Servants and Sons of the Savior.
**II.** She rejoices in the Peace made with the Supreme Pontiff <note>The "Supreme Pontiff" refers to the Pope; at this time, Catherine was instrumental in reconciling the city of Florence with Pope Urban VI following the death of Gregory XI</note>, and exhorts the aforementioned to give thanks to God for it.

## Letter 246.

For this reason, Pope **Urban VI**, who professed an austerity of life, was called a **Patarino** <note>A derogatory term originally referring to a 11th-century reform movement, but by Catherine's time used as a slur for a heretic or a hypocritically rigorous person</note> by those malicious people who opposed him in **Florence**.

[ C ] Now Peace is made. To handle this Accord, **Saint Catherine** delayed in **Florence** for several months, and after infinite hardships and grave danger to her life, she finally succeeded in establishing it in the month of **July** in the Year 1378. That this **Holy Virgin** had the greatest part in forging this Concord, swaying the hearts of the **Florentines** with her effective encouragements, is gathered from many of her **Letters**, in which it is known how much She exerted herself; and the **Blessed Raymond** <note>Raymond of Capua, Catherine’s confessor and biographer</note> has certainly left this record for us in his **Life of the Saint** <margin>Part 3, last chapter.</margin>. **Simone Pagano**, Auditor of the sacred **Rota** <note>The highest appellate tribunal of the Catholic Church</note> and **Bishop** of **Volterra**, and **Friar Francesco** of **Orvieto**, a religious Hermit of **Saint Augustine** <margin>Ammirato, Annals 1378.</margin>, were those who, by order of the Pope, released the City from the bonds of the censures of the **Church**.

( D ) Saturday evening the **Olive** arrived at the first hour of the night, and today at **Vespers** the other arrived. Not only among the ancient **Egyptians** and the **Secular Authors** was the **Olive** a hieroglyph of **Peace**, but it is also taken as its symbol by the sacred **Expositors** <note>Scholarly commentators</note> of the **Divine Scriptures**. The former took their reasoning from that Plant being dedicated to the mythological deity **Minerva**, reputed to be the Goddess of **Wisdom**, of whom **Peace** is the offspring; and the latter take it from the **Dove**, a peaceful bird, having long ago brought a branch of that **Tree** to **Noah** as a sign that the waters of the **Flood** had given **Peace** to the Earth by retreating from it. Hence it was an ancient custom recorded by **Dante** in this verse of his—
<margin>Purgatory, Canto 2</margin>
—*And like a Messenger who brings the Olive*—that **Ambassadors** sent to negotiate peace, or to bring news of it, would carry an **Olive Branch** as a signal of this, as noted by the **Commentators** of the work of that wondrous **Poet**. The formula that the **Saint** uses to denote the news of the **Peace**, saying, *the Olive arrived*, without any further addition, must be said to have been quite common in those times; we find it used at least three times in just a few pages by **Angelo di Tura di Grasso**, a **Sienese Chronicler** <margin>Manuscript text held by the Grassi gentlemen</margin> who lived in the times of Saint...

# To Sano di Maco, and to all her other secular children in Christ in Siena:

I. She exhorts them to ground themselves in the light of the Most Holy Faith.
II. Of the two Inviters who call us to themselves (as Faith teaches us), the first of whom is Jesus Christ.
III. Of the invitation he makes to us to drink from his wounds.
IV. That his Most Holy Body is a Book, and what may be read within it.
V. Who are understood to be the invited and the called by Jesus Christ.
VI. Of the other who invites us to himself, namely the Devil, and of the reward he gives to those who serve him.
VII. That the Lie is his way.
VIII. His Book is one's own sensuality.
IX. She exhorts them to follow Christ Crucified with true Charity toward their Neighbor, and with perseverance.
X. She excuses herself for not writing to them.
XI. She prays them to pray for the Holy Church and for the Supreme Pontiff.

->*In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary.*<-

Therefore, this light is necessary to us, for without it we would walk in darkness, and he who walks through the darkness is harmed by it.

**V.** He, as the **Fountain of living water** <note>original: "Fonte d’acqua viva"</note>, invites those who are thirsty to drink; and those who follow his **Doctrine** <term>Doctrine: here refers to the "Book of Christ Crucified," the teachings and life of Jesus as a blueprint for the soul</term> fill the vessel of their Soul with the water of **Grace**. By leaning their breast against his **Humanity** <note>A mystical image suggesting that by contemplating Jesus's human suffering and life, one draws closer to his divinity, much like the Apostle John leaning on Jesus at the Last Supper.</note>, they immerse themselves in this water in the way described, drinking with the mouth of holy desire the honor of God and the salvation of Souls. They do this with a hunger for the **Virtues**, which they believe they can acquire in this present time; therefore, they practice them with great diligence, so as not to be a loser, but to hold close the greatest treasure they have. 

These are the invited ones, unlike the negligent, who lie in the darkness of **mortal sin**, running along the dead way like blind men, obstinate in their miseries. These latter are indeed *called*, but not *invited*. They are *called* because God created them in his Image and likeness and recreated them in **Grace** through the **Blood of the Word** <note>original: "Sangue del Verbo"; refers to Jesus as the Word of God</note>, but they are not *invited* because they do not wish to be. The Law is made for everyone, but for whom shall we say it is? For those who observe it. So, who are those invited to drink? All of us who are called. Who then shall we say are the invited? Only those who have thirst and hunger for Virtue, and, like thirsty people, run through the **Doctrine of Christ Crucified**, placing before the **Light of Faith** the fountain to increase their thirst. With this thirst and Light, they reach the water, as has been said, but without the Light, they would never have reached it. I would have much to say about these who are invited, but I do not wish to expand further. But let us see who the other one is who invites us. We have said that sweet Jesus Christ invites us to the living water.

**VI.** The other is the **Devil** <note>original: "Dimonio"</note>, who invites us to that which he has for himself; in himself, he has death, therefore he invites us to the dead water. For if you asked him, "What will you give me if I serve you?" he would answer you: "That which I have for myself. I am deprived of God, and so you shall be deprived of God; I am in the eternal fire, where there is fire and gnashing of teeth; I am deprived of light and immersed in darkness; I have lost all hope; I am in the company of the tormented and tortured in **Hell** <note>original: "Inferno"</note> like myself." These are the joys and the refreshment that you will have as your reward. **Faith** demonstrates to you that it is truly so, and therefore the faithful man never goes by this way, or if he is on it, he repents. ### VII. 
What is the path of this **Inviter** <note>The Devil, contrasted with Christ the Inviter from the previous page.</note>? It is the path of the lie; for he is the **Father of lies**. This lie produces miserable self-love, through which one loves in a disordered way their social standing, the riches of the world, created things, other creatures, and themselves. In doing so, they do not care about losing God and the beauty of their own Soul. Instead, like a blind person, they make a god of themselves and of the world. Like a thief, such a person steals time; the time that they should spend for the honor of God, their own salvation, and the good of their **Neighbor** <note>original: "Prossimo"</note>, they instead spend on their own sensory delights, taking pleasure in themselves and giving ease and pleasure to the body outside of the **Will of God**.

### VIII. 
The **Book** that he <note>the Devil</note> places before you is one's own sensuality, in which are written all the **Vices** <note>original: "Vitij"</note>: movements of anger, pride, impatience, and infidelity toward one’s Creator; injustice, **lack of discernment** <term>indiſcretione: the inability to distinguish between good and evil, or a lack of moderation in spiritual and worldly matters</term>, impurity, and hatred toward one's Neighbor. It contains pleasure in Vice and a distaste for the **Virtues**, as well as dullness and detraction toward one's Neighbor, sloth, and confusion of mind, negligence, drowsiness, and ingratitude. He writes all these defects down. If the **Will** reads them and learns them, putting them voluntarily into action, that person follows—like an Infidel—the path of the Devil's lie. He drinks "dead water" within him, because he is deprived of **Grace** in this life; and in the next, dying in mortal sin, he receives eternal damnation and punishment along with the Devil.

### IX. 
Therefore see, dearest Children, how necessary the **Light** is to you, from how much evil it saves you, and to how much good it leads you. Considering this myself, and seeing that without this Light the **Will of God**—who created you to give you eternal Life—would not be fulfilled in you, nor would my own will (as I desire nothing else for you), I said that I desired to see in you the **Light of the Most Holy Faith**. And so I pray you, and I desire, that you always be faithful and true Servants of **Christ Crucified**. I want you to serve him totally and not halfway; in his way and not your own; choosing neither the time nor the place except as he wills, nor seeking your own consolation. Do not refuse pains or battles, whether they come from the invisible Devil, or the visible one <note>Likely referring to people who tempt or persecute the believer</note>, or the attacks of the fragile flesh; instead, embrace the path of suffering for the honor of God. Follow **Christ Crucified**, mortifying...

...chastising the body with fasting, with vigils, and with continuous, humble, and faithful prayer; kill your own will in the sweet Will of God. Let your conversation be with His servants. And when you are gathered, do not waste time <margin>B</margin> in idle words, nor in burdening yourselves with the affairs of others, devouring the flesh of your **neighbor** <note>original: "Proſſimo"; here used in the biblical sense of fellow human beings.</note> with gossip and false judgment; for God alone is the Supreme Judge of us and of everyone. Instead, show that you are gathered in the Name of Christ by speaking of His goodness, and of the virtues of the Saints, and of your own faults. 

Be strong, constant, and persevering in virtue; let there be no Devil, nor any creature, who through threats or flatteries might ever make you turn your head back; for only **perseverance** is crowned. Whoever is bound to the world, let them cut themselves from it immediately, and do not set about trying to untie the knots, for there is no time; and whoever does not cut, remains always bound. The memory of the **Blood** <note>The Blood of Christ, a central theme in Catherine's spirituality representing God's ultimate act of love and the price of redemption.</note> with the **Light of Faith** will make you perfectly cut away from all those things that are outside the Will of God. You will <margin>C</margin> be faithful to Him, and to me, a miserable woman, believing that even if I were never to write to you, I love you in truth, and with solicitude I seek your salvation before God; of this, I want you to be certain.

### X. 
It is true that through my own fault, and because of the many preoccupations that I have had, I have not written to you; but comfort yourselves, and love one another, for I desire more than ever to see you written in the **Book of Life** <note>A reference to the names of those saved by God, as mentioned in the Book of Revelation.</note>.

### XI. 
Drown yourselves in the Blood of the humble **Lamb** <note>Jesus Christ</note>. Do not cease to pray for the Holy Church, and for our Lord Pope <margin>D</margin> **Urban VI** <note>Pope Urban VI (reigned 1378–1389), whose reign was marked by the start of the Western Schism; Catherine was a staunch supporter of his legitimacy.</note>, because now is a time of the greatest necessity. Remain in the holy and sweet love of God. Jesus, sweet Jesus, Love.

# To Sano di Maco, and to the other Sons.

I. **S**he exhorts them to be true servants of God, not serving for their own profit, or out of servile fear <term>servile fear</term><note>In medieval theology, this refers to obeying God solely out of fear of punishment or hell, rather than out of love.</note>.
II. On the imperfection of such service.
III. On the faithful service of one who loves perfectly, that is, with the Light of Faith.
IV. That we must not grieve during times of battle <note>The "battles" here refer to spiritual temptations or internal struggles.</note>, believing we are offending God, but rather believe that they are sent for our own good.
V. On the perfection and peace of those who serve faithfully.
VI. She exhorts her said sons to abstain from murmuring, but to serve God faithfully, encouraging them with the hope of Paradise to be persevering.

## Letter 248.

### Written while in Ecstasy.
<note>original: "Fatta in Astrazione." This indicates that Catherine dictated the letter while in a state of mystic trance or religious ecstasy, a common occurrence for her.</note>

->In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary.<-

I. **D**earest sons in sweet Christ Jesus, I, Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious Blood, with the desire to see you as faithful servants to our sweet Savior; to serve Him is not to be a servant, but to reign; and a servant without faith cannot exist in truth; for if he is a servant and is not faithful, he is a mercenary; because he serves out of regard for his own profit, and he is a servant through servile fear.
II. And because this serving is not made perfect by the Light of Faith, it is therefore neither strong nor persevering, but catches every wind in its sails. Thus, if it is a wind of consolation, he moves with a lightness of heart; and if it is a wind of tribulation—

...consolation, he moves with impatience; and if there is a wind of battles <note>In Catherine’s writing, "battles" refers to spiritual trials, temptations, or internal conflicts.</note> and troubles from the Devil, he grows lukewarm and settles into weariness with a sadness of Heart. It seems to him that he is deprived of God when he sees himself deprived of consolation and of the felt sweetness in his Mind. All this happens to him because he loves the gift more than the Giver of graces, and because he serves more out of regard for himself than out of regard for the supreme and Eternal Goodness of God. Thus, just as his love is imperfect, so too is the Light of Faith imperfect.

<margin>Ezekiel 23 <note>While the margin cites chapter 23, the specific quote about the death of a sinner is found in Ezekiel 18:23 and 33:11.</note></margin>
III. But he who loves perfectly, serves faithfully, and with a living Faith. He believes in truth that whatever God gives or permits, He gives for his Sanctification; for God does not desire the death of the Sinner, but wants him to be converted and live. Such a person has seen, by the Light of Most Holy Faith, that with that same love with which He gives us great consolations, He also permits the Devil to trouble our Minds and allows other creatures to persecute us. Thus we see that God is supremely good, and from Him nothing can arise except supreme Goodness; and we see that nothing is done without God, except for sin alone. Therefore, the faithful Soul embraces everything with love, because everything is good and given for our salvation; and one cannot grieve, nor should one grieve, over what is for one's own good.

IV. And if you should say to me, Dearest Sons, "In the time of these battles it seems to us that we are rebels and that we are offending God, and therefore we grieve more for this than for the pain itself": I respond to you, that it is your own spiritual sensuality <term>spiritual sensuality</term><note>A technical term in mystical theology referring to an attachment to the "feel-good" emotions of prayer and spiritual life; when these feelings vanish, the "sensuality" suffers.</note> that is grieving as much as anything else. This passion, under the guise of the fear of offending God, has placed a bit of dust in the eye of the Intellect—right where the pupil of Most Holy Faith sits—which does not allow one to know or discern the truth. For if there were nothing before the eye of his Intellect, he would recognize that God gives him these battles in careful measure. He ought to see clearly that no battle, nor trouble from the Devil, nor from our own fragility of the Flesh <note>original: "fragilità nostra della Carne"</note>, is a sin; nor does one offend the Creator by these things, except when the Will consents to the thoughts of the heart. But the Soul that is a faithful Servant—that is, one who through the Light of Most Holy Faith knows the great gains to be made in the time of battles—builds a true foundation by departing from mercenary self-love; and the heart becomes pure, and...

...to, and the liberal affection. In the time of battles <note>In Catherine’s writings, "battles" refer to spiritual trials, temptations, or internal struggles.</note> he wages a great war against himself; and from that war, and from the **holy hatred** <note>Catherine uses the term "holy hatred" (odio santo) to describe a rejection of one's own selfish ego and sinful inclinations in favor of God's will.</note> which he has conceived and which has made him patient, like a faithful Servant, he always delights in remaining in the battle for **Christ Crucified**; and he grows in love, knowing his holy and good **Will** is not from himself, but from the supreme and Eternal goodness of God, who gave it to him by grace and not by obligation.

V. O glorious faithful service, which deprives the Soul of the perverse servitude of the **Devil**, the World, and of itself. He is liberated from the Devil because he has bound his **Will** with the bond of **Reason**; and he does not consent to his harassments, nor does he allow his soul to fall into disordered confusion because of his pains, but mocks him, delighting in staying on the field of battle; thus the Devil is then bound and scourged—I say, with the rod of **Charity**—and is bound with the bond of true **Humility**. So then the Man is made Lord, and does not fear the Devil; but the Devil fears him through **Christ Crucified**, through whom he can do all things. I say that he is made free and Lord of the World, because he does not allow himself to be dominated by its delights and greatness with disordered affection; rather, he is made Lord of them by despising them and mocking them; for he has seen and known by the Light of the Most Holy **Faith** that the wealth of the World is supreme poverty, and its delights and pleasures are miserable above all misery, and unpleasant. They seem so unpleasant to him that he despises them like a poisonous serpent, and he is not a servant of Men outside of the Will of God; for he does not want to conform to their will, except insofar as it is directed toward seeking and loving **Eternal Truth**. And why does he love and serve? Because he has seen with the sweet Light that his Neighbor is that medium which God has placed before him so that he may manifest his love for Him; and this serving makes him truly free, because he does not serve his Neighbor through the fault of sin. I say further that he is faithful and free, and not a servant of his own sensuality, which he has trampled under the feet of his affection, breaking it and striking it with the knife of hatred and of Love—that is, Love of **Virtue** and hatred of **Vice**. Thus he is indeed made King and Lord with this sweet servitude; for he has not sought himself for his own sake, but himself for God, because He is supreme and Eternal Goodness, worthy of being loved and served by

...us, and our Neighbor for God, and not for the sake of our own utility. What tongue would be sufficient to narrate the Peace of the faithful Soul? I do not say that she <note>In Italian, "Soul" (*Anima*) is a feminine noun; Catherine frequently personifies the soul as a "she."</note> is at peace because she is deprived of the waves and storms of the sea, but her **Will** remains at peace because it has been made one with the sweet **Will of God**. Wherefore the storm is her quietude, because she does not care for herself; she serves her Creator, whether He wishes for Wars or for Peace, and she holds War as dear as Peace, and Peace as dear as War. For by the **Light of Faith** she saw, and by seeing she knew, that both one and the other proceeded from the very same love. 

Such a person is never scandalized by their Neighbor, because they have not been made a Judge of the Will of Man, but only of the Will of God. Therefore, such a person is deprived of grumbling <note>The original term *mormoratione* refers to backbiting, gossip, or complaining against others.</note>. I do not believe that this perfection is yet in you; rather, often under the guise of goodness and compassion, you grumble and judge one another. This thing is not without offense to God; it is displeasing to Him, and most strongly displeasing to me. This **Doctrine** was not given to you for this, but so that you might love one another, bearing and supporting the defects of one another. No one is without defect; only God is without defect. 

All this happens to you because you are not yet made faithful **Servants**; for if you were faithful Servants, neither mockery, nor grumbling, nor scandal, nor disobedience would be found in you, neither in jest nor in anger. Therefore, considering your imperfection—and that your imperfection comes because the **Light of the Most Holy Faith** is not perfect in you—I said that I desired to see you as faithful Servants. This service will make you reign in this life by grace, and you shall master the World, the Flesh, and the Devil. Being made free, you shall be bound in the bond of <term>Carità</term> <note>Charity: In Catherine’s context, this is *Agape*, the highest form of selfless, divine love.</note>, humble and meek, and with true and holy patience. In the end, you shall reign with the true and sweet "tasters" in the enduring life, where the Soul is rewarded for every labor; there, there is satiety without boredom, and hunger without pain; for the pain of hunger and the boredom of satiety are far removed from that place.

# To Benincasa, her Brother in Florence.

**S**he exhorts him to conform himself to the Will of God, and to embrace patience after the example of Job.

## Letter 251.

->*In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary.*<-

**D**earest and most beloved brother in Christ Jesus. I, Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, comfort you in the precious Blood of the Son of God, with the desire to see you completely aligned and transformed by the Will of God. For I know that His Will is that holy and sweet yoke which turns every bitterness into sweetness; every great weight becomes light under this most holy yoke of the sweet Will of God. Without this submission, you could not please God; rather, you would taste the earnest-money <note>The original word "arra" refers to a down-payment or pledge. Catherine suggests that living in resistance to God's will provides a "foretaste" or guarantee of the sufferings of Hell.</note> of Hell. Take heart, take heart, dearest brother, and do not fail under this discipline from God, but have confidence that when human help fails, Divine help is near. God will provide for you. Consider that Job lost his possessions, his children, and his health; there remained to him only his wife as a constant scourge <note>Catherine refers to the tradition that Job’s wife was left to him not as a comfort, but as a trial to further test his patience (Job 2:9-10).</note>. Yet, after God had tested his patience, He returned everything to him twofold, and in the end, gave him eternal life.

<margin>Job 1:21</margin>
Patient Job was never troubled, but always exercising the virtue of holy patience, he said: *The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord* <note>original: "Dio me l'à date, Dio me l'à tolte; ſia il Nome di Dio benedetto."</note>. This is how I wish you to act, dearest brother: be a lover of virtue, with a holy patience and with frequent Confession <note>Catherine frequently advocated for frequent reception of the Sacraments as a source of psychological and spiritual strength during crises.</note>, which will help you to frequently carry your burdens. And I tell you that God will exercise His kindness and mercy toward you, and will reward you for every labor that you have borne for His love. Remain in the holy and sweet love of God. Sweet Jesus. Jesus Love.

# To three of her Brothers in Florence.

## Letter 252.

### In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary.

**I.** Dearest Brothers in sweet Christ Jesus. I am reminded of the immeasurable love that our sweet Savior had, who gave Himself over to death to give us the life of Grace. Our sweet Savior wished to do nothing else except—seeing that we had stepped out of the order of Charity <note>Catherine uses "Charity" in the sense of the Latin *Caritas*, meaning the selfless, divine love that binds humanity to God and one another.</note>—to restore to us this union of Charity, He willed to be united with the most shameful death He could choose. Alas, our Savior saw us sickened by the <term>disordered appetite</term> <note>A theological term for desiring earthly things more than God, which Catherine views as a spiritual disease.</note> that we have within ourselves for these transitory things, which pass like the wind and fail—either they fail us, or we fail them <note>This is a favorite phrase of Catherine’s, noting that either wealth is lost during life, or it is left behind at the moment of death.</note>.

<margin>1 Peter, ch. 1</margin>
**II.** And therefore I, Catherine, unworthy and useless servant, pray you that you would place your hope in God, and not trust in this mortal life, which is failing. I pray you, as ransomed Servants, that you place your desire and the affection of your Soul with all diligence upon your Lord, who has ransomed you, as Saint Peter says: *He has not ransomed you with gold or silver, but with His most sweet and precious Blood.* And therefore I pray you, Dearest Brothers, that you hold this sweet price very dear—that is, that you love Him. And to demonstrate that you love Him, always be lovers and observers of the commandments of God; and specifically I pray and compel you on behalf of Christ Crucified to keep the first and last commandment of God: that is, Charity and union with God.

Because I wish you to show me this Charity, I always want to see you united and bound with this sweet bond, so that neither the Devil nor the words of any person can separate you. I recall the word spoken by Jesus Christ, that *he who humbles himself shall be exalted* <note>original: "chi si umilia, sarà esaltato." A reference to Luke 14:11.</note>. Benincasa, you who are the eldest, I want you to be the least of all; and you, Bartolomeo, should want to be the least of the least; and you, Stefano, I pray that you be subject to God and to them. In this way, you will preserve yourselves sweetly in most perfect Charity. May God always give you His most perfect Grace. I write nothing more to you. Remain in the holy and sweet love of God. Jesus sweet. Jesus Love.

# To Stefano di Corrado Maconi.

I. She exhorts him to be strong and persevering in battles.
II. That this strength is acquired by drowning oneself in the Blood of Jesus Christ.
III. How in this Blood the Soul knows the truth of the Eternal Father.
IV. Of Charity and other effects produced in us by the Blood of Jesus Christ.
V. That once the foundation in the acquisition of Virtues is laid, every other thing is easily executed.

What was His truth? [ *A* ]. *Stefano di Corrado Maconi was from a very noble family, one of those in Siena called Consular <note>A "Consular family" (Famiglia Consolare) refers to the ancient nobility of Siena who held the office of consul during the early medieval Republic.</note>, finding that in the year 1168 a certain Macone (from whom the family perhaps took its surname) resided with the title of Consul in the Government of the Republic. He was afterwards her most faithful companion in many of her journeys, also very often lending her his assistance in the <term>ministry of writing letters</term> <note>Stefano was one of Catherine’s primary secretaries, transcribing her dictated letters and sometimes carrying them to their destinations.</note>.* <margin>Don Bartolomeo Scarpetta, in the Life and Letters of Blessed Stefano, at the end of Vol. 1.</margin> *By her express order, he later took the Sacred Habit of the <term>Carthusians</term> <note>The Carthusians are a strictly cloistered contemplative religious order; their monasteries are known as Charterhouses (Certosa).</note>, and in a few years made such progress in all the religious virtues that, having been made Superior very quickly after governing various monasteries, he was for some time General of the Order under the obedience of the Popes who were in Italy—even yielding that dignity of his own will, in order to return his illustrious Religion to its proper union, having long made every effort to induce the same in* <margin>Don Bartolomeo Scarpetta, cited place.</margin> *Don Bonifazio Ferreri, who was the head of those religious who obeyed the Pope—*

...offices of Avignon. He died already advanced in years in 1424, honored with the title of *Blessed*. Eleven *Letters* were addressed by the *Saint* to this *Stefano*, in addition to the one that is addressed jointly to him and to *Pietro di Giovanni Ventura*. She also wrote him another—the first she ever wrote with her own hand, as we learn from *Blessed Thomas Caffarini*—which has been lost.

How disorganized these *Letters* were, and out of their proper sequence, can be seen from this: the third of them claimed in its title to be the last, and yet after that one, there were eight others. This one, which held the penultimate place, is either the first or among the first that the *Saint* wrote to him, as it does not speak to him of any business, but is entirely focused on exhorting him to be well-founded in *Virtue*. In some of these *Letters*, a lowly and humble addition is found attached to *Stefano's* name—a quite manifest sign of it having been placed there by the *Blessed* man himself, and with it, he released the *Copies* that were later printed. It is read in the printed *Life* of *Blessed Stefano* that he contracted a feud in 1374 and achieved peace in 1375 through the work of the *Saint*; however, I do not know how much truth there is in this, since he himself assures us that he had no knowledge of *Saint Catherine* until about the year 1376. Therefore, this and the others must have been written after the beginning of the year 1376.

# To Stefano di Corrado Maconi

<margin>I.</margin> **S**he exhorts him to be a true Guardian of the City of his Soul.
<margin>II.</margin> Of the three Gates of this City, two of which—namely Memory and Intellect—are not in our power, but rather the third, which is the Will; for which we must give thanks to God for such liberty.

## Letter 255.

->**In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified and of sweet Mary.**<-

<margin>I.</margin> **D**earest son in sweet Christ Jesus: I, Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious Blood, with the desire to see you as a true Guardian of the City of your Soul.
<margin>II.</margin> O dearest son, this City has many gates; the primary ones are three: namely Memory, Intellect, and Will. Our Creator allows all of these gates to be struck, and even opened by force, except for one: namely the Will. Thus it sometimes happens that the Intellect sees nothing but darkness, and the Memory is occupied with vain and transitory things with many various and diverse thoughts and dishonest ideas, and similarly all the other senses of the body are disordered and prone to ruin. Thus it is clearly seen that none of these gates is freely in our possession, but only the Gate of the Will is in our liberty, which has for its [guardian]...

Free will is the guard, and this Gate is so strong that neither a Demon nor any Creature can open it if the Guard does not consent. And if this Gate is not opened—that is, by consenting to what the Memory, the Intellect, and the other gates <note>Catherine refers here to the physical senses as additional "gates" through which information enters the soul.</note> perceive—our City remains free forever. Let us therefore recognize, Son, let us recognize such an excellent benefit and such immeasurable abundance of Charity as we have received from Divine Goodness, having placed us in free possession of such a noble City.

### III. 

Let us strive to maintain a good and diligent Guard, placing alongside the Guard of free will the **Dog of Conscience**. When someone arrives at the Gate, this dog wakes up **Reason** by barking, so that Reason may discern whether it is a Friend or an Enemy. In this way, the Guard may let in the Friends—carrying out holy and good inspirations—and drive away the Enemies, locking the Gate of the **Will** so that it does not consent to the wicked thoughts that arrive at the Gate every day. And when the City is requested of you by the Lord, you will be able to return it safe and adorned with true and real Virtues, through His Grace. ## To Stefano di Corrado Maconi.

### Letter 256.

->*In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary.*<-

<margin>B</margin>
I. **D**earest Son in Christ Jesus: I, Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious Blood, with the desire to see you out of the hands of your Enemies. It seems to me, if I am not mistaken, that Divine Goodness is already making the Dawn appear, from which I hope that soon the bright day will come when the Sun is risen. You were captured, according to what you write to me, not in the time of night, but in the time of day. Then, through the working of the Mercy of the Holy Spirit, the Dawn appeared in the hearts of the incarnate demons <note>By "incarnate demons," Catherine refers to the actual men who had physically captured Stefano, suggesting their hearts were softened by God.</note>: and thus you were released. Consider, sweetest Son, that while you remain in the night of true self-knowledge, you will never be captured; but if your own passion should try to pass through the day of selfish sensual love, or if the Soul should try to pass to the day of the knowledge of God before the night of self-knowledge, it would be captured by its enemies. <note>Catherine uses "night" as a positive metaphor for the humble, dark introspection where one recognizes their own nothingness, which must precede the "day" of seeing God’s greatness.</note> Now there is no doubt that if the Soul does not remain with anxious and sweet desire in the knowledge of self and of God’s Goodness within itself, it would find itself led captive by the enemies of God. Immediately the enemy of presumption, with the bond of pride, along with passions, delights, worldly status, the Devil, and the Flesh, would all seize us. And therefore I want you to always rest between the day and the night—that is, knowing yourself in God, and God in you.

II. Then you will find that if your Enemies had bound you and crowded your heart with many and varied thoughts, your heart will receive the **Dawn** <note>The "Dawn" (Aurora) represents a middle state of spiritual progress: the transition from the dark "Night" of self-knowledge to the bright "Sun" of knowing God.</note>, and it will be said to you within your Soul—and you shall say it too: Go in peace, and rest in peace at the **Table of the Cross**, where you will find Peace and quiet while remaining in a stormy sea. What great Peace there was when, to you lambs in the midst of those wolves, it was said by them: "Go in peace." Even while in the midst of their War, you tasted Peace when you heard this; and so, think to yourself that when the Soul feels seized by many and different thoughts, and it conforms itself to the Will of God—seeing with how much love He allows it, and how much they lead us to a more perfect diligence and true **Humility**—the soul finds Peace there, even while in the time of War.

III. Now my soul desires that, since the sweet Eternal Spouse rescued you miraculously and drew you out of their hands, I pray Him that He might soon draw you away from those others who are even greater and more cruel Enemies than those men were. These were Enemies of the Body, but the others are Enemies of the Soul; and the truth is that a man's domestic associates, according to the world, are our Enemies <note>Catherine is referencing Matthew 10:36. In her view, family and worldly friends often distract the soul from God, making them "domestic enemies."</note>, and especially those who are more closely joined to us than it appears, who attend to nothing but their own utility. When you are liberated from them and have come out of prison, the **Sun** will be risen. Now you are in the **Dawn**, which still does not fully let you taste or discern **Virtue**, because you are not yet in the time of the Sun—that is, when you are untied from these domestic Enemies. ### [ D ] 
**I answer you regarding the matter of going to Mass. You do well not to go, and to have made yourselves household servants of Master James, etc.**

<margin>*History of Siena, part 3, book 2.*</margin>
<margin>*Ugurgieri, Sienese Glories, title VI.*</margin>
*The Saint gives a holy response to a query posed to her, which is mentioned only in passing, and thus cannot be fully understood. From what can be gathered, it seems that while the City of Siena was subjected to an <term>Interdict</term> <note>A decree by the Pope that prohibits certain religious rites and sacraments from being performed in a specific city or region, usually as a punishment</note>—as noted in the annotations to Letter 203—Stefano and others had enrolled themselves among the "familiars" or household members of this Master James. Due to his high rank, Master James was not forbidden from participating in Divine Offices even during that time, and Stefano had sought the opinion of his Holy Teacher <note>Saint Catherine</note> on this arrangement. There seems to be no doubt that this Master James was James of Sozzino Tolomei, a member of the Order of Friars Minor Conventual and Bishop of Narni, promoted to that dignity by Urban VI. No other person of such high rank with that name is known to have been in Siena during these years. This is further confirmed by public records cited by Tommasi, which state he was sent by the Pope to Siena as an Apostolic Nuncio <note>A high-ranking diplomat representing the Pope</note> to lift the Interdict from the city and negotiate the restoration of Talamone. Later, in 1383, he was promoted to the Bishopric of Grosseto and had significant disputes with the Sienese Republic; he and other members of his noble and powerful family plotted a conspiracy against the government, which was then a popular regime. He eventually died in 1387, an exile from his homeland. The Saint responds wisely to the request: since declaring oneself a "familiar" of someone does not truly make one a domestic servant or slave, it does not actually qualify a person to enjoy the privileges granted to the true household of such a dignitary. Therefore, Maconi could not rightfully enjoy the privileges granted to the Bishop's actual servants.*

### [ E ] 
**Whether Monna Lapa returns to Siena.** *Referring to the mother of Saint Catherine, who was perhaps staying in Florence with her other children.*

### [ F ] 
**And tell the Prior, that regarding Monna Lapa, etc.**

<margin>*Memoirs of the Archives of San Domenico in Siena*</margin>
*This refers to the Prior of the Convent of San Domenico in Siena. Lapa had already taken the habit of the <term>Mantellate</term> <note>A group of laywomen, often widows, associated with the Dominican Order who wore the habit but lived in their own homes</note>. Records show that in 1378 she became a "Sister" to her own daughter by joining that institute. For this reason, the Saint leaves the final decision regarding her to the Prior, who was her religious superior.*

### ( G ) 
**Your negligent brother, Barduccio.** *This refers to Barduccio Canigiani, one of Catherine’s most devoted secretaries and disciples.*

## To Stefano di Corrado Maconi.

I. She exhorts him to despise himself and every worldly thing for the honor of God.

### Letter 257.

->In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary.<-

I. **D**earest son in Christ Jesus: I, Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious Blood, with the desire to see you die consumed with longing for the honor of God—dying that death which gives life to the soul. This means that, for the honor of God, you do not care for yourself, but that I may see you run manfully to whatever place you can best fulfill His Will. It is time, my sweet son, to lose oneself and not care for anything, provided that we perform God's honor through much labor. I will say no more here.

II. I pray you, and I command you on behalf of Christ Crucified, that if the Prior <note>Likely the head of a religious house or monastery Stefano was associated with</note> etc., or others on his behalf, should request any service from you through letters or by messenger, you obey him as you would my own person, knowing that whatever he imposes upon you will be according to my will...

Here the Saint <note>St. Catherine of Siena</note> adopts this saying to express that it was necessary to have a little patience, and to restrain with moderation the longing for the grace that was being requested.*

[ E ] **To Matteo I am writing a Letter.** *Matteo di Cenni di Fazio, Rector of the Hospital of Mercy <note>a charitable institution in Siena</note>, to whom the Saint wrote three Letters. The one mentioned here is perhaps Letter 140, and in it she sends him the sacred Treasures of the Indulgences.*

[ F ] **That the Company of the Virgin Mary may give him as much help as you can.** *This Company, which was discussed in another place, manages many assets left to the piety and prudence of its Brothers, so that they may provide help to the needs of others.*

[ G ] **I am writing about it also to Pietro.** *The Letter written to this Pietro, who is perhaps the son of Giovanni Venture, is lost.*

[ H ] **May the negligent and ungrateful writer be recommended to you.** *This will be either Neri de' Pagliaresi or Barduccio Canigiani, the other two ordinary Secretaries of the Saint.*

## Letter 259.

### *In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary.*

**D**earest Son in sweet Christ Jesus: I, Catherine, servant and slave of the Servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious Blood, with the desire to see you emerge from the darkness and direct yourself toward the light without further delay. For time is running out for us, and we do not notice it because of our blindness; but we must indeed lift the cloud from before us and take the truth as our aim. The truth is this: that God wills and seeks nothing else from us but our Sanctification. For this reason, He created us in His Image and likeness, and for this reason, the sweet and loving Word <term>the Word: a title for Jesus Christ (the Logos), emphasizing His role as God's communication to humanity</term> willed to give His life with such a fire of love, and thus He manifests His truth to us. The Soul that looks upon this with light does not remain asleep; rather, it awakes from its slumber, seeking with great diligence the manner, the way, the place, and the time through which it may fulfill its purpose. It does not trust that it can wait until tomorrow, because it sees that it is not certain of having it. This is how I want you to act. Cast all darkness from you, so that this light is not hindered. You know that God has shown you—since you emerged from the darkness—that He has chosen you to know this truth. You would make yourself worthy of great reproach if you were to resist Him. You would be resisting Him if, through negligence, you set yourself to untying and not to cutting <note>Catherine often used the metaphor of "cutting" to describe a total, radical break from worldly life/secular career, as opposed to "untying" which implies a slow, hesitant process</note>; and because He wants you to cut, He has granted you the grace of having settled and concluded your affairs, from which conclusion there was great joy—

# To Stefano di Corrado <note>Stefano Maconi, Catherine’s beloved disciple and secretary</note> from her, his most unworthy and ungrateful daughter, she being in Rome.

I. The Soul is encouraged to cut itself off from the world and its own sensory feelings, showing it with what means and in what manner this cutting must be done.

II. She stimulates him to open his ears to the voices of God, who invites his faithful to fight for the glory and praise of His Name, for the Holy Church, and for the approval of Virtue.

## Letter 262.

->In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary.<-

Dearest son in Christ sweet Jesus: I, Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious Blood, with the desire to see you cut, and not set yourself to untying; because in untying, a span of time is required, and you are not certain of having it, because it passes quickly. Therefore, it is better to cut effectively with a true and holy diligence. Oh, how blessed my soul will be when I see that you have cut the world away from you, both in action and in mind, as well as your own sensory feelings, and that you are united with Eternal Life! This union is of such delight, and of such sweetness and suavity, that it extinguishes every bitterness and makes every great burden light. Who then will hold himself back from drawing forth the knife of hatred and of love <note>Catherine’s frequent metaphor for the hatred of one’s own selfish will and the love of God's will</note>, and with the hand of free will, cut himself away from himself? As soon as he has cut, this knife is of such power <term>Virtù</term> <note>Virtù here implies both moral virtue and an inherent, miraculous power or efficacy</note> that it unites him to God. But you will say to me: Dearest—

...my son; where do I find it, and where is this knife forged? I answer you: Find it in the **Cell of self-knowledge**, <note>A central concept in Catherine’s spirituality; she taught that one must always carry an "interior cell" of self-reflection and awareness of God's presence within.</note> where you conceive hatred for Vice and for your own fragility, and love for your Creator and for your Neighbor with true and real Virtues. Where is it forged? In the fire of **Divine Charity** upon the **Anvil of the Body of the sweet and loving Word, Son of God.** Therefore, he is truly ignorant and worthy of great rebuke who has the weapon within himself to be able to defend himself, and yet casts it away.

# To Stefano di Corrado Maconi, while she was in Rome; and this <margin>4</margin> was the last letter to him.

I. **S**he exhorts him to adorn himself with Virtues to draw souls to God by his example, and by the talent received from God.
II. That Virtue is acquired in the knowledge of ourselves, united with Prayer, and with the memory of the Blood of Jesus Christ.
III. That from the knowledge of oneself is born the most perfect love, and in what manner.
IV. That once Charity is acquired, we must use it for the benefit of our Neighbor.
V. She exhorts him to change his state of life <note>Catherine is encouraging Stefano to join a religious order.</note>, and informs him of the Prayers she continually offered for the same purpose.
VI. She responds to certain events about which he had written to her.
VII. She desires his departure from his kin, praying him to respond to the divine calls.

## Letter 263.

->In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of Mary sweet.<-

I. **D**earest and sweetest Son in Christ sweet Jesus: I, Catherine, servant and slave of the Servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious Blood, with the desire to see you as a mirror of Virtue, so that with the example of your Life, and with the doctrine of your word, and with continual and humble Prayer, you may be an instrument to draw souls from the hands of the Devil and lead them back to the Truth, Christ sweet Jesus, as God requires of us. This is so that a good account may be rendered of the talent <note>original: "talento"; a reference to the Parable of the Talents in Matthew 25, implying the gifts and responsibilities God gives to a person.</note> that He has given us to exercise virtue and the life of the Soul; for without it, we would be deprived of the life of Grace, and in this life we would taste the earnest-money <note>original: "arra"; a pledge or down-payment. Catherine means that the suffering of sin is a foretaste of Hell.</note> of Hell.

<meta>This page transitions from the historical commentary on the Great Schism and the Neapolitan Abbot Lisolo into the primary text of Letter 264. # To Pietro di Giovanni, and to Stefano di Corrado together, while she was in Rome.

I. **S**he encourages them to fight manfully against the three principal Enemies—namely, the World, the Devil, and the Flesh—showing them how the first two can be easily conquered, but not without great difficulty the third, which is the Flesh.
II. That hatred and Love are the weapons for fighting against sensuality.
III. She exhorts the aforementioned Pietro and Stefano to go to Rome swiftly.
IV. That God always pours graces into His holy Church.
V. She exhorts them all to perseverance.

## Letter 264.

->In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary.<-

I. **D**earest sons in Christ sweet Jesus: I, Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious Blood, with the desire to see you as manly knights <note>Catherine frequently uses the imagery of "knighthood" (*cavalieri*) to describe the disciplined, courageous life of a committed Christian.</note>, and in such a way that you may be victors over your three principal enemies. O sweetest sons, these three enemies are the Devil, the World, and the Flesh. It is an easy thing for us to conquer the first two; for the power that the Devil held over us was taken away by means of the Blood of the Son of God, to the extent that he has no power over us except what we ourselves grant him through our will toward sin. He can certainly cause us many troubles with various and diverse thoughts, but he cannot compel us to even the slightest sin; because in the said Blood of the Immaculate Lamb we are fortified and released from his servitude. What can the World do to us? Nothing at all. It can indeed strike the outer bark <note>Catherine uses "the bark" (*la corteccia*) to refer to the physical body or external circumstances, as opposed to the "pith" or "essence" of the soul.</note> of our body with many persecutions, mistreatments, scorns, and infamies,

...insults; but what does the **Servant of God** feel about all these things in the marrow of the **Soul**? Nothing at all. <note>original: "Non cavelle" – a characteristic Tuscan idiom used by Catherine meaning "nothing at all" or "not a bit."</note> The World wears itself out in giving him many **tribulations**, and he rejoices, because he has placed his affection in God, from whom all **joy** comes; He has chosen to endure for **Christ Crucified**; thus he considers it a blessing whenever he finds himself suffering without guilt, because then he conforms more to Him. 

So it is quite true that these two **Enemies** are easy to conquer. But the third—the **Flesh**, that is, our own **sensuality**—is a perverse law that always fights against the **Spirit**; hardly a moment passes that it does not want to rebel in some way against the **Will of God**. That is to say, it makes us cast behind our backs all the good inspirations that **Divine Clemency** sends into our hearts, so that it allows us to put none of them into execution, as long as we believe its lies. 

On the contrary, all the wicked thoughts that the **Devil** gives us—which are permitted by God to be given to us for the increase of perfection and **Grace** within us, and not so that we let ourselves be overcome—this perverse sensory passion makes us carry them all out. In short, it is that thing which deprives us of God and keeps us in continual bitterness in this life. We must, therefore, arm ourselves well against this **Enemy**.

<margin>[3]</margin>
II. Therefore, I want each of you to divide yourself into two parts: namely, **sensuality** and **Reason**, and let them be mortal **Enemies**. Let **Reason** arm itself, taking up the knife of hatred and of love. <note>The "knife of hatred and love" is one of Catherine’s most famous metaphors: hatred for one's own selfish will (sensuality) and love for God’s will.</note> And this war must not be undertaken sluggishly, but with efficacy; one must strive in every way to kill [the sensuality]; for that thing which takes the life of **Grace** from us and makes us rebel against God certainly ought to be killed. 

And sometimes this cursed law uses a great deception to make us fall with a harder blow: it will fall asleep and seem to be dead within us, since we find no struggle; instead, with burning fervor, all our acts and thoughts will be directed toward God with such sweetness that we seem to taste **Eternal Life**. But if we slacken the war, put down the knife, and do not exercise ourselves with diligence, it wakes up stronger than ever and sometimes makes us fall miserably. Therefore I want, my sons, for you to take up this war with the intention of never making peace, but of continually increasing it, giving to her...

I will say no more on this here.

### III.
I am responding to the **Letters** that you, Pietro, sent me. I shall see clearly if you truly have a desire to leave **Home** and come here; for if you have the will, you will strive with all diligence to dispatch yourself and bring to an end all the affairs that remain for you to do, so that, being unburdened, you may follow <term>Christ Crucified</term> <note>original: "Cristo Crocifisso" – Catherine’s primary name for Jesus, emphasizing His sacrifice and the blood of redemption.</note> in everything. 

But you are a negligent one, and you have not taken up that **knife** which was mentioned above; wherefore you do not put into execution the holy desire that God has given you. I know well that you do not 

<margin>B</margin> believe I wish to abandon you; for as surely as death comes to you and the others, I give birth to you anew every day in the sight of God through continual <term>Prayer</term> <note>original: "Oratione" – specifically the practice of deep, contemplative prayer.</note>, and most especially to those in whom I see the greatest need. Now strive to renew yourself, and I say the same to you, Stefano: that you study with diligence to lift yourselves from the **World** and run to **God**, who awaits us with open arms; come quickly.

<margin>C</margin> ### IV.
