* (A) This Letter is addressed to both Stefano and Pietro di Giovanni Venture, who was discussed in the annotations for Letter 235.*

* (B) *“May death come to you and the others just as I give birth to you anew every day in the sight of God.”* The French translator <note>This likely refers to the French versions of Catherine's letters circulated in the 17th century.</note> has taken the liberty of pulling these words toward a different meaning, giving them to us in his own language as: *And so may you live, you and all your brothers, as I give birth to you each day.* <note>original: "Et qu'ainsi vous puissiès viure, vous, & tous vos confreres, comme chaque jour je vous enfante."</note> I am inclined to believe that as the Saint burned entirely with the longing to die for the **Faith** and in defense of the **Pontificate of Urban VI**, she desired a similar fate for her **Sons**; thus she speaks by way of a wish, hoping they all might have the fortune of shedding their blood for this cause, as she perhaps expressed more clearly to them in person at other times.*

<margin>History of the Western Schism, book 1, page 94 and following.</margin>
* [C] *The Holy Church and Pope Urban VI, through the sweet Goodness of God, have had in these days the most significant news, etc.* In those days, happy announcements could have reached **Urban VI** regarding the steadfastness of the Emperor, the King of Hungary, England, and other Northern realms in recognizing him as the legitimate Pope, as France and the Spanish kingdoms had not yet taken the opposing side. Nor do I wish to fail to mention the boldness of **Maimbourg** <note>Louis Maimbourg (1610–1686), a historian known for his controversial views on the papacy and the Gallican church.</note> in reporting the facts pertaining to that **Schism**, always twisting them in favor of the party of **Clement** <note>Clement VII, the "antipope" elected in opposition to Urban VI, starting the Western Schism.</note> and to the disadvantage of **Urban’s** party. In numbering the Princes and States of Europe that held to this Pontiff, he claims most of them entered that party for political ends without examining the reasons, whereas, on the contrary, he claims France and Spain moved to Clement’s side after long and very mature counsel. Thus, the Emperor **Wenceslaus** followed Urban out of gratitude, as his Empire had been confirmed by him, and...

The English became **Urbanists** <note>Supporters of Pope Urban VI during the Great Western Schism.</note> for the purpose of opposing their French enemies in everything; they were followed by the Flemish, who were allied with England. The King of Hungary [joined] because he was an enemy of Queen Joanna, who was a supporter of **Clement** <note>Antipope Clement VII, the rival claimant to the papacy based in Avignon.</note>; and Italy joined out of a jealous pride for having an Italian Pope. <note>The following sentence was originally in French.</note> The greater part of Italy, for the interest of the Nation which no longer wanted an **Ultramontane** <note>original: "Oltramontain" – a term for a Pope from "beyond the mountains," i.e., non-Italian.</note> Pope, was for Urban. <margin>Ric. for the years 1379 & 1380.</margin>
to clarify the whole truth were merely for appearance, as others have said; and of the Spanish kingdoms, which also entered that party, led there by the maneuvers of the French King, as some have written—especially the Crown of Castile, which was closely united in interests with that of France. This was also the case for Scotland, which always followed the interests of the French Kings, partly to better oppose those of England. Aragon then, according to the words of this same author, although it had reason to complain about Urban—who had threatened King Peter with the intent of taking Sardinia from him, and warned him not to think of Sicily—and although Cardinal de Luna <note>Pedro de Luna, a powerful diplomat who later became the Avignonese Antipope Benedict XIII.</note> strongly urged him to give his obedience to Clement, remained neutral for a long time, eventually siding with the Avignonese Pope, perhaps due to the slights he received from the other.

( D ) **Which goes to the Bachelor.** Brother William of England, a Hermit of Saint Augustine at Lecceto, who was discussed in the annotations to Letter 134. Which of the six letters written to him by the Saint is the one she alludes to here, I do not dare to affirm. In Epistle 126, the Saint informs him of the good disposition of the **Judge of Arborea** <note>original: "Giudice d’Oriſtagni" – the ruler of one of the Sardinian judicates.</note> to undertake the **Crusade** <note>original: "il Paſſaggio" – literally "the crossing," a common term for a military expedition to the Holy Land.</note> with the full force of his people, and how the Republic of Genoa was also preparing for the Sacred War against the infidels; but these cannot be the "happy news" offered in this letter. These were not the matters of pressing concern at this time, nor were the minds of the Princes in any way disposed to favor this undertaking, contrary to what she expresses in that letter—especially the Genoese, who were entirely focused with their minds and their weapons on harming the Venetians, as that war was then at the height of its intensity. I believe, therefore, that this letter has also been lost, as this misfortune has happened to many others, much to our disadvantage.

( E ) The Grandmother. Perhaps they called one of the Saint’s companions by this name because she was more advanced in age; by chance, it was either *Alessia* or *Giovanna di Capo*. <note>Catherine often used affectionate nicknames for the members of her "famiglia" or circle of disciples.</note>

( F ) *Lisa*. The Saint's sister-in-law and her companion in her room in Rome.

<margin>Life of St. Catherine, book 2, ch. 11.</margin>
( G ) And all the rest of the poor little Family. This was usually composed of eight women and sixteen men, but most of the time it turned out to be much more numerous. Since the Saint welcomed with all charity the guests brought to her by either devotion or necessity, they sometimes reached over sixty in number. They were all maintained by the subsidies provided by the charity of others, sought from door to door, now by one of the companions, now by another; when the necessities of life were lacking—which happened more than once—the Saint provided for them through miracles. <note>The "Family" refers to Catherine's devoted followers, or "Caterinati," who lived and traveled with her.</note>

<margin>Bartolomeo the Carthusian in the Life of Blessed Stefano.</margin>
[ H ] When you, Stefano, arrive. Since the present letter is from the first of January in the year 1379—that is, one month after Saint Catherine’s arrival in Rome, having arrived there on November 28th of the previous year—this confirms what was said above: that the Blessed Stefano was not among the Saint's companions on that journey. This is true even though the author who left us the *Actions and Virtues* of this holy man wrote the contrary. <note>Stefano Maconi was one of Catherine’s primary secretaries; the author is correcting a historical error regarding when Stefano joined Catherine in Rome.</note>

( I ) Given in Rome, *January 1st, 1378* <note>original: "prima Januarii 1378"</note>. Whether the date of this letter is the Saint’s own, or was added by some Sienese person, there is no error in the year. We must conclude that they used the Era of the Incarnation of the Divine Word, which begins on March 25th, according to the Sienese custom. <note>The Sienese Republic used a calendar where the new year began on March 25th (the Feast of the Annunciation). Therefore, January 1378 in Sienese time is actually January 1379 in the modern calendar.</note> This must be affirmed so as not to give room for the suspicion of malicious people who might suggest these letters were forged. There is no doubt that on the first day of January 1378, Gregory XI was still alive, and there was no memory yet of Urban VI (who was created Pope three months later); likewise, it is certain that at that time the Saint was staying not in Rome, but in Florence. Therefore, the January listed here in the Sienese manner as 1378 was in truth the first month of the year 1379, according to the calculation of years commonly used in the rest of Italy. See what was observed in the annotations to Letter 102.

# To Niccolaccio di Caterino Petroni of Siena.

I. **H**e is exhorted to the observance of the Divine Precepts to participate in the life of Grace, but especially he is exhorted to Charity toward his Neighbor, which always goes hand-in-hand with the love of God.
II. That in whatever state one may be, good works must not be neglected, even in a state of sin.
III. How much more greatly God rewards works done in His Grace.

## Letter 265.

### In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary.

I. **D**earest Brother in Christ sweet Jesus: I, Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, <note>Catherine frequently used this title—a version of the Papal "Servant of the servants of God"—to express her deep humility.</note> write to you in His precious Blood, with the desire to see you as an observer of the sweet commandments of God, so that you may participate in the life of Grace. But this you could not do if you held displeasure and hatred for your Neighbor; for the second commandment of God is to love your Neighbor as ourselves. This affection of loving the Creature flows from the Fountain of Divine Charity; <note>The "Fountain" is a favorite metaphor for Catherine, describing God's heart as the source of all love.</note> therefore, whoever is not in the Charity of God is not in the charity of his Neighbor. Not being in it, he is like a limb that is cut off from the Body, which immediately loses its life and withers, because it is cut off from its source of life; and thus the Soul, separated by hatred from Divine Charity, is immediately dead to Grace, so much so that no good thing he does is of value to him regarding Eternal Life.

II. It is true, however, that one should not stop doing good, regardless of the state one is in, because every good is rewarded and every fault punished. If it is not rewarded with Eternal Life, God grants him this: either He grants him the time to be able to correct his life, or He will place some means through His Servants to draw him out of the hands of the De-

# To Agnolino di Giovanni d' Agnolino de' Salimbeni of Siena.

I. **S**he encourages him to fight manfully against our common enemies: the Flesh, the World, and the Devil.
II. That we must set the Dog of Conscience as a guard for our Soul. <note>Catherine frequently uses the "Dog of Conscience" as a metaphor for the inner voice that "barks" to alert the soul when sin or temptation approaches.</note>
III. That we must govern this with the fire of Charity, and with the Blood of Jesus Christ.
IV. How much Humility suits Man, and how Pride is unbecoming.
V. How Jesus Christ gives us strength to conquer our enemies.

VII. ## Letter 267.

### In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary.

I. **D**earest Son in sweet Jesus Christ: I, Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious Blood, with the desire to see you as a true combatant, and not one who dodges blows like a cowardly knight. These are the Flesh, with its disordered sensory delight; the World, with its honors and its pleasures; and the Devil with his malice. To hinder the holy desire of the Soul, the Devil sets many snares—either by himself or by means of a creature <note>In Catherine’s writing, "creature" generally refers to other human beings as created things.</note> using the tongues of his servants—speaking pleasing words of flattery, or threats, or gossip, or infamy. But we, like manly Knights, must resist and guard this City, and bolt the Gates of disordered feelings, and place the **Dog of Conscience** as a guard; so that when the Enemy passes, hearing the barks, he will thus awaken the eye of the <term>Intellect (Intelletto)</term> <note>In Catherine’s teaching, the Intellect is the soul's ability to discern truth through the light of faith.</note>, and see if it is Friend or Enemy—that is, whether it is Vice or Virtue that passes by. To this Dog, it is proper to give drink and food; he should be given Blood to drink and fire to eat, so that he may rise from the cold of negligence, and thus become diligent.

III. To you I say, Son Agnolino, give to this Dog of your Conscience the food of the most burning **Charity**, <note>decorative flourish</note> and the drink of the Blood of the immaculate Lamb opened upon the Cross, who from every part of His Body pours out Blood, so that we have something to give him to drink; and doing so, he will be completely reinvigorated, and you will become a true combatant. And take up the knife of hate and love—that is, hatred and displeasure for Vice, and love for Virtue; and may the Enemy of our Flesh, which is the worst and most wicked Enemy we can have, be slain, along with its delight, by this knife. And let Conscience show to the eye of the Intellect how dangerous this Enemy of carnal delight is as it passes into the Soul, so that it may be killed; and let him look upon the scourged Flesh of Christ Crucified, so that he may be ashamed to hold his own body in pleasure, in disordered delight, and in luxuries. And may the Devil, with his malices and the <term>snares (laccivoli)</term> he has set to catch Souls, be defeated by the Virtue of true **Humility**. Let this Dog of Conscience bark, awakening the eye of the Intellect, and see how dangerous it is to believe his [the Devil's] deceptions; and let man turn to himself and recognize that he is nothing <note>original: "l' Uomo sè non eſſere"—a central theme in Catherine's mysticism regarding the soul's nothingness without God</note>, so that he does not fall into pride; for Humility is that which breaks all the snares of the Devil.

IV. Indeed, Man should be ashamed to become proud, seeing that he is nothing, and that his very being comes from God and not from himself; and seeing God humbled for him; because through profound Humility He descended from the highest height to such lowliness as is our Flesh.

V. This sweet and beloved Lamb, the Word incarnate

The Flesh is defeated by the scourges and torments of Christ, and the World by the shame, mockery, villainies, and insults [He endured], and wealth by the voluntary poverty of Christ Crucified; for the highest Wealth is so poor that He has no place to rest His head while hanging upon the Wood of the Most Holy Cross. 

When the Enemy of the honor and the status of the World wants to enter within, make sure, Son, that the **Dog of your Conscience** barks at him, and awakens the guard of the <term>Intellect (Intelletto)</term> <note>In Catherine’s theology, the Intellect is the soul's power to discern truth through the light of faith.</note>, so that it may see that no worldly honor or status has any stability or firmness; no matter where they come from, the Intellect finds none at all. Then I want you to see that by giving oneself inordinately to these transitory things, which pass like the wind, no honor follows, but rather disgrace; because Man submits himself to something less than himself, and serves finite things, while he himself is infinite. For Man never ceases to be, although he may cease to be in <term>Grace (Gratia)</term> <note>State of being in a right relationship with God.</note> through mortal sin. And therefore, if we want honor and rest and fulfillment, it is necessary for us to serve and love something that is greater than us.

### VI.

God is our Redeemer, Lord, and Father, the highest and eternal Goodness, worthy of being loved and served by us; and we must do so by duty if we wish to participate in **Divine Grace**. He is the highest Power and fulfillment; He is the One who satisfies and fills the Soul, and strengthens every weak person; so that they remain in peace, in quiet, in <term>satisfaction (satietà)</term>, and in security. One cannot be satisfied elsewhere, and for this reason, every created thing is less than Man.

# To Matteo di Tomuccio of Orvieto

I. **H**e is exhorted to be constant, founded on the Living Stone, which is Jesus Christ.
II. That the Soul founded on this Stone is not moved by any contrary wind of adversity.
III. That the first wind which assails the Soul is the Devil with his temptations, and what they are in particular.
IV. Of the second wind, which is the World with its vanities, and the harms it produces.
V. How we must defend ourselves from it by remaining founded in Jesus Christ.
VI. Of the third wind, namely the Flesh, and how we must defend ourselves from it, particularly through humble Prayer.
VII. That many Servants of God fall because they are not well-founded on the Living Stone, which is Jesus Christ.

---

## Letter 268.

->In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of<-
->sweet Mary.<-

I. **D**earest Brother and Son in Christ sweet Jesus. I, Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ <note>Catherine frequently used this title, echoing the papal title *Servus servorum Dei*, to express her profound humility.</note>, write to you in His precious Blood, with the desire to see you as a firm Stone, and not a leaf that flies with every wind.

II. For the Soul that is not founded upon the living Stone, Christ sweet Jesus—that is, whose affection and desire are not founded solely in God, but rather in the transitory things of the World, which all pass away like the wind—fails, because it is deprived of Divine Grace. It is this Grace that preserves the Soul, from which it receives life and which gives it perfect light, depriving it of darkness and founding it in true and perfect patience, and in true and holy fear of God with perfect Humility and brotherly Charity toward one's Neighbor. Such a soul is not moved to impatience by the wind of tribulations, nor is it moved by disordered delight through the wind of consolations, nor does it swell with pri- <note>The text cuts off here at the start of the word "pride" (superbia).</note>

<summary>This page introduces a letter from Saint Catherine of Siena to Matteo di Tomuccio of Orvieto, outlining a spiritual framework for stability. Using the metaphor of the "Living Stone" from the New Testament, she warns against the "winds" of the devil, the world, and the flesh.</summary>

...[is distur]bed by the wind of wealth, and by the smoke of the honor of the World.

### III.
And all this happens to him because he does not move, because his foundation is <term>Christ Crucified<explanation>A central image in Catherine’s theology, representing the ultimate foundation of faith and the source of all grace.</explanation></term>; therefore, though those three principal perverse winds blow from which every other wind comes, he does not care about them. These are: the Devil, from whose mouth comes the wind of many and diverse thoughts and battles—sometimes the battle of vanity, which makes the heart light and immature, and through this vanity the appetite and desire for the <term>States of the World<explanation>The social ranks, political power, and material possessions of secular life.</explanation></term> grows; and sometimes it comes with the <note>original: "colore di Virtù"</note> appearance of Virtue. This is the most difficult wind to recognize that there is, and only the humble person is the one who recognizes it and cannot be deceived by it.

The appearance of Virtue that the Devil puts forward is this: if he finds the Soul ignorant and without the Virtue of Humility or true <term>self-knowledge<explanation>A core concept for Catherine; she taught that one must enter the "cell of self-knowledge" to find God within.</explanation></term>; suppose the soul has begun to desire God and show signs of Virtue, because it is still imperfect and lacks sufficient knowledge of itself, it begins to watch the actions of its Neighbor <note>meaning: fellow human being</note> in both temporal and spiritual matters. Then the Devil blows with the wind of false judgment, judging his Neighbor—whether they are Servants of God or servants of the world—wickedly, and he does not even realize it. 

Thus, such a person wants to take the Lordship of judgment out of God's hand; for only He is to judge them. Why does he not realize this? Because the Devil has cloaked this judgment with the mantle of Virtue, so that it seems to him that he acts for the sake of good; and this appearance is so deceptive that often it seems to him he is making a Sacrifice to God. But he is deceived by the <term>pride<explanation>In the medieval tradition, pride was considered the "root of all evils" and the direct opposite of Catherine's prized humility.</explanation></term> that is in him; for if he were truly humble and founded on true self-knowledge, he would be ashamed to see himself falling into such judgment. He would see that it is an attempt to set rules for God; for he wants to set rules for God when he is scandalized by His Servants, wanting to direct God's creatures in his own way, rather than according to how God calls them. 

And therefore, he who will be founded upon the living Stone, Christ, will resist these movements and will not consent, but with true Humility he will strive to rejoice and give glory to God for the habits and ways of His Servants, and to have compassion for the flawed, praying to Divine Goodness to turn the eye of Mercy...

<summary>Catherine explains the Devil's subtle temptation of "false judgment," where a person mistakenly believes they are being virtuous while actually usurping God's role as judge. She advocates for humility and self-knowledge as the only defenses against this spiritual pride.</summary>

over them, drawing them out of sin and leading them back to the Virtues; and thus he draws the Rose from the thorn. He keeps his <term>Mind<explanation>In Catherine’s writing, the ‘Mind’ often refers to the higher part of the soul where memory, intellect, and will reside.</explanation></term> pure and does not go about fantasizing, filling his memory with various fantasies of spiritual things—which he imagines he is receiving in the Mind—and of temporal things, as the mad, the foolish, and the presumptuous do. It is right, therefore, to flee from this with true and holy diligence.

### IV.
The other dangerous and perverse wind is the **World**, which delights in itself with disordered self-love and seeks its own pleasures and comforts. It fixes the eye of its <term>Intellect<explanation>The faculty of the soul that perceives and understands truth.</explanation></term> upon these things, covering up the darkness, misery, and lack of firmness and stability of the World with a mask of beauty, showing it to be beautiful and pleasing. And so it deceives the person, showing a long life though it is actually short; it makes it seem that all the delights, comforts, and riches of the World are stable and his own, though they are mutable and are only given on loan and for use according to his necessity. For it is inevitable that either these things be taken from Man, or Man be taken from them. Thus they are taken from us when we lose them at some time, or they are stolen from us by others, or through various other accidents that befall people, by which things are consumed and fail. I say that we are taken from them when the <term>First Sweet Truth<explanation>Catherine’s characteristic name for God, emphasizing that God is the ultimate reality and the source of all truth.</explanation></term> calls us, separating the <term>Soul<explanation>The immortal essence of the human person.</explanation></term> from the body, where the Body and the World with all its delights are abandoned; from this separation there is no one who can escape, neither through riches nor honor.

The weak and blinded Soul, then, which has not removed the dust of the World from its eye, but has even set it as its object, turns like a leaf on a tree in the wind of disordered self-love and of the World. From this cursed mouth comes an envy toward its Neighbor, with a high reputation of itself while murmuring, and many times it leads to hatred and resentment toward the Neighbor, and often makes [judgments] of others' affairs...

She emphasizes that all worldly goods are merely on loan and will be left behind at death when the 'First Sweet Truth' calls the soul.</summary>

his own, and to acquire them he will use oaths, perjury, and false witness; and he grows so much in this that he desires the death of his Neighbor, and those whom he ought to love as himself, he has become a devourer of both their flesh and their substance. He is without any steadiness, and whatever he begins in **Virtue**, he rarely brings it to completion. This man is founded upon the sand, where no building can be made that does not soon fall to the ground. He is deprived of the life of **Grace**, and has lost the light of **Reason**; he walks like an animal, and not like a rational **Creature**.

V. It is fitting, therefore, and necessary for us to be founded upon the <term>Living Stone<explanation>A reference to Jesus Christ, based on 1 Peter 2:4, symbolizing a stable and eternal foundation for the soul.</explanation></term>, upon which those who have placed the eye of the **Intellect** and their affection through holy desire cannot be struck, nor do they allow themselves to be struck by this wicked wind. Rather, they resist and defend themselves with a distaste for the **World** and its vanity and pleasures, and they strike down pride with deep **Humility**, and by desiring **Voluntary Poverty**. And he who has wealth and **Status** <note>original: 'Stato', referring to one's social standing or rank.</note> holds it, but does not possess it with disordered love outside the **Will of God**, but holds it with love and holy fear, and as a steward of **Christ**, helping the poor and nourishing the **Servants of God**, holding them in reverence, considering that they always offer **Prayers**, and burning desires, sweat, and tears before **God** for the salvation of every **Creature**. Such people rejoice at all times and in whatever state they are in, because they are deprived of the bitterness of the disordered will founded on self-love. Since, then, this foundation is so delightful, one must not wait for time to acquire it, because we are not certain of having [more] time.

VI. The other principal wind, I say, is the **Flesh**, which casts out such a miserable stench that it does not only stink before **God**, but it stinks to the **Demons**, and directly makes **Man** beastly; for he has the same shame as an **Animal**. This man acts like the **Pig** that wallows in the mud; thus he wallows in the mud of <term>impurity<explanation>The original 'disoneſtà' carries the weight of sexual immorality or lack of moral decency.</explanation></term>, and in whatever state he is, he ruins himself. Therefore, if he is bound to the state of **Marriage**, with disordered love he contaminates his state, and where he ought to approach that **Sacrament** with fear of **God**, he goes to it in a disordered way and with little decency. And these miserable ones do not look upon the great excellence in which our **Humanity** is held, because of the union that **God** has made in the

...our miserable **Flesh**; for if they were to open the eye of the **Intellect** to look upon it, they would choose death itself before giving themselves over to such misery. And do you know what a stench comes from this mouth, poisoning anyone who approaches it? The heart becomes suspicious, the tongue murmurs and blasphemes, believing that what is within itself is also in others. 

It is just like a sick man with a ruined stomach; because he is corrupted, food does not seem good to him. And it is not only common foods that taste foul, but even the specific medicine that the **Physician** <note>In this context, the Physician usually represents Christ or a spiritual confessor.</note> has given him to take. Seeing someone with a healthy sense of taste take that same medicine, it seems difficult and incredible to the sick man that it does not taste to them as it does to him. 

In this same way, the fools who give themselves over to **carnal delight** <term>carnal delight<explanation>From the Italian 'dilettatione carnale', referring to physical or sexual pleasures pursued outside of spiritual order.</explanation></term> have so ruined their appetite that they not only take offense at the "Community"—that is, those who are commonly seen in this same defect—but they are even scandalized by the healthy. They even find scandal in their specific "food," which is to say, in their own **Wife**, whom **God** has given to them to condescend to their fragile infirmity. Thus, this "food" <note>An analogy for the marital act, which the author argues is provided by God as a remedy for human weakness.</note> causes them harm because they use it in a **disordered** <term>disordered<explanation>A theological term meaning to love or use something in a way that places it above God or outside His established moral order.</explanation></term> way, as has been said. They frequently fall into suspicion and jealousy, judging a good thing to be evil, and coming to feel hatred and displeasure where there ought to be love.

This man has a **disordered** way of seeing, and this happens to him because his eye is sick; for if it were healthy, he would not act this way. O, how many miserable defects and inconveniences come from this miserable "wind," and he is always gnawing at himself from within. And after he has cast this stench from his mouth, he reaches a judgment of his **Spouse**; from which comes this other defect: that if a desire comes to him, through **Divine inspiration**, to rise up from this state and preserve a perfect state <note>Likely referring to a life of celibacy or religious devotion.</note>, the "worm" of **suspicion** has already entered the body. The odor of **Virtue** is extinguished in him, and he returns to his former **rot** <note>original: 'fracidume', implying putrefaction or moral filth.</note>. That which previously pleased him now displeases him, and he is neither constant nor persevering in **Virtue**. Instead, he turns his head back to look at the plow <note>A reference to Luke 9:62: "No one who puts a hand to the plow and looks back is fit for service in the kingdom of God."</note> and does not look at himself to recognize his own defect and his infirmity. 

All this happens to him because he did not build his foundation upon the **Living Stone**; and therefore he has been assailed and struck by this evil wind. It is necessary, therefore, for him to rise from the miserable foundation of the **carcass** <term>carcass<explanation>Original: 'carogna' (carrion). A derogatory term for the physical body when it is treated as an object of lust rather than a temple of the spirit.</explanation></term> and found himself upon the **Living Stone, Christ**. Then...

Let no one ever stay to struggle against it by entangling the **Mind** in the strong thoughts and movements that they feel coming; rather, let them intend to take up the remedies, and with the thought of the remedy, drive away the strong thoughts and imaginations; for this will create a water that will extinguish the fire of disordered movement. I desire, therefore, dearest **Brother** and **Son**, that you rise up from your lack of perseverance, and begin to enter within yourself; for it seems to me, as it is seen before the **Divine Goodness**, that you have already been outside of yourself for a long time.

Wherefore, considering for myself the remedies for your fall...

* (A) Leonardo Frescobaldi, of an ancient and illustrious family in the City of Florence, was a Lord also quite conspicuous for his own merits in his Republic, by which he was employed in very many affairs both in political and military government, as one who was no less wise than brave. He joined to these qualities another much more estimable one—that of Piety—because he was both dear to Saint Catherine and undertook the journey to the Holy Sepulcher in the year 1389. In 1413, he is found to have founded the Oratory of St. Luke of Gramaggio, donated by him to the religious Hermits of St. Jerome. It is found that this Lord, in 1379, changed his surname, entering the class of the People <note>In Florentine law, prominent "Magnate" families often officially changed their names to join the "Popolo" (the commoner class) to qualify for political office, as the city's laws often barred the old nobility from power.</note> according to the Law of the year 1361, there being this testimony in the public books of Florence:

# To Nigi di Doccio Arzocchi.

I. **H**ow we must follow the footsteps of Jesus Christ, desiring dishonors and torments, and enduring with true patience.
II. That we cannot learn the teachings of Jesus Christ without Humility.
III. That having acquired Charity, we must exercise it in the service of our Neighbor.
IV. She exhorts the aforementioned <note>Referring to Nigi di Doccio Arzocchi, a nobleman from Siena and one of Catherine’s dedicated secretaries and followers.</note> to exercise Charity for the Neighbor, succoring the Holy Church in its present needs.
V. That through the prayers of His servants, God shows mercy to the world.

## Letter 270.

->In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary.<-

<margin>John 14</margin>
I. **D**earest son in sweet Jesus Christ. I, Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious Blood, with the desire to see you a follower of the footsteps of Christ Crucified; for there is no other way we can hold to that would give us life. What is His life? It is this: mockeries, reproaches, insults, torments, and outrages, and to endure with true and perfect patience even unto death, and not wishing to turn one's head back because of any insult or murmuring that the world might give us. We must not, therefore, slow our steps, but with true perseverance return good to those who do us evil. This is the way which He teaches us, and which He Himself has become—that is, this sweet and salt-of-love <note>original: "innamorato," meaning filled with or characterized by divine love.</note> Lamb. Thus He said: that He was the Way, the Truth, and the Life <note>original: "Via, Verità, e Vita," quoting John 14:6.</note>; and truly He gives life to those who walk by this Way; for He gives us doctrine that, in this life, makes us taste the pledge <term>pledge<explanation>Italian: "arra," a legal or commercial term for a down payment or earnest money, used by Catherine to describe a foretaste of heaven experienced on earth.</explanation></term> of eternal life, participating in the life of Grace. This sweet Master has ascended onto the Chair of the Cross <note>The "Cattedra" or "Chair" refers to the seat of a teacher or bishop; Catherine presents the Cross as the ultimate pulpit of truth.</note> to give us doctrine founded in truth.

...to learn it, that is in the lowliness of true **Humility**, for it cannot be learned with pride; because pride thickens the **Intellect** of Man, and does not allow him to be capable of knowing God; but the Humble man is not like this; rather, he has the eye of the Intellect purified, and has removed the soil of every self-love and sensory tenderness, and is founded in true self-knowledge. In this knowledge he sees better and more subtly recognizes the supreme Eternal Goodness of God; whereby knowing more, he loves more, and the more he loves, the more he acquires perfect Humility and patience. For Humility is the Nurse and Foster-mother <note>original: "Balia, e Nutrice." Catherine frequently uses maternal imagery to describe how virtues support one another.</note> of **Charity**. So you see, Dearest Son, that it is fitting for us to sit low, as true Disciples, and in this way we shall learn the doctrine, and we shall run dead to every self-will along the way of sweet truth, and we shall delight ourselves on the Cross with anxious and agonizing desire, seeking the honor of God and the salvation of Souls.

III. Now is the time, Dearest Son, to rise from the sleep of negligence and ingratitude, and with diligence to be grateful and mindful, serving and loving our **Neighbor**; for we cannot show our gratitude to God through any benefit that can be done for Him, but we can certainly show it in serving our Neighbor. When was there ever a time, Dearest Son, that God required of us so much the desire for His honor and the salvation of Souls as now?

IV. At every time God requires it of us, because without Charity for the Neighbor we could not have Eternal Life; but the greater the need, the more it is required; wherefore, because we see now greater needs than perhaps were ever seen among Christians, we must never cease to continually offer tears and humble Prayers; and by this we shall be known as true Servants of God, and that we hold to the way of truth, and know His Doctrine well. Alas, it is no longer the time to seek oneself for oneself, but to seek **Christ Crucified**, and not to end our weeping over the miserable Souls that are seen in the hands of the Demons, until God turns the eye of His Mercy and appeases His anger toward us miserable ones. Alas, that the World perishes for so many miseries as are committed, and the irreverence and persecution of the **Holy Church**. I, a miserable cause of every evil, pray you for...

# To Ippolito degli Ubertini in Florence.

He urges him <note>The editor's summary uses the masculine "lo" (him) to describe Catherine's action toward Ippolito.</note> to promptly leave the world, according to how he felt himself called by God.

## Letter 271.

->In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified and of sweet Mary.<-

**D**earest brother in sweet Jesus: I Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious Blood, with the desire to see you with a manly heart <note>Catherine frequently uses the term "manly" (virile) to describe spiritual strength and courage, regardless of whether the recipient is a man or a woman.</note>, stripped of every passion and sensitive tenderness; which tenderness, proceeding from self-love, is an impediment to every holy desire and the worker of every evil. He who loves himself remains in a lukewarmness of heart; on one side God calls him, making him see how little time there is to live, and the misery and fragility of the world, and its lack of firmness and stability; and that every minor delight and concern that man takes inordinately <term>Inordinately (disordinatamente): In Catherine's theology, this refers to loving things outside of their proper order—loving the creature more than the Creator.</term> outside of God is miserably punished. The world becomes hateful and displeasing to him, and he willingly wants to leave it, seeing that he who leaves the world possesses the world—that is, he makes a mockery of its status, pomps, and delights—seeing that everyone is rewarded, and it will later be returned to him a hundredfold. He then disposes himself within his very self to abandon it entirely; but if self-love still lives in the soul, this desire grows lukewarm, and with a certain tenderness for oneself, he goes on attaching himself, taking delays of time. One must not act this way, but must kill all self-

Dearest Brother, since you are not <note>The Italian text reads "poichè sete sicuro," literally "since you are sure," but the context of the preceding and following sentences—"he is not certain of having time" and "time does not wait for you"—strongly suggests a missing "non" (not) or a rhetorical irony: "since you act as if you are sure of having time."</note> certain of having time, throw to the ground every self-love and sensitive tenderness, and do not set yourself to loosen, but to cut. *( A ) The Ubertini family was not only noble in the City of Florence, but also among the most conspicuous and most powerful that the Republic had in its state; hence, as a family of high affairs, it often fell under the suspicion of the popular government of the Fatherland. For this reason, various laws were established and from time to time renewed by the Magistrates, which, if they derived from the nobility, specifically targeted those who were of greater power and whom they wished, for their own security, to be humbled and even struck down—namely, the Ubertini, the Alberti, the Pazzi of Valdarno, and the Ubaldini. The same family also flourished in Siena, but this Ippolito was of the Florentine branch, which still flourishes, enjoying for a long age the Lordship of Chitignano, whereas the Sienese branch dried up several years ago.*

# To Neri di Landoccio de’ Pagliaresi. (A) <note>Neri di Landoccio was one of Catherine’s most devoted disciples, a nobleman and poet from Siena who served as her secretary and helped record her letters and "The Dialogue."</note>

In this context, the "Secolo" (the century/the age) refers to the secular world and its material concerns.</note>, and the opposition that exists between Christ and the world.

## Letter 272.

> ->**In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary.**<-

**T**o you, most beloved and dearest brother, and my son in Christ Jesus: I, Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, write to you and comfort you in His precious Blood, with the desire to see you united, transformed, and conformed to Christ Jesus. My sweetest son, the soul cannot do this—that is, be perfectly conformed to Christ—if it does not entirely detach itself from the conformity of the world; for the world is contrary to God, and God is contrary to the world; they have no conformity with each other. And truly it is so: we see that God-Man chose perfect poverty, insults, torments, scorns, outrages, hunger, and thirst; He despised human glory and honor, and always sought the glory of the Father and our salvation, always persevering with true and perfect patience. There was no pride in Him, but perfect Humility. O inestimable, beloved Charity, you are truly the opposite of the world! The world seeks glory and honors, delights, pride, impatience, avarice, hatred, resentment, and <term>self-love</term> <note>Original: "amor proprio." This is a central concept in Catherine’s theology—the selfish love of oneself that prevents a soul from loving God.</note> of one-

<summary>Catherine opens a letter to her secretary Neri di Landoccio, explaining that a soul must reject the values of the "world" to truly mirror the humility and suffering of Christ. She establishes a sharp contrast between worldly pride and the poverty and patience shown by Jesus.</summary>
<keywords>Neri di Landoccio, conformity to Christ, self-love, worldliness, humility, charity, Catherine of Siena</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Letter 272 to Neri di Landoccio. The text completes the sentence from the previous page: "the world is contrary to God; and they love **themselves** [original: *medesimo*] with such narrowness of heart..."</meta>

themselves with such narrowness of heart, that there is no room for their Neighbor for God’s sake. O, how much those foolish Men are deceived, who are conformed to this wicked World <term>Secolo</term> <note>Original: "Secolo" (the age/the century), referring to the temporal, secular world in opposition to the eternal kingdom of God.</note>; for wanting honors they are disgraced, and wanting riches they are poor, because they do not seek the true wealth. Wanting joy and delights, they instead have sadness and bitterness, because they are deprived of God, who is the supreme Joy. They want neither death nor bitterness, yet they fall into death and bitterness; they want firmness and stability, yet they distance themselves from the **living Stone** <note>A reference to 1 Peter 2:4, identifying Christ as the "living stone" rejected by men but chosen by God.</note>.

Now see then, Dearest Son, how great a difference there is between Christ and the World; and therefore the true Servants of God, seeing that the World has no conformity with Christ, strive with all diligence to have no conformity with the World. Instead, they rise up with hatred and displeasure <note>Catherine often speaks of "holy hatred" of one's own selfish will or ego.</note>, and become lovers of what God loves, and have no other desire than to conform themselves to Christ Crucified. They follow always in His footsteps, set ablaze and in love with true and real Virtues; and what they see that Christ chose for Himself, they want for themselves. In doing so, they receive the opposite of what the world expects: for by choosing poverty and lowliness <term>viltà</term> <note>In this context, "viltà" refers to a voluntary humble state or being of no account in the eyes of the world.</note>, they are always honored; they possess peace and delight, joy and gladness, and every consolation, being stripped of all sadness. And I do not wonder at it; for they are conformed and transformed by the supreme eternal Truth and Goodness of God, where every good is contained, and where true and holy desires are fulfilled.

## II.

Therefore it is right to follow Him, and to entirely lift oneself away and cut oneself off from this dark life. The knife of hatred and displeasure of yourself, and the pure love of God, will cut you away from it. I tell you, Dearest Son, that you could not have this knife and displeasure without the continual memory of God, and specifically of the abundance of the Blood of the Son of God. He has made a bath of that blood for you, bleeding from every vein and opening Himself with such fire and most ardent love upon the Wood of the Holy Cross. Now, here you will acquire this knife of hatred; for through hatred and displeasure of sin He died. Love keeps Him bound there; for as the Saints say, neither nails <note>Original: "Chiovi."</note> nor the Cross were sufficient to hold Him, were it not for the bond of Divine Charity.

## III.

Now here I want the eye of your understanding to always look and rest; there you will find and fall in lo—

This Rinieri was of a noble family, and among those who are called the "Greats of Siena" by some, but one of the many that have already been extinct for several years. # To Neri di Landoccio.

**SHE** prays him to exercise the light <note>The "light" refers to the gift of spiritual understanding or the "light of faith" often discussed in Catherine’s theology.</note> that God has given him with the contemplation of Divine Charity, in order to increase this light and acquire love toward his Neighbor.

## Letter 273.

->**In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary.**<-

**DE**arest Son in Christ sweet Jesus: I Catherine, servant and slave of the Servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in his precious Blood, with the desire to see you exercise the light that God has given you, so that the perfect light may grow in you; because without the perfect light we could not reach, nor love, nor clothe ourselves in the truth; and if we do not clothe ourselves in it, that first light would turn back into darkness for us. Therefore, there is a need to reach the perfect light, for God has chosen us for this. I desire, then, that with all diligence you place and fix your eye upon the truth, and upon the abyss of the Charity of God; and through this you will reach the perfect supernatural light, and you will reach the most perfect love of your Creator, and affection for your Neighbor. Thus will the Will of God be fulfilled in you, and my desire. I say no more. Remain in the holy and sweet affection of God. Sweet Jesus. Jesus Love.

->Letter 274.<-

->**In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary.**<-

<margin>I.</margin> **D**earest Son in Christ sweet Jesus: I Catherine, servant and slave of the Servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in his precious Blood, with the desire to see you with the true light, so that with the light you may know the truth of your Creator. His truth is this: that he created us to give us Eternal Life; but because of the rebellion that Man committed against God, this truth was not fulfilled, and therefore he descended to the greatest lowliness that he could descend, which was when he clothed the Deity <note>original: "Deità"</note> with our Humanity. And so we see with this glorious light God having been made Man, and this he did to fulfill His Truth in us; and with the Blood of the loving Word <note>original: "Verbo" — referring to Jesus as the "Word of God" made flesh (John 1:1).</note> he has clearly manifested it to us, so much so that what we held by faith is certified to us by the price of that Blood; and the Creature who possesses Reason cannot deny that it is not so.

<margin>II.</margin> Therefore I want your confusion <note>Catherine often uses "confusion" to describe a state of spiritual discouragement or scrupulosity that leads to despair.</note> to be consumed and to fade away in the hope of the Blood and in the fire of the inestimable Charity of God, and let there remain only the true knowledge of yourself, with which knowledge you will humble yourself, and grow, and nourish the light. And is he not more ready to forgive than we are to sin? And is he not our Physician, and we the sick? The bearer of iniquities? And does he not hold the confusion of the Mind in worse regard than all other defects? Yes, indeed. Therefore, dearest Son, open the eye of the Intellect

She exhorts him to true perseverance, and to grow every day in Virtue, and especially in patience.

## Letter 281.

->In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary.<-

**D**earest Son in sweet Christ Jesus: I, Catherine, servant and slave of the Servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious Blood, with the desire to see every personal sentiment <note>original: "proprio sentimento," referring to one's own will or ego</note> dead in you, so that your mind and your desire may never be contaminated by selfish passion, but rather that virtue may be increased in you. This you will do when you mirror yourself in the eternal Truth with the eye of the intellect; for in no other way could it be uprooted <note>original: "dibarbicare," meaning to pull up by the roots; Catherine often uses gardening metaphors for the soul</note>. Therefore, my sweet Son, I want you to mirror yourself in the supreme Eternal Truth, and lose not a moment of time, but always, according to your power, strive as much as you can to bear and endure the defects of fellow creatures <note>original: "Creature," a term Catherine uses for all human beings as creations of God</note>. <margin>A</margin> See that you are not negligent in Holy Prayer, and that you make an Easter of every Sunday <note>To "make an Easter" of Sunday meant to receive the Eucharist with the same preparation and joy as one would on the feast of the Resurrection</note> with Holy Communion; and do not worry that you are now physically far from me, for with holy desire and holy prayer I will always be near you. Take heart, and use force and violence <margin>Matthew 11</margin> so that you may seize the Kingdom of Heaven <note>A reference to Matthew 11:12: "the kingdom of heaven suffereth violence, and the violent take it by force."</note>. I say no more. Remain in the holy and sweet love of God. May God give you His sweet eternal blessing. Lady Lisa, Alessa, <margin>B</margin> Francesco, and Barduccio all greet you. Sweet Jesus. Jesus Love.

## Letter 282.

**DE**arest Son in sweet Christ Jesus: I, Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious Blood, with the desire to see every negligence and ingratitude extinguished in you; for negligence does not exist without ingratitude. Because the Soul that draws near to God and unites itself in Him through the affection of love, it necessarily follows that she be [dis]united <note>The printed text reads "unita" (united), but the context of the sentence and Catherine's typical theology suggests she meant "disunita" (disunited/separated) from creatures to be united with God</note> from the Creatures outside of God, and from the delights and pleasures and statuses of the World. If she loves the World, in the World there is nothing but pain; because through sin it sprouts thistles and thorns of great bitterness. Our Flesh gives nothing else but the stench and poison of sin and of corruption, so much so that by the Soul conforming herself to the Will of the Flesh and sensory passion, she receives poison from it, which intoxicates her in such a way that it brings death, stripping her of the life of Grace <note>The spiritual life given by God</note>, falling into the guilt of mortal sin. to love; he is always in sadness, and is unbearable to himself, because God has permitted that disordered affection <note>Disordered affection refers to love directed toward worldly things or self-interest rather than toward God.</note> be unbearable to itself. And conversely, the affection that is ordered in the sweet Will of God, united in Him by the affection of love, gives [peace] to the Soul of the one who has Him within. And therefore these things of the World cannot satiate Man, because they are less than he; thus he has peace and rest when he stays in Him [God], and participates in a largeness of heart, so that every Creature who has Reason within them fits inside through the affection of Charity <note>A common theme in Catherine's writing: the soul that loves God finds room in its heart to love all rational beings.</note>; rather, he strives to serve them, succoring his Neighbor, showing in him the love that he has for his Creator. Because God is supreme and eternal Purity, the Soul and the Body participate in it through the union made in Him, preserving his Mind and his Body in perfect Purity, choosing death rather than wanting to contaminate and defile the Mind and the Body through filth—not that he can [always] hold back the thoughts of the heart, nor often the movements of the Flesh, but movements and thoughts do not defile the Soul; only the Will [does], when it voluntarily consents to its fragility and to the cogitations <note>Latin-derived term for thoughts or musings</note> of the heart. But by not consenting, one commits no fault but earns merit, making a holy resistance, always drawing from these thorns the fragrant Rose of a perfect Purity; for through this one comes to a greater knowledge of self, and with a holy hatred <note>Catherine uses "holy hatred" to describe a spiritual loathing of one's own selfish or sinful inclinations, which drives the soul back to God.</note> rises against one's own fragility, and with love flees to Christ Crucified with humble and continuous Prayers, seeing that from so many evils there is no other way to escape. And we have already said that the closer one draws to Him, the more one participates in His Purity; therefore it is indeed true that from these battles one draws the purest Rose. This is the remedy against this miserable sin of the weak and fragile Flesh, and every other heaviness of sin: that we draw near and conform ourselves through the affection of love in God.

<meta>catchword: and not</meta>

<summary>Catherine explains that human desire can only be satisfied by God because the soul is superior to all created things but inferior to the Creator. She provides a spiritual strategy for maintaining purity, arguing that temptations (thorns) actually produce virtue (the rose) when the will refuses to consent to them.</summary>

...and let us not wait for time, most dear son, for it is brief and does not wait for us; we should not wait for it.

## II.
It is a great matter that Man wants to sleep in such blindness and not wake up from this sleep; but it is certainly true that we cannot wake up, nor come to this union, without the Light. It is necessary for us to recognize, by the Light of **Most Holy Faith**, our misery and guilt; and with a purified eye, place before ourselves as our object the ineffable love that God has for us. He has manifested this to us through the **Word** of His **Only-begotten** Son, and the Son has shown it to us with His **Blood**, shed with such a fire of Love, running like one in love to the shameful death of the **Most Holy Cross**. And how could the Soul, seeing itself so loved, hold back from loving? It could not. O most dear son, do not distance yourself from this Light, but with diligence dissolve the cloud of your self-love, and with a living Faith gaze upon the **Immaculate** and **slaughtered Lamb**, who calls you with such love; and by responding to Him, you will come to this perfect union. Being united, you will smell the fragrance of perfect **Purity**. Gazing upon the **Dignity** to which our Soul and miserable Flesh have come because of the union God has made in Man—joining the **Divine Nature** with our human nature—is a very good remedy against this **Vice** <note>In Catherine’s writings, "this vice" usually refers to impurity or lust, which she contrasts with the "purity" obtained through Christ's humanity.</note>. The Soul will be ashamed, and it will create a restraint against giving itself over to such misery, seeing itself raised above all the **Choirs of Angels**. Necessarily, when your Mind and your desire are raised so sweetly, the stench of Vice will be extinguished.

## III.
It is also necessary for us to chastise our Body and mortify it with vigils, and humble and continuous **Prayer**, clinging to the **Tree of the Most Holy Cross**. Flee as much as possible the company of those who live lasciviously; and do not doubt that God will grant you the greatest grace, provided you strive to cut <note>Original: "tagliare." Catherine often uses this metaphor to mean striking at the root of a problem rather than just "stripping leaves" (sfogliare) or dealing with superficial symptoms.</note> and not just stand there stripping leaves. Promptly arrange all your affairs; run with sweet and loving desire to the yoke of holy **Obedience**; in this way you will kill your own Will, mortify the Body, and taste the earnest-money <note>Original: "arra." An "arra" is a down-payment or pledge; Catherine uses it to describe a "foretaste" of heaven experienced during earthly life.</note> of **Eternal Life**. Let it not seem toilsome to you, for the labor will turn into the greatest delight. I am certain that if you make your dwelling through the affection of love with the sweet and good Jesus, you will do it, and not otherwise; and therefore I told you that I desired to see you united through the affection of love in **our Savior**, so that you might come to true Purity, and...

**Annotation to Letter 240.**
(A) Of this **Ser Antonio di Ciolo**, neither his homeland nor any other record is found. He was probably **Sienese** <note>original: "Saneſe"</note>; thus, according to the custom that ran in those times, even for noble families, he is called by his father’s name, as is still the custom in some parts of **Tuscany** to call people from the countryside. In **Muscovy**, however, those Sovereigns still maintain even today this manner of calling themselves by the father’s name, which is added to their own; hence the **Czar** who reigns at present is called **Peter Alexeyevich** <note>original: "Pietro Aleſſiouitz," referring to Peter the Great</note>, meaning "son of Alexis," just as his father was called **Alexis Mikhailovich** <note>original: "Aleſſio Micholouitz"</note>, which is to say "son of Michael." Perhaps from "Ciolo" was born the surname **Ciuoli**, which belonged to a noble Sienese family that is extinct in our day. The title of <term>Ser: a contraction of Messere, used as a formal address for notaries and certain professionals</term>, as was noted elsewhere, shows that he was a **Notary** by profession—an office which, in that age, brought no prejudice to nobility, although it may be a disadvantage now in some cities of Tuscany. The word *Ser*, as was said, is shortened from that of *Messere*, which was once of the highest honor, sounding the same as "my Lord," and was given to Kings and Great Lords; but in these times it has fallen in status, barely worthy of being given to people of low affairs, while that of *Ser* is still held presently by Notaries; thus the halved word is in greater honor than the full one.
</margin>

# To Pietro di Missere Jacomo Attacusi of the Tolomei of Siena.

## Letter 284.

->In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary.<-

I. **D**earest and most beloved Brother in sweet Christ Jesus: I, Catherine, servant and slave of the Servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in his precious Blood, with the desire to see you as a lover and servant of Christ Crucified; for in no other way can we please God, and this we must do out of duty. For every Creature that has Reason within itself is bound and obligated to love Him, because from God we have received nothing but service, delight, and pleasure. He loved us without being loved by us; for when we did not yet exist, He created us in His Image and likeness. And when we lost Grace through the sin of Adam's disobedience, He gave us the Word of His only-begotten Son solely out of love—not because He had received service from us, but rather offense. And because of that offense, we had fallen into war with God, yet God, though offended by us, gave us the Word of His Son and made Him our mediator and intermediary <note>original: "tramezzatore," meaning one who stands in the middle to broker peace</note>, making Peace in the great War with the precious Blood of the Lamb. Therefore, His obedience has defeated the disobedience of Adam; and just as through disobedience we all contracted sin, so through the obedience of the Son of God, we have all contracted Grace. And the Grace that...

<meta>This page continues the text of Letter 284 to Pietro di Missere Jacomo Attacusi of the Tolomei family, following the introduction where Catherine establishes God’s love as the reason for Christ becoming our mediator.</meta>

<page-num>445</page-num>
<sig>B</sig>

...we received through this Word; for as much as man offends, and returns to the Blood of Christ with sorrow and bitterness for his fault, so much does he receive mercy, as the Blood is administered to us through Holy Confession. For by vomiting the rot of our iniquities from our mouths—that is, by confessing well and diligently to the Priest—he then, in absolving us, gives us the Blood of Christ, and in that Blood the leprosy of the sins and defects within us is washed away. God gave us this entire gift out of love, and not because of any debt. Therefore, we are truly bound to love Him, and we must love Him if we do not wish for eternal damnation.

<margin>Augustine, Meditations, chapter 32.</margin>

II. But pay attention to one thing: that whoever acts against this Blood, or stands with those who persecute the Blood—that is, those who persecute the Spouse of Jesus Christ <note>The "Spouse of Jesus Christ" is a standard medieval metaphor for the Church.</note> with injury, scorn, and vitriol—such as these, if they do not correct themselves, will never share in the fruit of the Blood. No excuse will serve them for cloaking themselves in the faults of the Ministers of the Blood <note>The "Ministers of the Blood" refers to the clergy, who alone could administer the sacraments.</note>, saying: "We are only persecuting the defects of evil Pastors." For we false Christians have come to such a point that we think we are making a sacrifice to God by persecuting His Spouse. Even if we assume that the Ministers are incarnate demons and full of much misery, we must not be their executioners or Christ’s judges; for they are His Anointed, and He wishes for the judgment of them to remain with Him and those to whom He has committed it. Therefore, no temporal Lord or civil Law can interfere without falling into the death of their own soul, because God does not want it; such a person does not show a sign of loving his Creator, but rather shows a sign of hatred. Truly ignorant and wretched is the one who sees himself so loved and yet does not love in return; and great is the patience of God, who tolerates such iniquity. Let us not forget, then, to serve and love our Creator, for we are bound to love Him, as has been said; and to serve Him is no shame, because to serve God is not to be a slave, but to reign. The more perfect the service, and the more one submits to Him, the more one is free and made master of oneself, and is not ruled by that thing which has no being—that is, sin. For a man can be reduced to no greater misery than to make himself a servant and slave to sin, because he loses the being of Grace, and serves <term>nothingness</term><note>original: "non cavelle". A common Catherinian expression for "nothing," used to describe the ontological emptiness of sin compared to the "Being" of God.</note>, and becomes nothingness.

<summary>Catherine explains the necessity of Confession to receive the cleansing power of Christ's Blood and warns against those who justify attacking the Church by pointing to the corruption of the clergy. She concludes that serving God is the only true form of freedom, while sin reduces a person to nothingness.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Letter 284 to Pietro di Missere Jacomo Attacusi of the Tolomei family. Catherine has just finished explaining that the Blood of Christ is a gift of love and that Christians are bound to love God in return. <page-num>446</page-num>

## III.

<margin>1 Peter, chapter 1 <note>original: "1. Petr. c. 1." Catherine references 1 Peter 1:18–19 regarding being redeemed by the precious Blood.</note></margin>
<margin>Genesis 50 <note>original: "Gen. 50." Catherine likely refers to the theme of God turning human intentions toward a higher purpose.</note></margin>
It is truly a miserable thing for a blind and foolish man, lacking any light, to debase himself so much by failing to serve his Creator and instead serving the Devil and the world with its delights—which have no stability—and his own **sensuality** <term>sensuality: in medieval thought, this refers to the lower physical appetites and impulses that distract the soul from spiritual focus</term>. He abandons the service of that infinite Goodness who loves him so inestimably, and so sweet and glorious a Lord, who has redeemed us not with gold or silver, but with the precious Blood of His only-begotten Son. There is no one who can kick against Him <note>original: "ricalcitrare", an allusion to Acts 9:5, "It is hard for thee to kick against the pricks."</note>, because we have been bought, and we can no longer sell ourselves to the Devil or to any creature by serving created things apart from God. We are indeed bound and obligated to serve our neighbor, but not with a service that goes against the will of God.

O, how glorious is the **Mastery** <term>Mastery: Catherine uses "Signoria" (Lordship), implying that the soul who serves God becomes a "lord" over its own passions and the world's influence</term> that the soul acquires by serving its Creator! For she rules over the whole world and mocks its customs and its ways; she rules over herself and is not ruled by anger, nor by impurity, nor by any other vice, but rules them all with affection and love for virtue. Many there are who rule over cities and fortresses but do not rule over themselves; yet every mastery without this one is miserable and does not last. One always holds it imperfectly, with little reason and even less justice; instead, such a man will act with "reason" and "justice" according to his own sensuality and self-love, and according to the pleasure and will of men. 

Wherefore it is not then justice, but injustice; for justice will not be contaminated by self-love, nor by gifts of money, nor by flattery, nor by the desire to please men. Therefore, he who loves justice would rather die than offend God in this or any other thing. In this way, he is then a **faithful servant** and is made master of himself, ruling his own sensuality and free will with *Reason*.

Therefore, since the love and service of God are of such great dignity and necessary for our salvation, and the opposite is so dangerous and full of misery, I desire and pray you, dearest brother, that you serve Him with all your heart and all your affection. Do not wait for time, for you are not certain of having it; for we are condemned to death, and we do not know when. And therefore we must not lose the present time for the sake of a future we are not sure to have.

<meta>This page continues Letter 284 to Pietro di Missere Jacomo Attacusi. Having established that humanity is bound to love God in response to the Blood of Christ, Catherine now explains how that love must be expressed through service to one's neighbor, as God Himself needs nothing from us.</meta>

## IV.

And because we have said that we are bound to love God, I say that he who loves must be of benefit to the one he loves, and must serve him. But I see that we cannot be of benefit to God, because we bring Him no profit from our good, nor any harm from our evil. What then must we do? We must render glory and praise to His Name, and lead our life full of the fragrance of **Virtue**, and give the fruit and the labor to our **Neighbor**; that is, to be of benefit to them through our own labor and to serve them in those things that are according to God, and to bear and endure their defects with true **ordered Charity**, and not disordered. <term>ordered Charity: a theological concept where love is prioritized correctly—loving God above all, then one's own soul, then the souls of others, and finally physical life</term> **Disordered love** is to commit a sin in order to save oneself or to please one's Neighbor. It must not be so, because ordered love in God does not want to lose one’s own Soul to save the whole world. And if it were possible that by committing a single sin one could send every rational creature to eternal Life, one must not do it; but one certainly ought to give up one's physical life for the Soul of one's Neighbor, and one's physical substance to save their Body. Now, in this way and by this means of the Neighbor, it is necessary for us to love God, and thus we shall show that we love Him.

<margin>John 21 <note>original: "Jo. 21." Referring to Jesus' post-resurrection dialogue with Peter.</note></margin> Thus you know that Christ said to Saint Peter, when He asked: "Peter, do you love me?" And Peter, answering that he well knew that he loved Him, when the three times were completed, Christ said: "If you love me, feed my little sheep." It is as if He were saying: by this I will perceive if you love me; that is, since you cannot be of benefit to me, you must help your Neighbor, nourishing them and giving them your labor through holy and true doctrine. It is necessary for us, then, to help them according to our ability: some with Doctrine, some with Prayer, some with their substance, and those who cannot help with substance, let them help through friends, so that we may always be practicing Charity toward our Neighbor, being of benefit through this means that God has placed before us. Therefore I ask you, for grace and for mercy—and thus I declare the word of Christ: Peter, do you love your Creator and me? Now serve me in your Neighbor who is in want or necessity, according to our power, always placing the honor of God first without any offense.

...lemy II <note>The text likely refers to Ptolemy II of Egypt, from whom the Tolomei family claimed legendary descent</note>, settled in this City to dwell, establishing there his <term>Lineage</term> <note>original: "Prosapia"</note> known therefore as both the <term>Baldistricchi</term> and the <term>Tolomei</term>. It was later among the most powerful families of this Republic, and thus a rival to that of the <term>Salimbeni</term>, with whom it was in constant discord. These two powerful families waged war against each other in many of their territories with the shedding of much blood, as has been observed elsewhere. The family was illustrated by the valor of many of its Lords, counting as many as twenty-two who held supreme command of armies or achieved notable positions within them; and by the eminent prudence of a great number of personages, among whom was <term>Raimondo Tolomei</term>, the first to recover the honor of <term>Senator of Rome</term> <note>A high judicial and civil office in the city of Rome</note>, which for several years had been taken by foreigners. No less illustrious did the family prove to be on account of the holiness of its heroes, numbering eighteen of distinguished virtue, for which they received from the people—and some even from the Supreme Pontiffs—the blessed title of <term>Blessed</term> <note>original: "Beato"; a title indicating a person is recognized by the Church as having entered Heaven</note>.

** ( B ) Because they cloak themselves with the Mantle of the defects of the Ministers, etc.** In other letters, the Saint makes mention of this shield, which the Lords of Italy used for their defense when they usurped the goods of the Church and persecuted its ministers without any regard. They claimed they did so because the ministers' bad living had moved them to war, as if they thereby acquired rights over the Church and over the clergy; yet for the most part, these lords were far worse than those they criticized.

<margin>Bzovius, *Annales* for this year. <note>Referring to Abraham Bzovius, a historian who continued the *Annales Ecclesiastici*.</note></margin>
** ( C ) I have heard that Luigi delle Vigne, etc.** That which follows in this letter was missing from the old editions and has been taken from two handwritten texts cited above. This <term>Pietro Tolomei</term> was, as far as can be inferred, in the service of the <term>Prefect of Rome</term>, <term>Francesco di Vico</term>—a great enemy of the Popes, who in 1375 had usurped the Lordship of the City of <term>Viterbo</term>. <term>Luigi delle Vigne</term>, a Capuan nobleman and brother to the Blessed Raymond, the Saint’s confessor, was a subject of <term>Queen Joanna</term> of Naples by birth and campaigned on her behalf. This Queen was in excellent correspondence with the Popes until the time of <term>Urban VI</term>, and she was supported by them during the dangers she faced of losing her kingdom. Nor did she fail to provide aid to the Popes against those who waged war against the Papal State or who had seized control of any part of it. The imprisonment of this Luigi delle Vigne perhaps occurred in a clash mentioned by <term>Ammirati</term> <note>Scipione Ammirati, a prominent historian of Florence</note> in these words: "Being the..."

<meta>This page continues the historical commentary on the political and military environment of Italy during the time of Saint Catherine of Siena, specifically focusing on the conflicts involving the Papacy, the city of Viterbo, and the practice of ransoming noble prisoners.</meta>

<page-num>450</page-num>

<margin>Book 23. Year 1377.</margin>
The Pope sent 400 soldiers from Corneto <note>Modern-day Tarquinia</note> to harass the people of Viterbo, but the Prefect of Vico <note>Francesco di Vico, a powerful and often rebellious local tyrant</note>, coming out against them with troops from the Florentines, defeated them. Two hundred were taken prisoner, among whom were eighty gentlemen and twenty Knights of the Golden Spur <note>A prestigious papal order of knighthood</note>.

**[ D ] They set a ransom for him of four thousand Florins.**
*In ancient times, those who were taken prisoner in war remained servants, or slaves, as one might call them, to their conqueror. In wars between Christians, by a very ancient custom that has now become almost like law, common soldiers are rarely returned to liberty unless they are exchanged for others, or until the fighting has ended, though they are not held as slaves. Those who, by birth or office, are considered superior to others are often ransomed according to both ancient and modern custom. In the time of Saint Catherine, when the profession of arms was practiced by soldiers almost solely to enrich themselves with the goods of others through plunder and ransoms, redemptions were sought with greater rigor. From the sum of four thousand Florins that the Prefect’s men demanded for the ransom of this Luigi delle Vigne, it is clearly seen that he must have been a personage of great esteem due to some singular merit; for in those times, so poor in money compared to the years that followed, that sum was exceptionally large. As was mentioned elsewhere, Stefano Maconi <note>One of Saint Catherine’s most beloved disciples and secretaries</note>, a lord of clear nobility who fell prisoner to the Breton Mercenary Bands <note>The "Masnade de' Brettoni," notorious French mercenary groups active in Italy</note>, was only asked for 400 gold crowns to regain his liberty.*

**( E ) In reverence and obedience to the Holy Church.**
<margin>Annotation to Letter 22.</margin>
*Although this Lord <note>Referring to the Prefect of Vico</note> held the City of Viterbo—which belonged to the Church—unjustly occupied, he nevertheless returned to the Pope's favor in that same year of 1377 through the mediation of the Cardinal of Amiens <note>Jean de la Grange, a diplomat and cardinal</note>. Consequently, he was also reconciled by Pope Gregory with the Romans, with whom he was in open discord because of his office as Prefect of Rome, as has been said. Under the pontificate of Urban <note>Pope Urban VI</note> he was excommunicated, and later he was even killed by his own subjects.*
