# To Gabriele di Davino Piccolomini.
<note>Gabriele di Davino Piccolomini was a member of one of Siena's most powerful noble families. Catherine frequently wrote to the nobility, urging them to use their social standing for the service of God.</note>

I. Regarding the virtue of perseverance, exhorting him to it, and regarding the weapons we must use to conquer our enemies—namely, Charity and the hatred of oneself.
II. That many are ashamed to confess Jesus Christ.
III. That we must also keep Jesus Crucified before our eyes to conquer our fragility.

## Letter 285.

->In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified and of Sweet Mary.<-

I. **D**earest son in Christ sweet Jesus: I, Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, <note>Catherine frequently uses the title "servant and slave," echoing the papal title *Servus servorum Dei* (Servant of the servants of God), emphasizing her humility.</note> write to you in His precious Blood, with the desire to see you constant and persevering in virtue, in such a way that you never turn your head back; for in no other way could you be pleasing to God, nor would you receive the fruit of the Blood of the Humble and Immaculate Lamb; <margin>Matthew 10</margin> <note>Original: "Matt. 10," likely referring to verse 22: "the one who endures to the end will be saved."</note> for only perseverance is that which is crowned. Therefore, perseverance is necessary for us.

And if you should say to me, Dearest son: "In what way can I have this constancy and perseverance, seeing that I have many adversaries and many enemies around me—namely, the World and its creatures, <note>In this context, "creatures" refers to other human beings or worldly distractions created by God but misused by man.</note> with many persecutions, insults, and slanders, and my own sensuality, <note>The "sensuality" refers to the lower, physical impulses of the body that conflict with the soul's rational and spiritual desires.</note> which often resists me and rebels against Reason?"

I answer you, that in no way can the enemies be defeated except with weapons, and without fear, and by entering the battle willingly, disposing oneself to death, and loving the glory that follows after the battle. In this way we, who are placed in the field to fight against our enemies—namely, the World, the Flesh, and the Devil—could not fight without weapons, nor receive blows without them hurting us. What weapon, then, is it that we ought to have? A knife. It is necessary for you—

<summary>Saint Catherine begins a letter to Gabriele Piccolomini, emphasizing that the virtue of perseverance is the only path to spiritual victory and introduces the "weapons" needed for spiritual warfare.</summary>

...you must also have the breastplate of true Charity <note>Divine love (*caritas*), which Catherine identifies as the essential protection for the soul's "heart."</note>, which protects against the blows the World deals us in various ways, against the many temptations of the Devil, and against the blows of our own frailty, which fights <margin>3</margin> against the Spirit, as has been said. And it is fitting that this breastplate has a crimson surcoat <note>A *sopravesta* was the heraldic garment worn over a knight's armor; here it symbolizes the Blood of Christ covering the believer.</note>—that is, the Blood of Christ Crucified, joined, soaked, and kneaded with the fire of Divine Charity.

**II.** And it is right that this Blood be revealed—that is, that you confess it before every creature and do not hide it. Confess it through good and holy deeds, and with words when necessary. Do not act like the many fools who are ashamed before the World to remember Christ Crucified, or to confess that they are Servants of Christ. Such people do not want to put on the surcoat. O, what a confusion for the World! They are ashamed to remember Christ and His Blood, by which they were bought back with such a fire of love, yet they are not ashamed of their own iniquities, which so miserably deprive them of the fruit of that Blood. They have taken away the beauty of their souls and lost their dignity, becoming like brute animals <note>Literally "animali bruti," meaning irrational creatures who follow instinct rather than the divine "light of reason."</note>, made servants and slaves to sin. They do not even notice it, for they have lost the light of Reason and walk like the blind and the frantic, clinging to the things of the World. These things cannot be held according to our own will because they pass like the wind; either they fail us, or we fail them—that is, when we are summoned by the Supreme Judge <note>A reference to God at the moment of the soul's particular judgment after death.</note> and the soul is separated from the body. If they do not correct themselves, either during life or at the point of death—though no one should be so ignorant as to delay, since one knows neither the manner nor the state in which they will die, nor when—I say that by not correcting themselves, they are deprived of the good things of Earth and those of Heaven, and reach eternal damnation.

Therefore, my Son, since they are in such danger, I do not want you to be one of them. Instead, armed in the manner described, be constant and persevering in the battle until death, without any fear. It also fits that you have a knife <note>Or "dagger," used for close-quarters defense in medieval combat.</note> in your hand to defend yourself; let it be double-edged—that is, of hatred and of love: Love of Virtue and hatred of Vice. With this, you shall strike the World, hating its status, delights, pomps, vanities, and its infinite pride; and you shall strike...

Remain in the holy and sweet love of God. Sweet Jesus. Jesus Love.

...notably devoted <note>original: "signanter devotus"</note> to the Virgin of Siena <note>This refers to St. Catherine of Siena, whom the text identifies as "the Virgin."</note>, who saw and heard wondrous things concerning the Virgin, and who, leading a devoted life, finally rested in a blessed end. *The son of this Gabriele was the Blessed Giovanni Piccolomini, also a disciple of the Saint, who at her urging donned the Habit of Saint Dominic; in this holy Order, he lived with such piety and religious observance that he died on August 20, 1410, and earned from his fellow religious the glorious title of "Blessed."*

<margin>Pastorella's Testament, in manuscript</margin>
[ B ] It is fitting that the Breastplate have a **Scarlet Surcoat**. <margin>Historical Distinctions, Volume 3</margin> *The surcoat was a garment that horse-mounted soldiers were accustomed to wearing over their armor. Much like the **Paludamentum** <note>The paludamentum was a cloak or cape fastened at one shoulder, worn by military commanders in Ancient Rome.</note>, which was also a military garment of the ancient Romans and uniquely belonged to the supreme leaders, it was mostly dyed a scarlet or reddish color—that is, in purple. Thus, in emulation of the splendor of the commanders, the Knights wore the surcoat colored in scarlet, and it was called in Latin the **Chlamys** <note>original: "Chlamiis". The chlamys was a type of ancient Greek cloak, later adopted by Romans, often associated with military service.</note>. If this was in the style of the Paludamentum, it served more for the appearance of ornament than as a garment for covering, as seems to be suggested by what some ancient authors have written about it. However, the learned Budé <note>Guillaume Budé (1467–1540), a famous French humanist scholar.</note> suggests that the Paludamentum was a garment shortened to the knee and without sleeves, cut like those called **Coats of Arms** <term>Cotte d' Armi: A surcoat decorated with heraldic symbols</term> by the masters of the Heraldic Art or of Armory, used in the lands "beyond the mountains" <note>Referring to Northern Europe, likely France or Germany.</note> by Heralds or Kings of Arms in performing the functions of their office. These garments, being for mere pomp, have gone out of use in these times, when in warfare almost everything used for defense is now removed, let alone what is used for show, so that nothing at all hinders the Soldier.*

<margin>Dictionary of the Crusca.</margin>
[ C ] Like the fly from the boiling pot. *Flies do not approach a pot that is boiling, and this saying is an ancient phrase of the Tuscans. This is usually used as a proverb, meaning that when someone is truly angry, others should not go near them. Here, however, it does not hold the force of a proverb to express such a meaning, but is a simple simile used to explain her sentiment.*

# To Pietro di Tommaso de’ Bardi of Florence.

I. Concerning the Light of Holy Faith, demonstrating that it must not be separated from works, and that every good work is rewarded.
II. Concerning the hope that we must have in God alone, and which the soul illuminated by Faith possesses.
III. How Charity is born from these virtues.
IV. She prays him not to waste time, as those of the world do.

## Letter 286.

### Written while in a state of ecstasy. <note>original: "In Astrazione fatta". This indicates the letter was dictated while Catherine was in a mystical trance or deep state of prayer.</note>

#### **_In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary._**

<margin>James 2</margin> <note>The marginal note refers to the Epistle of James, Chapter 2, which famously argues that "faith without works is dead."</note>
**I. D**earest Brother and Son in Christ sweet Jesus: I, Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ <note>original: "serva, e schiava". Catherine frequently used these humble titles to emphasize her absolute devotion to God's service.</note>, write to you in His precious Blood, with the desire to see you illuminated by the Light of Most Holy Faith, and clothed in most perfect hope; because in no other way could you be pleasing to our Creator, nor participate in the life of Grace, for a living Faith is never without works. For if Faith were without works, it would be dead, and would give birth to its children of Virtue dead, and not alive; because he who is without the Light of Faith is deprived of the Virtue of Charity, and without Charity no good that he does, or act of Virtue, is worth anything toward Eternal Life—although no good should be left undone, because every good is rewarded, and every fault is punished. Let us consider that the good which is done while in the fault of mortal sin <note>In Catholic theology, a "mortal sin" is a grave action that separates the soul from God's grace.</note>—which at that time deprives one of the Light of Most Holy Faith—is not of value regarding Eternal Life, but it is of value for many other things, as one receives grace from God; that is, because the Divine Goodness does not wish for any good that a man performs to go unrewarded,

<meta>This page continues the text of Letter 286 to Pietro di Tommaso de’ Bardi. The previous page ended mid-word, discussing how God punishes faults and rewards every good deed.</meta>

...ed, He rewards it. Sometimes He rewards us by lending us time—a time in which we have the space to be able to correct ourselves; or He places us in the hearts of His servants, compelling them to desire our salvation. Through that desire and the prayers they offer for us, we emerge from the darkness of mortal sin and are restored to the state of Grace. Or, He rewards a person with temporal things if that person is not disposed, through their own fault, to receive spiritual rewards. So, you see that every good deed is rewarded, and therefore one must not cease doing good. Rather, we should strive to do good while in a state of Grace, so that it may be done with the Light of Faith. In this Light of Faith are born the living children of the Virtues <note>Catherine frequently uses the metaphor of "giving birth" to virtues to describe how a soul in union with God produces good works.</note>—that is, those works that give the life of Grace to the soul.

<margin>Jeremiah 17</margin> <note>The marginal note refers to Jeremiah 17:5: "Cursed is the man who trusts in man... blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord."</note>
**II.** O glorious Light! You strip the soul of darkness and divest it of hope in itself, in the world, in children, and in every created thing, and instead clothe it in true hope. This hope is placed in Christ Crucified, and therefore the soul never fears that it will lack anything, because through the Light of Faith it has recognized the Divine Goodness within itself. Thus, the soul knows that God is powerful enough to be able to help, and is most wise so that He knows how to help, and is most merciful because He wants to help His creature, who possesses reason. Whoever hopes in Him never lacks anything; He provides for us in the same measure that we hope in His generosity. Therefore, we will be provided for exactly as much as we hope.

And so, if a man knows himself through the Light of Faith, he does not trust in himself nor in his own hopes. He recognizes that, by himself, he clearly does not exist <note>A central theme in Catherine's theology is "the science of self-knowledge," where the soul realizes it is "she who is not" and God is "He who is."</note>; for if he were anything of himself, he would be able to possess the things he loves in his own way. But this is not the case: even when he wishes to be rich, he often finds it necessary to be poor; he might wish for health and a long life, yet he must be sick and his time runs out. Therefore, he is a fool—and cursed—who trusts in man, seeing that nothing comes from himself, and seeing that the world and other men do not serve him except for their own utility.

Whoever chooses to trust in them will always be deceived, because they keep faith with nothing. In wanting to grow rich, such a man impoverishes his soul, himself, and his children of their temporal substance. He becomes disordered and unbearable to himself, desiring that which he ought not to de—

...to consider. The soul that is disordered in desiring what it does not have is always in pain, because it is deprived of the Supreme Good, which pacifies, quiets, and satisfies the Soul.

### III.
O dearest Brother and Son, open the eye of your intellect with the Light of the Most Holy Faith, so that you may recognize the little firmness and stability of the world, and the great Goodness of God—firm and stable, He who never moves—who satisfies and nourishes the Soul in affectionate Charity. He clothes her in hope, as she hopes in her sweet Creator; she does well, for the Divine Goodness sees what she needs. Therefore, she offers her desire and her need to Him, serving Him with all her heart and with all her affection. She gives the labor of her body to her family, assisting and helping them as much as she can. With a good and holy conscience, she does what she can, and leaves the rest to the Divine Goodness, in whom she has placed her hope; for she knew through the Light of Faith His Goodness and Providence.

In no other way do I see how one could escape from the mud <term>loto</term> <note>Catherine frequently uses "loto" (mire/mud) to describe the sticky, degrading nature of worldly attachments and sin.</note> of the world without the Light of Faith, from which one draws hope and affectionate Charity, tasting in this life the earnest money <term>arra</term> <note>An "arra" is a down-payment or pledge. In Catherine’s theology, the peace felt by a believer is a "down-payment" on the joy of heaven.</note> of Eternal Life, because the soul's will is clothed in the sweet Will of God.

Thus I pray you, for the love of Christ Crucified, that you and your wife do this, so that you are not in a state of damnation. And that which might not have been done in the past, I want to be done in the present; do not wait for time to seek your salvation, because time does not wait for you, and therefore you must not wait for it. 

Do not act like the Raven, who says "cras, cras" <note>original: "cra cra". This is a play on words: "cras" is the Latin word for "tomorrow," but it also mimics the sound of a raven’s croak. And so they find themselves overtaken by death without realizing it. Then they want more time and cannot have it, because they have spent their time miserably with greed, cupidity, and illicit gains, and with much filthiness of mind and body, contaminating the Sacrament of Marriage. Such a person makes a god of his children and, like a blind man, places his hope where he should not. Thus he goes from blindness to blindness, so much so that if he does not correct himself and punish his fault with contrition of heart, and with Confession and satisfaction to the best of his power and his possibi-

# To Giovanni Trenta, and to Lady Giovanna, his wife, from Lucca.

**S**he exhorts them to union and to concord, in imitation of Jesus Christ, demonstrating how much we must humble ourselves since God has humbled himself for us.

## Letter 287.

->In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary.<-

**D**earest Brother and son Giovanni in Christ Jesus: I Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of God, bless you and comfort you in the precious Blood of His Son. With desire I have desired <note>Catherine frequently uses this biblical opening—referencing Luke 22:15—to express her intense spiritual longing for the recipient's well-being.</note>, my son, to see you and your family, and especially your bride, in such union and bond in Virtue, and in such a manner, that neither demons nor any creature can break it or separate it from you. O most dear daughter and son, let it not seem difficult or hard to do a small thing for Christ Crucified. Oh, how great would be the ignorance, the misery, and the coldness of heart to see the supreme eternal Greatness, Christ, descended to such lowliness as is our Humanity, and not humble ourselves! Now, do you not see Christ as a poor little one <note>original: "povarello"</note>, humbled in a manger between two animals, having rejected all pomp and human glory? Wherefore Saint Bernard <note>Saint Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), a Cistercian abbot whose writings on humility and the infancy of Christ deeply influenced Catherine.</note> says, commending the profound Humility and poverty of Christ, and to put our pride to shame: "Be ashamed, O proud man, who seeks honors, and delights, and the pomps of the world. Perhaps you believed that your King, the gentle Lamb, would have grand dwellings and honorable people?" The first sweet Truth <note>A characteristic title Catherine uses for God.</note> did not wish it so; rather, He chose for our example and rule, at His Nativity, such extreme poverty that He did not even have a decent swaddling cloth <note>original: "pannicello a sè condecente"</note> in which He could be wrapped.

*( C ) Of Guilt and punishment. This manner of speaking is quite common among ancient Tuscan authors when speaking of Indulgences granted by the Supreme Pontiffs. Thus Matteo Villani wrote that the Pontiff: Ordered an Indulgence of the Cross, pardoning guilt and punishment; that is to say, he published the Indulgence usually granted to those who took the cross to go and fight the Infidels <note>A reference to the Crusades</note>, through which both the guilt and the punishment were pardoned. This manner of speaking, therefore, I believe has its origin in the way the Pontiff is sometimes accustomed to dispense this Sacred Treasury. [ **E** ] *Believe, Son, with living faith and firm hope, etc.* Just as it is beyond doubt that one can, by virtue of the Indulgence, pass from this life immediately to Heaven, so it is commonly held as most certain by the Doctors <note>Theological authorities and scholars of the Church</note> that many, notwithstanding the plenary <term>Indulgence</term>, do not enjoy this advantage through their own fault. These are the ones who do not have the necessary disposition <note>The internal state of repentance and detachment from sin</note> required to receive an entire <term>remission</term> of the <term>punishment</term> due for their grave failings. Therefore, if the Saint gives this Gentleman such firm hope of Heaven as soon as he has died, she assumes him to be well-disposed in his Soul in that final hour to receive such a grace, and she was able to promise it to him based on his way of life.

# To Bartolo Usimbardi; and to My Lady Orsa his Wife, & to Francesco di Pipino Tailor, & to My Lady Agnesa his Wife from Florence.

### Letter 289.

->*In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary.*<-

**D**earest Sons and Daughters in sweet Christ Jesus: I, Catherine, servant and slave of the Servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in his precious Blood with the desire to see you burned and consumed in the fire of Divine Charity. This is that fire which, while burning, does not consume, but rather nourishes <note>Original: *fa ingrassare*. In the spiritual language of the time, "fattening" the soul meant making it robust, rich, and well-nourished by grace.</note> the Soul, and unites it and transforms it into itself—the fire of divine Love. This happens when the Soul considers that it has its very being from God alone out of love, and considers that, through love, God has granted it all the graces and gifts which are founded upon that existence. And then the soul will also see that, out of love, Eternal God has given us <term>the Word</term> <note>Original: *el Verbo*. This refers to Jesus Christ as the Eternal Word of God.</note> of his Son, so that he might pay the debt for us to which we were obligated, and draw us out of the dark prison and servitude of the Devil. From this prison, Man could not escape on his own. This Divine Word, becoming mortal Man, entered into the Field of Battle for us; and by defeating the Devil, he broke open the dark prison and drew us out of the miserable servitude in which all of humanity <note>Original: *tutta l'umana Generatione*.</note> had been for so long. With the Cross, he opened the gate of Eternal Life to us; and all this he has done out of love. Having therefore shown us the way and opened the gate, there remai—

*( A ) Although Usimbardi was of a noble family, and the other to whom this letter is also addressed was a Tailor by profession, they were nevertheless equals in the goodness of their lives and in their affection toward the Saint; and they were equally participants in the Government of the Republic. In that state, if the Nobles wished to enjoy the **Magistracies** <note>The governing offices or positions of authority in the city.</note>, they enrolled themselves in one of the **Guilds** <term>Arti</term> <note>The *Arti* were the professional and trade guilds of Florence. Joining a guild was a legal requirement for political participation, effectively making a nobleman a "citizen" or "man of the people."</note>, and in this manner they became part of the People and came to the administration of the offices of that Commune.*

*( B ) Monna Orsa. The word *Monna* is an abbreviation of *Madonna*, where both the one and the other mean the same as Lady, or My Lady. If one observes closely, however, the title of *Madonna* was held in much higher esteem than the other of *Monna*, just as *Monsignore* was more honored than *Signore*, *Dominus* <note>Latin: Lord or Master.</note> than *Domnus*, and *Domina* <note>Latin: Lady or Mistress.</note> than the shortened *Domna*. Hence it is that if in any of the Saint’s letters one finds sometimes one title and sometimes the other given to the same person—in which the whim or the oversight of whoever transcribed the letters may play a part—in...*

<meta>This page continues the editorial note (A) from the previous page, shifting from the specific family history of the Usimbardi family to a broader linguistic and sociological analysis of titles used in Catherine of Siena’s time, specifically the honorifics "Madonna" and "Monna."</meta>

<page-num>186</page-num>

<sig>A</sig>

...those [letters] which she addresses to Ladies of more illustrious birth, she employs the full name **Madonna** <note>literally "My Lady"</note> out of respect, which is never given to women of lower station. To the latter, she always gives the abbreviated title of **Monna** <note>a contraction of "Madonna"</note>, and even this was only granted to the noblewomen; common women remained with their simple name alone, without any addition of honor.
<margin>Migliore, *Illustrious Florence* <note>Likely referring to the work of Leopoldo del Migliore, a 17th-century Florentine historian.</note></margin> Some have said that the title of **Madonna** first honored a devout image of the Blessed Virgin called the **Madonna of Orsan Michele**—that is to say, "at the Gardens of Saint Michael" <note>the church of Orsan Michele in Florence was originally a grain market and garden</note>—in the City of Florence, and that the title then passed to the principal Ladies of the City in the fourteenth century. They claim it remained in use for the next two centuries, until the title became "dusty" <note>tarnished or common</note> by becoming a household term for the common people, at which point it was no longer deigned to be used by the elite.
I do not believe, however, that this claim is beyond doubt. If one observes, that Sacred Image began to perform miracles and be held in veneration in the year 1292, as narrated by Giovanni Villani <note>a famous Florentine chronicler (c. 1276–1348)</note>; yet neither he, nor the other authors of the following century—which is the **Golden Age of the Language** <note>referring to the 1300s, the era of Dante, Petrarch, and Boccaccio</note>—had given the Blessed Virgin this title, calling her **the Madonna**. Instead, they ordinarily called her **Our Lady** <note>original: *nostra Donna*</note>, whereas they continuously used the word **Madonna** to express the social status of the women of whom they spoke.
I believe it is easier to maintain the view that this title was already given to ladies of high standing; and since it was therefore even more fitting for the supreme Lady, who is the Most Holy Mother, it was easily adapted to express this greatness. Thus, while everyone said **Our Lady** or **Mistress**, some—as a greater expression of affection—called her **My Lady** <note>original: *mia Donna*, or *Madonna*</note>. This was then imitated by others in such a way that the title remained for her alone by excellence, without any other addition.

# **To Bartolo Usimbardi and Francesco di Pipino of Florence.**

**S**he <note>Likely an editorial summary by the 18th-century editor, Girolamo Gigli, describing the letter's intent.</note> exhorts them to gratitude toward God, from which all other Virtues proceed.

## **Letter 290.**

->**In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary.**<-

**D**earest Sons in sweet Christ Jesus: I, Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious Blood, with the desire to see you grateful and mindful of the benefits received from our Creator, so that the fountain of Piety may be nourished within you. This gratitude will make you diligent in practicing Virtue; for, just as ingratitude makes the Soul lazy and negligent, so this sweet gratitude gives it a hunger for time <note>A recurring theme in Catherine’s writings; the "hunger for time" refers to the urgent desire to use every moment for the glory of God rather than wasting it.</note>, so much so that not an hour or a moment passes that the soul does not work. From this gratitude proceeds every true Virtue. Who gives us Charity? Who makes us humble and patient? Only gratitude; and because the soul sees the great debt it owes to God, it strives to live virtuously, for it knows that God requires nothing else from us. And therefore, my sweet Sons, recall to memory with great diligence the many benefits received from Him, so that you may perfectly acquire this Mother of Virtues. I say no more. Remain in the holy and sweet love of God. Sweet Jesus. Jesus Love.

->*In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary.*<-

# To Francesco di Pipino, Tailor of Florence.

## She exhorts him to the virtue of perseverance and the abnegation of his own will.

### Letter 292.

->**In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary.**<-

**D**earest son in <term>sweet Christ Jesus</term> <note>Catherine frequently uses "dolce" (sweet) to describe Christ's mercy and accessibility.</note>: I, Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious Blood, with the desire to see you constant and persevering in Virtue, so that you may receive the **crown of glory**, which is not given to those who only begin, but to those who persevere until death <note>A reference to the biblical sentiment in Matthew 10:22: "the one who perseveres to the end will be saved."</note>. Wherefore I desire that you grow and persevere in Virtue; and let there be no tribulation, nor battle of the **Devil**, nor of creatures <note>In Catherine’s theology, "creatures" refers to any created being (other people), whose influence might distract a soul from God.</note>, that ever makes you turn your head back <note>An allusion to Luke 9:62: "No one who puts a hand to the plow and looks back is fit for service in the kingdom of God."</note>. Bathe yourselves in the **Blood of Christ**, drowning and killing every self-will and sensual passion; and then you will be made strong, and nothing will be able to move you, because you will be founded upon the <term>living Rock</term> <note>original: "viva Pietra." A common biblical metaphor for Christ as the foundation of faith (1 Peter 2:4).</note>, sweet Christ Jesus, and you will receive the reward for your labors. I say no more. Remain in the holy and sweet love of God. Sweet Jesus. Jesus Love.

## Letter 293.

->In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary<-

<margin>Matthew 10</margin>
**D**earest son and daughter in <term>sweet Christ Jesus</term> <note>original: "dolce Gesù." Catherine uses "sweetness" to describe the soul's experience of divine love and mercy.</note>: I, Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious Blood, with the desire to see you as true servants of Christ Crucified, constant and persevering until death, so that you may receive the **Crown of Glory**; for this crown is not given to those who only begin, but to those who persevere until the end <note>A reference to Matthew 10:22: "the one who perseveres to the end will be saved."</note>. I desire, therefore, that with all diligence you strive to run along the way of Truth, studying always to grow from **Virtue to Virtue**; because not to grow would be to turn back, since the soul cannot stay still in one state <note>A common medieval spiritual principle: in the spiritual life, if one is not moving forward, one is inevitably slipping backward.</note>. 

And what method shall we keep, dearest children, to grow the fire of holy desire within us? The method is this: that we place wood upon the fire. What wood? To bring to memory the many and infinite benefits received from God, which are innumerable; and most especially the benefit of the **Blood of the Only-begotten Word**, His Son, which manifests to us the ineffable love that God has for us. For by this, and by the many other benefits received, by remembering them, we shall come to love and grow in love. It also behooves us to consider attentively our many and innumerable defects, sins, and offenses committed against Him, and with bitterness and contrition to grieve, and to see how great His **Mercy** has been and is toward us, in not having made [the earth] swallow us <note>The text cuts off here with the syllable "inghiot-". The catchword "tire" at the bottom indicates the full word is "inghiottire" (to swallow).</note>

<meta>The catchword "tire" at the bottom right completes the word "inghiottire" (to swallow), referring to the biblical image of the earth swallowing sinners.</meta>

# To Francesco di Pipino, Tailor of Florence, and to Lady Agnesa, his Wife.

**S**he exhorts them to the holy fear of God, demonstrating to them how this drives out servile fear <note>In medieval theology, "servile fear" is the fear of punishment or hell, while "holy" or "filial" fear is the loving dread of offending God.</note>; and of the peace and perfection that is born in the Soul.

## Letter 295.

->*In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary.*<-

**D**earest Children in Christ sweet Jesus: I, Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious Blood, with the desire to see you founded in the holy fear of God, because without this fear you could not participate in the life of **Grace** <note>The supernatural life of the soul bestowed by God.</note> within you. This holy fear drives out every servile fear that might be in the Soul, and gives such security that, in order to fulfill the **Will of God**, the soul does not care for nor fear the displeasure of Men; such a soul does not care for reproach, torment, or villainy, nor does it fear losing temporal substance, or even life, so long as it sees itself performing its duty to render glory and praise to the Name of God. For such a person has lifted their eye from the Earth and placed it upon their **Creator**, following with great diligence the footsteps of Christ Crucified. 

All of their actions are directed and ordered according to the **Will of God**; they remain in the delight of **Charity** with all <term>Creatures</term> <note>original: "Creature." This refers to all human beings as created by God.</note> who possess **Reason** <note>The capacity for rational thought and moral choice.</note> within them. Every good, rest, peace, and quiet comes out of this holy and sweet fear, and every perfection follows for the Soul that is truly founded in it. And therefore I told you that I desired to see you founded in said holy fear, and so I pray you to do this for the love of Christ Crucified. I say no more to you. Remain in the holy and sweet delight of God. Sweet Jesus, Jesus Love.

<vocab>Catarina, Francesco di Pipino Sarto, Monna Agnesa, timore santo, timore servile, Gesù Cristo Crocifisso, Sangue di Cristo, Gratia, Volontà di Dio</vocab>

# Letter 296.

->*In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary.*<-

<margin>I.</margin> **D**earest children in Christ sweet Jesus: I, Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious Blood with the desire to see you stripped of yourselves and clothed in Christ Crucified, dead to every self-will and every human opinion and pleasure, and only His sweet truth alive in you. For in no other way do I see how you could persevere in **Virtue**; and by not persevering, you would not receive the Crown of **Bliss**, and thus you would have lost the fruit of your labors.

<margin>II.</margin> I desire then, my sweet children, that you study in everything to kill this perverse **sensitive Will** <note>The "sensitive will" refers to the part of the human soul driven by physical desires, emotions, and instincts, which Catherine views as often opposing the divine will.</note>, which always wishes to rebel against God. The way to kill it is this: to climb upon the Seat of your **Conscience** and hold court there <note>Catherine frequently uses the metaphor of the "court of conscience" where the soul acts as its own judge to maintain moral discipline.</note>, not letting one tiny thought pass outside of God that is not corrected with great reproach. Let a person make two parts of themselves—that is, <term>sensuality</term> and <term>Reason</term> <note>In Catherine’s psychology, "Sensuality" is the lower nature prone to sin, while "Reason" is the higher faculty that aligns the soul with God.</note>—and let this Reason draw out the **two-edged knife**, which is hatred of Vice and love of Virtue. With this knife, let Reason hold sensuality as a Servant, uprooting and tearing out every Vice and movement of Vice from the soul. Never give this Servant anything she asks for, but with the love of Virtue, trample her under the feet of the...

# To Francesco di Pipino, Tailor from Florence, and to Lady Agnesa, his Wife.

**H**e exhorts them to flee the company <note>original: "conversazione"; in this period, this refers to social interaction and "keeping company" with others, rather than just verbal speech</note> of sinners, demonstrating how dangerous it is, and to follow the company of the servants of God, which is very useful to the Soul; and [he shows] that for this, the living Light of Faith is necessary.

## Letter 297.

->*In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of Mary sweet.*<-

**D**earest Children in Christ sweet Jesus: I Catherine, servant and slave of the Servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in his precious Blood, with the desire to see you enlightened by true Light <note>original: "Lume"; light is Catherine’s primary metaphor for divine grace and the ability to distinguish between good and evil</note>, so that you may persevere in Virtue until death. Without the Light, Dearest ones, you would walk in darkness, and you would not recognize the truth; sweet things would seem bitter to you, and bitter things sweet. But having the Light, we will be cautious, and we will flee all those things that would diminish in us the Virtues and the love that we ought to have purely for our Creator. With this Light we will see how dangerous is the company of those who live without the fear of God; for such company is the foundation of our ruin. It causes our Conscience to become coarse; it takes away the "Mother of Prayer" <note>Catherine often refers to the "Mother of Prayer" as the state of soul that gives birth to all other virtues</note>; it removes abstinence, hinders fervor, expands our affection toward the vain delights of the World, steals holy Humility from us, takes away our Purity <note>original: "Oneſtà"; referring to moral integrity and modest living</note>, opens the senses of the Body, and blinds the eye of our Intellect <term>Intellect: the faculty of the soul that perceives spiritual truth through the light of faith</term>, so much so that it never seems as if the Soul has begun to know its Creator. And thus, little by little, the Creature does not notice, and finds itself transformed from an earthly Angel into a Demon of Hell. And where is the Purity that you used to have? Where is the desire to suffer for God? Where are the tears that you used to shed in the sight of God with hum[ble]...

...and continuous Prayer <term>Oratione; specifically the practice of mental or vocal prayer as a spiritual discipline</term>? Where is the brotherly Charity <note>original: "Carità fraterna"</note> that you used to have toward every rational creature? Nothing of it remains, because the Devil has stolen everything by means of his servants.

I do not want, my dearest and sweetest children, for this to happen to you; rather, let your social interaction <note>original: "conversazione"; in this period, it refers to who one spends time with and the nature of those social circles</note> be always with those who truly fear and love God. These people are the reason our cold hearts are warmed; they dissolve our hardness with sweet reasonings about God, speaking of His great Goodness and His Charity toward us. In this way, one person gives light to the other, seeking the Doctrine of Christ Crucified and the lives of the Saints. 

Hate all the selfish feelings of the body; with a holy modesty embrace Humility and her sister, lowliness <note>original: "viltà"; here meaning the humble recognition of one's own insignificance or unworthiness before God</note>, setting aside your own self-interest. In short, this is what follows from the company of the servants of God, just as every evil comes to us from the company of the servants of the world. Wherefore the Holy Spirit says through the mouth of the Prophet:

<margin>Psalm 17 <note>In modern Bibles, this is Psalm 18:25-26</note></margin>
*With the holy you will be holy, with the innocent you will be innocent, and with the chosen you will be chosen, and with the perverse you will be perverse.*

I want you, therefore, to be very careful to always associate with the servants of God—both men and women—and to flee from others like fire. Never trust in yourselves, saying, "I am strong, and I do not fear that these people will make me fall." Do not do this, for the love of God! Instead, with true Humility, let us recognize that if God Himself does not hold us up, we would be demons incarnate. We have such examples of this before us that we must always remain in trembling. 

I am certain that if you have the true Light, you will fulfill the Will of God and my desire in this and in every other thing; otherwise, you will not. And therefore I told you that I desired to see you enlightened by this Light. Because of my haste, I say no more for now. Remain in the holy and sweet love <term>diletzione; from the Latin "dilectio," a high form of spiritual affection or "delectation" in God</term> of God.

## Letter 298.

-> In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary. <-

I. **D**earest Son in sweet Jesus Christ: I Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious Blood, with the desire to see the fire of holy desire grow within you; for if it does not grow, you would turn back, and by turning back, you would be worthy of greater Judgment than if you had never set out; because more is required of the one who has received more. I want, therefore, that you manfully rise from the sleep of negligence, and with every effort strive to grow the Light <note>original: "Lume"; in Catherine's theology, this refers to the supernatural light of faith and reason granted by God</note> within you; for as the Light grows, love will grow, and as love grows, the Virtues and works will grow until death, and then you will render what is required of you—that is, to love God above all things, and your Neighbor as yourself.

II. And so I say to you, Agnesa, see to it that I hear you are growing in hunger for the honor of God and the salvation of Souls, and that you are pouring out rivers of tears with humble and continuous Prayer <term>Oratione; the practice of disciplined spiritual communication with God</term> before God for the salvation of the entire World, and especially for the reformation of the sweet Spouse of Christ <note>The "Spouse of Christ" is a traditional title for the Holy Catholic Church</note>, which we see falling into such darkness and such ruin. I say no more. Remain in the holy and sweet love of God. Sweet Jesus. Jesus Love.

<meta>This page marks the transition from Letter 298 (addressed to the tailor Francesco di Pipino and his wife) to Letter 299, addressed to Giovanni da Parma in Rome. # To Giovanni da Parma in Rome, October 23.

I. **T**hat we must be founded upon the living Stone, which is Jesus Christ, and on the manner of following His Doctrine.
II. That the Body of Jesus Christ is the Book where we learn it, and she explains what we read in the said Book.
III. She exhorts the aforementioned Giovanni to read in this Book of the Body of Christ, and not to be distressed on account of the Book that he had with him (which he wished to know by revelation if it were from God or from the Devil), exhorting him to leave it aside if he saw it was not in conformity with the Doctrine approved by the Holy Church.

## Letter 299.

->In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary.<-

I. **D**earest Brother in Christ sweet Jesus: I Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious Blood, with the desire to see you founded upon the living Stone, Christ sweet Jesus; for in no other way could a building be placed upon you that would endure, but if a contrary wind arrived, it would immediately fall to the ground. But the Soul that is founded upon this sweet Stone—that is, which follows the Doctrine of Christ Crucified—never fails. What Doctrine is this, which the sweet and loving Word <note>original: "Verbo"; referring to the Second Person of the Trinity</note> teaches us, He who is called the living Stone? And where does He teach it to us? Not in delights, nor in the pleasures of the World, but upon the Table of the Most Holy Cross <term>Mensa della Santissima Croce; a central image in Catherine’s theology where Christ acts as the food and the Cross as the table where the salvation of souls is consumed</term>. This teaches us to love God in truth, hating Vice and one's own sensuality, which is the cause of Vice, and to love Virtue and God Himself, who is the cause of every Virtue. It teaches us to obey the Commandments of the Law, and to bring us into love and counsel; it makes us conceive the desire to want to acquire them upon the Table of the Most Holy Cross, where the Soul clothes itself in the Charity of God and of its Neighbor. But take heed, for this cannot be...

--- Page 504 ---
<meta>This page continues Letter 299 to Giovanni da Parma. Catherine is expanding on the metaphor introduced on the previous page: the Body of Christ as a "Book" of doctrine that must be read with the "Light of Faith."</meta>

...to learn without the Light, nor without the object of the Book:
Therefore we have need that the eye of the Intellect be illuminated with the Light of the Most Holy Faith, and that the Book be written, so that in the Writing we may learn the Doctrine. If I look closely, Dearest Brother, God has given us the eye of the Intellect, and within it the Light of Faith, which light cannot be taken from us either by the Demon, nor by any creature, unless we ourselves take it away through self-love; and He has given us the written Book—that is, the Word of the Son of God—which was written upon the Wood of the Cross, not with ink, but with Blood, with the capital letters <note>original: "capoversi"; here referring to the highlighted initial letters or section headers of a manuscript, used here to describe Christ's wounds as the "headings" of the book of his body</note> of the sweetest and Most Sacred Wounds of Christ. And who would be so dense an unlearned person <term>Idiota; in the medieval sense, this refers to a person who is unlettered or lacks formal education, rather than someone of low intelligence</term>, and of such low understanding, that they would not know how to read them? I know of none, except those who love themselves, and this happens to them, not because they do not know how, but because they do not want to.

[ B ] *Your Book, because of which it seems you are so troubled,* etc. Regarding books that were considered harmful to the ancient religion of the Pagans <note>original: "Gentili"</note>, their reading was forbidden by Princes and Magistrates with rigorous prohibitions, as is found in the authors. With better reason, it is the custom in the Church to forbid the Faithful from reading those books if they in any way contradict the Catholic Faith or good morals; indeed, in the early days of nascent Christianity, amidst the first fervors of the new Christians, books that possessed too much dangerous curiosity were thrown into the fire, as is seen in the Book of the Acts of the Apostles, where it is narrated that books to the value of fifty thousand pieces of silver were burned—which, according to the calculation of Budé <note>Guillaume Budé (1467–1540), a French scholar and expert on ancient coinage</note>, is exactly five thousand Roman Scudi.

If one then moves through the centuries that followed, one encounters the strictest orders not only from Popes and Councils but also from Christian Emperors, forbidding the reading of books by heretics. Against other books not so openly hostile to Religion, there were no such rigorous laws, perhaps because they had not increased so much in number, nor were books spread everywhere so easily because they were too costly. But after the **Invention of Printing** [for which some have therefore given blame <note>A historical perspective suggesting that printing was responsible for the rapid spread of heresy</note>], their number having increased immeasurably and they being available at will, so that the Faithful might not suffer harm from such books pernicious to either Religion or Morals, the Holy Council of Trent <note>A 16th-century council that formalized the "Index of Prohibited Books"</note>, and according to its ordinances, the Supreme Pontiffs ordered and compiled the Catalogue <note>The Index Librorum Prohibitorum</note>, and with heavy but just penalties forbade both reading them and possessing them.

In the time of Saint Catherine, these provisions had not yet been made; thus this man, eager to read and yet fearful of drawing some harm to his soul, wished to have his doubt removed by the Saint—who was so enlightened by Heaven—as to whether the book contained any error that he might not have clearly recognized. I would not be far from believing that this book could be one of the many left to posterity by the famous **Raimondo Lullo** <note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1315), a Majorcan philosopher whose complex works were sometimes suspected of being heterodox</note>, who had died in that century—and as is held, by the hands of African Barbarians, out of hatred for the Holy Faith—

# To Marco Bindi, Merchant

On the virtue of patience, exhorting him to embrace it; and on the method of acquiring it, demonstrating that four things are necessary for this, and singularly the Light of Holy Faith.

## Letter 300

->In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary.<-

**C**arissimo Brother in Christ, sweet Jesus: I, Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious Blood with the desire to see you founded in true and holy patience <term>patience (patientia): in Catherine's theology, this is a "queen" virtue that proves the presence of charity, as it allows a person to endure suffering without losing peace</term>, for in no other way could we please God, but we would lose the fruit of our labors; and therefore there is a need for this glorious virtue of patience. And if you should say to me, dearest brother: "I have great labors, and I do not feel strong enough to have this patience, and I do not know how to acquire it," I answer you that there is no one who wants to follow Reason who cannot have it; but I well confess to you that we are fragile and weak in ourselves, according to our sensuality <term>sensuality (sensualità): here meaning the lower nature or the "flesh," which seeks comfort and avoids pain, as opposed to the "reason" of the soul</term>; and especially when a person loves themselves, and creatures, and temporal substance <note>worldly possessions and wealth</note> sensually; wherefore, loving them so much with a tender, sensitive love, when they later lose them, they receive intolerable pain. But God, who is our strength—if we will, with Reason, with the power of the Will, and with the hand of free will <term>free will (libero arbitrio): the capacity of the soul to choose between good and evil, which Catherine often depicts as a "hand" or "gatekeeper"</term>, trample upon our frailty—God will not despise the effort we make upon ourselves...

...limit ourselves <note>The original OCR 'defimi' likely refers to 'definimoci,' suggesting a setting of boundaries or defining one's response.</note> so as not to grieve inordinately; for He is the acceptor of holy desires, and He will give us this sweet and royal Virtue, and we will carry every toil with true and holy patience. So you see that everyone can have it, if they will use the **Reason** <term>Reason (Ragione): for Catherine, this is the "eye of the soul," the natural intellectual capacity given by God to distinguish good from evil and to govern the passions.</term> that God has given them, and not merely follow their own fragility; for it would be a very unseemly thing if we **rational creatures** did not use any other Reason than the brute animals; for they cannot use Reason because they do not have it, but we, because we have it, ought to use it, and by not using it, we fall into impatience and become scandalized by the things that God has permitted for us, and thus we offend Him.

What way, then, can we keep to have this patience, since I can and must have it, and without it I would offend God? There are four principal things it behooves us to have and consider. First, I say that it behooves us to have the **Light of Faith**, in which Light of Holy Faith we shall acquire every Virtue, and without this Light we would walk in darkness, just like the blind man for whom the day is turned to night; so it is for the Soul without this Light. That which God has done for love—which love is a light so bright above every other light—the soul perceives as night, that is, a night of hatred, holding that God permits the tribulations and the labors he has out of hatred. So then you see that it behooves us to have the Light of Most Holy Faith.

The second thing is that which is acquired with this Light: namely, that in truth it behooves us to believe—and not only believe, but be certain—that every thing that has being in itself proceeds from God, except for sin, which has no being <note>St. Catherine follows the Augustinian tradition that evil and sin are a privation or "nothingness," lacking the substance of being which comes only from God.</note>; the evil Will of Man, who commits the sin, He does not create, but every other thing—whether by fire, or by water, or by any other death, or whatever else it may be—everything proceeds from Him. It is like the point of a needle; therefore, it is indeed true that it is small. For I no longer have the labor that is past, because the time has passed; that which is to come I also do not have, because I am not certain of having the time, seeing as I must die and I do not know when. Only this point of the present exists, and no more.

Therefore, we ought to bear it with great joy, because every good is rewarded and every fault is punished. <margin>Romans 8</margin> And Paul says that the sufferings of this life are not worthy of that future glory received by the Soul that bears them with good patience. <note>original: "non sono condegne le passioni di questa vita a quella futura gloria" - a reference to Romans 8:18.</note>

And therefore I told you that I desired to see you grounded in true and holy patience, and so I pray you to do. *(A) To the Company of the Bigallo. The Company of the Bigallo <note>A charitable lay brotherhood in Florence, still active today.</note>, with which this man of the profession of <term>flax-worker</term> <note>original: "Linaiuolo"; a worker who processes or trades in linen.</note> resided, had been born in Florence a little more than a century prior. Its origin is traced to **St. Peter Martyr** of the sacred Order of **Preachers** <note>St. Peter of Verona (1205–1252), a Dominican friar.</note>, and great Defender of the Faith against the **Manichaean** heretics <note>The commentator refers to the Cathars, a dualist sect often called "Manicheans" by medieval and early modern writers.</note>, who in the thirteenth century corrupted a good part of Italy with their errors and had taken a large place in the City of **Florence**. He was at that time **Inquisitor General** in **Tuscany**, and for all the efficacy of his fervor, he had not succeeded in breaking the obstinacy of the wicked, nor in damming their advancements, lest they draw others to become their followers in **Heresy**. 

Full of Holy Zeal, as gentle remedies were of no use, he stimulated Catholics to secure their Fatherland with the sword from the danger of becoming completely infected, and to take vengeance all at once for the offenses that were committed more every day against Heaven by them. With much Blood on one side and on the* <margin>Migliore, loc. cit.</margin> *other, they fought near the Church of **Santa Felicita**, and finally those who had Justice on their side also had the Victory, the heretics being defeated and undone. A Column was raised as a perpetual memory of this event on the site of the battle itself, which is still preserved there today. Then the Saint wanted to provide for the future, should other errors ever be spread through the City; therefore, with this aim, he gathered many of the most influential Citizens, and to twelve of them he gave certain Banners, or Stand...* <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "gonfaloni" (banners).</note>

...white banners <note>original: "fanfaloni"; large processional standards or banners</note> with a vermilion Cross, so that whenever the need required it, they would go out with them into the field, and having gathered the People, they would create a military obstacle to Heresy and strike down the pride of those perfidious men. These Men, because they had the duty of leading armed groups and carrying Standards, were called by the Saint <note>St. Peter Martyr (1205–1252), a Dominican friar and inquisitor who organized lay groups to combat the Cathar heresy in Florence.</note> the Captains against the Heretics; and by Bzovio <note>Abraham Bzovius (1567–1637), a Dominican historian known for continuing the "Annales Ecclesiastici."</note>, they are called **Soldiers of the Militia of Jesus Christ marked with the Cross** <note>original: "Cruce signati Militiæ Jesu Christi"</note>. Later, the number of those who enrolled under these Banners—both Men and Women of every trade and condition—grew beyond measure, especially after the news spread of the glorious death of the Saint, who was killed by Heretics out of hatred for the Faith, leaving his name in the highest veneration in the City.

In those early times, this gathering was given the name **Company of Saint Mary**, and later that of the **Company of Mercy** <note>original: "Compagnia della Misericordia"</note>, on account of the many Works of Piety that they began to practice through it. This change occurred because there was no longer a need to fight in defense of Religion once the errors <note>Referring to the Cathar heresy.</note> had entirely vanished. Among the many places entrusted to this Company for the purpose of employing its Charity, one was the **Hospital of Saint Mary of the Bigallo**, located five miles from Florence in a place called **Fontana Viva**. It was situated on the road that leads from the City to **Arezzo**, and belonged to the Nuns of **Ripoli**, who had ceded it to the Company in the Year 1267. From this place, the Company and these Captains took their name, being called the **Company** and the **Captains of the Bigallo**.

That place had formerly been a retreat for those Nuns, who were the first to be established in these parts of Tuscany by the Holy Patriarch Dominic. Having later become a Hospital, as was mentioned, it was ceded in the Year 1503 by the Captains of the Bigallo to the Religious women of **Catignano**, who serve God by following the **Rule of Saint Benedict**. These nuns had abandoned their ancient Monastery which was falling into ruin from old age; they still maintain it today and are called the **Nuns of the Bigallo**. Where the name **Bigallo** originated is quite uncertain, and one can only guess at it.

The assets of that Company were later divided into two: one part being called **Saint Mary of the Bigallo** (or of **Saint Peter Martyr**), and the others being called the **Misericordia**. They were eventually reunited into a single body in the Year 1425 under the same Captains by order of the Florentine Senate. At present, these Captains—who form a particular Magistracy called the **Captains of the Bigallo**—have under their care the Hospital called **Saint Catherine**, where abandoned children and...

# To Salvi, son of Master Pietro the Goldsmith in Siena.

I. **She** exhorts him to be a true, faithful, and persevering man through the virtue of living Faith, demonstrating how Faith without works (we being adults) is dead.
II. That this Faith must be directed toward nothing but the Love of God; knowing the Will of God, which is our sanctification, manifested to us by His Only-begotten Son.
III. That whoever possesses the Light of this Faith bears all adversity with patience and despises prosperous things.
IV. How from this Light proceeds <term>charity</term> <note>original: "carità"; refers to selfless, divine love</note> toward one's Neighbor.
V. She responds to the Letters of Salvi, advising him how she was ready to stay or depart from her place according to the Divine Will, and gives him an account of what she does and longs to do for the salvation of Souls.
VI. She rebukes the Citizens of Siena, who were judging her and her companions unfavorably.

the work is dead. This is the working of faith: that we conceive virtues within ourselves through the affection of love, and these fruits will be born with true patience in the midst of our Neighbor, bearing and supporting the defects of one another. For it would not be enough for us, or for our salvation, to have received the form of Faith with Divine Grace when we receive Holy Baptism. It is indeed sufficient for the little child <note>original: "Fanciullo parvulo"</note> who, dying in his childhood, receives eternal life only by means of the Blood of the Lamb; but once we have come to a mature age <note>original: "età perfetta"; referring to the age of reason or adulthood</note>, having only Holy Baptism would not be enough if we did not exercise the light of Faith with love. 

Thus it happens to us as it does to the physical eye; for, although a man possesses an eye, and it is pure and healthy enough to see, if he does not open it with his <term>free will</term> <note>original: "libero arbitrio"</note>—which he has the power to do—and with a love for the light, it can be said that having the eye, he has no eye. He possesses the eye through the goodness of the Creator, but he does not possess the virtue of the eye because of the defect of his own will, which does not open it; one can therefore say that it is dead and bears no fruit. In the same way, Dearest Son, God through His infinite goodness has given us the eye of the <term>intellect</term> <note>original: "intelletto"; in Catherine’s theology, this is the faculty of the soul that perceives spiritual truth</note>, which He fills by giving us the light of Faith in Holy Baptism, and with it He gives free will, removing the bond of original sin. Now God requires, since we have come to a full age, that we have the knowledge to open this eye He has given us through our free will and with a love for the light.

II. Since the Soul therefore sees within itself the eye with which it is able to see, it must open it to its Creator. And toward what light should it be placed? To see in God nothing but love; for nothing can be done without love, whether spiritual or temporal. If I wish to love sensory things, the eye is immediately placed there to take delight in them; and if a person wishes to serve and love God, the eye of the Intellect opens, setting Him as its object. With love, it draws out love—that is, seeing that God loves him supremely, he cannot help but return that love. Thus, he then loses sensory love and conceives a true love, seeing himself created in the **Image and likeness of God** and recreated in grace by the Blood of His Only-begotten Son. This eye has found the Light, and having found the Light, it is made a lover of that Light,

## Letter 305.

You were made to be the **Temple of God** <note>original: "Tempio di Dio"</note>, which means you must receive God through grace, living virtuously, participating in the **Blood of the Lamb** <note>original: "Sangue dell' Agnello"</note>, where our iniquities are washed away. 

Alas, alas, my wretched Soul; I do not know how to set my hand to my iniquities and yours. Now, how could your Soul and your beastly sensory passion be so cruel and pitiless, that you, besides the sin against nature etc. Alas, let hearts burst, let the Earth split open, let the stones roll over us, let the wolves devour us, so they may not sustain such filth and offense committed against God and against your Soul. ## Letter 307.

->In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary.<-

I. **D**earest and most beloved Brother in sweet Jesus Christ: I, Catherine, servant and slave of God, write to you and comfort you in the precious Blood of the Son of God, with the desire to see you as a true servant of Jesus Christ, an observer of His commandments; for no one can have the life of Grace unless he is a fulfiller of these commandments. And when a Man sees that he is nothing of himself, and is entirely humbled by recognizing the benefit of the benefactor, he grows so much in love—recognizing the great Goodness of God working within him—that he would choose death rather than trespass against the commandment of his sweetest Creator. This holy trembling leads us to a very great love, and this love

## Letter 308.

> ->*In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified and of sweet Mary.*<-

I. **D**earest Sons in Christ sweet Jesus: I, Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious Blood with the desire to see you bound in the sweet bond of <term>Charity</term> <note>original: "Carità"; in Catherine's writing, Charity is the divine love that connects the soul to God and to neighbors</note> in such a way, and by such a manner, that neither Devil nor Creature may ever separate you from it.

<margin>Genesis 1</margin>
II. This is that sweet bond which bound God in Man and Man in God, when the Divine nature was united with Human nature; and this was that ineffable Love which gave being to Man, God drawing him out of Himself when He created him in His <term>Image and Likeness</term> <note>A reference to the creation of humanity in Genesis, signifying our inherent dignity and capacity for relationship with the Divine</note>. And because the Soul is made for pure Love, Love harmonizes the <term>powers of our soul</term> <note>original: "potentie dell' Anima"; referring to the three faculties of the soul—Memory, Intellect, and Will—which were central to medieval psychology</note>, and binds these three powers together: the will moves the intellect to see, wanting to love something; when the intellect perceives that the will wants to love, if it is a reasonable will, the intellect sets as its object the ineffable love of the Eternal Father, who has given us the Word of His Son, and the obedience and humility of the Son, who sustained with gentleness pains, injuries, manglings, scorns, and insults, which He bore with the greatest love. And so, toward that which the eye of the intellect has seen, the will with ineffable love...

III. O, how horrible a death is sin, which robs us of life! And the Soul, seeing this in the manner described, clothes itself in love and in perfect humility. It finds and tastes <term>charity</term> <note>original: "carità"; the divine, selfless love for God and neighbor</note> in the goodness of God, seeing itself participate in it through many gifts and graces, which it has received and receives continually. In the knowledge of itself and of the sin it finds through the perverse law within itself—which has rebelled and continues to rebel against its Creator—the soul conceives a hatred and displeasure toward this <term>sensuality</term> <note>original: "sensualità"; the lower, selfish appetites of the human person that resist spiritual growth</note>. And in this hatred, it finds a patience; which patience makes it strong to endure pains, scorns, insults, hunger, thirst, cold, heat, temptations, and molestations from the Devil. Therefore, it bears all things with such great patience, because charity—that ineffable love—has found its wet-nurse, namely humility, the servant of self-hatred, which for love's sake serves it with perfect patience. This patience takes vengeance and justice upon the enemies of Divine Charity; and its enemies are these: <term>self-love</term> <note>original: "amore proprio"; the selfish desire that seeks its own benefit above God's will</note>, which loves itself for its own utility and loves whatever it loves for its own sake and not for God; and also delights, pleasures, high status, honors, and riches. 

And what vengeance is this? It is a vengeance of such great sweetness that no tongue is sufficient to describe it; for from self-love, which brings death, the soul comes to Divine Love, which gives it life. From darkness, and from the hatred and displeasure of Virtue, it comes to the light and love of the Virtues, to such an extent that it would choose death before it would ever abandon Virtue. Furthermore, it gives itself to holding all those ways and paths through which it sees it can come to virtue and preserve virtue within itself. And because it sees that sensory delights, the softness of the body, and the company of wicked and perverse wordly people are harmful to it, it flees them with all its heart; and with all the affection of the body, it does the opposite. It takes vengeance on these things, macerating the body with penance, with fasting, vigils, prayers, and <term>disciplines</term> <note>Spiritual exercises or physical acts of penance intended to subdue the "sensuality" or ego</note>,

### IV.

Therefore, the Soul that is bound with Christ Crucified follows Him, taking vengeance—for the honor of God and for the salvation of itself and its neighbor—upon the <term>sensory part</term> <note>original: "parte sensitiva"; the lower appetites and physical desires of a person</note>. It drives out the enemies of its Soul—I mean the vices and the disobedience it has held against its Creator by disobeying His commandments—and it places and receives friends within. 

These friends are the true and real Virtues practiced in love and in perfect charity. One of the principal friends the Soul has is true obedience; for whoever is humble is also obedient, and obeys the holy commandments of God. The Soul that falls deeply in love with this obedience—which is a drowning and a killing of its own will—extends itself even further, desiring to observe the obedience of the Counsels of Christ, taking up the yoke of holy obedience in an approved <term>Order</term> <note>A "Religious Order," such as the Dominicans or Franciscans</note>. 

<margin>B</margin> And there is no doubt, my children, that this is a safer and more proven path. Even though we see "Religious" who are infirm <note>Spiritual "infirmity" or weakness; monks or friars who are not living up to their vows</note> because they do not observe the Rule of their Order, nevertheless the Order itself is never infirm, as it is founded and established by the Holy Spirit. Therefore, if you feel that God is calling you to obedience, answer Him; and if the thought should come to you to be dissatisfied because of the Orders that have so declined <note>original: "venute meno"; referring to the corruption or laxity in monastic life during the 14th century</note>...

# To the Prisoners on Holy Thursday in Siena

I. She begs them to place before their eyes the Blood of Christ Crucified, demonstrating to them how true patience is acquired from this.
II. On the effects of sin.
III. On the abundance of God's Mercy in meeting Death for our sake.

---

## Letter 309.

### In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary.

I. **D**earest Sons in Christ sweet Jesus: I, Catherine, servant and slave of the Servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious Blood with the desire to see you bathed with such great desire in the Blood of Christ Crucified. Place it as the object before the eye of your intellect; by doing so, you will acquire a true patience <note>Patience, for Catherine, is not just waiting, but a "queenly virtue" that proves one's love and endurance in the face of suffering</note>. This is because the Blood of Christ represents our iniquities to us, and represents to us the infinite mercy and charity <note>In this context, "charity" refers to *caritas*, the selfless, sacrificial love of God</note> of God. This representation makes us come to hate and feel displeasure for our faults and sins, and makes us come to love virtue. And if you were to ask me, dearest Sons, why our faults and His mercy are seen more clearly in the Blood, I respond to you: because the death of the Son of God was given to Him because of our sins.

II. Sin was the cause of Christ's death; for the Son of God had no need to enter into His Glory by way of the Cross, as there was no poison of sin in Him, and eternal life was already His. But we miserable ones, having lost it through our sins, had fallen into a great war between God and ourselves. Humanity was sick and weakened, rebelling against its Creator, and could not take the bitter medicine <note>The "bitter medicine" is a frequent metaphor in Catherine’s writings, referring to the suffering of the Cross which, though painful, heals the soul from the sickness of sin</note> that followed the fault committed. It was necessary, therefore, that God give us the Word of His Only Begotten Son; and thus, through inestimable Charity, He caused the Divine Nature to be joined with the Human Na-

<meta>catchword: Human Na-</meta>

<summary>Catherine of Siena writes to prisoners on Holy Thursday, exhorting them to contemplate Christ's Blood to find patience and understand both their sins and God's infinite mercy. She explains that Christ's sacrifice was the "medicine" required to heal the rift between humanity and God caused by sin.</summary>
<keywords>Catherine of Siena, prisoners, Holy Thursday, Blood of Christ, patience, mercy, sin, Divine Nature, Human Nature, atonement</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Letter 309 from Catherine of Siena to prisoners in Siena. The previous page established that the Blood of Christ reveals both human sin and divine mercy. This page expands on the metaphors of Christ as a Physician and a Nurse.</meta>

<page-num>518</page-num>

...Humanity, the infinite united Himself with our miserable, finite Flesh. He comes as an **Ill Physician** <note>original: "Medico infermo." This is a classic Catherinian paradox: Christ becomes "sick" with human mortality in order to cure the "sickness" of sin</note> and as our **Knight**. **Physician:** I say that with His Blood He has healed our iniquities, and given His Flesh as food and His Blood as drink. This Blood is of such sweetness and mildness, and of such great sweetness and strength, that it heals every infirmity and brings one from death to life. It removes darkness and gives light, because mortal sin causes the Soul to fall into all these misfortunes. Sin takes away grace, takes away life, and gives us death. It clouds the light of the **Intellect** and makes it a servant and slave to the **Demon**; it takes away true security and gives disordered fear, because sin always fears. He who allows himself to be ruled by sin has lost his mastery. Alas, how many have there been and are there who follow it? How many are the tribulations, anguishes, and hardships that are permitted by God solely because of sin? All these defects and these evils are extinguished in the **Blood of Christ Crucified**, because in the Blood the Soul is washed of its impurities when it brings itself to holy **Confession**. In the blood one acquires **Patience**; for, considering the offenses we have committed against God and the remedy He has provided to give us the life of **Grace**, we come to true patience. Thus it is very true that He is the **Physician** who has given us His Blood as medicine.

III. I say that He is **ill**—that is, that He has taken on our infirmity by taking on our mortality and mortal flesh—and upon that flesh of His most sweet Body He has punished our defects. He has acted like a **Nurse** who feeds a Child; when the child is ill, she takes the medicine for him, because the Child is small and weak and could not take the bitterness, for he feeds on nothing but milk. O most sweet Love, **Jesus**, You are the nurse who has taken the bitter medicine, sustaining pains, reproaches, torments, outrages; bound, beaten, flogged at the column, fixed and nailed to the Cross, sated with scorns and reproaches, afflicted and consumed by thirst without any refreshment. He is given vinegar mixed with gall with great insult, and He bears it with patience, praying for those who crucify Him. O inestimable love! Not only do You pray for those who crucify You, but You excuse them, saying:

they do what they know how to do. O **patience**, which exceeds all patience! Now, who was there ever who, being struck, beaten, mocked, and killed, pardons and prays for those who offend him? The **Crown of Thorns** was his helmet; his scourged **Flesh** was his <term>hauberk</term> <note>A piece of armor consisting of a shirt of mail or a breastplate.</note>; his nailed hands were his <term>plate gauntlets</term>; the lance through his **Side** was that knife which cut and severed death from Man; and his transfixed feet are the spurs. 

See how sweetly this Knight of ours is armed! We must indeed follow him and comfort ourselves in all our adversity and tribulation. Therefore I told you that the **Blood of Christ** manifests our sins to us and shows us the remedy, along with the abundance of **Divine Mercy** which we have received in his Blood. Bathe yourselves in the Blood of Christ Crucified, for in no other way could we participate in his **Grace**, nor reach the end for which we were created, nor could you patiently bear your tribulations; for in the memory of the blood, every bitter thing becomes sweet, and every great weight becomes light. 

I say no more to you because of how little time there remains. Remain in the holy and sweet love of God; and remember that you must die, and you do not know when. See that you prepare yourselves for **Confession** and for **Holy Communion**, those who are able, so that you may be resurrected in grace with Christ Jesus. Sweet Jesus. Jesus Love.
