# To Consiglio, a Jew

She begs him to be willing to come to the true faith by receiving Holy Baptism, showing him the Divine Mercy that was calling him.

## Letter 310.

->Praised be Jesus Christ Crucified, Son of the Glorious Virgin Mary.<-

**To** you, most beloved and dearest Brother, redeemed by the precious Blood of the Son of God just as I am; I, unworthy Catherine, write to you, compelled by Christ Crucified and by His sweet Mother Mary, to pray and urge you that you should come out and abandon your hardness and dark unbelief <note>original: "infedeltà." In a medieval context, this specifically refers to the rejection of Christian dogma.</note>, and that you should live again and receive the grace of Holy Baptism; for without Baptism you cannot have the Grace of God. Whoever is without Baptism does not participate in the fruit of Holy Church, but like a putrid member, severed from the Congregation of the Christian Faithful, passes from bodily death to eternal death. And reasonably he receives punishment and darkness, because he did not wish to be washed in the water of Holy Baptism and held in contempt the Blood of the Son of God, which He shed with such great love. 

O most dear Brother in Christ Jesus, open the eye of your understanding to look upon His inestimable charity, which He sends to you, inviting you through the holy inspirations <note>Internal movements of the soul believed to be prompted by God.</note> that have come into your heart; and through His Servants He requests and invites you, for He wishes to make peace with you, not looking upon the long war and injury He has received from you through your unbelief. For our God is so sweet and kind that since the Law of Love came, and since the Son of God came into the Virgin Mary and shed the abundance of His Blood upon the Wood of the Most Holy Cross, we can receive the abundance of Divine Mercy. Wherefore, just as the Law of Moses was founded on Justice and punishment, so the New Law given by Christ Crucified—the Evangelical life—is founded on love and mercy,

In Siena as well they continued their usury with the faculty of the Magistrates, and against such an abuse Saint Bernardino, with his usual zeal, made public complaints in one of his Sermons, which are held in manuscript. "If you," he says, <margin>Manuscript testimony of Mr. Ubertino Benvoglienti</margin> "have participated in this, that the Jew because of you, or by your help, lends at interest here in Siena—he who has consented with his ballot <note>original: "Lupino." <margin>E</margin> And as for the Lord King your Son, you can aid the **Holy Church** through prayer and holy desire, and you can also voluntarily and through love support her with human aid. Urge your dear Son strictly that, for love, he might offer himself and serve the **Holy Church**. And if our **Christ on Earth** <note>original: "Cristo in Terra." Catherine’s customary title for the Pope, highlighting his role as the visible representative of Jesus.</note> asks it of him, and wishes to lay this labor upon him, pray that he may faithfully accept his petition and request, thereby comforting the **Holy Father** and increasing in him the holy resolution to undertake the holy and sweet **passage** <term>passage</term> <note>original: "passaggio." A common medieval term for a crusade or military expedition to the Holy Land.</note> against the wicked infidel dogs <note>original: "Cani malvagi Infedeli." While harsh to modern ears, Catherine uses the standard crusading rhetoric of her time to describe the Ottoman forces.</note> who possess what is ours—and even more; for as I understand it, they are advancing further with all their power. <margin>F</margin>

It is surely a great shame for Christians to let them possess that **Holy and Venerable Place**, which by right is ours. It is no longer time to merely look on, but like children hungry for the honor of the Father, you must rise up <note>original: "lavare," likely a transcription error for "levare" (to rise/set out).</note> and reclaim what is ours for the salvation of their souls and the exaltation of the **Holy Church**. Consider if one of your own cities were taken from you: I am certain you would apply every remedy and effort possible, even unto death, to recover what is yours. Now, I pray you to do the same in recovering what has been taken from us; and you must attend to this with all the greater diligence and care, for this aids souls and the Holy Place, whereas defending your own city would serve only the land. 

I believe you have heard how the **Turks**, with all their might, are persecuting Christians and seizing the lands of the **Holy Church**; because of this, the **Holy Father** is disposed and prepared to initiate a holy **passage** against them. And I believe, by the goodness of God, that you and the others will dispose yourselves to help and comfort him in this matter in whatever way you can. I pray and compel you, on behalf of **Christ Crucified**, to be diligent and not negligent in this, so that this may be an instrument for you to receive and dwell in the fullness of **Divine Grace** and the fire of the **Holy Spirit**, with which my soul longs to see you filled. 

Know, Dearest Mother, that I have written concerning this same matter to the **Queen of Naples** <note>Joanna I, Queen of Naples (1326–1382). Catherine frequently corresponded with her, attempting to secure her loyalty to the Pope and her support for the Crusade.</note> and to many other lords, and they have all responded well and graciously, offering to give aid with their possessions or with...

( A ) *The Queen of Hungary, Mother of the King, to whom this Letter is written (found in the manuscript of the Convent of San Domenico and now appearing in print for the first time), can be no other than Elizabeth of Poland, daughter of Ladislaus, King of Poland, widow of Charles Robert—called for the sake of brevity "Caroberto," King of Hungary—and mother to King Louis, the first of that name. The proof of this is quite easy to provide, because this Prince reigned from the year 1343 until the year 1382. Since he began his reign before the birth of Saint Catherine and passed away two years after the death of this Virgin, it follows that she could not have written to any other Queen Mother of the King of Hungary except Queen Elizabeth, whose death occurred in the year 1380, which was also the final year of the life of this Seraphic Virgin. During the short time she lived after the birth of the <term>schism</term> <note>original: "scisima." The Great Western Schism began in 1378, when rival popes were elected, dividing Western Christendom.</note>, she showed herself most passionate in favor of Urban VI. To him she sent a gift of a very rich <term>Tiara</term> <note>original: "Triregno." Literally "triple-crown," the papal tiara signifying the Pope's spiritual and temporal authority.</note> adorned entirely with gems, to replace the one that had been carried away by the <term>Archbishop of Arles</term>, the <term>Camerlengo</term> <note>original: "Camarlengo." The high official who manages the Pope's temporal property and the interregnum between popes.</note> of the Holy Church, who had gone with it to the French Cardinals; unless, of course, this gift was from Queen Elizabeth her daughter-in-law, as Maimbourg seems to believe.*

## Letter 312.

->**In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary.**<-

<margin>2 1.</margin> **T**o you, my most Reverend and Dearest Mother in Christ Jesus: I, Catherine, servant and slave of the Servants of Jesus Christ, write to you and comfort you in the precious Blood of the Son of God, with the desire to see you as a true and perfect Daughter of God. You well know that a Servant will never want to offend in the presence of the Lord, because they fear the punishment that follows the fault committed; therefore, out of this fear, they strive to serve Him well and diligently. Likewise, I say that he who is a true Son chooses death rather than offending the Father—not for fear of punishment, nor for dread of Him, but only out of reverence for Him and for the love he has for the Father, he does not offend Him. This is the Son who shall receive the inheritance, for he has not renounced the Father’s **Will** <note>original: "Testamento," referring both to a legal will and the spiritual legacy of Christ</note>, but has observed and followed His footsteps. Thus I pray you, Venerable Mother in Christ Jesus, that you do likewise...

you, and like the true Servant, whom you know always stands before this Lord, and whose eye sees in secret and is always upon us; oh, the supreme eternal Truth sees well who he is who serves Him, or who fails Him. Therefore, the Soul <note>original: "Anima"</note> must fear to offend its Creator, because He is that true Lord who punishes every sin and rewards every good; and no one, neither by Lordship, nor by wealth, nor by nobility, can act or avoid serving this sweet Lord Jesus. Oh, how sweet and holy is this sweet servitude, which places a bridle and order on the Soul, and does not let it wander through the perverse servitude of sin, but rather flees all those things that could lead it into sin. All things that it sees are outside the will of the Lord, it hates, because it knows that if it loved them, it would fall under His judgment. Then, once the Soul has risen with fear, recognizing itself as a servant and knowing that it cannot hide from His eye, it begins to uproot the affection and the disordered love of the World, and orders and conforms them to the will of its Lord, because otherwise it could not please Him. <margin>Matt. 6.</margin> For, as Christ said: no one can serve two Masters <note>A reference to Matthew 6:24, "No man can serve two masters," illustrating that one cannot serve both God and worldly desires.</note>, because if he serves one, he is opposed to the other. So, since our Soul is drawn by fear, it runs with perfect diligence and drives away every sin and defect from itself. Rightly, this love acts like the Servant in the House who is appointed to wash the unclean vessels <note>In Catherine’s imagery, the "unclean vessels" represent the human heart or conscience filled with the "filth" of sin, which must be purified before higher love can enter.</note>. 

But once the Soul has come to be a Daughter—that is, to be and remain in perfect Charity <term>Carità (Charity): In this context, the highest form of Christian love, which is selfless and directed toward God</term>—she acts like the true Child, who loves their Father eternally. This child does not love with a mercenary love <note>original: "amore mercenario," meaning a love motivated by the hope of a reward or "pay," like a hired worker rather than a family member</note>—that is, for the profit they might draw from the Father—nor do they fear to offend Him out of a fear of punishment, but only because of the goodness of the Father and the substance of the nature that the Father has given them with love. Thus, nature gives them strength, and love constrains them to love and serve Him. Therefore, I say that such a person can be called a true Child. 

And so I say that our love toward the heavenly Father is this: that you do not love for the sake of any utility you might draw from Him, nor for fear of the punishment He might make you endure, but solely because He is supreme, and just, and eternally good through His infinite goodness, and worthy of being loved. Nothing else is worthy of being loved outside of God; but rather, we should love and serve all things in Him and through Him.

### [ B ] To you, Most Reverend and Dearest Mother

If one takes this title of *Most Reverend* <note>original: "Reverendissima"</note> correctly and in its true meaning, it will not seem strange that it is given to a Queen by the Saint, as it is also given in Letter *207* to the Marquis del Monte; for nothing else is intended to be expressed by it except being most worthy of reverence. This is why it was once given as a title specifically to Ecclesiastical persons because of their dignity—they being more worthy of reverence than others—as can easily be seen from the letters of the ancient Fathers, and in particular from those of *Saint Bernard*. Nor was it restricted to men alone, as *Abbesses* and *Nuns* were also honored with it by the Emperor *Justinian*, and by the ancient acts of *Saint Cuthbert*, which are brought forward as evidence by *Raynaldus*. It then came to be used as a title for people who were not of the Church by the masters of the *Tuscan tongue* <note>original: "Toscana favella"; referring to the prestigious literary language of Dante and Boccaccio</note>, provided they were of great merit or high lineage; thus *Dante* gave it to women of great affairs and to *Queens*, as did *Boccaccio*; and the eldest of the three *Villanis* <note>The Villani were a famous family of Florentine chroniclers</note> gave it to the Crown of *France*, calling it *Most Reverend*. But with the passing of the years, as the most solemn persons in the Laity moved toward other titles of higher pomp, that of *Most Reverend* remained only within the Clergy, used for its primary figures, whether Regular <note>belonging to a religious order</note> or Secular <note>parish priests and bishops</note>. The addition of *Mother* is likewise a sign of reverence and respect.

The title of *Venerable*—

# Letter 313.

->In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of Mary sweet.<-

I. **L**audable and Dearest Mother, Lady the Queen, your unworthy Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, writes to you in His precious Blood with the desire to see you as a true Daughter and a Spouse consecrated to our sweet God. You are called "Daughter" by the sweet primal Truth, because we are created by and have come forth from God. Thus He said: <margin>Genesis 1</margin> *Let us make Man in our Image and likeness.* <note>Genesis 1:26</note> The rational creature was made a Spouse when God took on Human Nature. ( B ) **That just as you are titled Queen of Jerusalem.** The first of the Kings of Naples to take the title of King of Jerusalem was the Emperor Frederick II of the House of Swabia <note>Also known as the House of Hohenstaufen, a powerful noble family that ruled the Holy Roman Empire and Sicily.</note>, who was at once King of Naples and of Sicily, by reason of having married Yolande <note>The text uses "Violante," the Italian form of Yolande of Brienne, also known as Isabella II of Jerusalem.</note>, the daughter and heir of John of Brienne, King of Jerusalem. By virtue of this marriage, as well as the promise given to the Pope and the vow made to God, he was meant to go and conquer that Kingdom; of which the King, his father-in-law, possessed nothing more than the mere name, the land having already fallen some years prior into the power of the Barbarians <note>A common historical term used here to refer to the Muslim forces (Saracens) who held the Holy Land.</note>.

<margin>Maimbourg, in the place cited.</margin>
But he gave little thought to this worthy undertaking; because of this, he and the Pope came into great discord, and he was even excommunicated by him. If in the end—to have his peace with the Pope and the Church and to be absolved—he went to the Holy Land, such a passage was of no advantage. For, satisfied with having entered the Holy City and having crowned himself there with his own hand, he quickly went away with the few troops he had brought with him, leaving that afflicted Christianity in abandonment. His son Conrad and his grandson Conradin continued to style themselves Kings of Jerusalem, as they were descendants of Queen Yolande.

<margin>See Maimbourg in the place cited.</margin>
With the unhappy Conradin <note>Conradin was the last legitimate male heir of the Hohenstaufen line; he was executed in Naples in 1268.</note>, the blood of that Princess was entirely extinguished. Therefore, the claims to that Kingdom were ignited in other Princes, even though it abounded much more in hardships than in riches; and at that time, some of them contended for the value of those claims, and their descendants, by styling themselves King of Jerusalem, still take pride in retaining them today. Two were they at that time—that is to say, in the thirteenth century—who entered into contention because of that Kingdom: namely, Hugh, King of Cyprus, and Mary, Princess of Antioch; and their claims were derived in this manner: Isabella, Queen of Jerusalem and daughter of King Amalric <note>The text uses "Amerigo," referring to Amalric of Jerusalem (reigned 1163–1174), the sixth Latin King of Jerusalem.</note> (who was the sixth of the French to reign in the Holy Land), from her first marriage to Henry, Count of Champagne in France, left the Princess Alice, who married Hugh Lusignan, the first of this name and King of Cyprus. From Alice and Hugh was born the Princess Isabella, married to Henry, Count of Poitiers, and mother of Hugh III, who was King of Cyprus after the death of King Hugh II, his cousin; and who claimed the Crown of Jerusalem when the lineage of the House of Swabia withered with the unhappy Conradin, against the claims of the Princess Mary.

This Lady <note>This refers to Maria of Antioch, who contested the throne of Jerusalem against Hugh III of Cyprus.</note> was the daughter of Bohemond IV, Prince of Antioch, and of Melisende, his second consort, who was herself the daughter of Queen Isabella of Jerusalem and Aimery, King of Cyprus, the last of her husbands. Therefore, King Hugh prevailed in this dispute by right of <term>descent</term> <note>Hugh was the grandson of the eldest daughter, which gave him seniority in lineage.</note>, as he was descended from the eldest daughter of that Queen, while the Princess [Maria] had the advantage over the King by being one degree closer in kinship <note>Maria was the granddaughter of Queen Isabella, whereas Hugh was a great-grandson, making her "closer" to the source of the claim in terms of generations.</note> to that Lady from whom both of them derived their rights to the Royal Crown.

King Hugh, however, immediately took up the Royal Insignia and was accepted as King of Jerusalem. The Princess, unable to support her claims in any other way, turned them all over in favor of Charles of France, Duke of Anjou and the first King of Naples, in the year 1272, with the approval of the Pope. From that time, he took the title of King of Jerusalem, and without any doubt, he would have added the possession of the land to the title, had the loss of Sicily <note>A reference to the "Sicilian Vespers" in 1282, a successful rebellion against Charles of Anjou's rule that stripped him of the island of Sicily.</note> not so severely shortened his reach and diverted his forces elsewhere. All of his descendants held the title of King of Jerusalem, placing it before that of King of Naples, and it passed as a heritage even to those who were his successors, whether in the dominion or in the pretensions over the Kingdoms of Naples and Sicily.

For this reason, the Catholic King <note>A title usually referring to the King of Spain, who at the time of this writing ruled Naples and Sicily.</note> keeps the title of King of Jerusalem added to his many other titles, displaying the Coat of Arms of that Kingdom alongside the many others with which the Royal Shield is adorned. On this same foundation, the Princes of the House of Lorraine raise the same banner, as they descend from the Kings of Naples of the second branch of the Dukes of Anjou through Yolande <note>original: "Violante"</note>, the only daughter of René, King of Naples.

On the other hand, the Royal House of Savoy keeps the same Arms of Jerusalem in its shield by reason of the claims to the Scepter of that Kingdom by King Hugh of Lusignan <note>Hugh III of Cyprus and Jerusalem.</note>; from whom the House gathered the rights to the Kingdom of Cyprus, ceded to them by Queen Charlotte when James of Lusignan, her illegitimate brother, took the paternal crown from her head. They also preserve in their bloodline the rights of Anna Lusignan, daughter of King Janus <note>original: "Giano"</note> and wife of Louis, Duke of Savoy, from whom all the Princes of this House descend. 

Now, since Queen Joanna was descended from King Charles, from whom she was four degrees removed, and since she enjoyed the Kingdom and the rights pertaining to it, she is urged by the Saint <note>Catherine of Siena</note> to the Enterprise of Jerusalem <note>The Crusades</note>, so that, as she says, it may be possessed by Christians with honor, and by you, as something belonging to you. ->( A )<-

The title of <term>Madama</term> <note>Literally "My Lady."</note>, which is the same as "my Dame" or "my Lady," came to Italy from nearby Provence, like not a few other Tuscan words. I would take the word "Dame" to be the same as <term>Donna</term> <note>The Italian word for "woman," derived from the Latin "Domina" (Lady).</note> or "Lady"; hence the Tuscan authors, just as they once addressed the most holy Virgin as "Our Lady" <note>original: "nostra Donna"</note> by excellence, so too they called her "Our Dame" <note>original: "nostra Dama"</note>. Just as the title of "Madonna"—that is to say, "My Lady"—was given by them only to ladies of respectable birth, so also that of "Madama" was held in high esteem and reserved for the titles of Queens or Empresses. Now even this title has lost its luster; and if it is not quite as sullied as that of "Madonna"—which remains only for women of low affairs—it has nonetheless fallen in value, as every lady is now honored with it in one language or another. In the time of Saint Catherine, it maintained its ancient place of honor; thus, she does not use it for others except for this Queen, and in this letter alone, since (as was noted elsewhere) the Saint did not pay much mind to these titles, varying them almost every hour. In that century, the style of giving titles was not well-fixed, not even in the courts of Great Princes or Lords, nor toward supreme Monarchs. To prove this, let it suffice to bring here a few examples of the titles given by various Cardinals to King Philip the Fair of France.

<margin>Baluze, Vol. 2, Collection of Ancient Acts.</margin>

To the most Serene Prince, his most dear Lord, Lord Philip, by the grace of God, the most Illustrious King of the Franks. Peter, by Divine mercy, etc. <note>original Latin: "Serenissimo Principi Domino suo carissimo, Domino Philippo, Dei gratia, Illustrissimo Francorum Regi. Petrus miseratione Divina &c."</note> To the most Excellent Lord Philip, by the grace of God, illustrious King of the Franks. Arnaldus &c."</note> To the most Serene Prince and Magnificent Lord Philip, etc. <note>original Latin: "Serenissimo Principi, & Magnifico Domino Philippo &c."</note> To the most Excellent Prince, Lord Philip, by the grace of God, illustrious King of the Franks, most dear friend, etc. <note>original Latin: "Excellentissimo Principi Domino Philippo, Dei gratia, Regi Francorum illustri, amico carissimo &c."</note> For this reason, one should not marvel if in this epistle this Joanna is called: "Most beloved, most Reverend Mother, Sister in Christ Jesus, My Lady the Queen," while in another she is called

[ C ] **The Holy Father will proclaim it against the Turks.** *Many times Pope Gregory XI resolved in his mind to proclaim a Crusade against the Turks, provoking the Christian Princes to the enterprise with effective invitations. All the celebrated movements made to the detriment of the Infidels of the East, which were called "Crusades" because those who prepared to go placed a red Cross on their left shoulder, were proclaimed by the Sovereign Pontiffs. The first, which also resulted in the greatest advantage, was proclaimed in Clermont, France, by Urban II in the year 1095; the second in 1144 by Eugenius III; the third in 1188 by Clement III; the fourth in 1195 by Celestine III; the fifth by Innocent III in 1198; the sixth by Honorius III in 1216; and the seventh and last to take effect was published by Innocent IV in the year 1245, during the First Council of Lyon.*

The Queen did not fail to provide aid in the form of people to the Pontiff, as is gathered from what is found in Letter 284.*

# To the Queen of Naples

I. Exhorts [her] to deprive herself of self-love to acquire the Light necessary to know the truth.
II. That many lovers of themselves poison others as well with self-love.
III. Detests the wickedness of those Prelates who, having elected Urban VI as Supreme Pontiff, then refused to recognize him as such, convincing them with various reasons. <note>This refers to the beginning of the Great Western Schism in 1378, when a group of cardinals declared Urban VI's election invalid and elected an antipope.</note>
IV. Exhorts the aforementioned Queen not to adhere to their blindness, but to render obedience to the true Pontiff, Urban VI.
V. Of the efficacy of Prayer made by the Servants of God.

## Letter 315.

->In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of Sweet Mary.<-

I. **D**earest Mother in Christ, sweet Jesus: I, Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious Blood with the desire to see you with true and most perfect light, so that in all your actions you may receive light. This light is a life of grace, because all actions performed with the light of the fear of God give life; but without this light, all are performed in death. We walk through darkness in such ignorance and blindness that we discern truth as a lie, and a lie as truth, light as darkness, and darkness as light. From this it proceeds that the soul’s taste is sickened, so that suddenly good things appear evil to it, and evil things appear good. The knowledge of oneself is lost, so that one does not know one's own evil. This happens to the soul through the deprivation of light. Alas, alas, dearest Mother, all this proceeds from the cloud of <term>self-love</term> <note>original: "Amor proprio"; in Catherine’s writings, this is the root of all sin, an obsessive focus on one’s own will over God's.</note>, which obscures the eye of our intellect so that it does not let us discern the truth. It makes us weak and fickle, so that we turn like a leaf in the wind. It is a poison that infects the soul, and it does not infect or poison oneself without [poisoning] others, because

But if you distance yourself and join the opinion of those who hold the contrary falsely against their own conscience, you would cast forth the fruit of death from a disobedience that generates death.

( C ) **Oh men who are not men, but rather visible demons.** Perhaps some of the French Cardinals were staying with Queen Joanna, the great protector of the newly elected <note>The "newly elected" refers to the Antipope Clement VII, whose election sparked the Great Western Schism.</note>; therefore, the Saint turns her speech to them, full of zeal, and with the strongest reasons makes them see that the election of Urban was legitimate in every respect. The arguments she uses to provide very valid proof of this have been used by authors who wrote later in favor of this Pontiff, and by the Saint herself in her other letters for the same purpose, particularly in Letters 31 and 187, where they have also been discussed at length in the annotations made to them.

( D ) **For the Dignity of the Hat.** The ornaments of their dignity were received by the <term>Cardinals</term> <note>The high-ranking clergy who elect the Pope and serve as his primary advisors.</note> at different times and from several Pontiffs. The most noble of their sacred garments can be said to be the **red hat**, since while others are taken up without a great display of ceremonies, the Pontiff himself gives this one, and the new Cardinal goes to receive it with a solemn retinue; hence it is added as an ornament to the coat of arms and is hung at the tomb as a mournful remembrance. Therefore, while the Saint remains silent about the other ornaments that were also used by the Cardinals in her time, she mentions only the hat. This was granted to them in the year 1245 at the First Council of Lyon by Pope Innocent IV as a fitting ornament of the dignity they held. He wished that in it they would look closely at the duty they had to the Church to shed even their blood, if necessary, in its defense—particularly at that time when the Emperor Frederick II outraged and oppressed the Church with such perfidy. A few years earlier, in 1241, having captured some of them who were traveling to the Council, the Emperor did not hesitate to put several of them to death with a cruelty never before heard of in a Christian prince; because of which Pope Gregory IX had also died of grief.

<margin>Rainaldi, Annals, year 1343 and following</margin>
( E ) **Faithful servant as you have been since ancient times of the Holy Church.** As was noted elsewhere, Queen Joanna always remained in obedience to the Church, and from the Supreme Pontiffs she received great help in the calamities that befell her, through which she was able to regain the Kingdom taken from her by the King of Hungary.

# To the Queen of Naples.

In two main ways it is necessary for us to know this Truth. Let us suppose that it is necessary to know it in everything—that is, that everything which has being in itself should be loved in God and for God, who is Truth itself, and without him nothing, for otherwise it would move away from Truth and walk toward the lie, following the Devil, who is its Father; I was saying that in two ways particularly it is necessary for us to know it. 

The first is that we know the truth of God, who loves us inestimably, and loved us before we were—even creating us out of love. The second and final way is that we must know and see the truth in our Neighbor, whether great or small, whether subjects or Lords—that is, when we see them perform any action to which they might invite us, we must see and know if it is founded in Truth or not, and what foundation that person has made who is moved to perform this action. [you have] stood by the lie, and the Devil, who is its Father, having abandoned the counsel of the **Holy Spirit**, and taken the counsel of **incarnate Demons**; from a member bound to the **True Vine** <note>A reference to John 15:1-5, where Jesus describes himself as the vine and his followers as branches; Catherine argues the Queen has severed her spiritual connection to Christ.</note>, you have cut yourself off from that vine with the knife of self-love; from a legitimate Daughter tenderly loved by the Father, the **Vicar of Christ on Earth, Pope Urban VI**, who is truly the **Pope and Supreme Pontiff**, you have departed from the breast of your Mother, the **Holy Church**, where for so long you were nourished. It does not appear that you have known the truth of God in the manner described; for if you had known it, you would have chosen death before offending God mortally. Nor have you known it in your Neighbor, but with great ignorance, moved by your own passion, you have followed the most miserable and shameful counsel, putting into operation the worst thing you could ever have done.

And what greater shame can be received than that of one who was a Christian, held to be a Catholic and virtuous Woman, and then acts like the Christian who renounces the Faith, abandons good and holy customs, and the due reverence she once practiced? Alas, open the eye of your **Intellect** <note>In medieval philosophy, the "intellect" was the faculty used to perceive spiritual truth.</note> and sleep no more in such misery; do not wait for the moment of death, after which it will not help you to make excuses, nor to say: "I believed I was doing well." For you know that you are doing evil, but like a sick and passionate woman, you let yourself be guided by passion. I believe well that this counsel came from others rather than from yourself. 

Desire, desire to know the truth: who those men are, and why they make you recognize a lie as truth—saying that **Pope Urban VI** is not the true Pope, and making you see the **Antipope**, who is truly an **Antichrist** and a member of the Devil, as if he were Christ on Earth. And with what truth can they tell you this? With none at all; they speak with lies and falsehood, lying upon their own heads. What can these wicked Men say—not Men, but incarnate Demons? From whichever side they turn, they cannot see that they have done anything but evil. Even if it were true (which it is not) that **Pope Urban VI** were not the Pope, for this alone they would deserve a thousand deaths as liars caught in falsehood. For if in the beginning they had elected him out of fear, and not in truth— <note>This refers to the claim by the dissenting Cardinals that they elected Urban VI only because they were intimidated by the Roman mob, a claim Catherine vehemently rejected.</note>

Do not wait for this rod, for it will be hard for you to kick back against **Divine Justice**. You must die, and you do not know when.

...manly heart <note>original: "cuore virile." You cannot escape the hands of God; whether by **justice** or by **mercy**, you are in His hands. Correct your life so that you may escape the hands of Justice and remain in Mercy; do not wait for the time when you might wish to do so but will no longer be able. 

O little sheep, return to your sheepfold! Let yourself be governed by the **Shepherd**, otherwise the **infernal Wolf** <note>The Devil.</note> will devour you. Take back the guidance of the servants of God, who love you in truth more than you love yourself. Take back good, mature, and discreet counselors. You will weep yet, saying, "Alas, alas!" if you do not change your ways; regarding that fear placed in me by wicked counselors, I am the one who has deprived myself of it. But there is still time to make amends, Dearest Mother, before the judgment of God. Return to **obedience**...

( C ) **And from a Lady you have become a Servant.** Among the Tuscan authors of the "Good Century" <note>The *buon secolo* refers to the 1300s, considered the golden age of the Tuscan Italian language.</note>, the word **Donna** <note>original: "Donna"</note> is continually used to mean **Mistress** or **Lady** <term>Domina: the Latin root of 'Donna,' implying a woman of high rank or authority</term>, and it is in this sense that the Saint employs it here, as she does in other letters.

<margin>Reasoning of the English Clergy in Bzovius, Rainaldi, and Baluze.</margin>

<margin>Baluze in Notes on the Lives of the Avignon Popes; Maimbourg, page 52.</margin>
( E ) **The wicked life without any fear of God of these, etc.** The Saint laments not only in this letter, but in almost every one she wrote to Gregory XI, that most of the Cardinals of that time did not lead the life of a churchman, nor even of a Christian who cares for his own salvation. The strongest argument of those who have sided with the cause of Clement is drawn from the protests of the Cardinals, whose integrity they insist should not even be under suspicion. However, this had no effect on the Saint; on the contrary, from the manner of their unregulated living, she forms an argument to the opposite, showing that they are not worthy of being believed by others.

<margin>Platina, Cracow, Anonymous Life of Clement VII in Baluze; Maimbourg, History of the Great Schism, book 1, page 87 and following.</margin>
( F ) **Where is the just Man, whom they have elected as Antipope?** The Antipope Clement VII was formerly called Robert, and was the son of Amadeus III, Count of Geneva. He was the last of his illustrious lineage, the ancient line of those Counts failing with him, after which that noble county passed to Humbert of Villars, who was his sister’s nephew. He was admitted to the College of Cardinals in the year 1371 by Gregory XI, by whom he was sent to Italy in 1376 with the title of Legate. On the occasion of the rebellion of the cities of the Papal States against the Pontiff, he led numerous bands of English and Breton soldiers. The Clergy of England, in giving the reason for their adherence to Urban and the motives that moved the minds of those people, speak thus of Clement: 

<margin>16th Reason of the English Clergy in Bzovius, Rainaldi, and Baluze, Column 1085.</margin>

The other was the more-than-barbaric cruelty used by his men against the Castle of Monte Giorgio, twelve miles from Bologna; having surprised it, they killed everyone there from the age of six upward, and they did the same toward the City of Cesena. The people of Cesena had suffered most grave outrages from the Legate’s troops, and suffered more every day; nor were their just complaints heard in a way that offered any remedy for their ills or placed any restraint on that immoderate license. Finally, with their patience overcome by the weight of the injuries, those miserable people took up arms and with them took cruel vengeance for the outrages committed against them, killing over eight hundred of those soldiers. Fearing no pardon for their fault, they were planning to rebel and ally themselves with other peoples defiant of the Church, unless they were granted a pardon by the Legate, remitting all punishment and giving full security by means of an oath. *Maimbourg depicts him for us in the guise of a Prince, which he was by birth, not as he was reputed to be by election; nor does he refrain from accusing him of being ambitious and a squanderer of Church goods, which he employed in worldly pomp.*

> Besides, he says, wanting to live in all the splendor and magnificence of a great Prince, and to provide his Cardinals with the means to maintain their Court and their worldly pomp proportioned to his own, he was reduced to the unfortunate and cruel necessity of oppressing the Gallican Church <note>The Catholic Church in France, which maintained a degree of autonomy from Rome.</note> by insupportable exactions, etc.

*But he reveals the vices of Robert more precisely when he mentions his election as a false Pontiff.*

<margin>Book 1, page 88</margin>
> Having the inclinations and manners of a great Prince, but with a bit too much excess; living in a brilliance and magnificence that went much further than what the state of a Prince of the Church demands; and subsequently never having enough to provide for his excessive expenses and the profusions he made—giving everything away more like a prodigal than a liberal Prince, etc.—greatly loving his relatives and allies, whom he took great care to elevate; little applied to business and unscruplous, etc.

*Another French author, speaking of his death,* <margin>Briet, at the year 1394.</margin> *gives him a title truly worthy of such a Pontiff, calling him* **a man more concerned with money than with religion.** <note>original Latin: "Vir pecuniæ quam Religionis sollicitior." Reference to the Jesuit historian Philippe Briet.</note> *If he was such a man, then, when they elected him Antipope, it is no wonder if the Saint <note>Saint Catherine of Siena (1347–1380), who strongly supported the legitimacy of Urban VI against the Avignon claimants.</note> spoke of him with contempt—he having made himself worthy of it precisely through those vices that she so hated and abominated in ecclesiastics. <margin>Rinaldi, for the year 1380, no. 2.</margin>

But it is certain that they reasoned poorly, not seeing that it is possible for a Saint, acting in good faith, to be mistaken like other men—especially regarding facts where, in the confusion of disputes, it is difficult to untangle the true from the false; and that the gift of Prophecy and discernment, with which God sometimes honors His Servants, is not a fixed and steady habit to make them always infallibly discover what is certain, but only a passing light that illuminates them on certain occasions and leaves them on others, to leave them with that [light] which they may have through natural means. *What is said here by this Author proves well that no strong argument in Clement’s favor can be drawn from the holiness and miracles of the Blessed Peter; but it does not weaken the proof of Urban’s legitimate Pontificate gathered from the holiness of this Virgin <note>Catherine of Siena</note>. Because, as was said elsewhere, it is one thing to be a follower of a party embraced by many nations, having in its favor many reasons seemingly clothed in truth, and to stay in it in good faith; it is quite another to make oneself its head and supporter, to fight the opposite side with all one's power, openly labeling it as false, and bringing forth the clearest revelations from Heaven as proof. Of the first kind...*

Blessed Peter conducted himself as was stated above; the Holy woman <note>Saint Catherine of Siena</note> did the same for the second cause. Therefore, the sentiment of this Author—which, as is easy to believe, is intended indirectly to strip the efficacy of this Holy Virgin of all Authority and value in favor of the Cause of Urban <note>Pope Urban VI (reigned 1378–1389), whose election triggered the Great Western Schism</note>—does not weaken it in the slightest. For if it is beyond doubt that God could permit some to be deceived in adhering to one of the two Parties (not being bound to discover the truth to others, nor even to great Saints), it must also be held as certain that sometimes in similar cases He has revealed it to someone. Indeed, no one can deny that He revealed it to Saint Catherine, except for those who have either not read her *Legend* <note>The *Legenda Maior*, a biography written by her confessor, Raymond of Capua, which recounts her mystical visions</note> or think little of calling that Holy Man a liar, who so wisely compiled it, as was noted in the Annotations to Letter 187. <margin>Book I. page 125.</margin>

Inasmuch as they rightfully use the Authority of Legal Authors, since the Saint—a full three years before the <term>Schism|A split within the Catholic Church from 1378 to 1417, where multiple men claimed to be the true Pope</term>—foretold to Blessed Raymond <note>Raymond of Capua (c. 1330–1399), a leading Dominican who was Catherine's spiritual director</note> that this was going to happen through the fault of the Cardinals, who did not wish to reform their manner of living as the Pontiff required of them; they take this as an argument to show that he was the legitimate Pope. And if everything she did or wrote in favor of that Party are not "effects of her holiness" as he writes, they are still so in some manner despite him; because she labored so much with voice and pen, not for any political end—as he even had the audacity to write—but because of the revelation she received that Urban was the true Pope, and having such a revelation is itself a sign of eminent Holiness. But this author makes no mention of the Saint's revelation, either to avoid bringing prejudice to his own party by citing it, or to avoid bringing it upon himself by attacking it.

# To Queen Joan of Naples.

I. **S**he persuades her that we cannot be defeated by our enemies unless we choose to be, for it is we who provide them with the weapons to conquer us.
II. She reproaches her for her obstinacy in persecuting the Holy Church, threatening her with the punishments of God and of the Supreme Pontiff Urban VI <note>Urban VI was the Pope whose election sparked the Great Western Schism; Catherine was one of his most vocal supporters</note>, and finally exhorting her to amend her ways and have pity on her own soul.

## Letter 317.

->Written in a state of spiritual ecstasy.<- <note>Italian: "In Astrazione fatta." This indicates the letter was dictated while Catherine was in a mystical trance.</note>

### In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified and of sweet Mary.

1. **D**earest Mother in sweet Jesus Christ: I, Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious Blood with the desire to see you show compassion to yourself, both in Soul and in Body; for if we are not merciful to our own soul, the mercy and pity of others will benefit us little. The Soul commits a great cruelty against itself when it places the knife into the hand of its enemy, with which that enemy may kill it; for our Enemies have no weapons with which they can harm us; they may wish to do so, but they cannot, because the Will alone is what offends. Neither a Demon nor any other Creature has the power to move the Will or force it into the slightest fault more than it is willing to go. Therefore, the perverse Will, which consents to the malice of our Enemies, is the knife that kills the Soul when it is handed over to those Enemies by the hand of <term>free will</term> <note>Latin: "liberum arbitrium." The theological concept that humans have the power to choose between good and evil without being forced by external necessity.</note>. Who shall we say is more cruel: the Enemies, or the person who receives the blow? We are more cruel to ourselves, because we consent to our own death. We have three principal Enemies, namely the Devil, who is weak unless I make him strong by consenting to his malice; he loses his strength through the virtue of the...

Catherine uses the metaphor of the "knife of the will" to urge the Queen to take responsibility for her spiritual state and her opposition to the Church.</summary>

### [ G ]
**And this, I do not say, is denigrated.** <note>original: "dinigrato"</note> The word *denigrated* is not found used by other authors, and from what can be gathered from what follows, it means the same as *at a whim*, or *without foresight*. The author of the French translation has said *at random* <note>original: "a la volée"</note>, that is to say, *inconsiderately*. <margin>To the Year 137<note>likely an abbreviation for 1379 or 1380 based on the context of the Schism</note></margin> Farri, and Rinaldi—who reports a large part of this Letter in his Annals—have kept the same word *dinigrated*. Perhaps it should be read as *Digrato*, which would mean the same as if one said voluntarily, or of one’s own <margin>Book 9, p. 208.</margin> whim. Such a word is used by Matteo Villani <note>Matteo Villani (c. 1283–1363), an Italian chronicler</note> who says: "The King of France, to show his magnificence beyond the terms of the Peace, of his own will <term>digrato<gloss>meaning voluntarily or as a free gift</gloss></term> gave La Rochelle to the King of England."

### [ G ]
**And from the other Lords, who will assist me.** The Queen’s hopes were based on the aid of France, and particularly on that which she could expect from Louis, Duke of Anjou, brother to the French King, which, however, failed her in her time of need. For since King Charles V died the following year, and his brother the Duke having taken over the government of the <margin>Maimbourg, History of the Great Schism, book 2, p. 170.</margin> Kingdom during the minority of his nephew <note>Charles VI of France</note>, affairs became so disordered that it was not possible for that Prince to be ready to offer the required help to the Queen. Thus, she fell into the power of the Victor <note>Charles of Durazzo</note>, losing her Kingdom, her Liberty, and then her Life as well, at the very time when he had set out on the march to give her aid.

### [ I ]
**That from such a side he will send him help, that we cannot imagine it.** The help for Urban <note>Pope Urban VI</note> was brought by Charles of Durazzo with the army of Louis, King of Hungary, from whom it did not seem one could reasonably hope for aid, as that Prince was involved in a bitter war against the Republic of Venice, which at that hour was at its highest heat. The Saint <note>Catherine of Siena</note> wrote to both Princes on this matter; and the Letters were perhaps carried by Martino da Taranto, a confidant of the Pontiff, who was directed by him to that King to ask him for help.

### [ L ]
**Stay in the middle for so long, until it is declared to you.** In this manner the Kingdoms of Castile <margin>Maimbourg, book 3, page 186.</margin> and Aragon remained for some time without siding with either of the two Popes. The same course was proposed to the French King by many of his Council, and in the end it was also embraced by that Kingdom, seeing the obsti-

### Letter 318.

## In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary.

**D**earest and Reverend Mother, you will be dear to me when I see you being a daughter, subject and obedient to Holy Church. Reverend to me insofar as I shall render you the due reverence; for you will make yourself worthy of it when you abandon the darkness of heresy and follow the light. I, Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious Blood with the desire to see in you a true knowledge of yourself and of the true Creator. This knowledge is necessary for our salvation, because every virtue comes out of this holy knowledge. <note>Self-knowledge is the cornerstone of Catherine's spirituality; she often describes the "cell of self-knowledge" as the place where the soul discovers its own nothingness and God's infinite goodness.</note> Where is true humility found? In the knowledge of ourselves; for the soul that knows it is nothing of itself, but knows its very being comes from God, cannot lift its head against its Creator through pride, nor against its neighbor; for that which of itself is nothing cannot become proud. Where does the soul weigh its fault? In the knowledge of itself, with a holy consideration—that is, thinking who she is who offends God, and who God is, who is offended by her. And she sees herself to be fertile mud <note>original: "loto fecondo," a common medieval metaphor for the physical body and human frailty.</note>, her humanity made from the dust of the earth. And truly she is a sack full of stench, for from every part she casts out filth, subject to many miseries and needs, and subject to death, and waits for...

O human blindness! To what greater misery can we come than to be brute animals? And if someone were to say to us: "You are a brute animal," we could not bear it; indeed, we would strive to take revenge on whoever had said it. And nonetheless, so great is our fragility that we make ourselves brute animals; yet we do not take revenge upon our sensory appetite and our own self-love, which are the very things that make us brute animals.

And all this happens to us because we do not know ourselves. Therefore, we do not weigh the gravity of our faults. Why do we not weigh them? Because we do not know what follows after the fault, nor what the fault makes us become. For by knowing it with that true consideration mentioned before, we would lift ourselves up from every vice and from disordered living, and we would embrace Virtue. Whereupon we would then render honor to God, we would preserve the beauty and the Dignity of our soul, and we would follow the Doctrine and the truth; and by following it, we would become children of that truth.

O sweetest Mother, I desire to see you founded in this truth, which you will follow by staying in the true knowledge of yourself—and not otherwise. And this is why I told you that I desired to see you know yourself. I invite you to know this truth so that you may be able to love it. This is the truth: that God created you to give you eternal life; and if you look upon the humble Lamb <note>Refers to Jesus Christ as the "Lamb of God."</note>, in His Blood He has manifested to you that this is the truth. I called while you had the time; once that time has passed, you will have no further remedy. ( A ) <margin>Refers to "Deh" (Alas/O), page 64.</margin> *O Dearest Mother. This note of compassion or of sorrow, used here as "Do" <note>original: "Do," a variant of "Deh," an archaic Italian exclamation of pleading or grief</note>, is found used by Passavanti <note>Jacopo Passavanti (c. 1302–1357), a Dominican friar and author known for his elegant Tuscan prose</note> and by other most refined writers of that century.*

[ B ] <margin>Historical context of Joanna's reign.</margin> *Which you have ruled for so long, with such diligence, and with such peace. She succeeded her grandfather, **King Robert**, in the year 1343; thus, the year 1379 was the thirty-sixth year of her reign. She faced war twice brought against her by **King Louis of Hungary**, and from then on she had no other grave turbulence; thus the Saint could truly and justly say that she had held the government with such peace until that hour.*

[ C ] <margin>Textual sources for this letter.</margin> *Alas, how does your heart not burst, etc. From these words until these others—"and do you not see"—the text has been supplemented by the work of two handwritten manuscripts from **San Domenico** and **Buonconti**, as this entire section of the letter was missing from the editions printed by **Aldo** and **Farri** <note>Reference to the famous Aldine press of Venice and the printer Farri, who produced early editions of Catherine’s letters</note>.*

( D ) <margin>The symbolism of the Roses.</margin> *And let one hold the **White Rose**, and the other the **Red**. If the Queen, along with most of her subjects, held to the side of **Clement** <note>Clement VII, the Antipope in Avignon</note>, others among them—and especially the city of **Naples**—were in spirit with **Urban**; whence, as usually happens from differing sentiments, discords arose with the shedding of blood. The Saint here mentions the **White Rose** and the **Red Rose** as if these were divided, so that the two parties who held either to Urban or to Clement might be distinguished from one another, some having the White Rose as their insignia and the others the Red <note>original: "vermiglia"</note> Rose. Of these recent factions of the two roses arising on this occasion in the **Kingdom of Naples**, no memory is found in any other author; but that they truly existed cannot be disputed, unless one doubts the authority of the Saint, who was speaking of an event that was actually occurring at that very hour.*

*...one must confess, however, that these names of factions soon appeared in Italy, for if they had enjoyed a long life, some mention of them would be found in the histories of those times—just as, unfortunately, one finds in those most dismal records of the **Guelfs** and **Ghibellines**, or the **Whites** and the **Blacks** <note>These were rival political factions in medieval Italy; the Guelfs and Ghibellines famously split over support for the Pope versus the Holy Roman Emperor</note>. In England, not many years later, there arose a most calamitous division between the two Royal Houses of **York** and **Lancaster**, concerning the rights that each claimed to have to that Crown. The followers of one party took the heraldic device <note>original: "l' Assisa," referring to a livery or badge</note> of the **White Rose**, and the others that of the **Red Rose**; thus, from these two roses, the two passionate factions came to be named. With such strange events that, in the short space of about thirty years, they brought death to four Kings and more than eighty Lords of the Royal House; and in thirty battles that were fought, several hundreds of thousands of people perished there. It would not be a great stretch to suggest that these names of opposing factions passed from Italy into England, since in those years there were very many Englishmen who fought in these parts under the banner of **John Hawkwood** <note>original: "Gio. The House of York was favored by those of the White Rose, and the House of Lancaster by those of the Red Rose; and perhaps in the Kingdom of Naples, the partisans of **Clement** <note>Antipope Clement VII</note> wore the white rose, as this color was the emblem of the House of France which supported him, and those who followed **Urban** <note>Pope Urban VI</note> took the red, which was perhaps held by Urban as a device, seeing as six red roses are visible on the shield of **Cardinal Francesco Prignani**, his nephew.*

<margin>A</margin>
# To My Lady, the Wife of Bernabò Visconti.
<note>Beatrice Regina della Scala (1331–1384) was the wife of Bernabò Visconti, the ruler of Milan. Catherine often wrote to influential women to reach their husbands, who were frequently in conflict with the Papacy.</note>

I. She urges her to clothe herself in the Garment of Charity to set an example for her husband.
II. Demonstrating how this Charity is acquired: namely, through knowledge of oneself and of the Divine Goodness.
III. That it is necessary for us to love Jesus Christ in no other way than by following His example through suffering and dishonor.
IV. That when possessing States and riches, we must not love them inordinately, nor outside of God.
V. Concerning the union with God, which we acquire by means of the Love of Jesus Christ.
VI. She prays her to be willing to lead her husband back to the Love of Jesus Christ and to obedience to the Supreme Pontiff.

## Letter 319.

->In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of Sweet Mary.<-

<margin>B</margin> I. **R**everend Mother in Christ Jesus: I, Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious Blood with a desire to see you clothed in the garment of most ardent Charity; so that you may be the means and the instrument to reconcile your husband with sweet Jesus Christ, and with His Vicar, "Christ on Earth" <note>original: "Cristo in Terra." This was Catherine's favorite title for the Pope, emphasizing his role as the earthly representative of Jesus.</note>. I am certain that if the virtue of Charity lives within you, it will be impossible for your husband not to feel its heat. For thus the First Truth <note>original: "prima Verità." A common Catherinian name for God.</note> wills: that you two be one in spirit, in affection, and in holy desire. This you could not do if this love were not within you.

II. But you will say to me: "Since I do not have this love, and without love I cannot do this, what way can I take to have it?" I tell you that love is not acquired except through love; for he who wishes to be loved must first love—that is, he must have the will to love. After he has had this...

<meta>This page continues Letter 319 to Beatrice della Scala, picking up from the previous page's discussion on the necessity of Charity. Catherine is explaining that to influence her husband, Bernabò Visconti, Beatrice must first ground herself in self-knowledge and divine love.</meta>

<page-num>585</page-num>

[...impossible for you not to want his salvation. To fulfill] this will, it is necessary for her to open the eye of <term>knowledge</term> <note>original: "cognoscimento." For Catherine, this is "spiritual self-awareness"—the practice of looking into the "cell of the soul" to see one's own nothingness and God's greatness.</note>, and see where this love is found, and how it is found. She finds it in herself. How? By knowing that she herself is nothing, seeing that she does not exist by her own power, she gives credit and acknowledges that she has her being from God, and every grace that is founded upon this being—that is, the spiritual and temporal graces and gifts that God gives us; for if we did not exist, we could receive no grace. Thus, everything she has, she finds that she has through the inestimable Goodness and Charity of God. When the Soul has found and seen in herself such great Goodness from her Creator, she rises up and grows in such love and desire that she despises and holds in contempt herself and the World with all its **delights**. And I do not wonder at it, because it is the nature of love that when the Creature sees itself loved, it immediately loves in return. Since she loves, she chooses death rather than to offend the one she loves. She nourishes herself in the fire of love because she has seen herself loved so much, when she sees that she herself was that Field and that stone where the **Banner** <note>original: "Gonfalone." A military standard or flag. Catherine depicts the soul as the very ground in which the Cross was planted.</note> of the Most Holy Cross was fixed; for you know well that neither the Earth nor the stone would have held the Cross, nor would nails nor the Cross have held the Word of the Only-Begotten Son of God, if love had not held Him. Therefore, the love that God had for our Soul was that stone and those **nails** that held Him.

<margin>Isaiah 53</margin>
III. Now this is the way to find love; since we have found the place where love dwells, in what way must we love? O reverend and sweetest Mother, He is the rule and the way, and there is no other way but this one. His way, which He teaches us and which we must follow if we wish to walk in the light and receive the life of grace, is: to go through pains, through **reproaches**, scorns, **torments**, and insults, and persecutions; and with these pains to conform oneself with Christ Crucified. He was that immaculate Lamb who despised the riches and Lordships of the World, **even though** <note>original: "conciosiacosache."</note> He was God and Man; nevertheless, as our rule and way, He teaches it to us, having become an observer of the Law and not a transgressor. He is humble and meek, so that His cry is not heard through any **complaining**. He has opened Himself up; through the breadth of love He becomes a taster and an eater of our salvation, not seeking nor seeing Himself, but only the honor of the [Father]...

<meta>This page continues Letter 319 to Beatrice della Scala. In the preceding text, Catherine urged Beatrice to ground herself in self-knowledge to find the fire of divine love. She now transition from the soul's inner state to the imitation of Christ’s poverty and suffering.</meta>

<page-num>585</page-num>

[...the will of the] Father and the good of His <term>Creatures</term> <note>original: "Creature." Catherine uses this term to refer to all human beings as created by God.</note>; He does not shy away from pains, but rather pursues those very pains. It is a great thing to see the sweet and good Jesus, who governs and feeds the whole World, yet is Himself in such misery and necessity that there is no one like Him. He is a beggar to such an extent that Mary did not have decent cloth in which to wrap her Son. In the end, He dies naked on the Cross to reclothe Man and cover his nakedness. [Man] had been made naked because of the sin committed, having lost the garment of <term>Grace</term>, so He strips Himself of life and clothes us with it. I say that the Soul that has found love in the affection of Christ Crucified will be ashamed to follow Him by any other way than by Christ Crucified; she will not want **delights**, nor Status, nor pomp, but will rather want to stay like a pilgrim or traveler in this life, who only waits to reach her destination; neither for prosperity found on the way, nor adversity—if he is a good pilgrim—does he slow his pace, but rather goes manfully through the love and affection he has placed in his goal, which he expects to reach.

<margin>D</margin>
IV. This is how I want you to act, sweetest Mother and Sister in Christ sweet Jesus. I do not want you to look at the high status you have, nor at great riches and delights, nor at adversity or tribulation that you might see coming; let neither delight nor pain hold you back, but with a <term>manly heart</term> <note>original: "cuore virile." Catherine frequently uses this term for both men and women to describe spiritual fortitude and the courage to persist in virtue regardless of circumstances.</note> run along this path, always delighting in <term>Virtue</term> and in carrying pain for Christ Crucified, who so sweetly taught it to us. Take things of the World for the necessity of <term>Nature</term>, and not for disordered affection, which would be too displeasing to God—that you should place your love in something that is less than you, for that would do nothing but lose your dignity; for the <term>Creature</term> becomes whatever thing it loves. If I love sin, sin is nothing; thus, I become <term>nothing</term> <note>original: "non covelle." A Sienese dialect term meaning "nothing at all." Catherine teaches that since God is Being itself, sin (which is the absence of God) has no true existence; therefore, the soul that loves sin loses its own spiritual "being."</note>; one cannot come to a greater vileness. Sin proceeds from nothing other than loving what God hates, and hating what God loves; therefore, by loving the transitory things of the World and oneself with a sensory love, one offends, because that is the thing God hates, and it displeased Him so much that He wanted to perform justice and vengeance upon His own body. He made an **anvil** <note>original: "ancudine." A powerful image of Christ's body receiving the hammer-blows of human sin to forge the "tool" of our salvation.</note> of Himself, forging our iniquities upon it. Now, what great misery and blindness is that of the <term>Creature</term> to see itself created...

...to His <term>Image and likeness</term> <note>original: "Immagine, e similitudine." A reference to Genesis 1:26, where humanity is created in the divine image.</note>, and also reformed in <term>Grace</term>, after he lost it through <term>mortal sin</term> <note>A serious sin that, in Catholic theology, "kills" the life of grace in the soul.</note>, with the abundance of His Blood He reformed this image. And yet the soul is so blind that she abandons the affection and the Love that made her great through His goodness, and gives herself to loving those things that are outside of God—that is, by drawing her affection and love away from Him, and loving created things and herself without Him. It is not that the high status, the delights of the World, nor the <term>Creatures</term> <note>Meaning all created beings or things.</note> are themselves blameworthy, but rather the affection that the person places in them, transgressing the sweet commandment of God for the sake of this [disordered] affection.

V. So, on the contrary, when love and affection lift themselves up from the self and place themselves entirely in Christ Crucified, the soul comes to the greatest dignity she can achieve, because she becomes one thing with her Creator. And what better could she have than to be united in Him, who is every good? She cannot attribute that dignity and union to herself, but to love; for a Servant-girl would be considered great if she were taken as a Bride by the Emperor, because as soon as she is united with him, she is made Empress—not through herself, for she was a Servant, but through the dignity of the Emperor. 

In this way, think, Dearest Mother in Christ sweet Jesus, that the Soul in love with God—who is a servant and a slave ransomed by the Blood of the Son of God—comes to such dignity that she cannot be called a servant, but an Empress, a Spouse of the eternal Emperor. This accords well with the word of the first Truth: <margin>Augustine, *Meditations*, chapter 32.</margin> to serve God is not to be a Servant, but to reign; it also removes the servitude of sin and makes one free. 

Truly, then, this perfect union is strong, which beyond the dignity of her creation, through the union of love and the Virtues, makes perfect this first dignity of being—that is, through the union she has made with her Creator. This soul has stripped off the <term>Old Man</term> <note>A Pauline concept (Ephesians 4:22-24) referring to the sinful human nature before spiritual renewal.</note> of her old self and clothed herself in the new Christ sweet Jesus. Then the Soul is fit to receive and hold Grace, with which in this life she tastes God, and finally in the end she sees His eternal vision, where she is pacified and has perfect rest and quiet, because her desires are fulfilled. This is the reason that in this life one cannot have peace, because one's desire is not satisfied until reaching the union of the Divine Essence; one has only hunger and desire while one is a traveler...

...you, and a pilgrim in this life; he has a desire to take the straight path and hungers to reach the goal and his end. Therefore, I want you to grow in holy and true desire to follow this way, which brings you to the goal. Know that it is not dark, nor gloomy, nor full of thorns; rather, it is bright with true light, and He paved this road with His Blood—Jesus Christ, who is that Light. There are no thorns here, for it is fragrant and full of flowers and sweet fruits, so much so that as soon as the <term>Creature</term> <note>In Catherine’s writing, "the creature" refers to any created being, specifically the human soul.</note> begins to take this sweet path, she tastes such sweetness that she would sooner choose death than to leave it. 

And although thorns may be seen on this path—appearing as the thorns of many <term>tribulations</term> <note>Historical term for trials, sufferings, or spiritual tests.</note> and the illusions of the Devil, and the World standing before us with swollen pride—I say that the soul who delights in this way does not care for them. Instead, she acts like one who goes to a rose garden, who picks the rose and leaves the thorn alone. Thus she leaves behind the tribulations and anxieties of the world and picks the fragrant rose of true and holy patience, placing before the eye of her knowledge the Blood of the Lamb, who gives life, stationed at the head of this Road. 

Therefore, run, Mother, and let us all faithful Christians run toward the object of this Blood, following its scent. Then we will truly become drunk on that Blood, burned and consumed in <term>Divine sweet Charity</term> <note>Charity here means "Caritas," the highest form of Christian love, which Catherine often describes as a fire.</note>, and we shall be made one thing with Him. We shall act like the drunkard, who thinks not of himself, but only of the wine he has drunk and that which remains to be drunk. 

Intoxicate yourself with the Blood for the sake of Christ Crucified; since you have it before you, do not let yourself die of thirst. Do not take just a little, but so much that you become intoxicated, so that you lose yourself. Do not love yourself for your own sake, but for God’s sake, nor love the Creature for the creature’s sake, but only for the praise and glory of God’s Name; nor love God for yourself, for your own benefit, but love God for God’s sake, insofar as He is the supreme Goodness, worthy of being loved.

**( A )** *The handwritten text, which is preserved in the famous <term>Certosa di Pavia</term> <note>The Charterhouse of Pavia, a magnificent monastery and complex in Lombardy.</note>, built with royal magnificence by <term>Giovanni Galeazzo Visconti</term> <note>The first Duke of Milan and nephew to the lady addressed in this letter.</note>, first Duke of Milan, and nephew to this Lady, was left to that Monastery—so it is said—by the <term>Blessed Stefano Maconi</term> <note>One of Catherine’s most devoted disciples and secretaries, who later became Prior of the Certosa.</note>, who served as Prior there, in place of this title.* **To Madame, wife of Bernabò Visconti**, *it bears this other, more grand title:* **To My Lady the Queen, Lady of the aforementioned Lord of Milan.** *What title the Saint herself placed on this Letter cannot be known. Nonetheless, I believe it is more credible that she used the first, rather than the second of these titles, since, as anyone can see, the Saint was not accustomed to making much of such things, keeping for the most part to a moderation and simplicity that would not allow for excessive or vain flattery. I believe, therefore, that such an addition of "Queen" was placed there by the person who transcribed the Letter, giving that Lady the title of Queen because it was the custom of every subject in those lands to address her by that exalted name of honor, accommodating themselves to her wishes. Her name was Beatrice, and she was the daughter of <term>Mastino III della Scala</term> <note>Known as Mastino the Great, the ruler of Verona.</note>, called the Great Lord of Verona and other cities; a woman of noble lineage, singular beauty, and extreme ambition. It is reported by some authors that although her husband held no title other than Lord of Milan, she nevertheless insisted on being called Queen. The epitaph placed upon her tomb, flattering her vanity even after death, also gives her this title, beginning as follows:*

->The splendor of Italy, Beatrice, Queen of the Ligurians. <note>original Latin: "Italiæ splendor, Ligurum Regina Beatrix."</note><-

<margin>Corio, History of Milan, part 3.</margin>
*Bernabò, her consort, in informing his subjects of her death, likewise calls her Queen:* **Our consort, the Lady Queen of the Scala family.** <note>original Latin: "Consors nostra Domina Regina Scaligera."</note> *And the Milanese historians also give her this name, but at the same time, they depict her as a bold, proud woman, insatiable for wealth, impious, and one who steered the state and her husband’s will according to her own desires. It seems believable, both from the husband’s letter and the writing on the tomb, that she held both names—that is, Beatrice and Queen—and that since she preferred the second, as it gave greater fuel to her ambition, many took to giving it to her as a title of honor; hence, they called her simply "The Queen," without any further addition, rather than "Queen and Lady of Milan."*

### Letter 320.

->In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary.<-

I. **D**earest Daughter in Christ sweet Jesus: I, Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious Blood with the desire to see you clothed in the garment of Divine Charity—true and perfect love—in such a way that every other love departs from your heart and affection. For the soul cannot be clothed in two loves at once; if she is clothed in the World, she cannot be clothed in God, because they are very contrary to one another. The love and affection placed in the world loves itself with sensory love <note>original: "amore sensitivo," referring to love driven by physical feelings and worldly desires rather than spiritual intellect.</note>, always seeking honor, status, and riches, delights, pleasures, and sensory consolations, which delights lead the soul to eternal death. For he who loves the world and its delights inordinately is always rooted in pride, and from pride all vices are born. Oh, to what misery is that heart reduced which is completely drowned in the perverse solicitudes of the world! It acquires death and loses the life of Grace; it enters into darkness and loses the light; it falls into the perverse servitude of sin, and thus becomes a servant,

# To Lady Niera, wife of Gherardo Gambacorti, in Pisa.

I. On the faith we must have in God alone, and of the fruits of that faith; and on the trust that Men place in <term>Creatures</term> <note>In Catherine’s spiritual language, "creatures" refers to any created person or thing—money, family, or status—as opposed to the Creator.</note>, exhorting her to place said faith in God.

## Letter 321.

->**In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary.**<-

I. **D**earest Daughter in sweet Christ Jesus: I, Catherine, servant and slave of the Servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious Blood with the desire to see you a faithful servant and Daughter of the Eternal Father. You know that Love is the thing that makes us faithful; in the thing that a person loves, he has faith. Thus we see that the true Servants of God, because of the love they have for their Creator, lose all faith and hope in themselves, so that they do not hope in their own virtue, nor in their own wisdom, for they know and see that they are <term>nothing</term> <note>original: "non essere." This reflects Catherine's famous vision where God told her, "I am He who is, and you are she who is not."</note>; they attribute their being to God, possessing it by grace and not by right. As soon as one loves with faith, one has a living hope—not in oneself, but in Him who is. These people have a living faith, not a dead one, accompanied by sweet and holy works. What are the works that demonstrate a living faith founded on true Love? Patience against injury or pain in whatever way God allows it to come to us; Divine Charity against the selfish sensory love of oneself; and humility against the swollen pride that Man acquires through status, luxuries, honors, and the delights of the World. This humility will despise the World with all its pomps; but no one can have it unless they recognize their own defects and see God humbled for them. As the Sou- <margin>ni-</margin>

...soul regards the supreme **Highness** descended into such lowliness as is our humanity; then, human pride is ashamed, seeing God so greatly humbled. Now, these are the fruits brought forth by **Faith**, when it is living and placed in its Creator alone. Such people enjoy and savor God in truth; they feel no pain from any suffering or torment they may endure, because they firmly believe that God seeks, wills, and permits nothing except for our sanctification. And all of this proceeds from **Love**; for if Love were not there, they would have no faith.

Thus you see that, on the contrary, those who have placed their affection and their concern upon the **World**, find that all their faith and hope rests in themselves and in the World. Therefore, they live in continual pain and bitterness, because they place their love in something that is neither firm nor stable, and so they find themselves deceived. What stability is there in a Father, or a Mother, or honors, or riches, or **Power**? None at all, for everything passes like the wind: today alive, and tomorrow dead; just now healthy, and just now sick; just now rich, and just now poor. One moment a person delights in their children, and the next moment they are gone. Thus one suffers by placing love and disordered desire there, because these things are not enough, and one cannot hold onto what one loves.

And therefore, my sweetest **Daughter**, I desire that you have no affection, nor faith, nor hope in yourself, nor in any corruptible thing. Instead, I desire that you take all your delight in serving **Christ sweet Jesus**, in whom all delight and consolation rest. There, the **Soul** is inebriated by the Blood of the **Immaculate Lamb**; it burns and dissolves in the fire of most ardent **Charity**, and receives such strength that neither the Devil nor any <term>Creature</term> <note>Catherine uses this term to refer to any created being or worldly thing, emphasizing their temporary nature compared to the Creator.</note> can take this good away. Therefore, hide yourselves in the wounds of **Christ Crucified**; place your affection, your faith, and your hope in Christ Crucified. With this sweet and true Lamb, you will pass through this dark life and reach the lasting life, where the true and sweet tasters are fed. I wish to say no more.

**II.** Regarding what you sent to me, speaking of settling your <term>Boy</term> <note>original: "Garzone." While it can mean a servant or apprentice, Catherine is here referring to Niera’s son, for whom a marriage is being arranged.</note> in marriage, I reply to you: look not to wealth, nor to great family connections, but only to the **Virtue** and the good character of the **Girl**. When you find this, proceed securely; and whatever you do, do it with the fear of God, always keeping Him as the object before the eyes of your Soul.
