# To Lady Tora, Daughter of Master Pietro Gambacorti of Pisa.
<note>Pietro Gambacorti was the ruler of Pisa and a significant political ally and friend of Catherine.</note>

She exhorts her to be a true servant and bride of Jesus Christ, renouncing entirely the <term>sensory love</term> <note>Love directed toward physical things or people rather than spiritual truths.</note> of creatures, and loving Him with all her heart; since her husband has died, she advises her to enter <term>Religion</term> <note>In this context, 'entering religion' specifically means joining a monastic order or becoming a nun.</note> to better serve God; exhorting her to prayer, frequent attendance of the Holy Sacraments, the reading of Holy Books, and other exercises of piety.

## Letter 322.

### In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of Mary sweet.

Dearest Daughter in Christ sweet Jesus: I Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious Blood with the desire to see you as a true servant and bride of Christ Crucified, so, and in such a way, that for His love the world becomes tedious to you with all its delights, because they have in them no firmness nor any stability; and you see well, my daughter, that this is the truth. The world showed itself to you with great beauty and pleasure, and now it has shown that all its joys and pleasures are vain and fleeting, and they germinate sadness with great bitterness for the soul that possesses them in a <term>disordered way</term> <note>A theological term meaning love that is out of its proper priority, placing the creation above the Creator.</note>, and they take away the life of Grace, and give death, and the soul falls into extreme misery and poverty.

...ity. It is right, then, to flee it, and to hate one's own <term>sensuality</term> <note>The sensory appetite or physical desires that conflict with the spirit.</note>, and every worldly delight, and to despise them with all our heart and all our affection, and to serve only our most sweet Creator. To serve Him is not to be a slave, but rather it makes one reign; for it makes us all Lords in the life that endures, and in this life, the soul becomes free, because it is loosed from the bond of mortal sin, from the love of the world, and from its own sensuality. **Reason** is made the Mistress, and by ruling over [sensuality], she is Mistress of all the world; for she mocks the world, and there is no one who can fully possess it, except the one who perfectly despises it. And would that soul not be quite foolish and mad, who could be free and a Bride, yet makes herself a servant and a slave, selling herself back to the Devil as an adulteress? Certainly so; and this is what the soul does, which, having been liberated from the servitude of the Devil and bought back by the Blood of
<margin>1 Peter 1</margin>
Christ Crucified—not with gold, nor with silver, but with Blood <note>A reference to 1 Peter 1:18-19: "knowing that you were not redeemed with corruptible things, like silver or gold... but with the precious blood of Christ."</note>—holds itself as something vile. She does not recognize her own dignity, and she despises and debases the Blood with which she was bought with such a fire of love. God having made her the Bride of the Word, His Son, which sweet Jesus wedded to Himself with His own flesh; for when He was Circumcised, as much flesh was removed in the Circumcision as is the edge of a ring, as a sign that, as a Groom, He wished to wed the Human Race. And if she loves anything outside of Him—whether Father, or Mother, or Sister, or Brothers, or kinsmen, or riches, or worldly Status—she becomes an adulteress and not a loyal Bride, nor faithful to her Groom; because the true Bride loves nothing but her Groom—that is, nothing that would be against His will. And so must the true Bride of Christ do: that is, love Him alone with all her heart, with all her soul, and with all her strength, and hate what He holds in hatred, which is vice and sin. He hated it so much and it so displeased Him, that He willed to punish it upon His own Body for our salvation. She must love what He loves: namely, the Virtues, which are proven in **Charity for one's Neighbor**, serving him with brotherly charity in his necessities, according to what is possible for us. And therefore I want you to be a faithful servant, and I do not want you to be without a Groom. From what I have understood, it seems that God has called your husband to Himself; if he disposed himself well...

Clothe yourself not in mourning—that is, the blackness of self-love and the pleasures of the world—but in the whiteness of purity, preserving your mind and your body in the state of <term>continence</term> <note>Specifically, the practice of refraining from sexual relations, often used here to describe the life of a widow dedicated to God.</note>. Over this purity, place the crimson mantle of the **Charity** of God and of your neighbor, fastened with perfect humility and adorned with the trimming of true and real virtues, through humble and continuous prayer. Without this means, you would not be able to attain any virtue. 

See that you wash the face of your soul often through **Confession** and with contrition of heart, which will be a fragrant ointment making you pleasing to your Spouse, blessed Christ. Thus adorned, go to the Table of the Altar to receive the **Living Bread** <note>The Eucharist.</note> that gives life—the food of Angels. That is the proper time for it, as it is during Easter and the feasts of sweet Mary, and as God disposes you for other such solemn feasts. 

Delight in staying continually at the table of the Most Holy Cross, and there hide and lock yourself in His chamber—that is, in the side of Christ Crucified. There you will find the bath of Blood which He has prepared for you to wash the leprosy of your soul; and there you will find the secret of His heart, showing you through the opening of His side that He has loved you and loves you inestimably. 

Reflect that this sweet **Spouse** is very jealous; He cannot bear to see His spouse depart from Him even a little without becoming indignant and withdrawing His grace and sweetness from the soul. I desire, therefore, that you flee the conversation of worldlings and worldly matters as much as you can, so that you do not fall into anything that would cause your Spouse to depart from you. Therefore, be a dweller of the **Cell** <note>In Catherine’s teaching, this refers to both a physical room and the "cell of self-knowledge" within the mind.</note>, and take care that you do not waste your time, because much more will be required of you now than before. Always employ your time either with prayer, or with <term>reading</term> <note>Latin: "lettione"; the practice of spiritual reading or Lectio Divina.</note>, or with some manual labor, so that you do not fall into idleness, for that would be a dangerous thing. By resisting manfully and without any fear, you will ward off the blows with the Shield of Most Holy Faith, trusting in your Spouse Christ, who will fight for you. 

I know that you will enter now—or perhaps you have already entered, more accurately—into the field of the many battles of the **Devil**, who throws many...

She was shut in a room with a strict prohibition against anyone else—except for a certain Stefano, a domestic servant of her father—even seeing her, much less speaking to her. She remained as a prisoner for five months, during which only once was she permitted to hear Mass. Passing through **Pisa** in those days was **Alfonso**, formerly **Bishop of Jaén** <note>Alfonso Pecha de Vadaterra (c. 1330–1389) was a Spanish bishop who resigned his see to become a hermit and later became a close friend and advisor to Saint Catherine of Siena.</note> and later a hermit, who was mentioned elsewhere and who was well known to **Pietro** <note>Pietro Gambacorti, the ruler of Pisa and Tora’s father.</note>, as they had been together in the Holy City of **Jerusalem**, where both had made a pilgrimage at the same time. He was asked by Pietro to speak to his daughter and try to dissuade her from such a noble purpose <note>original Italian: "generoso Consiglio," referring to her vow of poverty and religious life.</note>.

**Alfonso** met with **Tora**, and having admired the firmness of her spirit in the path she had already chosen, instead of moving her from it, he encouraged her even more. Subsequently, by the force of his zeal, he even induced her father to consent to his daughter’s will. Having obtained the longed-for permission, she returned to her former monastery <note>The monastery of San Martino.</note>, with the power to leave it to move to another of the **Order of Saint Dominic**, which was to be built by **Pietro**. After four years of staying in that of **San Martino**, she went in the year 1382 to the new monastery of **Santa Croce** of the Order of Saint Dominic. She was then twenty years old, and was joined by four companions who wished to clothe themselves in the habit of the **Dominican** sisters along with her.

She lived in this monastery for thirty-seven years with the highest praise for her consummate virtue, as can be seen in her *Life* <note>original: "Leggenda," a term for a hagiographical biography.</note> written by **Serafino Razzi**, by the continuators of **Bollandus** <note>The Bollandists, an association of scholars who compiled the *Acta Sanctorum*, a massive encyclopedic work on the lives of saints.</note>, and by others. These authors, not having paid attention to these **Letters of Saint Catherine**, make no mention of her, although, as is clearly seen, Catherine played such a great part in directing **Tora’s** soul toward the path of perfection. Her death occurred on the seventeenth day of April in the year 1420, which was the fifty-eighth year of her life. God demonstrated her holiness through miracles, and the people honored her with the title of **Blessed**.

# To Lady Tora, Daughter of Master Pietro Gambacorti in Pisa.

I. She exhorts her to strip herself of the love of the world and of creatures, and to love Jesus Christ alone, demonstrating the instability of worldly goods and the firmness of the true good, God.
II. Concerning prayer and its effects, exhorting the said Tora to practice it.

### Letter 323.

->In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified and of sweet Mary.<-

<margin>Matthew 6</margin>
I. Dearest daughter in sweet Christ Jesus: I, Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious Blood with the desire to see your heart and your affection stripped of the world and of yourself; for in no other way could you clothe yourself in Christ Crucified, because the world has no conformity with God. Therefore, disordered affection for the world loves pride, while God loves humility; the world seeks honors, status <note>The term "Stato" here refers to social standing or political power in the Pisan Republic.</note>, and greatness, but blessed Christ despised them, embracing shame, mockery, insults, hunger, thirst, cold, and heat, even to the shameful death of the Cross. By this death, He gave honor to the Father, and we were restored to grace. This disordered affection seeks to please creatures, not caring about displeasing the Creator; yet He never sought anything but to fulfill the obedience of the eternal Father for our salvation. He embraced and clothed Himself in voluntary poverty <term>povertà volontaria: the religious practice of giving up all personal possessions to rely entirely on God</term>, while the world seeks great riches. Truly, then, the one is different from the other, and therefore it is necessary that if the heart is stripped of the world, it be filled with God, and if it is stripped of God, it be filled with the world. Thus said our Savior: no one can serve two masters, for if he serves one, he holds the other in contempt <note>original: "contempto"</note>. We must, therefore, with great solicitude <note>sollecitudine: a focused, diligent care or concern</note> lift our heart and affection from

[the heart from] this tyrant of the world, and place it entirely free and pure in God; and without any mediator, not double-hearted, nor loving falsely, because He is our sweet God, who keeps His eye upon us and sees the hidden secret of our heart. Our simplicity and foolishness is too great; for seeing that God sees us, and that He is a just Judge who punishes every fault and rewards every good, we are as if blinded and without any fear, waiting for that time which we do not have, nor are we sure of having. We are always attaching ourselves, and if God cuts off one branch, we grab another; and we care more about losing these transitory things and creatures than we care about losing God.

All this happens to us because of the disordered love we have placed in them, holding and possessing them outside the will of God. Whence in this life we taste the <term>down payment</term><note>The original term "arra" refers to earnest money or a pledge given to guarantee a contract. Catherine uses it to mean a "foretaste" or "advance installment" of the suffering of Hell.</note> of Hell; for God has justly permitted that whoever loves these things in a disordered way becomes unbearable to themselves, and always has war in soul and body. For one suffers for what they possess, out of fear of losing it; and to preserve it so it does not fail, one toils day and night. One also suffers for what they do not have, because they crave to have it; and thus the soul is never quieted in these worldly things, because they are all less than the soul itself.

They were made for us, and not we for them; and we are made for God, so that we may taste His supreme and eternal good. Only God, then, can <term>satisfy</term><note>original: "fatiare", meaning to sate or fill to the point of complete satisfaction.</note> the soul; in Him it is pacified, and in Him it rests, because it cannot will or desire any thing that it does not find in God. He knows, is able, and wants to give to us more than we know how to desire for our salvation; and we experience this; for not only does He give when we ask, but He gave to us before we even existed. Without us ever praying to Him, He created us in His image and likeness, and recreated us in grace through the Blood of His Son.

So, then, the soul finds its peace in Him and not in another; for He is the one who is supreme wealth, supreme <term>wisdom</term><note>original: "sapientia"</note>, supreme goodness, and supreme beauty—so much so that no one can estimate His goodness, greatness, and delight except Himself alone. Thus He knows, is able, and wants to satisfy and fulfill the holy desires of whoever wants to strip themselves of the world and clothe themselves in...

Therefore, I want us to apply all our effort to this: namely, to strip our heart and our affection of all earthly things and of creatures, loving every person in God and for God, and nothing outside of Him. <note>In Catherine’s theology, "creatures" refers to anything created (people, objects, or animals). To love them "outside of God" means to love them for one's own selfish pleasure rather than as gifts from the Creator.</note>

II. To this I invite you, sweetest daughter: namely, to place and to fix your heart and your mind on Christ Crucified. Seek Him and think of Him, delighting in being always before God with humble and continuous <term>prayer</term><note>original: "oratione". For Catherine, this is not just reciting set prayers but an internal state of constant communion with God.</note>, which I give to you as your principal exercise, so that you spend all your time in it as much as you can. For this prayer is that Mother who conceives true virtues in the <term>charity</term><note>original: "carità", meaning the selfless, divine love of God.</note> of God and gives birth to them in charity for one’s neighbor. In this prayer, the <term>soul</term><note>original: "anima"</note> learns to strip itself of itself and clothe itself in Christ. In it, you will taste the fragrance of <term>continence</term><note>original: "continentia", meaning self-restraint and spiritual purity.</note>; in it, you will acquire a strength such that you will not care about the battles of the Devil, nor the rebellion of the fragile flesh, nor the words of any creature who might wish to remove you from your holy <term>purpose</term><note>original: "proponimento", referring to a religious resolution or vow.</note>. Against everything you will stand strong, constant, and persevering even unto death. In this prayer, you will fall in love with suffering so as to conform yourself to Christ Crucified. In it, you will find a supernatural light with which you will walk the path of <term>Truth</term><note>original: "verità".</note>. I would have many other things to say to you about this Mother of Prayer, but the brevity of time does not allow it. Study yourself, therefore, in it, and always strive to know yourself and your defects, and the great goodness of God in you, and the affection of His charity, and His infinite blessings. I say no more. Remain in the holy and sweet delight of God. Sweet Jesus. Jesus Love. <note>original: "Gesù dolce. Gesù Amore." A signature closing for Catherine's letters.</note>

# To Lady Jacoma, wife of Master Trinci of Foligno.

I. **O**n the virtue of patience, exhorting her to it, and showing it to be necessary to strip oneself of one's own will, which hinders it.
II. On the conflict that exists between God and the World, and between the servants of both.
III. On the disordered love for creatures, and how we ought to love them. <note>As noted previously, "creatures" refers to any created being or thing, including family members and friends.</note>
IV. On the steadfastness of God, and of love toward Him.
V. She exhorts her to serve God, comforting her in the loss of her husband who died for the Church. <note>Jacoma's husband, Giovanni di Messer Trinci, was a supporter of the Papacy and was killed in 1377.</note>
VI. On the ease and method of practicing patience, namely through the memory of the Blood of Jesus Christ.
VII. Other motives that she brings forward for this virtue.
VIII. She prays her to guard against hatred of one's neighbor, showing its harms.

## Letter 324.

-> In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary. <-

I. **D**earest Sister in Christ sweet Jesus: I, Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious Blood with the desire to see you established in true and perfect <term>patience</term><note>original: "patientia". For Catherine, patience is not just waiting, but a courageous endurance born of love for God.</note>. Considering myself, I see that the Soul cannot please God, nor remain in His grace without the virtue of patience; for once a soul has become impatient, it is deprived of God through grace. This is because impatience proceeds from <term>self-love</term><note>original: "amor proprio". This is a central theme in Catherine’s writing: the "cloud" of selfish interest that obscures the light of God.</note>, clothed in one's own sensory will; and self-love and one's own sensuality are not in God. Therefore, you see that the Soul that is impatient is deprived of God.

We see it clearly, for today we are rich and tomorrow poor, today Lords and tomorrow vassals, today alive and tomorrow dead; so we see, then, that he is not firm. This is what it seems that glorious Paul meant when he said: <note>Catherine is likely paraphrasing St. Paul’s warnings on the transience of the world (e.g., 1 Corinthians 7:31).</note> "Take care of those who presume to trust in themselves and in the world, for when you believe you are doing well, you fail," and such is the truth. How long is our time? The Saints say that it is like the point of a needle, which has no height or length to speak of. Such is the life of our body, for it suddenly fails when it pleases Divine Goodness to draw us from this life.

VI. Their unwillingness only adds hardship upon hardship through their own will, in which all pain resides; for a hardship is only as great as the will makes it.

### VII

Every tribulation, with true knowledge of our own defects—that we deserve every hardship—and of the goodness of God within us, where we find such mercy; for by our faults we would deserve infinite punishment, yet He punishes us with these finite pains. And simultaneously, sin is paid for, and we merit eternal life through His grace, which...

O sweet patience, full of gladness and joy! For when it proceeds from Charity—that is, bearing every tribulation for God's sake, whether through death, or life, or in whatever way God grants it—I say that under this yoke of patience, acquired through the sweet mildness of God's will, every bitterness becomes sweet, and every heavy burden becomes light. The Soul clothes itself in this holy and sweet garment when it dresses itself in the will of God, who desires nothing other than our sanctification. Whatever He gives or permits to happen to us, He gives for our own good, so that we may be sanctified in Him. 

Therefore, do not let it seem difficult to you, Dearest Mother and Sister in Christ Jesus, for the **Physician of eternal life** <note>A common medieval title for Jesus, portraying Him as a doctor who heals the soul through spiritual "medicine."</note> came into the world to heal our infirmities. And truly He acts as a true Physician, giving us bitter Medicine and drawing blood from us to preserve our health; and you know that a person will endure any thing, even the pains of Hell, out of respect for their own health. 

Alas! Why do we behave worse toward the heavenly Physician than toward an earthly one? For He does not desire the death of the sinner, but wants him to be converted and live. Thus, sweetest Mother, the sweet God gives bitterness to our sensuality, but not to our reason; and He draws blood when He draws [our loved ones] to Himself, depriving us of our children, or our health, or our prosperity, or whatever else it may be. 

Be comforted then, since He has not done this to bring you death, but rather to give you life and to preserve your health. Therefore, I pray you by the love of that sweetest and most abundant Blood, which was shed for our Redemption, that the will of God may be fulfilled in you, and that all these bitter things may turn to your sanctification. Just as the will of God intends, you should truly clothe yourself in the virtue of patience, as has been said.

II. And I do not want you to think of your Son who remains with you as your own property; for he is not yours—otherwise we would be thieves—but use him as a thing lent to you for your needs.

You know well that it is so; for if it were yours, we could keep it and use it according to our own will. III. The first is the brevity of time; the second is the will of God, who has drawn them to Himself, as you sent word to tell me. The third thing is the harm that would follow from impatience. Comfort yourself, then, for the time is short, the labor is small, and the fruit is great. I say no more. The peace of God be with you. Remain in the holy and sweet love of God. Sweet Jesus, Jesus Love. # To Lady Pantafilea, Wife of Ranuccio da Farnese.

1. She desires to see in her the true Light, which is sought to know one’s own misery, and the Divine Goodness and Charity toward us; showing how from such knowledge one acquires true patience in adversity and hope in God.

## Letter 326.

->In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary.<-

I. **D**earest Sister in sweet Christ Jesus: I, Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious Blood, with the desire to see you with true light and knowledge of yourself and of God, so that you may know the wretched fragility of the World. For the soul that knows her own misery well knows that of the world; and whoever knows the Goodness of God within themselves—which they find in their very being, that is, knowing themselves to be a rational creature created in the image and likeness of God—immediately then, once the soul has come to this holy and true knowledge, she loves God in truth. And what she loves, she gives back to her Creator: every gift and every grace. She always accords herself with His will, and with whatever God does or permits for her, she is content; for she sees that God wills nothing other than her sanctification.

Therefore, since the death and the Blood of Christ manifest to us the inestimable love that God has for us, and that He wills nothing but our good, we ought to bear every toil with true patience,

He gives these things to us in measure, and if the labor increases, He gives greater strength so that we do not falter. It is therefore necessary for us to bear them and hold them in reverence for the sake of **Christ Crucified**, and because they are the cause and instrument of our salvation; for the hardship and tribulation of this life make us humble and quench our pride, and they make us lift away our disordered affection for the **World**, and direct our love toward **God**. They also make us conform to **Christ Crucified** and feel something of His pains and reproaches. Thus, they are of great necessity to us if we wish to enjoy the eternal vision of God; they make us feel and wake us from the sleep of negligence and ignorance, because in times of need we run to Christ, knowing that He alone can help us. In this way, we become grateful for the benefit received and that we are receiving, and we better know His **Goodness** and our own misery; for He is He who Is, and we are those who are not, and we have our very being from Him. <note>This is a central theme in Catherine’s theology, based on her vision where God told her: "I am He who is, and you are she who is not." It emphasizes that human existence is entirely dependent on God's sustaining power.</note> You see this clearly and manifested, for sometimes we desire life, and it is necessary for us to have death; we want health, and we are infirm; or we wish to hold onto our **Children**, and riches, and the delights of the **World** because they please us, and yet it is necessary to leave them. This is the truth: either they leave us by **Divine providence**, or we leave them by means of death as we depart from this dark life. So you see that we are nothing <note>original: "cavelle" — a Sienese dialect term meaning "anything" or "something," used here in the negative to mean "nothing at all."</note> of ourselves, except full of sins and much misery; this alone is ours, and every other thing belongs to God.

II. By doing this, you will not make a God of your children, nor of any other...

I pray you, for the love of **Christ Crucified** and for your own benefit, that you do this; thus you will fulfill in yourself the will of God and my desire. I say no more. Remain in the holy and sweet love of God.

## To Countess Giovanna of Mileto and of Terra Nuova in Naples.

I. She exhorts her to contempt for the world and its delights, demonstrating how harmful it is to love them.
II. That true wealth consists of true and real virtues.
III. Regarding Charity, which alone remains in the next life.
IV. Regarding the disordered love that people have for created things.
V. She exhorts her to the contempt of herself—that is, to humility—showing that the way to obtain it is the consideration of the humility and charity of Jesus Christ.
VI. How, once she has acquired the virtues, she should order her own actions and those of her family.

**II.** This is a lasting wealth that removes every poverty; it feeds us with grace, it covers our nakedness, it gives an account for us in the final extremity of death before the Supreme Judge; it pays the debt to which we are obligated—that is, to return to God the debt of love. This love is returned and demonstrated through virtue. It accompanies us in this life of pilgrimage, which is a road on which we have many enemies who stand before us to bring us death; but among others, three are the principal ones: namely, the **World**, the **Devil**, and the **fragile Flesh**. Each of these strives to shoot poisoned arrows: the World with its false delights and vain pleasures; the fragile Flesh and our sensuality with disordered love and vain, light pleasure; the Devil with many thoughts, by taking our things away from us, and by making our neighbor do us some other injury to deprive us of brotherly charity and make us feel hatred and displeasure toward our neighbor.

...is given light, and with that light He leads us to the gate of **Eternal Life**, which gate is unbolted by the **Blood of Christ**; inside enters **Charity**, which is the Mother of all the other virtues. The others remain outside, and she brings in the fruit of them all; for when the **virtuous soul** <note>A soul that has lived in accordance with God's will and practiced the virtues.</note> departs from this life, it enters **Eternal Life** with the virtue of **Charity**. The other virtues are not necessary in that enduring life, and therefore they are not carried there. There the virtue of **Faith** is not needed, because the soul is certain of that which it used to believe; and **Hope** is not needed there, because she has that which she hoped to have; and so it is with all the other virtues, which it is necessary for us to have in this life—for without them we would be deprived of God—but there only **Charity** is needed, that is, love, because **Eternal Life** is nothing other than love, with which we taste God in His essence. His love has made us worthy to see Him face to face, in which seeing lies our beatitude. Love makes us share in the good of one another, and the good of the entire **Angelic nature**, and of all those who are in **eternal life** through love. God makes us enjoy Himself; even more, in Him we all enjoy, full and satisfied in the peaceful Sea of His essence. And being satisfied they still have hunger <note>Catherine describes a mystical paradox: the souls in heaven are completely satisfied yet always "hungry" for more of God, but this hunger is joyful rather than painful.</note>, but the pain of hunger and the boredom of satiety are far away. There is so much love and fraternal charity among them that the small has no envy of the great, but all are content and rest in one another's good, so that only **Charity** is necessary there, and without it no one can go there.

To acquire vice, one leaves virtue; for death, one loses life; for the finite thing, one leaves the infinite; for the goods of the Earth, one leaves the goods of Heaven; for the **Creatures**, one leaves their Creator. To serve the Devil and follow him by the way of lies, one ceases to serve **Christ Crucified** and follow His doctrine—He who is the Way, the Truth, and the Life—and whoever goes through Him goes through the light and does not go through the darkness. ### V.

I do not want this to happen to you, but I want—and I have said that I desire it—that your heart and your affection be entirely stripped of this; that is, that you love and hold all creatures and created things for God’s sake, and without Him, consider them nothing. Love Him and serve Him with all your heart and all your strength, without any intermediary, with true and profound humility, loving your neighbor as yourself. 

But you will say to me: "How can I have this humility, when I feel full of self-love and inclined toward every act of pride?" 

I answer you that if you will it, through **Divine Grace** <note>The spiritual help given by God to help humans lead a virtuous life and attain salvation.</note>, you will soon cut these away from you; for this grace is given to anyone who wants it. The way is this: that with light <note>The "light" of faith or reason infused by God.</note> we look upon the humility of God and the fire of His **Charity** <note>Divine love, often described by Catherine as a fire that consumes the soul's imperfections.</note>. This humility is seen to be so deep that every human intellect falls short of it. 

Now, was there ever such a thing in a creature? Certainly not. Is there any greater thing than to see God humbled before Man? To see the supreme height descended to such lowliness? To see Him clothed in our humanity, God visibly conversing among men, carrying our infirmities, poverty, and miseries upon Himself, and humbling Himself even to the shameful death of the **Cross**? 

Greatness has made itself small to confound the bloated and proud who always seek to be greater; but they do not realize that they fall into the lowest depths and misery. Thus, in Him you will find the vein of humility, which has drawn near into the soul of every rational creature, if we look upon His **Charity**. 

And where was it ever seen that the one who has been offended should voluntarily pay with his life for the one who offends? Only in the humble, spotless **Lamb** <note>A title for Jesus Christ, referring to his sacrificial role in Christian theology.</note> do we find it; He paid that debt for us wicked debtors, which He Himself never contracted. We were, and are, the thieves, and He willed to be nailed to the wood of the most Holy **Cross**; He took the bitter medicine to give us health, and made for us a bath of His **Blood** <note>Catherine frequently uses the imagery of Christ's blood as a purifying "bath" for the soul's sins.</note>. Like one in love, He opened His Body for us, so that from every...

...part, He pours out Blood with such generosity and fire of love, and with such patience that His cry was not heard through any grumbling <note>original: "mormoratione." ### VI.

So we have found the way by which we come to virtue: that is, through the knowledge of the goodness of God, and through the light with which we see His humility and charity. In Him we shall acquire it, seeking it within our own soul; elsewhere, or in any other way, we shall never find it. This is the foundation, the principle, the middle, and the end of every virtue and of our perfection. From this you will come to a contempt for the world and for your very self; this will set your life in order at every time and in every place where you may be. And not only you, but it will cause you to guide and raise your entire family in His pleasure with holy and good customs, just as a mother ought to do for her children and a lady for her servants, with holy Confession and Communion at the place and time ordained by the Holy Church. We must obey the Church, and **Pope Urban VI** <note>Catherine was a fierce supporter of Urban VI during the Western Schism, a period when the papacy was contested.</note> until death. Now, in this way, order yourself in all your actions. 

Thus, I sweetly pray you to look upon the humble and loving Lamb with great diligence, so that together with Him we may rejoice in this life through grace, and in the end, with the Mother of Charity, enter into the glory of lasting life. I say no more to you. Remain in the holy and sweet love of God. Sweet Jesus. Jesus Love.

# To a Great Neapolitan Lady who is with the Queen.

Concerning the holy fear of God and servile fear, and the opposition that exists between the one and the other. Exhorting the named Lady to clothe herself in this holy fear and to strive to lead the Queen's heart to know the truth and adhere to the Holy Church. <note>The Queen mentioned is likely Joanna I of Naples, whom Catherine frequently urged to remain loyal to Pope Urban VI during the Great Western Schism.</note>

## Letter 328.

->In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified and of sweet Mary.<-

<margin>A</margin>Dearest Sister in sweet Christ Jesus: I, Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious Blood, desiring to see you stripped of all **servile fear** <term>servile fear: a fear based on the dread of punishment rather than love for God</term>; so that you may proclaim the truth far and wide and persevere in the **holy fear of God**. This fear makes the soul courageous <note>original: "virile." In medieval spiritual writing, this term denotes strength of character and fortitude, applied to both men and women.</note>, so that it fears neither pain, nor death, nor any persecution; it does not fear displeasing creatures, because it wishes to please only its Creator. It only fears offending God, and nothing else. How sweet a thing it is for the soul to dwell in this holy fear, because it proceeds from the sweetness of **Charity** and the fear of due reverence; just like a good son who, out of <margin>a</margin>love and reverence, fears displeasing his Father—not out of fear of beatings, but to avoid offending Him. This is what the soul does that has freely given itself to serve its Creator with all its heart and all its affection, not serving Him out of fear, nor with **mercenary love** <term>mercenary love: an "employer-employee" relationship with God, where one only does good to receive a reward or avoid a penalty</term>, but with **liberal love** <note>original: "amore liberale." This refers to the love of a free person (Latin: "liber") who gives out of generosity and friendship.</note>. And just as its love and service are free, so its fear is free; for without fear of punishment it offers itself, and with holy fear, it stands ready to endure every pain. We have a great need to possess this holy fear in these times that run upon us today—though we ought to have it in every time, state, and place—and to flee that wretched **self-love**, from which proceeds the servile fear that is so afraid that its own shadow causes it terror. Oh, how...

<vocab>Catherine of Siena, holy fear, servile fear, Charity, reverence, mercenary love, liberal love, self-love, Queen, Holy Church</vocab>

<summary>In this letter opening, St. Catherine distinguishes between "servile fear" (dread of punishment) and "holy fear" (reverent love), urging a noblewoman at the Neapolitan court to be brave in speaking the truth. She argues that true spiritual strength comes from loving God as a child loves a father, rather than as a servant fearing a master.</summary>
<keywords>St. Catherine of Siena, Naples, Queen Joanna I, Great Schism, servile fear, holy fear, divine love, fortitude, Papal loyalty</keywords>

...how miserable is this fear; it debases the soul and constricts the heart within the affection of <term>Charity: in this context, the selfless love of God and neighbor</term>, which does not allow it to perform the works of God, nor to love the neighbor through delight and love. It makes the soul timid, such that seeing God and one’s neighbor being offended, out of fear one will pretend not to see the offense done to one's Creator; even sometimes, to please or avoid displeasing others, one shows oneself to conform with those very defects one sees being committed, acting always against one's conscience, which tells one that both the act and the actor are doing wrong. 

O cursed self-love, you who have ruined the whole world and deprived souls of the treasure of virtues! By accompanying yourself with **servile fear**, you impoverish the soul, you take away its light, and you ruin its taste, so that bitter things seem sweet and sweet things seem bitter. You strip the soul of **holy fear** and clothe it in servile fear and extreme misery, so that even in this life it tastes the <term>earnest money of Hell: a "down payment" or foretaste of suffering</term>. The soul becomes unbearable to itself. 

This miserable fear brings every evil with it. Well should the soul therefore hate it, rising above itself and climbing onto the seat of its conscience to hold court <note>original: "tener ragione." This refers to the spiritual practice of "the court of conscience," where the soul acts as its own judge.</note>, not letting the movements of the affection of fear pass without being corrected by the light of reason. 

Dearest Sister, I invite you to leave this servile fear behind. With the light of truth and the holy fear of God, begin to sow the truth in the heart of the Queen, so that Divine Judgment does not fall upon her, and so she no longer keeps the Holy Church and the entire Christian congregation in such bitterness and sadness.

# To Countess Benedetta, Daughter of Giovanni d'Agnolino Salimbeni of Siena.

## Letter 329.

->In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary.<-

I. **D**earest daughter in Christ sweet Jesus: I, Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious blood with the desire to see you as a servant and spouse of Christ Crucified, considering for myself that to serve God is not to be a servant, but to reign. It is not like the perverse servitude of the world, which makes the creature base and makes them a servant and slave to sin and the devil; this sin, which is **nothingness** <note>original: "non cavelle." Catherine uses this archaic Tuscan term, meaning "not anything," to describe sin as a lack of true being.</note>, brings man to nothingness. Know, dearest and sweet daughter, that the soul that serves created things and riches outside of God—that is, which inordinately hungers for and desires the riches, delights, and vanities of the world with self-pleasure—loses...

...which are all vain, without any firmness or stability; just like a leaf that turns in the wind, it falls into death and debases itself, because it submits itself to those things that are lesser than itself. For all created things are made for the service of the <term>rational creature: a human being, endowed by God with the power of reason</term>; and the creature who possesses reason within themselves is made to serve their Creator. And therefore we deceive ourselves, for the more Man craves these transitory things, the more he loses that sweet Lordship which is acquired by serving his Creator. Instead, he submits himself to that thing which is nothing—for by loving in a disordered way outside of God, he offends God.

So it is indeed the truth that from the servitude of the World we come to <note>original: "non cavelle"</note> nothingness. Oh, how mad and foolish is the one who gives himself to serve that which holds no Lordship, except over that thing which is nothing—that is, **Sin**. The Devil does not rule over anyone except those who are workers of iniquity. And in what way does he rule them? Through torment, giving them punishment in eternal damnation. And the World also—meaning the disordered affections that we place upon the World; for the things of the World are good in themselves, but the evil will of the person who uses them makes them bad, returning to them and desiring them without fear of God. 

And in this way, I say that these are the servants who bind us to the Devil in torment. I say that this servitude to death takes away the light of reason and gives darkness; it takes away the wealth of grace and gives the poverty of vice. I do not want, my daughter, since it is so dangerous, for you to give yourself over to the perverse servitude of the World, but I want you to be a true **Servant of Christ Crucified**, who has redeemed you with His precious blood. 

He is our sweet God, who created us in His image and likeness. He has given us the **Word** <note>The "Word" refers to Jesus Christ (the Logos), the second person of the Trinity.</note> of His only-begotten Son to take death away from us and give us life; with His Blood, He took away the servitude of sin and made us free, pulling us from the Lordship of the Devil, who possessed us as his own. The Blood furthermore has made us strong and has put us in possession of Eternal Life, for in it are all the keys that have unlocked the door which stood closed because of the sin that had been committed. This sweet Word, mounting his horse <note>Catherine uses the vivid metaphor of the Cross as a stallion and Christ as a Knight going into battle to win back humanity.</note> upon the Wood of the **Most Holy Cross** as a true Knight, has defeated His enemies and has put us in possession of enduring life; and in such a way,

...I say, that neither the Devil nor any creature can take it away from us, unless we so will it. And thus I said that I desired to see you as a servant and Bride of Christ Crucified; for as soon as you are made a servant—because to serve God is to reign <note>original: "el servire a Dio è regnare." A common medieval paradox: true freedom and power are found only in submission to the divine will.</note>—step by step you become a Bride. You have seen clearly that it held no stability for you; and so consider that it will do the same to you again if you trust it further, for the end is just as mortal as the beginning.

Rise up, then, from all tenderness and self-love, and enter into the Wounds of Christ Crucified, where there is perfect and true security. <margin>I</margin> It is that sweet place where the Bride fills the lamp of her heart; for truly the heart is a lamp. It ought to be like a lamp that is narrow at the base and wide at the top—meaning that its desire and affection should be narrow toward the World and wide above; <margin>I</margin> that is, to broaden the heart and its affection in Christ Crucified, loving Him and fearing Him with true and holy care. Then you will fill this lamp at the <term>Side of Christ Crucified: the wound in Jesus' side, which Catherine frequently describes as an entrance to the "secret of the heart" or the depths of divine love</term>. The Side has shown you the Secret of the Heart: that what He has done and given for us, He has done out of pure love. There one finds true and profound humility, which is the oil that feeds the fire and the light in the heart of Christ’s Bride. What greater breadth of love can you find than seeing that He has laid down His life for you? And what greater lowliness can be seen, or ever found, than seeing God humbled before Man?

# To Countess Benedetta, Daughter of Giovanni d'Agnolino Salimbeni.

I. Concerning true and perfect Charity, and its effects.
II. What Charity is, and how it is acquired.
III. Concerning worldly love, and its sad effects.
IV. That our Soul is a tree of love, which must be cultivated and worked by free will, and planted in the valley of humility, and not on the mountain of pride.
V. Which flowers and fruits this tree must produce.
VI. That the Earth, where this tree is planted, is true humility in the enclosed garden of self-knowledge. <note>original: "giardino chiuso," a reference to the 'Hortus conclusus' of the Song of Solomon, symbolizing a soul set apart for God.</note>
VII. That the Soul, knowing itself, joins its own affection with the affection of Christ Crucified, and with love draws love to itself.
VIII. That the aforementioned tree must be watered with the water of Charity toward one's Neighbor.
IX. What the love of the Neighbor should be, and what its operations are.
X. How through Charity one acquires true patience, and perseverance in doing good.
XI. With how much diligence one must seek the acquisition of Holy Charity, and how it must be preserved until death.

## Letter 330.

->In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary.<-

This charity is a wedding garment <note>original: "vestimento nutiale." Charity extinguishes and consumes sin in its heat, and without this garment, we cannot enter into the lasting life to which we are invited.

Through love; for love is not acquired except through love, and from love. But you will say to me, Dearest Daughter: "What method must I have to find and acquire this love?" I answer you in this way. All love is acquired through **light**, for a thing that is not seen cannot be known, and not being known, it cannot be loved. It is necessary, therefore, to have light so that you may see and know that which you ought to love. And because light was necessary for us, God provided for our necessity, giving us the <margin>▲</margin> **light of the Intellect** <term>Intellect (Intelletto): in Catherine's theology, the faculty of the soul that perceives spiritual truth</term>, which is the most noble part of the Soul, with the pupil of **Holy Faith** <note>Catherine frequently uses the metaphor of the eye, where the "Intellect" is the eye and "Faith" is the pupil that allows it to see God.</note> inside it. And I tell you that even if a person offends their Creator, they do not pass their time, nor do they live, without love or without light; for the Soul, which is made of love and created through love in the image and likeness of God, cannot live without love, nor would it love without light.

### III. 
Hence, if one wishes to love, it is necessary that one sees. But do you know what the "seeing" and "loving" of the Men of the World <note>A term for those living purely secular lives, focused on material rather than spiritual concerns.</note> is? It is a dark and obscure seeing, and through the dark night the truth is not discerned. It is a mortal love, for it brings death to the Soul, stripping it of the life of **Grace** <term>Grace (Gratia): the divine life of God present in the soul</term>. But why is this seeing obscure? Because it has placed itself in the darkness of the transitory things of the World, having placed them before itself, apart from God—that is, it does not regard them in His Goodness, but only regards them for **sensory delight**; this delight and sensory love moved the Intellect to see and know sensory things. Therefore this affection, which is nourished by the light of the Intellect—even if we assume the affection moved the intellect first, as was said—brings death, committing a fault and stripping away the life of Grace. This is because nothing can be loved or seen outside of God without bringing us death; and therefore, that which is loved must be loved in Him and through Him—that is, recognizing oneself and everything else as coming from His Goodness. So you see that this person loves and sees, because without loving and seeing one cannot live. But the love of the Men of the World, which gives death, is different from the love of the Servant of God, which gives life; for the love that is acquired from the **Supreme and Eternal Love** gives the life of...

### IV. 
And this tree is so well made that there is no one who can prevent it from growing, nor take away its fruit, if the tree itself does not wish it. And God has given to this tree a worker to cultivate it, because it pleases Him, and this worker is <term>free will</term>. And if the <term>Soul</term> did not have this worker, it would not be free; not being free, it would have an excuse for <term>sin</term>, which it cannot have, because there is no one—neither the <term>World</term>, nor the <term>Devil</term>, nor the <term>fragile Flesh</term>—that can compel it to any fault if it does not wish it. For this tree has within itself reason, if <term>free will</term> wishes to use it, and it has the eye of the <term>Intellect</term> which knows and sees the truth, provided the fog of <term>self-love</term> does not obscure it. 

And with this light, the soul sees where the tree must be planted; for if it did not see, and did not have this sweet patience <note>original: "patientia." In mystical theology, this refers to the soul's capacity to remain open and receptive to God's light.</note> of the <term>Intellect</term>, the worker would have an excuse and could say: "I was free, but I did not see where I could plant my tree, whether on high or down low." But he cannot say this, because he has the <term>Intellect</term> which sees, and reason, which is a bond of reasonable love with which he can bind it and graft it into the <term>Tree of Life</term>, <term>Christ sweet Jesus</term>. He must, therefore, plant his tree, since the eye of the <term>Intellect</term> has seen the place and in what earth it must stand if it wishes to produce the fruit of life. 

Dearest Daughter, if the worker of <term>free will</term> then plants it where it ought to be planted—that is, in the <term>Earth of true humility</term>—for he must not place it upon the <term>mountain of pride</term>, but in the <term>valley of humility</term>, then it produces <term>fragrant flowers of virtue</term>. And uniquely, it will produce that supreme <term>Flower of Glory</term> and praise to the Name of God; and all its works and virtues, which are sweet flowers and fruits, will receive their fragrance from this.

### VII.

Since the peak—that is, the affection of the **Soul**, which follows the **Intellect** as has been said—has known the object of Christ Crucified and the abyss of the fire of his **Charity**, which it recognized in this <term>Word</term> <note>original: "Verbo." ### VIII.

Since the vessel of the Heart is full, it waters the tree with the water of Divine Charity for one's Neighbor, which is a dew and a rain that waters the plant of the tree and the Soil of true humility, and enriches that Soil and the garden of <term>self-knowledge</term> <note>A central pillar of Catherine's teaching: by looking into the "cell" of the self, one finds both their own nothingness and God's infinite love.</note>; for then it is seasoned with the seasoning of the knowledge of God’s Goodness within itself. warmed by the heat of the Sun of **Divine Charity**; it would not bear the fruit of life, nor would its fruit be ripe.

### IX.

Once the tree has grown, it spreads its branches, offering fruit to its **Neighbor**, that is, the fruit of most holy, humble, and continuous prayers, providing an example of a holy and good life. It also extends these branches when possible by aiding the neighbor with material possessions with a large and liberal heart—sincere and not feigned. That is, one should not show one thing in action while being another in fact, but should serve with sincerity and affectionate charity in whatever service one can; and whatever need one sees, one should meet it to the best of one's power. **Charity** does not seek its own interests, and does not seek itself for its own sake, but itself for God’s sake, to return the flowers of glory and praise to His Name. It does not seek God for its own sake, but God for God’s sake, insofar as He is worthy of being loved by us because of His goodness. And one does not love, nor seek, nor serve one's **Neighbor** for one's own sake, but only for God, to pay that debt which one cannot pay to God. <note>Catherine explains that since we cannot directly benefit God, who lacks nothing, we must "repay" our debt to Him by serving our neighbor.</note> I already told you that we cannot be of any use to God, and therefore God has us be of use to our **Neighbor**, who is a means placed before us by God to test our virtue and to show the love we have for the sweet and eternal God.

### X.

This **Charity** tastes eternal life; it consumes and has consumed all our iniquities, giving us perfect light with true patience. It makes us strong and persevering, so much so that we never wish to turn our heads back to look at the plow; <note>A reference to Luke 9:62: "No one who puts a hand to the plow and looks back is fit for service in the kingdom of God."</note> rather, we persevere until death, delighting to stand on the **Battlefield** for **Christ Crucified**, placing His Blood before us so that it may encourage us in the battle like true **Knights**. Therefore, since this **Charity** is so useful, necessary, and delightful—for without it we live in continual bitterness, receive death, and our shames are uncovered—and on the last day of **Judgment** we would be shamed before the whole world and before the Angelic Nature and all the Citizens of lasting life (where there is life without death and light without darkness, where there is perfect and common **Charity**, sharing and tasting one another's good through the affection of love), we must embrace this sweet **Queen** and <term>wedding garment</term> <note>original: "vestimento nuttiale." Referring to the state of grace or love required to enter the heavenly banquet.</note> of **Charity**, and with anxious and sweet desire dispose ourselves to death in order to be able to acquire [it].

<margin>Pompeo Sansedoni, Title 34 <note>Pompeo Sansedoni was a 17th-century Sienese hagiographer and historian who documented the lives of local holy figures.</note></margin>
It is suggested that the daughter of Giovanni Salimbeni was the wife of Paolo Trinci of the Lords of Foligno, as it is found in the Sienese memoirs that during these times a certain Lisa Salimbeni was married to that Lord. **[ B ]** *I recall that, according to the world, you made yourself feared.* This confirms what was said regarding the status of this Lady; that is to say, she was placed in a high position and belonged to a family of power and dominion.

**( C )** *On the matter of the Habit,* etc. Perhaps this refers to her taking the habit of the <term>Mantellate <note>Members of the Dominican Third Order, so named for the black "mantles" or cloaks they wore over their white tunics. **[ D ]** *Of your glorious Father St. Francis.* The Trinci family held the Order of the Seraphic Father Saint Francis in special veneration; and a few years earlier, Brother Paolo Trinci had returned several convents of the Order to the ancient rigor of the Rule <note>Paolo Trinci (1309–1391) was a leader in the "Observant" movement, which sought to restore the original strict poverty and discipline of St. Francis to the Franciscan order.</note>.

**( E )** *Of the deeds of the Countess.* That is, of the Countess Benedetta, who was commonly called Bandeca, her sister, who was also eager to enter the religious state.

II. Concerning the fear and the love that God requires from us.
III. Concerning two things that are necessary to preserve in ourselves Faith in God, particularly in times of adversity.

The other is that you should truly believe that whatever happens to us—whether by death or by life, by illness or by health, by wealth or by poverty, or by injury done to us by friends, or by relatives, or by any Creature—I want you to believe that it is by the permission and will of God, and without His will not a leaf falls from a tree. ( A ) *This Lady was the wife of Lodovico, commonly called by everyone by the shortened name Vico da Mogliano, <term>Senator of Siena</term> <note>The Senator was the highest judicial and police official in the Republic of Siena, usually a foreigner to ensure impartiality.</note>. He entered the office of Senator in February of the year 1373 and remained there for eighteen months, according to the testimony of Angelo di Tura del Grasso in his Chronicle, where he is mentioned. On the eighth day of February, Vico da Mogliano, from the territory of Fermo, arrived as Senator of Siena in the year 1372 (<note>original: "giusto al computo Sanese"</note> correct according to the Sienese reckoning, but 1373 by the common style <note>Siena calculated the start of the year from March 25th, the Feast of the Annunciation, rather than January 1st.</note>), and on the eighth of August 1374, he was succeeded by Antonio da Saramondo of Puglia.*

<margin>Memoirs obtained from Fermo</margin>
*This Lord was the Master of the Land of Mogliano, which is one of the most populated, wealthy, and honored with refinement of all those within the State of Fermo. The City of Fermo at that time was essentially a free city and was ruled by the People, with the Nobility having no part in the Government. Despite this, the nobility did not cease to be held in high esteem, particularly those who held the Lordship over some Castle or some Land of the State; such a person was considered a Noble—that is, the Lord or Lady of that place—and for the most part took their surname from it, as has happened in many other places. With the passing of the years, the City occupied the domains of the Castles and Lands near it; the same happened in other states, and particularly here in Siena. Consequently, those Lords took refuge in the cities they once dominated, feeling they could not with dignity live as subjects in the very places where they had been Lords, and using distance to soften the bitterness of their lost power. These Lords, or Nobles, of Mogliano had been in possession of that land since the year 1226; there is a record in the secret Archive of the City of Fermo, kept in the Convent of the Dominican Fathers, of an agreement between the government and the Nobles and Barons of Mogliano, along with other Lords, signed in that year. The son of this Lodovico, named Maffio,*

( B ) *Regarding the incident that had occurred to the Senator.* As was noted in another place, the government of the City of Siena had fallen, beginning in the Year 1368, into the <term>Balìa</term> <note>A special committee or governing body with temporary dictatorial powers, common in Italian city-states.</note> of the People, favored in this by the Emperor Charles IV, who was in Tuscany at that time; the entire Nobility remained completely excluded from the government. For some time, only those of the "People" who were more substantial <note>The "Popolo grasso," or the wealthy merchant class.</note> had the management of affairs, while the smaller and more lowly commoners <note>The "Plebe," or lower-class laborers and artisans.</note> were held in no account, being rejected—as is usually the case—as incapable of turning the wheels of government with the correct motion. However, this lower class, noticing from the change already made that they were the most powerful because they were the greatest in number, and having taken a whim to be equal in dominion with those who were only slightly above them in condition, seized the entire Lordship of the Republic for themselves in the Year 1371 by force—which in such works counts for more than any reason. Many were the seditions that were stirred up from hour to hour in those first years by the lowest commoners, who were never well-settled because they were always searching for novelty in the hope of a better fate. Consequently, as the Senator had several times used the arms of Justice against some of the rabble who were disturbers of the peace, he had fallen into contempt with many. For this reason, he ran no slight danger of losing his life in those tumults, murdered by those...

# To Lady Orietta Scotta at the Cross of Caneto in Genoa.

I. She exhorts her to the virtue of patience, as the Daughter of Charity, discussing its effects and the virtues that proceed from it.
II. She prays her to be willing to have compassion for the many offenses that were being committed against God at that time, and to offer her prayers to prevent them.
III. She exhorts her to drown her own will.

## Letter 334.

->In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary.<-

I. **D**earest Mother and Daughter in sweet Jesus Christ: I, Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious Blood with the desire to see you founded in true and perfect patience. This patience demonstrates whether we truly love our Creator or not; because it is the marrow <note>original: "mirollo", an archaic form of marrow, used here to mean the essential core or pith.</note> of Charity, for Charity is not without patience, nor patience without Charity. It is a virtue so pleasing and necessary to our salvation that without it we cannot be pleasing to God, nor receive the fruit of our labors <note>original: "fadighe", referring to the trials or toils of life.</note> which God permits for our salvation; indeed, we would taste the earnest <note>original: "arra", a legal term for a down payment or deposit, here used to mean a "foretaste" of Hell.</note> of Hell in this life. This virtue demonstrates the light that is in the soul that possesses it; that is, it demonstrates that the soul, through the light of most holy faith, has seen and known that God wants nothing other than its good, and that what He gives and permits to us in this life, He gives for our sanctification. And therefore the soul that has known this is immediately patient, almost saying to itself, when the pro-

one's own sensuality might want to rise up through impatience, and do you want to complain about your own good? ## II.
O dearest Mother and Daughter, now is the time to embrace this true and real virtue, seeing that the World persecutes those who are lovers of truth with many injuries and reproaches. It is fitting for us to be patient in our own injuries and toils, but for the toils of others we must have great compassion, and be impatient toward the vice of the one who offends. <margin>..8 3..</margin> Dearest Mother and Daughter, if there ever was a time for compassion and bitterness because of offenses against God, it is now; if today in such darkness and bitterness we see the World placed only through the cloud of self-love of ourselves, which has poisoned and corrupted the World. Whoever has patience has perfect charity; having perfect Charity, one grieves—and must grieve—more for these evils that one sees than for one's own pains and tribulations. Alas, what is to be seen, that our eyes see our Faith contaminated, even as we are Christians marked with the Sign of Christ? With the darkness of Heresy they lose the Blood of Christ; well should it grieve us, and with this grief drive out every other grief. I invite you to bear with true patience,

...places mentioned above, and there, privately and by night, Pope **Gregory XI** himself arrived to confer with her regarding his journey to Rome. The Cardinals had wished to divert him from this path with all their power. He came to beg for her **Prayers** in those most pressing needs of **Holy Church**, as reported by **Blessed Tommaso Caffarini** in the **Supplement to the Legend** <note>original: "Supplemento alla Leggenda." The **Residence** of this Lady was on the street that was called, and is still called, **Caneto**. This street leads directly from the Banks <note>The 'Banchi' area was the commercial and financial heart of medieval Genoa.</note> to **Saint George** and to **Castello**, the very ancient and famous Convent of the **Religious of Saint Dominic**, which for this reason is called "in Caneto." Because the streets intersect there in a certain way, for greater clarity it is titled: **at the Cross of Caneto**. To this day, the **Memory of the House** of this Lady is preserved because this **Holy Virgin** stayed there, even though it has passed to another Family—specifically that of certain **Merchants of the House of Piatti**, who are its current masters. Within it, one may see the **Room of Saint Catherine**, which is used as a **Sacred Chapel**.

<margin>*Sansovino, Illustrious Families of Italy*</margin> 
The **Scotti Family**, to which this Lady belonged, is rightly numbered among the most **Illustrious of Italy**. They held the Lordship of the **City of Piacenza** along with many Lands and Castles. While the family still flourishes today in various **Cities of Italy**, particularly in **Lombardia**, it is not extinct in **Genoa**, where it has thrived for many years in one of its branches, though differing only in name. This most illustrious Family came to this City around the year 1120, brought by two brothers named **Amico** and **Gabriele**, sons of **Guglielmo Scotti** called "**the Younger**." This distinguishes him from the other **Guglielmo** of the famous lineage of the **Scottish Douglas Counts**, who, according to the opinion shared by many authors, came to Italy with **Charlemagne** and established the family in **Piacenza**, giving it the name **Scotta** because of its Scottish origin <note>It was common for noble families of this period to claim legendary origins from famous foreign knights or emperors like Charlemagne to bolster their prestige.</note>.

<margin>*Memoirs of the Centurione Family*</margin> 
These two Lords were brought into service by the Genoese, who gave them command of the military in the enterprise against the **Pisans**, which was brought to its desired conclusion by them with courage and success. From **Balduino Scotti**, son of **Amico**, the family was propagated in **Genoa**. From him descended, in direct succession from father to son, **Barnaba Scotti**, who was the husband of this **Orietta**. **Lodovico Scotti**, his son, was the grandfather of another **Lodovico**, who assumed the **Insignia** and the surname **Centurione**, due to the **Union** <note>This refers to the Genoese "Albergo" system, where different noble families merged into a single political and legal entity, often adopting the name and coat of arms of the most prominent member.</note> made in that

# To My Lady Lariella, Wife of Master Cieccolo Caracciolo of Naples.

I. That one must not trust in Created Things <note>In this spiritual context, "creatures" or "created things" refers to anything that is not God, including other people, wealth, or status.</note>, but only in God.
II. She rebukes her because she was suffering distress on account of her husband, who was in Rome, exhorting her not to place her trust in Created Things, as she seemed to be doing, but only in God.
III. That hope in God proceeds from love; therefore, it contains all the goodness of love and the virtues that flow from it.
IV. That we must practice our love toward God for the benefit of our Neighbor.

...trusts in man. For when we believe we hold onto these things securely, they fail us, either by divine dispensation <note>original: "divina dispensatione"; meaning God's plan or providence</note>, which takes them from us for our own good, or by means of death, separating us from this dark life. At times, we believe we are making a great profit and attaining a very high status, only to lose what we already have; and even if we do keep it, it is not without great labor and a disordered fear and dread of losing it. Thus, the Man becomes unbearable to himself. Truly, it is a vain and foolish thing for a Man to place his hope there. 

I say that it harms us because it takes away our Sovereignty and freedom, and makes us Slaves. For if we love Creatures <note>In Catherine’s theology, "creature" refers to any created thing—people, riches, or titles—as opposed to the Creator.</note> and created things in a disordered way outside of God, we offend Him; and by offending God, we make ourselves slaves of sin (which has no real being) and of created things, all of which are less than we are. Indeed, all things were created to serve us, and we were made to serve God. But we do the exact opposite, for we serve them and do a disservice to our Creator. 

These things deprive us of light and do not let us see or discern the truth. Just as a diseased eye cannot look at the light, so the eye of the Soul—into which has come the unfaithfulness and infirmity of self-love and disordered love—loses the light in such a way that it can know neither itself nor God; that is, it cannot know His infinite Goodness nor its own misery. It loses the wealth of the virtues because it is cut off from the affection of <term>Charity</term> <note>original: "Carità"; here referring to the theological virtue of selfless, divine love</note>, in which all the virtues are bound together. There, there is no love of God nor love of the Neighbor, and one does not serve him except for one's own profit. There is no true humility, because there is only one's own reputation, in which one delights in being held as great and having high status. All of one’s study is to please Creatures, and because such a person pleases themselves, they would rather please them than the Creator; and if they receive an injury, they bear it with great Impatience; and if they serve their Neighbor or their relatives, yet receive no personal profit or honor from it, they are not patient and would willingly abandon that service.

Then the service will be pleasing and acceptable to God, and an honor and a benefit to you. I mean a benefit of grace, which is the benefit that God requires us to seek with great diligence. This you will do if your hope is placed in God; otherwise, you will not. 

And so I told you that I desired to see you place your affection and hope only in Him; and truly you must do so, since you see how harmful it is to place it in oneself, or in Creatures, or in created things apart from God. Such a choice holds the Soul in much bitterness <note>original: "amaritudine"</note> and causes great damage, as has been said. The opposite is true of the hope a person has in God, because hope proceeds from love; a Creature always hopes in the one she loves. Therefore, he who loves a Creature hopes in the Creature, and if he loves his Creator, he hopes only in Him; and love—that is, the affection of <term>Charity</term>—always gives the greatest joy to the heart that possesses it. <margin>B</margin>

Being master of himself, he is made master of the World, because he mocks it, refusing its pomps and its delights, for he sees that they are neither firm nor stable. Therefore he has removed his hope from them and placed it in his Creator, who is firm and stable, who never changes, and cannot be taken from us unless we so will.

Here I want your diligence to be placed, so that you may receive that supreme and eternal good which is prepared for you. I say no more to you. Remain in the holy and sweet love of God. Sweet Jesus. Jesus Love.

# To Lady Pentella, Married in Naples, a Servant of Christ.

I. Regarding the light that is necessary for us to know the truth of the Eternal Father—which is our sanctification—and of the way we must keep to obtain salvation, which is the imitation of Jesus Christ.
II. That it is not impossible for us to follow this way, if we so desire.
III. Regarding a most singular sign of the Servants of God, which is the love of suffering.
IV. Regarding the debt we have to give honor to God.
V. That we must give this honor through Charity toward our Neighbor (even though they may be ungrateful) in imitation of Jesus Christ.
VI. That we must not desire their death, but pray to God that He might enlighten them.
VII. She exhorts her to seek a true light to know the truth and the error in which she found herself, since she desired the death of her Husband and of one of her slaves (on account of whom she was mistreated by her husband), demonstrating that no virtue can exist alongside such a desire.
VIII. She exhorts her to endure this tribulation with patience and to turn her hatred against herself.

<meta>This page continues the text of Letter 336 from Saint Catherine of Siena to Lady Pentella. The text follows the theme of the "light of truth" mentioned at the end of the previous page, transitioning into a discussion on how Jesus Christ (the Word) is the model for the Soul's journey toward God.</meta>

...[doc]trine, and His footsteps, keeps to the way of truth; and whoever keeps to the way of truth receives within themselves the life of <term>Grace</term> <note>original: "Gratia"; divine favor and the supernatural life of the soul</note>. What way should the Soul take to walk this path? What way did He take? This was the way: that with the light—which light He Himself was, and is—He contemplated the Will of the <term>Eternal Father</term> <note>God the Father</note>. This Will, for our sanctification, wished to manifest His eternal truth, which truth was this: that He had created Mankind to give them eternal life, so that they might enjoy the Supreme Eternal Good. And because of the fault committed <note>A reference to Original Sin</note>, this truth was not being fulfilled in us; therefore, it was necessary, in order to fulfill it, that the fault be purged. Thus, God willed to both purge the fault and fulfill His truth in Mankind. And so, this aforementioned truth constrained the Eternal Father, and through the ineffable love He had for us and for His truth, He gave us the truth of the <term>Word</term> <note>original: "Verbo"; Jesus Christ, the second person of the Trinity</note> of His Son, and clothed Him in our humanity, so that in it, by enduring suffering, our faults might be satisfied, and thus His truth might be fulfilled in us. 

Hence, the sweet Word of the Son of God, receiving the great obedience from the Father, ran like one in love to the shameful death of the **Most Holy Cross**; and by fulfilling obedience, He fulfilled the truth—that is, that we were restored to grace as far as His part is concerned, provided that we, for our part, do not resist with our miseries and defects. And this sweet Word, knowing that without enduring suffering He could not restore life to us, fell in love with pains, satiated Himself with reproaches, and clothed Himself in the insults of hunger, thirst, scorn, villainy, and the displeasure of vice. He was so displeased by vice that, although there was no poison of sin in Him, He punished it upon His own Body. He held such love for the virtues that He brought all virtues to ripeness in His own Blood. Like a 
<margin>B</margin> **Tree of Life**, He produced for us these fruits of the virtues; for after the redemption we received in the Blood, the fruits of the virtues have all been made available to us for eternal life. 

What did this Word seek, and for what did He grieve? He sought the honor of the Eternal Father and our salvation; and He grieved more over the offense committed and the harm that followed after the fault than over His own pain. Thus we see that He grieved more for the damnation of Judas than for the betrayal that Judas committed against Him. This is that sweet way which He has taught us, and which we must keep. And if you should say to me: "He was the true Son of...

II. III. We would rejoice as much as we saw ourselves trampled upon by the World; this, and seeing ourselves suffer without fault, would be our glory. And this is one of the most singular signs that can be seen in a <term>Servant of God</term> <note>original: "Servo di Dio"</note>, whether he is enlightened in knowing this truth or not. O sweet life, how sweet you are to the Soul that tastes you, which is lost and drowned in itself! This knowledge makes the soul run, dead to every self-will; being dead, it has no one to wage war against it, because only the will is what brings war and bitterness, not the tribulations and persecutions of the World. Rather, these are the delight and consolation of the true Servant of God; he feels as much well-being as he sees himself suffering. More than that: when he sees that the World holds him in any reverence or good opinion, he becomes saddened, fearing that in this life God does not wish to reward him for that little good he does, and because he would wish to conform himself with <term>Christ Crucified</term> <note>original: "Criſto Crocifiſſo"</note> and follow His footsteps. Such a person does not grieve over the one who does him injury, nor would he wish that the one who makes him suffer were taken away from him; instead, he grieves for the offense against God and the damage to the Soul of his Neighbor. Wherefore he does not cease to hold that person in God’s presence with great desire, offering humble, continuous, and faithful <term>Prayers</term> <note>original: "Orationi"</note> for him.
