IV. Why does he do this? Because in the light and in the doctrine of Christ Crucified, he has known the truth; and because with that same light, he has seen that he ought to do it out of duty. Therefore the Soul must answer the Devil and its own fragility when they want to fight against reason and virtue in any and every way, saying: "I must not consent to you, but I must serve my Creator with all my heart, with all my affection, and with all my strength; and this service I must demonstrate through endurance <note>original: "sostenere"; Catherine uses this to mean the patient bearing of trials and the Cross</note>." Why do you do this? Because it is my duty and a commandment, which I am bound and obligated to obey. Beyond the commandment, I am bound by grace, for by grace I have received my being and every grace added to that being; hence, even if it had never been commanded of me, I would still be bound to do it because of the graces received. Therefore, I do not want to be crude <note>original: "villana"; implying someone who is unrefined in spirit or lacking the nobility of gratitude</note> or ungrateful for so many benefits, but I want to give back what is not mine. For I work with what belongs to my Creator, and in this way, I give back to God; I am not giving Him anything of my own, but returning what I owe Him. Oh, how deserving of punishment is the <term>mercenary servant</term> <note>original: "servo mercenajo"; a common theme in Catherine's writing, referring to those who serve God only for personal reward or to avoid pain, rather than out of pure love</note> who tries to take what is not his own! Such people are greatly rebuked in the sight of God and in their own consciences, for they ought to give the honor to Him, yet they give it to themselves. Why is he worthy of such punishment and rebuke? Because he is bound to serve purely, without regard for his own consolation or delight—whether from God or from a creature for His sake—and also because he is bound to give glory and praise to His Name. With mercenary service, he could not give this glory in the manner he is obligated. Let us suppose that God, on His part, would draw glory from it, but on our part, it would not be so; nor would that Eternal Truth be fulfilled in us—He who created us and re-created us in grace through the Blood to give us eternal life. Therefore the Soul, looking with this light upon the debt it must repay, and also upon the grace—for it sees it is loved by God through grace—and seeing that all the spiritual and temporal graces it has received were given in this same form and in the same way, feels compelled to respond to God. It feels compelled not to depart from those ways it finds in Him, nor to leave the pattern of the <term>footsteps</term> <note>original: "vestigia"; the tracks or marks left by Christ, which the soul is called to follow</note> of Christ Crucified.

V. It is true that we cannot return the love of grace to Him, because He loved us before we even existed; thus we are held by debt, as has been said. She returns it purely, so that no matter the labor she finds in him, nor the reproach she might receive from him, nor the ingratitude for the services she has done him, she never lets up. This is because the light has made her constant and persevering, learning from the **humble Lamb** <note>A title for Jesus Christ, emphasizing His patience and sacrifice</note>. Sometimes they do this under the guise of not offending God, and sometimes by wanting her to acknowledge the ingratitude of her Neighbor, which comes to her colored with the guise of **Justice**.

VI. Sometimes he wants to throw her to the ground by making her desire the death of her Neighbor, under the guise of having more peace and more quiet in her mind. This is because her blindness, the demon of her own sensuality, and the indignation and displeasure she has taken toward the neighbor do not let her see or recognize the truth. To have him entirely, it is necessary for you to love sincerely, as has been said, without any regard for yourself, and to follow him by the way of the **Cross**, never choosing to be crucified in your own way, but in his. ## VIII.

Now see how "wise" you truly are. Does not the slave of your **humanity** <note>original: "umanità"; here referring to the lower, physical nature or the senses</note> do more harm to you—along with the Spouse of **free will**, who voluntarily consents to this slave and with her tramples and debases **reason**, who is the Lady? Certainly so. Therefore, you ought to hate that which is within you more than the Slave and the Husband who are outside of you; for the latter strike only the bark <note>meaning the exterior or surface</note> of the Body with injuries and pains, but the former strike the **Soul**, which is beyond comparison much more noble than the Body. Indeed, every nobility the Body possesses comes from the Soul, and the Soul comes from **God**. 

Therefore, for his honor, you must be solicitous to attend to that part which is more noble, turning all hatred toward yourself. Let it be a mortal hatred—that is, may you always desire the death of your own perverse will, so that only the eternal **Will of God** lives in you. Bathe yourself in the Blood, drown yourself in the Blood of **Jesus Christ Crucified**, which will make you love God and his creatures sincerely. See to it that what has been until now is no more. I say no more to you. Remain in the holy and sweet love of God. Sweet Jesus. Jesus Love.

so that you could taste it, God redeemed you with the **Blood** of his Son; but consider, most dear daughters, that this **Food** is not eaten on Earth—that is, in earthly affection—but on high. Therefore, the Son of God raised himself on high upon the wood of the **most Holy Cross**, so that on high, and upon the said Table, we might take this Food. But you will say to me: "What is this <term>Angelic Food</term> <note>original: "Cibo Angelico"; Catherine uses this to describe the spiritual union where human desire and God's desire meet.</note>?" I answer you: It is the desire that resides in the affection of the **Soul**, which desire draws to itself the desire of God, so that the one and the other become one and the same thing. This is a Food that, while we are pilgrims in this life, draws to itself the scent of true and real virtues; these virtues are cooked in the fire of **Divine Charity** and eaten upon the **Table of the most Holy Cross**—that is, by enduring pains and labors for the love of virtue and by resisting one's own sensuality. 

<margin>Matthew 11.</margin> 
In this way, with force and violence, one seizes the realm of the **Soul**, which is called "Heaven" because it conceals <note>original: "cela"; Catherine is using a common medieval wordplay where "Cielo" (Heaven) is linked to "celare" (to hide or conceal), suggesting the soul is a hidden heaven where God dwells.</note> God within itself by grace. This is the Food that makes the **Soul** angelic, and therefore it is called **Angelic Food**. Because once the Soul is separated from the Body, it tastes God in His essence, and He satisfies it so much and in such a way that it desires nothing else, nor can it wish for anything except that which may more perfectly preserve and increase this Food. It hates what is contrary to it; hence, being prudent, it looks with the light of the **most Holy Faith** (which light resides in the eye of the **Intellect**) at what is harmful and what is useful. Once it has seen, so it loves and scorns—it scorns, I say, its own sensuality, holding it bound under the feet of its affection, along with all the vices that proceed from that sensuality. 

The soul flees all causes that might incline it toward vice or impede its perfection; wherefore it denies its own will, which is the cause of every evil, and submits it to the yoke of holy **obedience** to the commandments of God—to which obedience all faithful Christians are bound. And there are many others who run to the obedience of the **Holy Order**; this is a greater perfection. Hence, when the Soul is truly obedient, it subjects itself not only to the commandments of God (or, if a **Religious** woman, to her order), but to every other **Creature** for God's sake. <meta>This page continues Catherine of Siena's Letter 337 to the sisters of San Gaggio. It transitions from the metaphor of the "Angelic Food" to a practical guide on the three levels of prayer: continuous, vocal, and mental.</meta>

...she flees them with the greatest diligence, and loves and seeks that which increases and preserves her in virtue.

IV. And because she has seen that she tastes this food better by means of **Prayer** <note>original: "Oratione"; Catherine uses this term to mean both formal prayer and a general state of communion with God.</note> made in the **knowledge of self**, therefore she exercises herself in it continually, and in all those ways by which she may approach God. Prayer is made in three ways. The first is **continuous**, that is, the continuous and holy desire, which desire prays in the presence of God in everything the <term>Creature</term> <note>meaning any created human being</note> does; for this desire directs all our spiritual and temporal actions to His honor, and thus it is called "continuous." Of this, it seems that the Glorious Saint Paul speaks when <margin>To the Thessalonians 5</margin> he says:

> Pray without ceasing. <note>original: "Orate senza intermissione"; a reference to 1 Thessalonians 5:17.</note>

The second way is **vocal prayer**, that is, when speaking with the tongue one recites the Office or other vocal prayers; and this is intended to lead one to the third, namely **mental prayer**. The Soul reaches this when, with prudence and humility, she exercises the mind in vocal prayer—that is, while speaking with the tongue, her heart is not far from God, but she strives to fix and establish her heart in the affection of Divine Charity. And when she feels her mind being visited by God—that is, if it is drawn in any way to think of her Creator—she ought to abandon the vocal prayer and fix her mind with the affection of love on that which she feels, where God is visiting her. Then, if that visitation ceases and she has time, she should resume the vocal prayer, so that the mind remains full and not empty. 

And because in prayer many battles might abound in various ways, and darkness of mind with much confusion—with the Devil making us see our Prayer as not pleasing to God because of the many battles and the darkness we experience—we must not leave off for this reason. Instead, we must stand firm with strength and long perseverance, recognizing that the Devil does this so that we might depart from the **Mother of Prayer**. God permits it to test our strength and constancy, and so that in these battles and darkness we may know that we are nothing, and in our good will we may know the Goodness of God; for He is the giver and the preserver of good and holy wills, and He does not deny them to anyone who wants them. And in this way, one reaches the third and final Prayer, namely **mental**, in which she receives the fruit of the labor <unclear>that she sustained</unclear> in imperfect vocal prayer. She then tastes...

...hell. <note>The text continues from the previous page: "...the virtue that conquers hell."</note> **O true and sweet patience, which fashioned that virtue** that was never conquered, but always conquers; you alone are the one who shows whether the Soul loves its Creator or not. And once he has conceived them within, he places himself upon the tongue and makes them be given birth through the word; and with the word he achieves his effect. In this way, he divides the lover from the beloved, from which then come impatience, hatred, and rancors, depriving us of the life of Love.

Therefore, he is not to be believed; instead, one must ascend the seat of one's conscience and hold oneself to account, setting against this dangerous wave the hatred and displeasure of yourself <note>A reference to "holy self-hatred," or the rejection of one's own selfish ego and will.</note> by opening the eye of the Intellect and recognizing the Goodness of God and His eternal will. For the love of virtue is proved and finds its source through our Neighbor; and it teaches us to love God for God’s sake—insofar as He is the supreme and eternal Goodness and worthy of being loved—and to love oneself for God, and the Neighbor for God, and not for one's own utility, nor for delight, nor for the pleasure found in them. Rather, we love them insofar as they are creatures loved and created by the supreme Eternal Goodness, to serve them and help them in that which we cannot do for God; for since we cannot do anything for God...

Therefore, let us serve God alone with all our heart and all our affection, for He is that good which pacifies and satisfies the heart.

->II.<-

Since then this patience is so necessary and useful, it is right that we acquire it. But in what way shall we acquire it? I tell you: through light, by opening the eye of the Intellect <note>original: "Intelletto." The faculty of the soul that perceives spiritual truth and the nature of God.</note>, and recognizing that one is nothing <note>Catherine frequently uses the "nothing/everything" dichotomy: the soul is "nothing" on its own, but God is "all."</note>, and attributing one's being to the inestimable Charity of God. Since one has seen that they are loved by God, they see that out of love He gave us the Word <note>original: "Verbo." And since, therefore, He gave His life with such a fire of love, we must hold firmly that every toil <note>original: "fadiga." This implies hardship, labor, or the suffering of life's trials.</note>, from whichever side it comes—whether prosperous or adverse—is given out of love and not out of hatred; it is for our own good, so that we may reach the end for which we were created. And we must also see how great the toil is, and we will find that it is small; for it is only as great as time, and our time is only as much as the point of a needle <note>original: "punta d'aco." A vivid image used by Catherine to illustrate the brevity of human life compared to eternity.</note>, which in neither width nor length is anything at all <note>original: "cavelle." An archaic term meaning "nothing" or "something of no account."</note>. So then our toils are small and finite: we no longer have the toil that has passed, because that time has fled; we do not have the toil that is to come, because we are not certain of having that time. Since then we have seen its brevity...

# To Monna Nella, the lady who was the wife of Niccolò Buonconti of Pisa.

She exhorts her to bathe herself in the Blood of Jesus Christ through the memory of it, in order to acquire the virtue of Charity, and through it, the virtue of patience.

## Letter 339.

-> In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary. <-

**D**earest Mother in Christ sweet Jesus: I, Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious Blood with the desire to see you bathed by holy desire in the Blood of Christ Crucified. In this Blood, the soul is purified of every fault of sin, and there finds the warmth of Divine Charity, seeing that it was shed out of love. Because of this, the soul becomes intoxicated with love and senses the fragrance of patience; and through the love found in the Blood, it strips itself of all self-love and bears every adversity and tribulation of the world with meekness, passing through them with true patience. Likewise, it passes through the prosperities and delights of the world, and its social standing, and the love of its children with a true and holy fear, loving them as things lent <note>original: "cosa prestata." This reflects a core concept in Catherine’s spirituality: the idea that our lives, families, and possessions are not our own property but are on loan from God, which should prevent us from becoming too attached to them.</note>, and not as its own. Every person who possesses reason ought to act in this way. By doing so, one does not offend God, and tastes the down payment <note>original: "arra." A legal or commercial term for a deposit or pledge that guarantees a future transaction. Catherine uses it to mean a "foretaste" of eternal life experienced here on earth.</note> of eternal life in this life through brotherly charity with one's neighbor. The soul finds all of this in the memory of the Blood. And truly it is so; for as long as we keep the benefit of the Blood in mind with yearning desire, we will be grateful and appreciative, rendering back to Him the debt of the affection of Charity and of true and real virtues. For the creature <note>original: "Creatura." In this context, it refers to any human being created by God.</note> offends for no other reason than because it does not keep the memory of the Blood and other benefits, and therefore it is not grateful; and not being grateful, it does not care about—

### III.

Let us rise up courageously, most dear Mother and Daughter, abandoning the pomp and vanity of the World; so that at this point in time, grieving for lost time, you may wish to restore it in the present time you have, and consider that time will be demanded of us at the final extremity of death. Love one another, love one another together, most beloved Mother and Sister. Remain in holy and sweet love. Praised be Jesus Christ. Sweet Jesus. Jesus Love.

# To Madonna Laudomia, wife of Carlo degli Strozzi of Florence.

I. **She exhorts her** to the service of God, demonstrating the benefit and the good that it brings.
II. That one cannot serve the World and God together, and of the contradictions that exist between the will of God and that of the World; from which it follows that we must renounce the second to serve the first.
III. On the manner of loving Creatures, and on the value of Divine Grace.

## Letter 341.

->*In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary.*<-

<margin>Augustine, Meditations, ch. 6, 32.</margin>
I. **Dearest** Sister in Christ sweet Jesus: I, Catherine, Servant and slave of the Servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious Blood with the desire to see you a true Servant of Christ Crucified. To serve Him is not to serve, but to reign <note>original: "servire non è servire, ma è regnare." This is a common medieval theological paradox: by submitting to God's will, the soul is liberated from the "slavery" of its own vices and thus becomes a "ruler" over itself.</note>; it makes the Soul free, pulling it from the servitude of sin. It takes away our blindness and gives us perfect light; it takes away death and gives us the life of Grace. It gives us peace and quiet, stripping us of all war, and it clothes us and satisfies us with the garment of Charity and the food of the Lamb. This Lamb was cooked **and** roasted on the wood of the Most Holy Cross with the fire of love for the Father’s honor and for our salvation. It makes a person secure, taking away all servile fear <note>servile fear: A fear of God motivated only by the dread of punishment, as a slave fears a master. Catherine contrasts this with "filial fear," which is a loving respect for God.</note>. Truly, then, there is great sweetness **and** inestimable dignity in this sweet serving of God.

<margin>Matthew 6</margin>
II. We must, therefore, serve Him with true and perfect diligence with all our heart and all our affection. But take heed: this Lord wants no company, nor does He want to be served halfway, but totally; for it would be impossible to serve God **and** the World. Thus did blessed Christ say: No one can serve two masters <note>A reference to Matthew 6:24: "No one can serve two masters; for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other."</note>, because serving

<meta>This page continues Letter 341 to Madonna Laudomia. It elaborates on the irreconcilable conflict between the "World" (the ego and its attachments) and the service of God.</meta>

...ing one, it is in conflict with the other, because they have no conformity together. The World gives exactly the opposite of what we have said; for whoever serves their own <term>sensuality</term> <note>sensuality: in Catherine's thought, this refers to the "lower nature" or the part of the soul driven by physical impulses and selfish desires rather than reason and spirit.</note>, delights, status, riches, honors, and sensory pleasures—or children, or a husband, or any creature with sensual love, that is, loving them for one's own sensuality outside of God—it gives them death, blindness, and nakedness. This is because it causes one to be deprived of the garment of Charity, and brings them shame, losing their dignity; and they have sold their <term>free will</term> <note>free will: the power given by God to the soul to choose good or evil. Catherine views sin as a voluntary surrender of this power to the devil.</note> to the World and to the Devil, binding it to the servitude of sin, placing their affection and love in things that are less than themselves. Thus they sin by offending God; for all created things were made to serve us, and we were made to serve God. Therefore, by giving myself to serve them outside of God, by offending Him, I become a servant and a slave of sin (which is nothingness), and I become a non-thing, because I am deprived of God, who is He Who Is <note>original: "colui, che è." A reference to Exodus 3:14. Catherine often contrasts God's absolute "Being" with the "non-being" of sin and the soul that turns away from its Creator.</note>.

It is therefore necessary for us to renounce the World entirely and serve God. But why is the World so contrary to God? Because Blessed Christ invites us and teaches us to serve Him with <term>voluntary poverty</term>; for if a person possesses riches in actuality, they must not possess them mentally—that is, with desire—but should strip their affection of every earthly thing. The World loves pride, and God loves humility; and this virtue pleased Him so much that we see that God humbled Himself to us, and His Son, with great humility and patience, ran even to the shameful death of the Cross for us. He invites us and requires the virtue of true patience with hope and living faith—I say patient in bearing whatever God grants us, and for His love, forgiving those who offend us. The World wants exactly the opposite; for it wants to take revenge and remain in hatred and rancor toward its neighbor. 

Hope and faith must be placed in God, who is a firm and stable thing, and not in creatures; rather, one must trust and be faithful to Christ Crucified, and not to one's own sensuality. Then one will have living faith when she gives birth to the living children of the virtues through holy and good works. God also loves justice, and the World loves injustice. Let us therefore act, let us perform a holy justice upon ourselves; when our sensory feeling wants to rebel against its Creator, let it be lifted up with the affection of love and with the light of Conscience...

...knowledge, and accuse it <note>This refers to the soul accusing its own sinful nature before the judgment of the conscience.</note> to the Lord—that is, to the <term>free will</term>—and bind it with the bond of hatred, and with the knife of Divine Love, kill it. Now let us do this, Dearest Sister, for by doing so we shall be faithful Servants, and by being Servants, we shall be Lords. You have seen what great excellence and utility comes to the Soul from this holy service, and without it we cannot reach the end for which we were created; and we have also seen how dangerous it is, and to what vileness and misery the Soul is led that serves the World and its delights and pleasures. Christ loves virtue and hates sin; and He so loved virtue and hated sin that, to clothe us in it, He stripped Himself of life, fashioning our iniquities upon His own Body with many scourges, pains, shame, and reproach, and finally the painful death of the Cross. Since, therefore, sin displeases Him so much, we must flee it and hate it unto death; for it offends the Soul in no other way than in loving what God hates and in hating what He loves.

### III.
Now, therefore, let us raise up holy desire, and with the affection of love let us serve God, stripping the heart of every vanity and every disordered love of Children, of Husband, and of riches. Possess them and love them as things lent to us, for everything is given to us as a loan and for our use; let them suffice us only as much as pleases God, who has given them to you. It is unseemly to possess a thing that is not one's own as if it were one's own; but Divine Grace is ours, and we must possess it as our own. That thing is truly ours which neither the Devil nor any Creature can take from us unless we wish it; and truly ignorant is he who deprives himself of such a great treasure. Now, let us not be stingy with ourselves <note>original: "non ce ne facciamo caro." This suggests we should not hold back or be overly self-protective when such spiritual abundance is available.</note>, since there is such great wealth available. And so that you may better possess and preserve it, hide yourselves in the Wounds of Christ Crucified, and bathe yourselves in His precious Blood <note>This "blood mysticism" is a hallmark of Catherine's writing, symbolizing total immersion in God's mercy and the sacrifice of the Cross.</note>. I say no more. Remain in the holy and sweet love of God. Sweet Jesus. Jesus Love.

Carlo, the husband of this Lady, was held in the highest esteem for his prudence in his time, and for this reason, he was employed by the Republic <note>The Republic of Florence.</note> in various affairs. He established a peace very advantageous to the homeland with the Republic of Pisa in the year 1369; however, this turned out to be so unpleasing to the People—who, because of the victory gained over the enemies, had advanced their desires much further beyond the boundaries established by Strozzi—that he was in no small danger of being killed by the common folk <note>original: *plebe*</note> who had risen in a riot. He likewise handled other significant affairs entrusted by the Republic to his prudence and valor with supreme skill. Maddalena Strozzi, daughter of Carlo and Laodamia, was the wife of Luchino Visconti, cousin to Bernabò, Lord of Milan. The name Laodamia entered the family once again in the sixteenth century <note>original: *secolo decimofesto*</note> through the marriage of Piero Strozzi, Marshal of France, to Laodamia, daughter of Pier Francesco de’ Medici.

( A ) Giovanna Pazzi was one of the devoted companions of Saint Catherine, whom she accompanied for some time in various places; hence she is mentioned several times in these Epistles. From this, a doubt may arise as to whether this Lady was a Florentine of that most illustrious and celebrated Pazzi family, or rather of the noble Cinughi family of Siena, since it is held as certain that this House originated from that one; and this is proved quite conclusively by Francesco Campana in his *Advices* <note>original: "Consigli"; legal or expert opinions often published by scholars</note>. For some Lords of that great House, due to rebellion against the Commune of Florence, came to live in Siena in the year 1260, where their descendants were later called "of the Cinughi," forming the surname from two names, namely Cino and Ugo, son and father; thus it is found that Niccolò, who was the founder in 1340 of the Charterhouse of Belriguardo, is called in the Bull of Urban VIII (cited in the notes to Letter 59) *Nicholas [son] of Cino [son] of Ugo* <note>original: "Nicolaus Cini Ugonis"</note>. From this, one sees that the surname Cinughi had not yet been formed, and as he was called by the names of his father and grandfather, he kept the ancient surname of the House, perhaps not using it to be more pleasing to the People who ruled in Siena; and consequently this Giovanna, who was perhaps the daughter of this Niccolò, could herself still maintain it. This can be further confirmed by the fact that there is no memory of any of the Saint's companions being from any other homeland than Siena.

## II.

It is necessary, then, for us to apply a remedy to such malice from the <term>Devil</term>, and to respond within ourselves to these thoughts that come to us, by turning our eyes toward our Creator and saying:

> I confess that I am mortal, which is a very great grace to me, because through death I shall reach my end—that is, God, who is my life. And I also confess that my life, with the works I have done, deserves nothing but Hell; but I have faith and hope in my Creator, and in the Blood of the consumed and slain Lamb, who will forgive my sins and give me His grace. And I will strive to correct my life for the present time; and even if death should come to me before I have corrected my life—that is, if I have not yet done penance for my sins—I say that I trust in my Lord Jesus Christ, because I see that there is no comparison between Divine Mercy and my sins. Furthermore, if all the sins that could be committed were gathered into one single creature, they are less than a drop of vinegar in the middle of the Sea. This is how sins are in respect to Divine Mercy, provided the Soul wishes to return and receive it with a true and holy disposition, and with a displeasure for the fault committed—in which displeasure it loses the tenderness of its body and every created thing. In this way, the Soul becomes secure, its love for its ultimate goal grows, it loses the <term>servile fear</term> <note>Fear based on the threat of punishment (like a slave), rather than "filial fear" which is based on love for a father.</note> of confusion, and it delights with the greatest joy in its beloved Christ Crucified, awaiting the hour of death with the greatest happiness and peace. And not only does the Soul await it, but it desires to see itself taken from the world and to be with Christ.

## III.

Come now, then, my sweet Daughter, no more fear, but with joy pass through this point of time with a desire for virtue and with true patience, enduring every bodily and mental pain, whether through infirmity or in whatever way God might grant them to you. Do not shun pains for me, but cling to them and embrace the Cross and the sufferings; for every pain you have is granted to you by God for your own benefit: because He wants to have something for which to reward you when you leave the <term>stormy sea</term> <note>A common medieval metaphor for life on earth, which is seen as a perilous voyage toward the "port" of heaven.</note> of this dark life, and go

## Letter 344.

->***In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary.***<-

<margin>I.</margin> **D**earest daughter in sweet Christ Jesus: I, Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious Blood with the desire to see you living dead to your own sensuality, because in no other way could you participate in the life of Grace. Therefore, I wish that with the greatest affection and desire, you strive to raise yourself up from the fragility of the world. For it is not a fitting thing that we—who are made to taste the dwelling of Heaven by nourishing ourselves with the food of the virtues—should instead taste the Earth and nourish ourselves with selfish, sensory love, from which all vices proceed. Rather, we must rise and climb to the height of the virtues, opening the eye of the Intellect to gaze upon the Wood of the Cross, where we find the Lamb, the tree of life, who has made a ladder of His own Body.

<margin>II.</margin> The first step that He has taught us to climb is the feet; that is, the affection. For just as the feet carry the body, so the affection carries the Soul. Having climbed the first step—that is, with your feet fastened and nailed to the Cross—you will find your affection stripped of disordered love. Reaching the second step—that is, the open Side of Christ Crucified—you will see the second [step] of the Heart, with what ineffable love He has made for us a bath of the Blo... <note>original: "San-". The text cuts off here; the catchword "gue" indicates the word is "Sangue" (Blood).</note>

<margin>Medicine chapter 22.</margin>
...in His blood. On the first step, the soul rises and strips itself of [selfish] affection; on the second, it tastes the love it finds in the open Heart of Christ. Reaching the third step—that is, the mouth of the Son of God—it nourishes itself in peace. Once the soul is clothed in the love of Christ Crucified and stripped of the perverse sensory love <note>The "sensory love" or *amore sensitivo* refers to an instinctive, selfish attachment to worldly things and physical comforts rather than spiritual truth.</note> that wages war against it, it has found patience, and every bitterness seems sweet. It even delights in the persecutions and tribulations of the world, from whatever side God allows them, because it has found the peace of the mouth. The person who gives peace becomes one with the person to whom they give it; thus, the soul clothed in virtues with an affection of love tastes God, and joins the mouth of holy desire to the desire of God, and in that desire of God is united with peace and quiet. 

So you see that Christ Crucified has made a **Ladder of His own Body**, so that we may climb to the height of the Heaven of eternal life, where there is life without death, light without darkness, satiety without boredom, and hunger without pain. For as **Saint Augustine** says, boredom is far from satiety and pain is far from hunger, because the citizens who are in eternal life are satisfied in the eternal vision of God with that for which they have hunger and desire. Truly ignorant and miserable is that soul which, through its own fault, loses such great good and makes itself worthy of much evil. 

Rise up then, **Dearest Daughter**, and do not wait for time that you do not have, but with great affection of love, rise from the perversity of your sensory love, which takes the light of reason away from you and makes you love the world and your children immoderately <note>original: "senza modo," meaning "without measure" or beyond the bounds of reason and faith</note>; for in no other way could you reach the end for which you were created.

# To Lady Lodovica di Granello

I. **S**he exhorts her to the virtue of Charity <note>original: "Carità"; in this context, it refers to "Agapē" or divine, selfless love rather than just monetary giving.</note>, comforting her in the temptations that she seemed to be suffering.
II. That to acquire love toward God it is necessary to strip oneself of self-love, and with the light of Holy Faith to think of the Divine Charity with which He has loved us, and thinking that tribulations are sent to us by God for our own good.
III. On the knowledge of ourselves, which is necessary to us, and of the Goodness of God within us.
IV. That Charity makes us bear every labor.
V. That impure thoughts are not credited to us as sin without consent.
VI. She thanks her for the alms given to certain Religious <term>Religious</term><note>A technical term for members of a monastic or mendicant order, such as monks or friars.</note>.

## Letter 345.

->*In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary.*<-

**D**earest Daughter in Christ sweet Jesus: I Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ <note>A characteristic humble greeting Catherine used, modeling herself after the papal title "Servus servorum Dei."</note>, write to you in His precious Blood with the desire to see you founded in true and perfect Charity; because without Charity no virtuous act would have life in itself; because every virtue has life from Charity. She is that Mother who gives birth to the living Children of the Virtues; who gives us the life of grace, and not death. This sweet Charity has with it the light of Most Holy Faith, which, through the love it has for its Creator, believes in truth that God wills nothing other than our Good, and whatever He gives us and permits, He gives for our sanctification. Through this knowledge <note>original: "cognoſcimento"; a central theme in Catherine's theology, referring to the deep, experiential realization of one's own nothingness and God's all-encompassing love.</note> and light which one receives from the affection of Charity, one comes to patience, and is not scandalized nor troubled in their mind by anything that happens: rather, one holds it in due reverence. O dearest Daughter and Sister in Christ sweet Jesus, it seems to me that Divine Goodness permits you many labors, troubles, and temptations of the Devils <note>original: "Dimonia"; Catherine often speaks of spiritual warfare and the psychological pressure of demonic temptation as a refinement of the soul.</note> for your own good—not so that you may be conquered, but so that you may conquer. For these pains and battles, there is a great necessity to

<meta>This page continues Letter 345 to Lady Lodovica di Granello, following the introduction of Charity as the "Mother of Virtues" who carries the light of faith.</meta>

...to have in you this love with the light of Most Holy Faith: and if you have it, bitterness will turn into great sweetness, and heavy weights will become light; because with the light you will know that God gives them to you for your good; you cannot grieve over your own good. But you will say to me: Since having this Charity <note>original: "Carità"</note> is of such delight and such necessity, in what way can I have it, and where do I find it? I answer you very briefly, that love cannot be had except from love, and without the light it cannot be found; for by going without the light, we would seek it where it is not, and so we would walk in darkness.

II. Therefore it is necessary for us to take away from ourselves that thing which takes the light from us, that is, self-love <note>original: "amore proprio"</note>, which is a cloud that does not let us know nor see the truth of what we ought to love. This is that cloud which, in darkness, makes one love what is loved outside of God, not with the love of reason, but with the love of one's own sensuality <note>original: "senſualità"; in this period, this referred to the lower, physical nature of man as opposed to his rational soul.</note>. It is right to dissolve this cloud, rising up with hatred and displeasure for this perverse law, which always fights against the Spirit with this perverse and disordered love. After the eye of the Intellect has remained clear with the light of Faith, it will place as its object the ineffable love that God has manifested to it by means of the Incarnate Word <term>Incarnate Word</term><note>A theological term for Jesus Christ, the second person of the Trinity, taking on human flesh.</note>, His Only-Begotten Son. And this sweet and loving Word, the Immaculate Lamb, manifested it to us by means of His Blood. In this Blood the Soul becomes inebriated <note>original: "inebria"; Catherine frequently uses the metaphor of being "drunk" with the Blood of Christ to describe mystical ecstasy.</note>, seeing it shed for her with such a fire of Love. In this Blood she knows eternal life; that to fulfill this truth in the Soul and give us the end for which He created us, He gives and permits that the World, the Devil <note>original: "Dimonio"</note>, and the enemy of our Flesh should molest us, solely so that our affection does not expand to place its end in the World nor in our own sensuality; but so that it might rise from the dark thorns of the World, from these transitory delights, which truly are thorns and pass away like the wind. Oh, how mad and foolish is he who places his desire and affection there! One should not place it there for anything; rather, the Creature who has reason within itself must appreciate them for what they are worth and no more; to love them and hold them for God, and not without God, using them as a thing lent and not as one's own, with the grace and affection of—

III. But where shall we find it? In the holy knowledge of ourselves <term>self-knowledge</term><note>A central theme in Catherine’s spirituality; she taught that the soul must enter the "cell of self-knowledge" to recognize its own nothingness and God's infinite goodness.</note>, seeing ourselves loved before we even existed; for the love that God had for us constrained Him to create us in His image and likeness. In ourselves we find the blood that manifested the love God has for us—in which Blood we received our redemption—and having lost the state of Grace <note>original: "Gratia"</note>, we were re-created to grace. We are that vessel which has received the Blood, because it was shed for us alone. Therefore, let us not depart from the dwelling of self-knowledge, in which light—through the affection of Charity that we shall acquire from that light—we will bear [all things] with true and real patience. We shall not despise or shrink from hardships in whatever way they come to us, but accept them with love; because through love we see that He gives them to us, and not out of hatred—not so that we lose our salvation, but so that we may acquire it. Therefore, I desire, my dearest and sweetest Daughter <note>original: "Figliuola"</note>, that you strive with great diligence to acquire this love with the light of Faith <note>original: "Fede"</note>. Remain in the delight of Charity, for otherwise the children of the virtues would not be born alive, but dead, and we would ruin in this life the earnest-money <note>original: "arra"; a legal term for a down-payment or pledge, here used to describe the soul's current spiritual state as a precursor to eternity.</note> of Hell <note>original: "Inferno"</note>.

IV. Considering within myself that there was no other way, I said that I desired to see you founded in true and perfect Charity. This will make you bear every hardship; and God, who is no despiser of holy desire or of the hardships you will bear for the glory and praise of His Name, will take away our hardships or bring them to an end or a limit, by our putting an end to our own will, so that it may accord with the sweet will of God.

V. I do not want you to fall into confusion of mind, nor into despair because of any temptation or trouble that the Devil <note>original: "Dimonio"</note> might want to give you, putting foul and diverse fantasies into your mind with many dishonest thoughts; but with a true hope and living faith, embrace the Most Holy Cross <note>original: "Santissima Croce"</note>, where you will see that these things are given to you out of love, and He gives you no more than you are able to bear. And I want you to know...

# To Lady Stricca, widow of Cione di Sandro de' Salimbeni. <note>The Salimbeni were one of the most powerful and wealthy noble families in Siena.</note>

**I.** She exhorts her to the virtue of patience, demonstrating how it is acquired through the light of Holy Faith, by which we know the love of God toward us, and that all tribulations and prosperity come to us from God for our own good.

to [slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious blood, desiring to see in you a living faith, in which we recognize] <note>The sentence completes a standard formula used by Catherine: "servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ."</note> that God is God; and that he has created us in his image and likeness; that he has given us the Word of his Only-begotten Son, born in the sweet Womb of Mary, and died on the wood of the Most Holy Cross to take death from us and give us the life of Grace, which we lost through the disobedience of Adam; and through the obedience of the Word, we all receive Grace, just as before we all received death through the first sin. I say then that as soon as the Soul has so sweetly acquired the light of Faith—seeing such ineffable love as God bears for her, and that to give us hope for our resurrection (which we shall have on the last day of Judgment), he has manifested his own resurrection—the Soul falls in love with such light and such sweetness of love as she sees God has for her. She begins to see with this same eye <note>The "eye of the intellect" or "eye of faith" is a recurring metaphor in Catherine’s writings for spiritual perception.</note> that God wants nothing other than our sanctification; and whatever he gives us and permits in this life, he gives for this end: tribulations and consolations, insults, mocks, and slights, persecutions of the World, and temptations of the Devil, hunger and thirst, infirmity and poverty, prosperity and delights—he permits everything for our good. 

Wherefore he permits wealth to us so that we may be dispensers to the poor; and delights and worldly status, not so that we may lift our heads in pride, but rather we ought all the more to humble ourselves with a holy thanksgiving for Divine Goodness. Tribulation, from whatever side it comes, and poverty, he gives to us so that we may reach true and perfect patience, and so we may know the little firmness and stability of the World, so that we may remove our affection and desire from it and place them only in God with true and real virtues; thus we shall receive the fruit of our labors. For every labor that we sustain for his love is rewarded, and the fruit of everlasting life is preserved for us—where there is life without death, and light without darkness, satiety without boredom, and hunger without pain.

Thus says **Saint Augustine**:
> "Far removed is boredom from satiety, and pain from hunger; in the next life every good is rewarded, and every fault is punished." <note>original: "dilonga è el fastidio dalla satietà, e la pena dalla fame, nell'altra vita ogni bene è remunerato, & ogni colpa è punita."</note>

Therefore the Soul that has this living **Faith** brings forth true and holy works, and is truly patient in sustaining every pain and labor for God, and for the remission of her sins. Furthermore, she holds every pain in reverence, considering who he is,

him who gives them, why he gives them, and to whom he gives them. Who is he who gives them? It is God, the supreme and eternal Goodness, who gives not out of hatred, but out of singular love. Thus he said to his disciples: <note>original: "Io vi mando..." This refers to Christ’s commissioning of the Apostles, warning them of coming trials.</note> I send you to be persecuted and martyred in the world, not out of hatred, but out of singular love; and with that same love with which my Father has loved me, I love you. For love, as has been said, and for our sanctification, so that we may be sanctified in him. And who are we, to whom these labors are given? We are those who "are not," <note>Catherine frequently uses the ontological distinction that God is "He who is" and humans are "those who are not" (nothingness) without Him.</note> but through our own fault we are worthy of a hundred thousand hells, if we could receive so many; because since we offend the infinite Good, an infinite punishment should follow. Yet God, in his mercy, punishes us in finite time, giving us finite pain; for tribulations in this life last only as long as time itself, and no longer. Therefore, every great labor is small because of the brevity of time.

II. Our time, say the Saints, is but the point of a needle. A man's life is as <term>nothing</term> <note>original: "cavelle," a Sienese dialect term for "nothing" or "naught."</note>, so little is it. Therefore, every great labor is small; the labor that is past we no longer possess, and that which is to come we are not certain to have, because we are not certain of having the time. Only this present point exists for us, and no more. Arise then, sweetest daughter, from your sleep, and let us sleep no longer, but follow with living faith the footprints of Christ Crucified with true and holy patience. Bathe yourself in the Blood of Christ Crucified. I say no more. Remain in the holy and sweet love of God. Sweet Jesus. Jesus Love.

Indeed, it was not only a woman's name, but also a man's, as Dante mentions a certain Stricca Marescotti, <margin>Inferno, Canto 29.</margin> who with Niccolò Salimbeni and Sano Maconi were leaders of a famous <term>Company</term> <note>Known as the "Brigata Godereccia" or Spendthrift Brigade, this was a group of wealthy Sienese youths famous for their profligacy.</note> called the "Joyful Brigade," formed of noble youth for the purpose of having a grand time in the most lavish banquets and other excessive expenses. The husband of the aforementioned woman, named Cione, was a man of great authority in the <term>Republic</term> <note>Referring to the Republic of Siena.</note>, but restless and fierce. To seek vengeance for the death of a member of his family, he took up arms against his homeland and broke its squadrons, which were encamped at the <margin>Malavolti, Part 1, Book 8, page 142.</margin> Castle of Boccheggiano, receiving encouragement from the Abbot of the Great Monastery, who was the Pope's Vicar in Perugia; he later laid down his arms after the Republic <margin>The same author, in the place cited, page 147.</margin> of Florence intervened to mediate peace. He then came into discord with Agnolino Salimbeni, head of that family, and gave him much trouble in the enterprise of the Castle of Montorio, which had been entrusted by the Sienese to the valor and prudence of that lord. 

Of no less authority, and even greater <margin>Malavolti, Part 1, Book 10, page 196.</margin> power, was his son Niccolò, called Cocco; it is recorded that in 1404 he ruled over Chiusi, Radicofani, and the neighboring lands and castles. The daughter of Cocco, named <margin>Pompeo Sarnelli, Title 34.</margin> Antonia, was the consort of Francesco Casale, Lord of Cortona, and later of the famous Sforza Attendolo of Cotignola, and she was the mother of Buoso Sforza, Count of Santa Fiora, from whom the other counts and lords of the said branch of this most noble lineage are derived.

# To Lady Franceschina in Lucca

I. An exhortation to be a Servant and Daughter of Jesus Christ, to love His Cross, and to grow always in Charity and in other virtues with true perseverance, in imitation of Saint Mary Magdalene.
II. Concerning the love of Jesus Christ toward us, demonstrating how we are compelled to love Him in return.

## Letter 347.

### In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary.

**T**o you, most beloved and dearest Sister and Daughter in Christ sweet Jesus: I, Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, write to you and comfort you in His precious Blood, with a desire to see you a true servant and Daughter of the sweet and good Jesus, bathed and clothed in the Blood of the Son of God, so that every garment of self-love may be stripped from you, as well as every negligence and ignorance. Wherefore I want you to follow that sweet and enamored <term>Magdalene</term> <note>Saint Mary Magdalene was Catherine's primary model for the "apostolic" and "contemplative" life; she often refers to her as the "enamored" one who found total transformation through Christ's love.</note>, who never detached herself from the Tree of the Most Holy Cross, but with perseverance she became inebriated and bathed in the Blood of the Son of God. She so filled her memory, her heart, and her understanding that she could never turn to love anything else but Christ Jesus. 

In this way, I want you to act until the very end of your life, growing from virtue to virtue, and not ceasing to persevere through your days like a true pilgrim, not turning back for any weariness. Do not sit down out of negligence, but I want you to take up the staff of the Most Holy Cross—where all the virtues are planted and founded—beholding the <term>Lamb bled dry</term> <note>original: "Agnello svenato." This refers to the visceral image of Christ as the sacrificial lamb whose lifeblood was completely poured out.</note> for us with such a most burning fire. This fire should burn and consume every coldness and hardness of heart, or any self-love that might remain in the Soul. Oh, how could the Spouse <note>The "Spouse" refers to the individual soul in its mystical marriage to Christ.</note> fail to follow the footsteps of her Spouse, that is, with love...

to endure, and to walk the way of suffering in whatever way God grants it to us. Now rise up with patience and true humility to follow the <term>gentle Lamb</term> <note>original: "Agnello mansueto." A favorite title Catherine used for Christ, emphasizing His submissive sacrifice.</note> with a generous, broad, and charitable heart, and abandon yourself for Him. Learn from Jesus himself, who, to give us the life of grace, lost the love of His own body <note>meaning He sacrificed His physical life and well-being</note>; and as a sign of His generosity, He opened His whole self. This mercy gives grace and leads to everlasting life, where there is life without death, fullness without boredom, hunger without pain, and perfect, complete joy without any bitterness. There, the taste and the appetite of the creature are satisfied.

### II.
O inestimable and ineffable <term>Charity</term> <note>original: "Carità." Catherine uses this term to describe the selfless, agonizingly intense love of God for humanity.</note>, who forced you to give us this true good? Only your measureless love, with which you created your creature—not because of any debt you owed, for we are obligated to you, not you to us. But consider, most beloved sister in Christ sweet Jesus, that the soul cannot come to such a great good as seeing God if first, in this life, it does not strive to taste Him through most ardent and burning love, which love encloses and draws to itself all virtues. No virtue is lacking to the soul that is wounded by the arrow of <term>Divine Charity</term>, which Charity is acquired at the <term>Table of the Most Holy Cross</term>, where the <term>immaculate Lamb</term> is the table, the food, and the servant. 

Now, how could the soul restrain itself from loving its sweet Savior, seeing itself so loved by Him? It is the custom and habit of love to always return love for love, and the thing that loves is transformed into the beloved. Thus the <term>Soul as Bride of Christ</term>, seeing herself loved by Him, should show that she wishes to return the favor by rendering love to Him; that is, that for love she might want to bear pains and reproaches for Him. Thus she is transformed and becomes one thing with Him through love and desire, and she loves what God loves, and hates what God hates, because she sees that sweet Jesus took supreme delight in carrying the Cross of many labors for the love of...

## Letter 348.

> ->In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary.<-

**T**o you, daughter in Christ sweet Jesus: I, Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, write and comfort you in His precious Blood with the desire to see you united and transformed in the fire of <term>Divine Charity</term> <note>original: "Divina Carità." This refers to the selfless, supernatural love of God.</note>, in such a way that there may be no creature nor any other thing that separates you from that Charity. ### III.

Now, in this way I want you and the others to love: look only toward giving honor to God and giving your labor to your neighbor; for though it may seem a hardship to you to see that thing which one loves taken away, nevertheless it is accepted without weariness if it is true love, founded only on the honor of God, and regards the salvation of the soul more than itself. Act, act, so that I may no longer see you in pain, for this would be an intermediary <note>original: "mezzo." Catherine uses this term to describe anything that stands between the soul and God. And truly it seems that it acts like the Master <term>Mason</term> <note>original: "Maestro." Then this wall is preserved, because they are many Creatures, and they are <margin>1 Corinthians 9</margin> one. *(A) By ancient tradition, it is held that Saint Catherine, during her stay in Lucca, was hosted by the Lords Balbani—whose family is among the ancient and illustrious of that city—in a villa not far from there; there is no record of where she stayed when she was in the city itself. She went there from Pisa in the year 1375, as was observed in the annotations to the first letter (page 200), and there she formed friendships with various people, and particularly with this lady, her hostess. Since this lady was exceedingly grieved by Catherine's departure, it may be believed that shortly thereafter she revealed the bitterness of her soul to the Saint; hence this letter, which is a reply, likely dates from that same year, or the first months of the following.*

*(B) "Go to that most sweet and venerable Cross." These adjectives of "most sweet" and "venerable," which the Saint applies to the Cross, seem not to be given to just any cross, but specifically to that one which is venerated with such piety in the city of Lucca, to which she exhorts this Lucchese lady to have recourse in her needs. Although it is not a simple Cross—as it also features the image or statue of the Crucified Lord, which is also called the <term>Holy Face</term> <note>original: "Volto Santo"; a famous cedar-wood crucifix in Lucca, traditionally believed to have been carved by Nicodemus.</note>—nevertheless, everyone calls it the Holy Cross. It was already held in the highest veneration before the time of Saint Catherine, as can be seen from the writings of Dante <note>Dante Alighieri (c. 1265–1321), the author of the Divine Comedy.</note>, who died in the year 1321, in those verses of his where he speaks of a man from Lucca:*

After having been hidden for over 700 years in the Holy Places of Palestine, through a heavenly sign, the Holy Crucifix was revealed to <margin>Cesare Franciotti, *Lives of the Saints of Lucca*.</margin> a Piedmontese Bishop, <unclear>who was</unclear> in those parts to venerate the memories of our Redemption. By him, it was placed upon a vessel <note>The original Italian "Legno" (wood) here refers to a wooden ship or boat.</note> under the guidance of Divine Providence, and it came to the port of the ancient and now-destroyed city of Luni. However, Heaven did not wish to favor that city with such a beautiful treasure, as it was already destined for the city of Lucca; God's will was revealed through miraculous events. Thus, it arrived in Lucca at the end of the eighth century, where by new miracles it chose for itself its own location. This is the very spot where, several centuries later, Pope Alexander II—who was at that same time still the Bishop of Lucca—built the Cathedral Church in honor of Saint Martin the Bishop. In this magnificent temple, this miraculous <term>Simulacrum<gloss>A sacred statue or physical representation of a holy figure.</gloss></term> of the Crucified Lord is still venerated today.

# To Lady Colomba in Lucca
<note>Monna (Lady) Colomba was a widow in Lucca and a follower of Catherine.</note>

I. She exhorts her to give a good example, making herself a mirror of virtue, and detests the bad example given in the world by men.
II. That one must not have regard for friends or relatives in the exercise of virtue, but only for Jesus Christ.
III. Of the losing and finding of Jesus Christ in the Temple, and how we also must find Him.
IV. She exhorts her to mercy toward the poor, to true obedience, to the negation of her own will, and to the contempt of herself, and to all the other virtues that befit widows to be true spouses of Christ.

## Letter 349.

### In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of Sweet Mary.

I. **T**o you, most beloved sister and daughter in Christ sweet Jesus: I, Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, write in His precious Blood with the desire to see that you might be a fruitful field, yielding fruit by receiving the seed of the word of God for yourself and for others. Since you are now old in the world and loosened from the bonds of secular life <note>original: "Secolo." In this context, it refers to the worldly life outside of religious orders or strict spiritual devotion.</note>, you should be a mirror of virtue to the young women who are still bound in the world by the bonds of their husbands. Alas, alas, I perceive that we are unfruitful ground, allowing the seed of God's word to be choked by the thorns and briers of disordered affections and worldly desires, walking along the path of its delights and pleasures, striving to please creatures rather than the Creator. And there is even greater misery: our own evil is not enough for us, but where we ought to be an example of virtue and honesty, we set ourselves as an example of sin and vanity. It seems that just as the Demon did not wish to fall alone but wanted much company, so too do we invite others to those same vanities, delights, and pleasures that are within us. You must withdraw <margin>yourselves</margin>

**II.** Perhaps you would make some excuse by saying: "It is only right that I should condescend to my relatives and friends and do this, otherwise they would be troubled and scandalized against me." And thus fear and perverse pleasure take life from us and often give us death; they take away the perfection to which God elects and calls us. This excuse is not acceptable to God, for we must not condescend to men in anything that offends God and our soul; nor should we love or serve them except in those things that are in God and according to our state. Alas, miserable, wretched me! Was it relatives, or friends, or any creature who redeemed us? No: only Christ Crucified was that Lamb who, with ineffable love, bled and opened His Body, giving Himself to us as a bath, as medicine, as food, as clothing, and as a bed where we can rest. He did not look to His own self-love or sensory delight, but with pain, sustaining insults and shames, He humbled Himself, seeking the honor of the Father and our salvation. It is not right that we, miserable and wretched, should hold to any other path than that which the first sweet Truth <note>Catherine frequently uses the term 'Sweet Truth' or 'First Truth' to refer to Jesus Christ.</note> held.

**III.** You know that God is not found in luxuries and delights. Hear what it says: that He was lost while going to the Feast. <meta>This page continues Letter 349 from Saint Catherine of Siena to Monna Colomba of Lucca. Having just argued that one must not offend God to please relatives, Catherine now explains how to find God through the "bitterness" of repentance and the internal "temple" of the soul.</meta>

let us seek Him with her <note>Likely referring to Mary, who searched for the child Jesus in the Temple after He was missing for three days.</note>, that is, with bitterness; the grief and displeasure for the fault committed against our Creator in order to condescend to the will of Creatures. It is necessary for us, then, to go to the Temple, and there He is found. Let our heart, our affection, and our desire rise up with this company of bitterness, and go to the Temple of her Soul, and there let her know herself. Then, knowing that she herself is nothing <note>A core tenet of Catherine's mysticism: the soul is "she who is not," while God is "He who is."</note>, she will know the goodness of God within her, who is He who is. Then the will will rise up with diligence, and will love what God loves, and will hate what He hates. Then the memory, standing to debate within itself, will reprimand the things it has received into itself—the delights and pleasures of the World—and how it has not received nor reserved within itself the graces, Gifts, and great benefits of God, who has given Himself to us with such a fire of love. It will reprimand the intellect, which has given itself more readily to understanding the will of Creatures and observing the opinions of the World than the will of its Creator; and thus the will and sensory love have turned to loving and desiring these coarse, sensory things that pass away like the wind. She must not do this, but must understand and know the will of God, who

God did not release you from the World <note>By making her a widow.</note> so that you would be suffocated and drowned in the World by your affection and disordered desire. Now, do you have anything other than one Soul? No; for if you had two, you could give one to God and the other to the World; nor do you have more than one Body, and this will be worn out by every slight thing.

# To Lady Franceschina, and to Lady Caterina, and to two other spiritual companions in Lucca.

I. She exhorts them to the virtue of charity, and to follow Jesus Christ by the way of the Holy Cross as His true spouses.
II. How the true spouse of Christ must be persevering in virtue and recover lost time.

## Letter 350.

->*In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary.*<-

<margin>To the Romans 12 <note>original: "Ad Rom. 12." — Referring to St. Paul's exhortations on living a Christian life.</note></margin>
**T**o you, most beloved and dearest daughters and sisters of mine in Christ Jesus: I, Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of God <note>Catherine adopted this humble title, used by Popes, to emphasize her role as a spiritual messenger</note>, write and comfort you all in the precious Blood of the Son of God, with the desire to see you as true daughters and spouses consecrated to the Eternal Spouse, who with such fire of charity gave His life for us. Act in this way, then, and manfully <note>In medieval spirituality, "manfully" (virilmente) meant acting with courage and strength of spirit, regardless of one's gender</note>, and with most burning desire follow the banner of the Most Holy Cross; that is, follow His footsteps by way of pain, and torments, and loving desires. For the Son must always delight in following the Father, and the spouse her husband: hence if He suffers pain, she conforms herself to Him in pain; and if He has delight, she conforms herself in delight. Just as the Apostle Paul, enamored [of Christ], said of himself: *I rejoice with those who rejoice, and I weep with those who weep* <note>original: "Io godo con coloro, che godono, e piango con coloro, che piangono" — a paraphrase of Romans 12:15</note>. This is what the soul does when it remains in perfect charity, and by doing so, the word of this same Apostle Paul is fulfilled in it; that is, whoever shares in the tribulation—which is the Cross of Christ—will share in the consolations—which is to say, they will be in Glory with Christ. Reasonably, God will give them His inheritance, because for love they have left behind the worldly inheritance and the cares of the world, and left behind worldly delight and consolations, following the Cross

I pray you therefore, for the love of Christ Crucified, that since our sweet and good Jesus is so courteous and generous, we should delay no longer, but take into our hands the brevity of our time, and recover with sorrow and holy bitterness the time lost and spent with little diligence; and in this way, we shall acquire the time passed. I say no more. I pray the Primary Truth <note>Catherine's characteristic name for God, emphasizing that all reality and goodness stem from Him.</note> that He may increase you from virtue to virtue until you reach that end, where there is life without death, satiety without boredom, hunger without pain, joy without sadness, and where there is every good without any evil. May the peace of God be always in your souls. Remain in the holy and sweet love of God. Sweet Jesus. Jesus, Jesus.

# To Lady Bartolomea, Wife of Salvatico of Lucca.

I. She exhorts her to the virtue of Charity, and to the Love of God, showing how patience and the desire to suffer for the love of Christ must proceed from it.
II. How we must strip ourselves of our own will, and place it in God in all tribulations.
III. She exhorts her to Humility and the abasement of herself.
IV. She encourages her to persevere in her holy purpose.
V. Concerning three Virtues necessary for perseverance.
VI. She encourages her to despise worldly opinions, following the example of Saint Mary Magdalene.

## Letter 351.

### In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary, Mother of the Son of God.

I. **T**o you, most beloved and dearest Sister in Christ Jesus, I Catherine, Servant and Slave of the Servants of Jesus Christ, write in His precious Blood with the desire to see you always feeding and nourishing yourself at the breast of the gentle Mother Charity <note>Catherine frequently personifies "Charity" (divine love) as a mother who breastfeeds the soul with the "milk" of Christ’s blood and grace.</note>, considering that without this milk, which this glorious Mother gives us, no one can have life. She is so sweet and so gentle to the soul who tastes her, that everything bitter in her becomes sweet, and every great burden light. I do not wonder that it is so; because by staying in this charity and love, one stays in God.
<margin>1 John 4 <note>original: "1 Jo 4." — A reference to 1 John 4:16: "God is love, and whoever abides in love abides in God, and God abides in him."</note></margin>
Thus says Saint John, that God is Charity, and he who stays in charity stays in God, and God in him. Therefore, having God, one cannot have any bitterness, because He is the supreme delight, supreme sweetness, and joy; and this is the reason why the Servants of God always rejoice. Hence, even if they are sick they rejoice, or in hunger, or in thirst, or poor, or afflicted, or troubled, or persecuted by creatures—even if everyone

### III. 
I desire, therefore, that we lift from ourselves the burden of every worldly vanity and of self-love. Do you know why it says that the gate through which we must pass is narrow? Because we must restrict <note>The Italian *ristregnere* implies both narrowing and restraining.</note> our love and our desires for every delight and consolation of the world, and transform ourselves into that sweet Mother of Charity, as was said before. I say that you must bow your head because the gate is low; for if you carried it high, you would break it. You must bow through holy and true humility, considering that God humbled himself for us. You ought to consider yourself—and I want you to consider yourself—the lowliest of all others, and see to it that you do not turn your head back for anything: neither for the illusions of the Devil, nor for words you might hear, whether from your spouse or from any other creature.

<margin>Luke 9 <note>original: "Luc. 9" — A reference to Luke 9:62: "No one, having put his hand to the plow, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God."</note></margin>
### IV. 
Persevere manfully <note>In Catherine’s writing, the term "manfully" (virilmente) denotes spiritual strength, courage, and maturity, regardless of the recipient's gender.</note> in the holy resolution you have begun; for you know what Christ says: Do not turn back to look at the plow, because perseverance is the thing that is crowned. Turn with affectionate love alongside that sweet, enamored Mary Magdalene, embracing that venerable and sweet Cross; there you will find sweet and royal virtues, because there we find both God and Man. Consider that the fire of Charity has pressed that venerable and sweet Body so much that <margin>Isaiah 53 <note>original: "Is. 53" — A prophecy of the Suffering Servant: "He was oppressed and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth."</note></margin> from every side he pours out Blood with such love and holy patience that the cry of this Lamb is not heard in murmuring; he is humble and despised, and sated with reproaches. Let your heart and your soul be split open by the heat of love at this breast of Charity by means of the flesh of Christ Crucified. In no other way could you taste or possess virtue, because he is the way and the truth, and whoever holds to it cannot be deceived. Make up your mind that even if the whole world were against you, you—with a manful and royal heart—must not turn your head back, but stand forward with your shield in hand to receive the blows.

### V. 
You know that a shield has three corners; likewise, it is necessary for you to have three virtues within yourself: hatred and displeasure for the offense you have committed...

### VI.
There is no blow, whether from the Devil or from a creature, that can harm you if you have this shield of hatred, love, and true patience; for these are those three strong columns that preserve the soul and take away its weakness. The sweet Magdalene <note>Saint Mary Magdalene, who Catherine often presents as a model of the "inebriated" lover of God.</note> took up this path in such a way that she no longer saw herself; rather, with a royal heart, she clothed herself in **Christ Crucified**. She no longer desired status, nor greatness, nor her vanities; she lost every pleasure and delight of the world. In her, no other care or thought could be found except for the way in which she could follow Christ. And as soon as she placed her affection in Him and knew herself, she embraced Him and took the path of lowliness. She despised herself for God’s sake because she saw that she could not follow Him or please Him by any other way. She considered herself to be the lowest creature to be found. Like a woman who is drunk <note>A reference to "sober intoxication," where the soul is so filled with divine love that it appears "drunk" or oblivious to the world.</note>, she no longer noticed whether she was alone or accompanied; for if she had noticed, she would not have stayed among those soldiers of Pilate, but she went and remained alone at the Monument <note>The Tomb of Christ.</note>. Love did not let her think: "How will I appear? Will evil be said of me because I am beautiful and of high standing?" She does not think of this here, but only of how she can find and follow her Master. Now, this is the companion whom I give to you, and whom I want you to follow, because she knew the way so well that she has been made a Teacher for us.

Run, my daughter and my daughters! Do not stay asleep any longer, for time runs and does not wait a moment. I do not wish to say more. Comfort Lady Colomba <note>Madonna Colomba of Rieti, a contemporary mystic and follower of Catherine's spirit.</note>, to whom I send word as I do to you, and also to Mon—

...so that we may taste His supreme and eternal good. Therefore, only God can satisfy the soul.

## II.

In Him the soul finds peace, in Him she rests; for she can neither desire nor want anything that she does not find in God. Finding Him, she lacks for nothing, for she finds the wisdom to know how to give to her, and the will to want to give to her. And we experience this, because not only does He give to us when we ask, but He gave to us even before we existed; for without us ever praying to Him, He created us in His image and likeness, and recreated us in grace through the **Blood of His Son**. <note>In Catherine’s theology, "recreation" refers to the Redemption—mankind was created once at the beginning, and "recreated" or restored through the sacrifice of Jesus.</note>

Thus the Soul finds peace in Him and in no other, for He is supreme wealth, supreme Wisdom, supreme Goodness, and supreme Beauty. He is an inestimable good; for there is no one who can estimate His goodness, greatness, and delight; but He alone understands and values Himself. Therefore, He can, does, and wills to satisfy or fulfill the holy desires of anyone who wishes to strip themselves of the **World** and clothe themselves in Him. 

Therefore, I do not want us to sleep any longer, my dearest daughter, but let us rouse ourselves from sleep, for our time is continually drawing closer to death. I want you to regard transitory and temporal things and creatures as things for use, loving them and holding them as borrowed items <note>original: "cose prestate"</note>, and not as your own property. You will do this by detaching your affection from them, and not otherwise; and it is necessary to detach oneself if we wish to participate in the fruit of the **Blood of Christ Crucified**. 

Hence, considering that there is no other way, I said that I desired to see your heart and your affection stripped of the **World**. Therefore, my dearest daughter, detach yourself entirely from these bonds <note>original: "legacci," referring to worldly attachments or "ties" that bind the soul.</note>, so that you may be a true servant of **Christ Crucified**, and follow His most sweet will; this will invites you to the wedding of eternal life, for He desires nothing other than your **sanctification**. <margin>Matthew 25</margin> 

But take heed, dearest daughter, that you must be like those wise Virgins, and not like the foolish ones, who delayed until the very end to provide for their lamps, and because of their delay, they later found the door locked; but the wise and diligent ones, because they had heeded the invitation of the **Bridegroom** and loved Him, provided for themselves before their time ran out. You, then, who ought to be a **faithful Bride**, <meta>catchword: ought to (debbi)</meta>

<summary>Catherine exhorts Lady Bartolomea to find total satisfaction in God rather than the world, using the Parable of the Ten Virgins to emphasize the urgency of spiritual preparation before death.</summary>
