<meta>This page continues Letter 351 from Catherine of Siena to Lady Bartolomea. The previous page established that the soul can only find rest in God and must detach itself from "borrowed" worldly things to participate in divine grace.</meta>

...insults, hunger, and thirst, cold, and heat, even unto the shameful death of the **Cross**; and by that death, He returned honor to the Father, and we were restored to grace. Man seeks to please **Creatures** <note>In Catherine’s writing, "creatures" refers to any created thing or person other than God.</note>, not caring if he displeases the **Creator**; but Christ sought nothing except to fulfill the obedience of the Eternal Father for our salvation. He embraced and clothed Himself in **voluntary poverty** <term>voluntary poverty: the spiritual practice of choosing to live without material wealth to better imitate the life of Jesus</term>, while the **World** seeks great riches. 

There is a great difference, then, between the one and the other; and therefore it is necessary that if the heart is stripped of God, it must be full of the World; and if it is stripped of the World, it must be full of God. As our Savior said: 
<margin>Matthew 6</margin> 
"No one can serve two masters; for if he serves one, he is displeasing to the other." <note>A reference to Matthew 6:24: "No one can serve two masters... You cannot serve God and mammon."</note> We must, therefore, with great diligence lift our heart and affection from this tyrant that is the World, and place it—entirely free, pure, and without any intermediary—in God; not with a divided heart or a love kept secret, because He is our sweet God, who keeps His eye upon us and sees the hidden secrets of the heart. 

Our simplicity and foolishness are far too great, for we see that God sees us, and that He is a just Judge who punishes every fault and rewards every good; yet we remain as if blinded, without any fear. We wait for a time that we do not have, nor are we certain of having; instead, we go on constantly attaching ourselves to things. If God cuts one branch away from us, we simply grab another. We care more about not losing these transitory things, which pass away like the wind, and these **Creatures**, than we care about losing God. 

All this happens because of the disordered love we have placed in ourselves. Thus, by holding and possessing things outside of the will of God in this life, we taste the down payment <note>original: "arra"—a legal or commercial term for a deposit paid to confirm a contract; Catherine uses it to mean a "foretaste" of the afterlife.</note> of **Hell**. For God has permitted that anyone who loves inordinately shall become unbearable to themselves. Such a person always has war in their **Soul** and in their body; for they suffer pain over what they possess, for fear of losing it, and they exhaust themselves day and night to preserve it so it does not fail them. And they suffer pain over what they do not have, because they hunger to possess it; and not having it, they suffer. 

Thus, the soul never finds rest in these things of the **World**, because they are all "less" than the soul itself. They were made for us, and not we for them; for we are made for God...

*The name Peronella is a corruption of Petronilla, as the Saint was adapting to the manner of speaking used in Naples; for in Siena, the name Petronilla becomes Petornella, not Peronella. -> [ B ] <-

He was sent to Naples by the Saint for important matters for the benefit of Holy Church, as she herself wrote to the Blessed Stefano Maconi in Letter 263. However, the letter she refers to here is lost, since in none of the eleven letters written to this Neri that survive does she mention what is alluded to here.*

<meta>This page begins Letter 353, written by Catherine of Siena to three devout women in Naples. It follows a letter to Lady Bartolomea (also a Neapolitan resident) and continues Catherine’s mission of providing spiritual direction to laywomen through the metaphor of spiritual nursing and the necessity of suffering to achieve true charity.</meta>

# To Three Spiritual Neapolitan Women.

<margin>a.</margin> **S**he exhorts them to the Virtue of Charity, demonstrating how this is drawn from the Humanity of Christ Crucified, and from it is born the desire for suffering and for dishonor. Of the effects of the same, and how we must end our lives in weeping to pray to God to illuminate the Holy Church.

## Letter 353.

->In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary.<-

**D**earest Mothers and Daughters in sweet Christ Jesus, I, Catherine, Servant and Slave of the Servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in his precious **Blood** <note>For Catherine, the "Blood of Christ" represents the ultimate expression of God's love and the source of all spiritual life.</note> with the desire to see you founded in perfect **Charity** <term>Charity: From the Latin *caritas*, meaning a selfless, divine love for God and neighbor.</term>, so that you may be true nurses and governors of your Souls; for we could never nourish our neighbor if we did not first nourish our own Soul with true and real virtues. And one cannot be nourished by virtue if one does not first attach oneself to the breast of divine Charity, from which breast the milk of divine sweetness is drawn. 

For you, dearest Sisters, it is necessary to do as the Child does, who, wanting to take milk, takes the Mother's breast and puts it in his mouth, whereby through the medium of the flesh he draws the milk to himself. This is what we must do if we wish to nourish our Soul: we must attach ourselves to the breast of **Christ Crucified**, in whom is the **Mother of Charity** <note>Catherine frequently uses maternal imagery, describing Christ's side-wound as a breast that feeds the soul.</note>; and through the medium of his Flesh we will draw to ourselves the milk that nourishes the Soul and the children of true Virtues. This is done through the Humanity of Christ; because it was upon his Humanity that the pain fell, and not upon his Divinity. We cannot nourish ourselves on this milk, which we draw from the Mother of Charity, without pain; and the pains are of different kinds. Often they are the pains of great battles with the **Devil**, or persecutions from Creatures with much infamy, mistreatment, and injury; these are pains

<summary>Catherine uses the vivid metaphor of a nursing infant to describe how the soul must draw spiritual nourishment from the wounds of Christ. She explains that true charity is inseparable from the willingness to endure suffering and persecution.</summary>

in them, but not in the **Soul**, which has set itself to nourish at this sweet and glorious breast, from which it has drawn love—seeing in **Christ Crucified** the ineffable love that God has shown us by means of this sweet and loving **Word** <term>Word: Referring to the "Verbo" or the Son of God, the second person of the Trinity.</term>, and in that love it has found hatred for its own guilt and for its perverse law, which always fights against the Spirit. But above all other pains borne by the Soul that has come to this desire of hatred, are the excruciating and loving desires that it feels for the salvation of the whole World. For **Charity** does this: she becomes sick with those who are sick, and she is healthy with those who are healthy; she weeps with those who weep, and she rejoices with those who rejoice <note>A paraphrase of Romans 12:15, a favorite scripture of Catherine's to illustrate perfect empathy.</note>; that is, she weeps with those who are in the time of weeping for mortal sin, and rejoices with those who rejoice in the state of grace. Then she has taken up the Flesh of **Christ Crucified**, bearing the Cross with him with pain—not an afflictive pain that withers the Soul, but a pain that "fattens" it <note>Catherine uses "ingrassa" (fattens) to describe how spiritual suffering, unlike worldly stress, nourishes and strengthens the soul's virtues.</note>, delighting and striving to follow his doctrine and his footsteps; and thus she tastes the milk of divine sweetness. And with what has she taken it? With the mouth of holy desire. So much so that, if it were possible for her to have this milk without pain, and with it give life to the virtues—which all have life from the milk of "ablaze" Charity—she would not want it. Rather, she chooses to want it with

pain for the love of **Christ Crucified**; because it does not seem right to her that under a **thorny head** there should remain **delicate members** <note>Catherine is quoting St. Bernard of Clairvaux’s famous sentiment that it is unseemly for followers of Christ to live in luxury while their "Head" (Christ) suffered on the Cross.</note>. Instead, she chooses to bear the thorn together with him, not choosing stings in her own way, but in the way of her head, Christ. By doing so, she does not carry the weight, but her head, **Christ Crucified**, is made the bearer of it. Oh, how sweet is this sweet Mother of Charity! She does not seek her own things—that is, she does not seek herself for her own sake, but herself for God’s sake—and whatever she loves and desires, she loves and desires in him and for him, and outside of him she wishes to possess nothing. In every state in which she finds herself, she spends her time doing the will of God. If she is **secular** <term>Secular: Here meaning a layperson living in the world rather than in a cloistered monastery.</term>, she wishes to be perfect in her state; if she is a **Religious** subject, she is a perfect earthly Angel in this life, and she does not crave nor place her love in the world, nor in temporal riches, not wishing to possess anything as her own, because she sees that this would go against the vow of **voluntary poverty**. whatever state the **Soul** is in, it is in a widowed state <note>In Catherine’s mystical theology, a "widowed state" refers to the soul that has detached itself from the "world" (its former spouse) to wait in purity for God, its true Bridegroom.</note>, and in every way having within itself that sweet Mother of **Charity**, <margin>a</margin> nourishing itself at the breast of **Christ Crucified**, she tastes this sweet and mild milk with burning desire and with the most perfect light; because she has cast off the darkness of the perverse and miserable self-love. # To Lady Giovanna di Corrado

I. She exhorts her to withdraw into the knowledge of herself to acquire the virtue of Charity, and to strip herself of sensory love for Created Things.
II. She consoles her regarding the difficulty she felt at the departure of Stefano.
III. That the Soul, through the knowledge of itself, becomes a delightful Garden.

## Letter 354.

-> In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of <-
-> sweet Mary. <-

**D**earest Mother in Christ sweet Jesus. I, Catherine, servant and slave of the Servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in his precious Blood with the desire to see you make a dwelling in the Cell of self-knowledge <term>Cell of self-knowledge: A central theme in Catherine’s teaching, referring to an interior mental space where one reflects on their own limitations and God's infinite grace.</term>, so that you may come to perfect love. Consider with me that he who does not love his Creator cannot please him, because He is Love itself, and wants nothing but love. This love is found by the Soul that knows itself; for seeing that it is nothing in itself, but has its very being through grace and not by right, and that every grace founded upon that being is given to us with inestimable love; then it finds within itself so much of God's goodness pouring out that the tongue is not sufficient to describe it. And once it sees itself so loved by God, it cannot help but love in return. It loves reason and God within itself, and hates sensuality <note>In Catherine's works, "sensuality" refers to the lower impulses and self-centered desires that compete with the spirit.</note>, which inordinately wants to take delight in the World—whether it delights in status, or riches, or in pleasing Created Beings more than the Creator—grounding itself in its own opinion, the delights and pleasures of the World, or its own will. There are those who love their children, some their Spouse, and others their Mother or Father inordinately with a love that is too sensory; such love acts as a barrier between the Soul and God, which does not...

<summary>In the opening of Letter 354, Catherine of Siena encourages Lady Giovanna to practice interior reflection in the "cell of self-knowledge" to overcome worldly attachments. She explains that recognizing one's existence as a gift from God, rather than a right, is the key to developing divine charity.</summary>
<keywords>self-knowledge, sensory love, Giovanna di Corrado, Stefano Maconi, divine love, sensuality, spiritual dwelling</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Letter 354 from page 730. Catherine is writing to Monna Giovanna di Corrado, mother of her secretary Stefano Maconi, explaining how interior detachment from family and the "world" actually leads to a more perfect, God-centered love for them.</meta>

...letting one clearly know the truth of true and supreme Love; <margin>Matthew 10</margin> and therefore the first sweet Truth <note>Catherine frequently uses the title "Sweet Truth" to refer to Jesus Christ.</note> said: whoever does not abandon Father and Mother, Sister and Brother, and even themselves, is not worthy of me. True servants of God well realized, and do realize, that they must immediately strip their heart, affection, and soul of the world, its pomps, and its delights, and of every creature apart from God; not that they do not love the creature, but they love it only for God’s sake, insofar as they are creatures immeasurably loved by the Creator. But just as they hate the sensory part <note>The "sensory part" refers to the lower, self-centered impulses that resist spiritual growth.</note> that rebels against God within them, so they hate it in their neighbor, whom they see offending the supreme eternal Goodness. So I wish you to do, dearest Mother in Christ sweet Jesus: love the goodness of God in you and His immeasurable Charity, which you will find in the cell of self-knowledge. In this cell you will find God, who just as God holds within Himself everything that participates in being, so in you, you will find memory, which holds and is fit to retain the treasure of God’s benefits; you will find understanding, which lets us participate in the Wisdom of the Son of God, understanding and knowing His will, which <margin>1 Thessalonians 4</margin> desires nothing but our sanctification. Seeing this, the soul cannot grieve or be disturbed by anything that happens, knowing that everything is done with God's providence and with greatest love.

## II.
With this knowledge, I want and pray you for the love of the bloodied Lamb <note>original: "svenato Agnello" — literally the "bled-out" or "slaughtered" Lamb, a visceral image of Christ’s sacrifice.</note>, to heal the eschar <term>eschar: A piece of dead tissue or a painful sore; Catherine uses this medical term as a metaphor for the raw, stinging grief of a mother’s separation from her son.</term> and the difficulty you felt because of Stefano’s departure. Rejoice and exult, for it will not be without an increase of grace in his soul and yours; by God's grace you shall see him soon. Also I say that in the knowledge of yourself, you will find the sweet clemency of the Holy Spirit, which is that part that gives nothing but love, and is nothing but love; and all that He does and works, He works for love. This affection you will find in your soul, because the will is nothing but love; every affection and movement of it moves for no other reason than love; it loves and hates what the eye of knowledge has understood and seen. Now it is truly so, dearest Mother, that within the cell of the soul you find all of God, who gives such sweetness,

refreshment and consolation, which cannot be disturbed by anything that happens, because it has been made capable of receiving the will of God.

### III.
Immediately the Soul then becomes a Garden full of fragrant flowers of Holy desire, and in the middle is planted the tree of the Most Holy Cross, where the immaculate Lamb rests; He pours out Blood, which washes and floods this sweet and glorious Garden, and He holds within Himself the mature fruits of true and royal virtues. If you want patience, meekness is founded there, to such an extent that no cry was heard <margin>Isaiah 53</margin> from the Lamb by way of any grumbling; [you will find] profound humility, seeing God humbled to Man, the Word humbled to the shameful death of the Cross. If you want Charity, He is Charity itself; even <margin>1 John 4</margin> more than the force of love and charity, it was this that held Him fastened and nailed to the Cross. Nails and the Cross were not sufficient to hold God and Man, if the power of charity had not held Him. I do not wonder if the soul, who has made herself a Garden through self-knowledge, is strong against the whole World, because she is conformed and made one thing with the supreme strength. Truly she begins to taste the earnest money <note>An "earnest money" or "pledge" (arra) refers to a partial payment given in advance as a guarantee of the full reward of heaven.</note> of eternal life in this life; she masters the World, because she mocks it. The demons fear to approach the Soul that burns in divine charity. 

Now then, dearest Mother, I do not want you to sleep any longer in negligence, nor in sensory love <note>The original "amore sensitivo" refers to love based on physical feelings and family ties rather than spiritual purpose.</note>, but with a most ardent and immeasurable love, rise up, bathing yourself in the Blood of Christ, and hiding yourself in the wounds of Christ Crucified. I say no more. I am certain that if you stay in your cell <note>The "cell" refers to the interior "cell of self-knowledge" mentioned on the previous page.</note>, as has been said, you will find nothing other than Christ Crucified; and say the same to Corrado, that he should do this very thing. Remain in the Holy and sweet love of God. Sweet Jesus, Jesus Love.

...remedy the <term>yearning</term> <note>ascaro: a regional term for a specific type of emotional longing or tender sorrow.</note>, and the difficulty, etc. *This word <term>ascaro</term>, derived from <term>ascara</term>, which is still in use today in the City of Lucca, expresses a tenderness at seeing the things one holds most dear; it is normally used to describe that grief felt when one is away from those they love most.* The Knight Scipione Bargagli <note>Scipione Bargagli (1540–1612) was a Sienese scholar and writer.</note>, in his most beautiful dialogue entitled the *Turamino* <note>Il Turamino (1602) is a celebrated work by Bargagli that discusses the Sienese dialect and its merits relative to the broader Italian language.</note>, makes mention of this word. He does not reject it, though he considers it unique to the people of Lucca. However, from this text by Saint Catherine, we see it was already used by the Sienese, and in a letter addressed to a person from Siena; therefore, it seems one must conclude that this word was common and ordinary in Siena as well during that era. The French translator, not understanding this word, believed it referred to a member of the illustrious Lascari family <note>The Lascari were a famous noble family of Byzantine origin; the translator likely saw the unfamiliar word "ascaro" and assumed it was a proper noun.</note>, translating this passage in this way:

## Letter 355.

->In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary.<-

<margin>Matthew 6.</margin> To you, dearest Sister and Daughter in Christ Jesus, I, Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in his precious Blood with the desire to see you clothed in the wedding garment <note>vestimento nuttiale: a biblical reference to the Parable of the Wedding Garment (Matthew 22), representing the soul being in a state of grace or charity.</note>; considering for myself that without this garment the Soul cannot please its Creator, nor find itself at the wedding of eternal life. I desire, therefore, that you be clothed, and so that you may better clothe yourself, I want you to strip yourself of every proper sensitive love <note>amore sensitivo proprio: self-centered emotional attachment.</note> that you have for yourself, for your Children, or for any other created thing outside of God. You must not love yourself, nor any other thing [for its own sake], because it is impossible for Man to serve two masters; if he serves one, he is discontent with the other. There is no one who can serve God and the World, because they have no conformity with each other. The World seeks honor, status, wealth, Children in high positions, nobility, pleasure, and sensitive delight, all rooted and founded in perverse pride; but God seeks and wants the exact opposite. He wants voluntary poverty, humiliation of heart, contempt for oneself and for every delight and pleasure of the World; he does not want one's own honor, but the honor of God and the salvation of one's Neighbor, and he seeks only how one may clothe oneself in the fire of most burning Charity, with the adornment of the sweet and royal

You must not wish to choose their states of life <note>original: "stati," referring to one's vocation or social position, such as entering a religious order versus remaining in the world.</note> according to your own way; for that would be a sign that you loved them outside of God; but according to the state to which God calls them, be content with that. For often the Mother who loves her Children in the perversity of the World says: "It pleases me well that my Children should please God, and they can serve Him just as well in the World as in another state."

This is because such pride and ignorance reigns in those who act this way, wishing to impose laws and rules upon the **Holy Spirit** who calls them. These people do not love them in God, but with a self-centered sensory love outside of God; for they love the bodies more than their souls. Never, most beloved **Sister** and Daughter in Christ sweet Jesus, could one clothe oneself in Christ...

Come now, sweetest Daughter, let us delay no longer; let us recover the lost time with true and perfect love; so that in this life, by clothing ourselves through grace in the aforementioned garment, we may enjoy and exult in the wedding of the lasting life—you together with the Spouse and your children;

II. # To Nanna, daughter of Benincasa, a young virgin, her niece in Florence. <note>Nanna was the daughter of Catherine’s brother, Benincasa. Catherine often wrote to her family members to guide their spiritual development.</note>

I. She teaches her the true way to be a Bride of Jesus Christ in imitation of the wise virgins described in the Gospel, demonstrating what her lamp must be—namely, her own Heart.
II. That inside this lamp one must pour the oil of Humility, which is acquired through the knowledge of oneself.
III. That one must join the knowledge of the divine Goodness within us.
IV. Of the light of the Most Holy Faith, with which this lamp must be lit.
V. Of the mortification <note>In this context, the discipline or "putting to death" of physical desires to strengthen the spirit.</note> of the senses of the Body.
VI. Of Charity, which we must have for God above all things.
VII. Of fleeing the praise and applause of Men.

## Letter 356.

-> In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary. <-

<margin>Matthew 25.</margin>
I. **D**earest daughter in sweet Christ Jesus, I Catherine, servant and slave of the Servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious Blood with the desire to see you as a true Bride of Christ Crucified, and to see you flee everything that would prevent you from having this sweet and glorious Spouse. But you could not do this if you were not among those wise virgins consecrated to Christ, who had lamps with oil, and the light within them; and therefore see, that to want to be a Bride of Christ, it is necessary for you to have the lamp, the oil, and the light. Do you know what this means, my daughter? By the lamp, we understand our heart, because the heart must be made like a lamp; you see well that the lamp is wide at the top, and narrow at the bottom, and thus the heart is made, to signify that we must always keep it wide at the top, that is, through holy thoughts,

to be made <note>original: *sieri*, a variant of *si ha da essere*. This continues the sentence from the previous page: "By the lamp, we understand the heart..."</note> through holy imaginings and through continuous prayer, always keeping in memory the benefits of God, and especially the benefit of the Blood, through which we are redeemed. For blessed Christ, my daughter, did not buy us back with gold, nor silver, nor pearls, or other precious stones; rather, he bought us back with his precious Blood. Therefore, such a benefit should never be forgotten, but always carried before one's eyes with holy and sweet thanksgiving, seeing how inestimably God loves us—He who did not care to give his Only-begotten Son to the shameful death of the Cross to give us the life of grace. I said that the lamp is narrow at the bottom, and so is our heart, to signify that the heart must be narrow toward these earthly things—that is, in not desiring them, nor loving them inordinately, nor hungering for more than God wishes to give us, but always thanking him, seeing how sweetly he provides for us; so that nothing <note>original: *cavelle*, an archaic Sienese term meaning "anything" or "something." Catherine uses it here to mean that God's providence never leaves us wanting.</note> ever fails us. Now, in this way, our heart will truly be a lamp; but think, my daughter, that this would not be enough if there were no oil inside.

**II.** By the oil is understood that sweet little virtue of profound humility, because it is fitting that the Bride of Christ be humble, and meek, and patient; and she will be as humble as she is patient, and as patient as she is humble. But we cannot reach this virtue of humility except through true self-knowledge <term>self-knowledge (cognoscimento di noi medesimi): a foundational concept in Catherine’s spirituality, involving the recognition of one's total dependence on God.</term>, that is, knowing our misery and fragility, and that we, by ourselves, cannot perform any virtuous act, nor lift from ourselves any struggle or pain; for if we have a bodily infirmity, or a pain, or a mental struggle, we cannot take it away or remove it; because if we could, we would take it away immediately. Therefore, it is indeed true that we are nothing by ourselves other than shame, misery, stench, fragility, and sins; for which reason we must always stay low and humble. But to stay only in this knowledge of oneself would not be good; for the Soul would come to weariness and confusion, and from confusion it would come to despair; wherefore the Devil wants nothing else but to make us come to confusion, to then make us come to despair.

## III.
It is therefore fitting to remain in the knowledge <note>original: *cognoscimento*, a key Catherinian term referring to a deep, experiential understanding of spiritual truths</note> of the goodness of God in Himself, seeing that He has created us in His image and likeness, and recreated us in grace through the Blood of His Only-begotten Son, the sweet incarnate Word; and seeing how the goodness of God continually works within us. But see, to remain only in this knowledge of God would not be good, because the soul would then fall into presumption and pride. It is therefore necessary that the two be mixed together: that is, to remain in the holy knowledge of the goodness of God *and* in the knowledge of ourselves; in this way we will become humble, patient, and meek, and in this manner we will have the oil in our lamp.

<margin>James 2</margin>
<margin>Matthew 25</margin>
## IV.
It is now necessary that there be light, otherwise [the rest] would not be enough. This light must be the light of Most Holy Faith; but the Saints say that **Faith without works is dead**; therefore it would not be a living or holy faith, but a dead one. Thus, there is a need for us to continually occupy ourselves virtuously, and to leave behind childish ways <note>referencing 1 Corinthians 13:11, "When I became a man, I put away childish things"</note> and our vanities. We must no longer behave like worldly young women, but like faithful Brides consecrated to Christ Crucified. In this way we will have the lamp, the oil, and the light. But the Gospel says that those wise virgins were five; therefore I tell you that it is necessary for each of us to be "five," otherwise we shall not enter the wedding feast of eternal life.

## V.
By this "five," it is understood that we must subjugate and mortify our five senses <note>original: *sentimenti*, referring here to the physical senses of sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch</note> of the body in such a way that we never offend with them, nor take disordered delight or pleasure through them or any one of them. In this manner we will be "five"—that is, we will have subjugated our five bodily senses.

## VI.
But consider that this sweet Spouse, Christ, is so jealous of His Brides that I could not describe it to you; and therefore, if He perceived that you loved others more than Him, He would immediately become indignant with you. If you did not correct yourself, He would not open the door where the immaculate Lamb, Christ, holds the wedding feast for all His faithful Brides. Instead, like adulteresses, we would be driven away, just as those five foolish virgins were; for while they gloried only—and vainly—in the integrity and virginity of their bodies, they lost the virginity of their souls through...

corruption of the five senses <note>original: *cinque sentimenti*; in the spiritual language of this period, "sentimenti" refers to the five physical senses (sight, hearing, etc.) which must be guarded against temptation</note>, because they did not carry the oil of humility with them; thus their lamps were extinguished. ## VII. 
For all flatterers and worldly praisers sell this oil. It is almost as if it were said to them: "In exchange for your virginity and your good works, you did not wish to purchase eternal life; rather, you wished to purchase human praise, and you performed your works to receive that praise. Go then and buy your praise, for you shall not enter here." And therefore, my daughter, guard yourself against the praise of men, and do not desire praise for any work that you might do; otherwise, the door of eternal life will not be opened to you. Therefore, considering that this was the best path for me, I said that I desired to see you as a true Bride of Christ Crucified <note>The "Bride of Christ" is a traditional term for women, especially nuns or those living a consecrated life, who dedicate their souls exclusively to Jesus</note>, and thus I pray you, and command you, to strive to be so. I have nothing more to say to you. Remain in the holy and sweet love of God. Sweet Jesus, Jesus love.

# To Lady Bartolomea di Domenico in Rome.

I. She exhorts her to walk the path of this life in the manner of a Pilgrim, bearing every tribulation and toil with patience.
II. Regarding the staff of the Holy Cross, which we must use on this journey to resist our enemies.
III. She exhorts her to often gather the Blood of Jesus Christ by means of Holy Indulgences <note>In Catherine’s time, indulgences were seen as a way to access the "treasury of merits" earned by Christ's sacrifice</note>.

## Letter 357.

->In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary.<-

<margin>I.</margin> **D**earest Mother and Daughter in sweet Christ Jesus, I Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious Blood with the desire to see you as a good and true pilgrim, keeping to the way that the true pilgrim and traveler keeps in this life. And because we are running toward the end, which is death, I want you to act courageously like the wise pilgrim, who never looks back at the toils or the pleasures he might find along the way, but looks only to the goal and focuses on where he wishes to arrive. Thus we travelers must not turn aside for tribulations, nor for injuries, nor for the reproaches that might be said or done to us in this life. Do not turn away out of impatience, but with true and holy patience as a person who is not meant to stay here <note>Catherine emphasizes that the world is a temporary lodging, not a permanent home</note>. I say also that we must not turn toward pleasures or consolations out of disordered appetite or delight, but we must pass through them courageously and not stop for the sake of delighting in them; and it is necessary for us to have the staff in hand on this journey, so that we can defend ourselves from the wild beasts and from our enemies.

<sig>II.</sig>

## II. 

This, Mother and my dearest Daughter, shall be the staff of the Most Holy Cross. Upon this staff you will find the slaughtered Lamb <note>original: "Agnello svenato". This refers to the sacrificial nature of Christ on the Cross.</note> consumed by love, who defends us from the enemy of our <term>sensuality</term> <note>In Catherine’s vocabulary, "sensuality" refers to the lower, physical nature and selfish desires that pull a person away from God.</note>; for the Soul, beholding such a fire of love, mortifies and kills its own perverse will. I say that it defends us from the Animals—that is, from the thoughts of the Devil, and from the false flatteries of the World, and from the disordered love of Children, and of every Creature. O how sweet is this glorious wood, upon which the Soul leans, and which makes it run and reach its destination. Our destination and end is Eternal Life. I want you to place this object before the eyes of your mind, and in this way, you will be a true pilgrim and reach the port of salvation.

## III. 

Bathe yourselves, bathe yourselves in the Blood of Christ Crucified; go about licking the Blood of Christ Crucified through these <term>Pardons</term> <note>The "Pardons" or "Perdoni" refer to the spiritual graces and indulgences offered by the Church, which Catherine envisions as the literal application of Christ's blood to the soul.</note>, for the Creature does nothing else when going for Pardons but gather the Blood, because the Pardon is given to us through the Blood of the immaculate Lamb. Remain in the holy and sweet love of God. Sweet Jesus, Jesus Love.

* ( A ) *Go about licking the Blood of Christ Crucified through these Pardons.* <note>This visceral image of "licking" the blood is typical of Catherine’s mystical style, suggesting an intense, intimate, and desperate need for divine grace.</note> *The name "Pardon" is used not only for the act of forgiving an offense committed against oneself, but it also refers to the Church or another sacred place where there is an indulgence; therefore, "going to gather"—or as the Saint says, "licking"—the Blood of Christ Crucified through these pardons, expresses nothing other than frequenting the Churches where, there being Indulgences, one gathers the fruits of the Blood of Christ our Lord by obtaining the pardon for the punishments deserved by one's own faults, as the Saint herself expresses.*

# To Monna Bartolomea d' Andrea Mei of Siena

I. She is exhorted to strive for the acquisition of true virtue, and [taught] how we must strip ourselves of selfish sensory and spiritual love <note>In Catherine’s theology, "sensory and spiritual self-love" refers to loving God only for the physical or emotional comforts He provides, rather than for God Himself.</note>, which is the desire to choose tribulations according to our own way rather than according to the divine will, or indeed serving God for one's own consolation more than for the glory of God.

II. Regarding the Love of God in our creation and redemption, of which we render ourselves unworthy by committing any mortal sin and by maintaining the aforementioned sensory and spiritual self-love.

## Letter 358.

->*In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary.*<-

**D**earest Mother and Daughter in sweet Jesus Christ, I Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious Blood with the desire to see you founded in true and real virtue; for without the means of virtue we cannot please our Creator, since God has always willed to give the life of grace through a [prescribed] means. You know well that the first man, Adam, having fallen into guilt through disobedience—which was followed by eternal death—and [God] wishing to restore us to grace and give us eternal life, He did so through the means of His only-begotten Son, commanding Him that through obedience He should kill our disobedience, and through the means of His death He should restore life to us, and consume and destroy our death. And truly so it was; for making a <term>Torniello</term> <note>original: "Torniello". This refers to a tournament or a wrestling match. Catherine envisions the Passion of Christ as a heroic athletic struggle or a knightly combat.</note> upon the wood of the Cross, this sweet and beloved Word wrestled hand-to-hand with death. With death He conquered death, and death killed life—that is to say, the death of our guilt killed the Son of God upon the wood of the most holy Cross. Thus, with His death, He took away our death, and

...rendered life perfect. Therefore Life remained the Victorious Lady <note>The original Italian "Donna" stems from the Latin "Domina" (Mistress/Lady). Catherine personifies "Life" as a queen who has triumphed over the lordship of Death.</note> and has defeated the infernal Devil, who held and possessed the lordship over Man—of whom no other should be Lord but only God, the eternal Lord. From this [selfishness] we come to the first death, and we lose the life which we have by means of the Blood of Christ; that is, when the Soul begins to serve its own **sensuality** <term>sensuality: In Catherine's theology, this refers to the "sensitive" or lower part of human nature that seeks physical or emotional comfort over spiritual growth.</term> with disordered desires, whether for status, or wealth, or children, or any other created thing, or in whatever way it may be that is not ordered and founded in God. 

Also, at times, the Soul will spiritually become a servant and a slave to its own will under the guise of spirituality and for the sake of "having more of God"; that is, when we desire consolation, or tribulation, or temptation from the Devil, or a specific time or place according to our own fashion, saying sometimes: "I would like to have the tribulation in another way, because in this current way it seems to me that I am losing God; I would bear that other one patiently, but this one I cannot. If I were not offending God, I would want it; but because it seems to me that I am offending God by it, I am therefore grieved." 

Dearest Mother, if you open the eye of your intellect, you will see that this is your own sensory will cloaked in a spiritual mantle. For if the soul were wise, it would not act so, but with living faith would believe that God does not permit more than one can bear, nor does He permit anything without it being necessary for one's salvation, <margin>1 Thessalonians <note>original: "1. ad Tessal." Catherine refers to 1 Thessalonians 4:3: "For this is the will of God, even your sanctification."</note></margin> because He is our God, who wants nothing other than our sanctification. 

And so we often act regarding the mind’s own consolations; for not feeling them when one wants, nor in those times or places one desires—but rather feeling battles and disturbances, and a sterile, dry mind—one falls into pain, bitterness, affliction, and the greatest weariness. And often through the deceptions of the Devil, he makes it appear that what the soul then says and does is not pleasing or acceptable to God, as if he were saying to her: "Since it does not please Him, because you are so wicked, let it be for now; perhaps another time you will feel better and will be able to perform your prayer." This **Prayer** gives us the weapons of true **Humility** and most ardent **Charity**, because holy **Prayer** makes us perfectly know ourselves and our own fragility, as well as the infinite Charity and Goodness of God.

And both are better known during the battles of the **dry mind** <term>dry mind: Often called "spiritual aridity," this is a state where a person feels no emotional joy or "sweetness" in their religious practice, often felt as a desert-like emptiness.</term>, and from this one draws more perfect humility and diligence. Therefore, if the soul is prudent, so that she does not serve her own will under the guise of consolation, and does not believe the Devil, but courageously and with a holy hatred of herself perseveres in **Prayer** in whatever way God grants it to her—whether with a feeling of sweetness or a feeling of bitterness—she gains more in the aforementioned way of bitterness and pain (in whatever way God allows it) than she does in sweetness. 

For in her need, she goes with all humility and runs with true diligence to her benefactor, knowing that by herself she can do nothing, and that God alone is the one in whom she hopes, who can and will come to aid her. Therefore, to bring us to true virtue (for without this means we would not reach proven virtue, though it might well be conceived through desire), it is necessary to sustain with true and royal patience the tribulations of the mind—that is, those given to us by **Creatures** <note>In this context, "creatures" refers to other human beings or any created thing other than God.</note> through infamy or other scandals brought against us. 

In this way we come to virtue, because these are the means that allow us to give birth to virtue; for it is tested in toils just as gold is tested in the fire. If one has not made a true test of patience in these toils, but instead shuns them in the manner described above, or through any other thing that might happen, it would be a manifest sign that one is not serving their Creator. Such a person would not let themselves be ruled by Him by receiving humbly and with love what their Lord gives them, and they would show no sign of **faith**—that is, the belief that they are loved by the Lord. For if they truly believed it, they could never be scandalized by anything, but would weigh and hold the hand of adversity in as much reverence as the hand of prosperity, and with—

II. We see clearly that we were not created for ourselves, but He Himself made us by means of His Charity; for through His pure love He created us in His image and likeness, so that we might participate in and enjoy His eternal vision. And so the fire of the abyss of His Charity found the way to make this peace; and so that Justice might be satisfied, He united Himself—that is, the eternal Deity, the divine nature—with our human nature. And with the infinite God united to the finite nature of Man, Christ-Man was sufficient, by suffering the pains upon the wood of the Most Holy Cross, to satisfy His Father and appease the wrath that was coming upon Man. But we, ungrateful and <term>unrecognizing: scognoscenti; those who fail to acknowledge the gifts they have received</term>, often lose <term>grace: gratia</term> through our sins and enter into war with God. Sometimes it is a mortal war, and sometimes it is the indignation of a friend. 

A <term>mortal war: guerra mortale</term> occurs when the <term>Soul: Anima</term> lies in the death of <term>mortal sin: peccato mortale</term>, making a god out of the world, the flesh, and miserable pleasures; thus, these people have lost life entirely. It is quite true, however, that through <term>Confession</term> and by means of the <term>Blood of Christ</term>, one can recover it while one still lives. So then you see that without the "means," one cannot live in grace, nor reach everlasting life. 

The <term>indignation of a friend: sdegno di amico</term> is found in those men and women who serve God, free from mortal sin, and are in grace, and wish to be true servants of God; but often through <term>ignorance: ignorantia</term>—which proceeds from their own spiritual will, which they have made their lord—they are distanced from the truth. It is not that they depart from the truth so far as to fall into mortal sin, but they offend the <term>perfection: perfettione</term> to which they truly wish to come, by wanting to choose the time, the place, the consolation, and the tribulation or temptation in their own way. 

Then God takes indignation with the Soul that is His friend, because it does not seem to Him that it walks, nor does it walk, with that pure freedom with which it ought to walk. Wherefore He has provided a "means" for us and requires that we use it if we want the indignation and displeasure to be removed, and our progress toward sweet perfection not to be hindered; that is, that we drown our own will, so that it seeks and wants nothing else but <term>Christ Crucified: Cristo Crocifisso</term>. Then all its delight would be to rest in the <note>original: "obbrobrj di Cristo"—the insults, shames, and reproaches Christ suffered.</note> reproaches of Christ, giving birth to the <term>virtues: virtù</term> conceived through such great desire in the <term>charity: carità</term> of one's neighbor with true <term>humility: umiltà</term>. 

Therefore, by means of enduring pains and hardships as God grants them, and "sterility of mind" <note>A state of spiritual dryness where one feels no emotional comfort in prayer.</note> with true and holy patience, we will be founded in true and real virtue; and we will have the strength and <term>knowledge: cognoscimento</term> of an adult, and not of a child who does not want to walk or do anything except in its own way. I see no other way by which we can pass, and therefore I told you that I desired to see you founded in true and real virtue; and wanting your soul to be united to God through the affection of love, I said that it could not be done without the "means" of virtue, because everything must be done through a means, as has been said. # To Lady <note>original: "Monna"; a traditional Italian title of respect for a woman, contracted from "Madonna."</note> Montagna, a great Servant of God in the District of Narni in Capitone.

I. On the virtue of perfect Charity toward God, and of Humility its Nurse.
II. On temporal and spiritual self-love, neither of which can exist with perfect Charity.
III. On the union of the Soul with God, which arises from perfect Charity.
IV. That this is acquired with the light of Holy faith in the knowledge of oneself.
V. She desires to see herself and her drowned in this virtue of perfect Charity.

## Letter 359.

### In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary.

<margin>I.</margin> **D**earest and most beloved Mother in Christ sweet Jesus, I Catherine, servant and slave of the Servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious Blood with the desire to see you burned and consumed in the fire of divine Charity <note>original: "Carità"; in Catherine’s theology, this refers to the selfless, supernatural love of God (agape) rather than mere almsgiving.</note>, which Charity does not seek its own ends—that is, it does not seek itself for its own sake, nor the neighbor for its own sake, nor God for its own sake, but itself and the neighbor for God, and God for His own sake, insofar as He is worthy of being loved as the highest and eternal goodness. This fire burns and does not consume—and yet it does consume; that is, it does not afflict or wither the Soul, but rather enriches <note>original: "ingrassala"; literally "fattens" it, meaning to make the soul spiritually robust and fertile.</note> it, anointing it with true and perfect humility, which is the <term>wet-nurse: baglia; a woman who cares for and suckles a child</term> and nurtures this Charity. And it consumes all spiritual and temporal self-love, and every other thing it might find in the Soul that is outside the sweet will of God.

<margin>II.</margin> I say that it consumes temporal self-love, because with the light [of faith] she recognized herself and recognized that temporal and transitory things [are passing]

...to be instruments of death, which kill the Soul that possesses them in a disordered way; and therefore the Soul begins to hate them, and to cast them out of its heart and out of its mind. And because the Soul cannot live without love, it immediately begins to direct its affection and love toward the wealth of virtues; whereby this fire of Love, by the force of its heat, consumes every other love. 

Once the Soul has thus consumed it <note>Referring to disordered or worldly love.</note> within itself, it is still not perfect; for until it reaches its perfection, there remains a certain spiritual self-love, directed either toward Creatures or toward the Creator—though one is not without the other, because with the same perfection with which we love God, we love the rational creature <note>original: "Creatura ragionevole"; in Catherine’s thought, this refers to human beings, who are the only created beings on earth endowed with reason and an eternal soul.</note>. 

How is it recognized that this spiritual self-love is in the Soul? When the person loves their own consolation within themselves, for the sake of which they would neglect to work for the salvation of their neighbor, or when, in that holy work, they see their peace and the quiet of their mind diminished—or other exercises which they wished to do for their own consolation—and so they withdraw. 

Or when at times they love a Creature with a spiritual love, and it does not seem to them that this Creature responds to their love, or if that person should have more intimate conversation or show more love to another person than to them; then they suffer the heaviest pain, indignation, and displeasure, and often harbor judgment in their mind, and distancing themselves from that Creature under the color of humility and the desire to have more peace; and yet it is simply the self-love that they have for themselves. 

These are the signs regarding the Creature, showing that spiritual self-love is not yet consumed in the Soul toward the Creator. It is also seen when the mind receives some darkness, or battles, or the deprivation of its usual consolations; if the Soul because of this falls into weariness <note>original: "tedio"; a state of spiritual boredom, listlessness, or "accidie" where holy things become tasteless.</note> or confusion of mind—through which confusion and weariness it will often leave the sweet exercise of Prayer <note>original: "Oratione"; specifically referring to the practice of mental or vocal prayer as a discipline.</note>. This is something the Soul must not do; but by every means it must take up the Mother of Prayer and not let her go. 

For if the Soul leaves this especially, or leaves any virtuous act, it is a sign that its love is mercenary <note>original: "mercennaio"; love that serves only for the sake of reward or "wages" rather than out of pure devotion.</note>—that is, that the Soul loves only for its own consolation, and that the self-love of spiritual delight is still rooted in its Soul. I say that the fire of divine Charity <note>original: "Carità"; the supreme virtue of selfless love.</note> consumes this and removes the imperfection; it makes the Soul perfect in the love of God, and in the affection for the neigh-

...they do not care. For the honor of God and the salvation of Souls, they are willing to lose their own consolations; they do not refuse labor, but rather delight in being at the <term>table of the crucified desire</term><note>A signature image in Catherine’s writing: the "table" represents the work of salvation, where the soul "eats" the food of souls through suffering and desire, imitating Christ's sacrifice.</note>, accompanying the humble, immaculate Lamb. She <note>The Soul, referred to as "she" (ella) in the feminine gender in Italian.</note> weeps with those who weep, and becomes weak with those who are weak; for she considers the faults of others as her own; she rejoices with those who rejoice, expanding her heart in charity toward her neighbor, to the point that she is almost more content with the well-being, peace, and consolation of others than with her own. Whatever she loves, she wishes that everyone would love; she is not scandalized because she sees others loved more than herself, but with true humility she remains content, because she considers herself deficient and others virtuous; and thus it seems to her a just and fitting thing that the one in whom virtue is found should be loved more than she is.

### III. 

This charity unites the Soul in God, drowning its own will, and clothes it and unites it with His eternal will, so that the mind can be scandalized or disturbed by nothing except the offenses committed against its Creator and the damnation of Souls. This is a fire that converts everything into itself, and causes the Soul’s affection to rise above itself, receiving such union through the elevation of the mind—which has been made in divine Charity—that the vessel of its Body loses all sensation. To the point that, seeing it does not see, hearing it does not hear, speaking it does not speak, walking it does not go, touching it does not touch; all the senses of the Body seem bound, and their power seems lost, because the affection has lost itself and is united in God. Thus God, with His power and charity, has drawn that affection to Himself, and therefore the senses of the Body fail; because the union that the Soul has made in God is more perfect than that of the Soul in the Body. He draws the <term>powers of the Soul</term><note>Catherine follows the Augustinian tradition which identifies the three powers of the soul—Memory, Intellect, and Will—as the image of the Trinity within a person.</note> to Himself with all their operations. Because the memory has been filled with the remembrance of His benefits and His great goodness; the intellect has placed before itself the doctrine of Christ Crucified given to us for love, and therefore the will runs with the greatest affection to love it. Then all operations are ordered and gathered in His name. She tastes the milk of divine sweetness; she becomes intoxicated with the Blood of Christ, and like a drunkard, she wishes to be satisfied by nothing but reproaches; embracing scorns, insults, and outrages, cold, and

...enduring cold and heat, hunger and thirst; persecutions from men, and harassments from demons; in all these things she <note>The Soul, personified as feminine.</note> glories with the **glorious Paul** in **Christ sweet Jesus**. I said that **Charity** did not seek itself, because it does not choose place nor time in its own way, but according to what is granted to it by the divine Goodness. Therefore, every place is its place, and every time is its time; tribulation weighs as much upon it as consolation, because it seeks the honor of God in the salvation of souls with the desire to acquire and grow in true and real virtues. Here she has made her beginning—not in her own mental consolations, nor in revelations, nor in killing the body, but in killing her own will. She has seen with the light that the perfection of the soul does not consist in those other things, but rather in killing one's own spiritual and temporal will; and therefore, she freely throws it into the furnace of divine Charity. Since she is within it, it is necessary that she be burned and consumed in the manner described. Now that we have seen—though it is nothing compared to what it truly is—what this sweet Mother of Charity gives, let us see in what place it is acquired, and with what.

### IV.

I tell it to you in few words: it is acquired with the light of **most holy Faith**, which Faith is the <term>pupil of the eye of the Intellect</term><note>A classic Catherinian metaphor: just as the physical pupil is the part of the eye that actually sees, Faith is the essential core of the mind's ability to "see" spiritual truths.</note>. With this light, the soul sees what she ought to love and what she ought to hate; seeing, she knows, and knowing, she loves and hates. She loves, I say, what she has known of the divine Goodness, and she hates what she has seen of her own malice and misery, which she sees as necessary for her salvation. What was the cause? The light, from which came knowledge, and from knowledge, love. For a thing that is not known cannot be loved; therefore, the light leads us to this fire, and one is united with the other; for fire is not without light, nor light without fire. 

Where do we find it? In the <term>house of self-knowledge</term><note>Catherine's famous "cella del cognoscimento di sé," an internal spiritual space where one discovers their own nothingness and God's infinite love.</note>. In ourselves we find this sweet and loving fire, because through love God has given us our being in His **image and likeness**; through love we are re-created in grace through the **Blood of Christ Crucified**; for love held Him fastened and nailed to the Cross. We are those vessels that have received the abundance of the Blood, and all the spiritual and corporal graces given to us beyond our very being; we have received them through love; so that in itself the soul finds...

She emphasizes that knowledge of God's goodness and one's own misery leads to a love fueled by the Blood of Christ.</summary>

...and knows this sweet fire. Therefore, with the light, let us go into the **House of self-knowledge** <note>A central theme in Catherine’s spirituality; she believed one must enter the "cell" or "house" of the heart to know both one's own nothingness and God's infinite love.</note>, and there we will nourish ourselves on <term>divine Charity</term><note>Carità: in this context, it refers to the theological virtue of selfless, sacrificial love (Agape).</note>, seeing ourselves loved by God inestimably. This Charity nourishes the **children of the virtues** at its breast and makes the soul live in grace; without it, we would be sterile and deprived of life.

### V.

Considering this, I said that I desired—and so I desire in myself along with you—to see us burned and consumed in the furnace of **divine Charity**. I pray to the clemency of the **Holy Spirit** that he might do this for us through grace, so that the **divine Goodness** may be glorified in us, consuming our lives in sorrow and bitterness for the offenses that are committed against him. Let this be done with humble, faithful, and continual prayer for the **Holy Church** and for every creature that possesses reason. Let us drown ourselves in the <term>Blood of the Lamb</term><note>original: "Sangue dell' Agnello." Catherine frequently used the image of being "drowned" or "bathed" in Christ's blood as a symbol of purification and total immersion in God's mercy.</note>. I say no more to you. Remain in the holy and sweet love of God. I humbly commend myself to you. **Sweet Jesus, Jesus Love.**

(A) *Every effort made to obtain any information about this woman—celebrated in old printings as a great servant of the Lord—has been in vain. There is no memory of her in **Capitone**, neither in writings nor on sepulchral marbles <note>Tombstones or memorial plaques.</note>, nor even in the stories passed down by local fame. Perhaps because that land was ransacked in the following century by the rapacity of **Sforza’s** soldiers <note>Referencing the mercenary troops of the Sforza family, who were active in power struggles across Italy in the 15th century.</note>, both the public and private documents that could have provided some knowledge of her were lost. If the stones of the graves preserved any record, they all perished when the Parish Church was renovated (the only place where bodies are given burial), which was a project of the early years of the seventeenth century. The land of **Capitone** is located in **Umbria**, approximately three miles from the city of **Amelia**, four from **Narni**, and seven from **Terni**. It depends on the city of Narni for both its spiritual and political government; therefore, it is said to be in the "Contado" of Narni—that is to say, within its territory. The old printings wrote "Narui" instead of "Narni," so that error has been corrected in this new edition.*

# To Lady Agnes of Tuscania, Servant of God and woman of great penance.

I. **C**oncerning the true foundation we must build for the edifice of our soul, which is found in self-knowledge through the light of Holy Faith.
II. Concerning the hunger for divine honor that must be placed upon this foundation, and love toward one's Neighbor.
III. How one must totally kill one's own Will, both temporally and spiritually.
IV. Concerning bodily penance, and how our main foundation must not be placed in it.
V. Concerning the diversity among the Servants of God.
VI. Concerning the method for building the aforementioned foundation and growing in the virtues.
VII. She dissuades her from going yet to the <term>Holy Sepulcher</term><note>The tomb of Christ in Jerusalem. At this time, Catherine often discouraged pilgrimages to the Holy Land, believing the "Holy Land" to be the soul itself or the reform of the Church in Rome.</note>, praying her to choose to weep for the present calamities of the Church due to the <term>Schism</term><note>The Great Western Schism began in 1378 when a group of cardinals elected an antipope (Clement VII) in opposition to Urban VI, whom Catherine supported.</note> that has arisen against the election of Urban VI.

## Letter 360.

### In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified and of Mary the sweet.

I. **D**earest Sister in Christ sweet Jesus, I, Catherine, servant and slave of the Servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in his precious Blood with the desire to see you build a true and real foundation, so that every great and good edifice may be placed upon it, which no contrary wind could throw to the ground. Do not wonder why I say that I desire to see you build a true foundation, which seems like such talk as if we were just now beginning to build the <term>City of our Soul</term><note>Catherine frequently uses architectural metaphors, comparing the spiritual life to a city or a house that requires a deep foundation to withstand the "winds" of temptation or hardship.</note>. It has been such a long time since it appeared that we wanted to begin to build this foundation, though I confess that I myself never did it; but the reason why I say that we are beginning to do it now is because every day the Soul must begin anew to make this start. Since

<meta>This page continues Letter 360 to Agnes of Tuscania. The previous page established that a spiritual building requires a firm foundation. Here, Catherine describes the "site" of that foundation—self-knowledge—and warns against a common pitfall: killing one's self-will only "halfway" by remaining attached to spiritual comforts.</meta>

...we have seen that it is necessary for you to make this foundation; now let us see where, how, and in what. I tell you: the place is the true knowledge of ourselves, which knowledge is dug in the valley of true Humility. And in what manner? With the light of Most Holy Faith, digging with the hands of hatred <note>Catherine frequently uses "hatred" to describe a holy turning away from one's own selfish or "disordered" impulses.</note> for the affection of disordered love—which is that earth that clutters the Soul—and wanting to fill it with the stones of true and real virtues, with the hand of love with burning and holy desire.

II. And what shall we place upon it? The hunger for the honor of God and the salvation of Souls, learning from the humble and immaculate Lamb <note>original: "Agnello"; a reference to Jesus Christ.</note>, following his doctrine. This doctrine teaches us nothing else but to love him above all things and our Neighbor as ourselves. Therefore, the prudent Soul—having made her beginning in the holy knowledge of herself in the manner described, where she has known the great goodness of God and the ineffable love he has for us—falls in love with him and with what he loves, that is, the Creature who possesses reason. Therefore, she immediately sets herself at the Table of holy desire to take the food of Souls, and to kill in herself her own will, and to clothe herself in virtues for the honor of God. And this will must be killed <gloss>or perhaps "is often killed"</gloss> halfway, and not entirely.

III. Do you know when it is killed only halfway? When the Soul cuts its affection from these transitory things, cutting off sensual love, and undertakes to do the will of God—who wants us to strip ourselves of it. It remains half dead, being dead in this, and half remains alive—namely, in spiritual things—seeking its own consolations <note>original: "conſolationi"; these are the emotional or spiritual "highs" one feels in prayer.</note>, choosing times, places, and comforts in our own way and not in God’s way, which thing must not be done. Rather, we should freely and purely serve our Creator, and let him decide the times, places, and comforts in his own way. For he is the Physician, and we are the Sick; therefore, we must receive and take the medicine in his way. Truly foolish and mad is that Soul who wants to go her own way; it seems she considers herself to know more than God, and she does not perceive it. Yet it is indeed so, because she is veiled with this color <note>A "color" or "cloak" in this context is a deceptive appearance or a rationalization.</note>, appearing to her to be more pleasing to God in her own way than in that which is permitted by God. <meta>This page continues Letter 360 to Agnes of Tuscania. In the previous section, Catherine explained how a soul’s will might only be "halfway killed" if it remains attached to spiritual pleasures. ...she often receives very great deceptions. And what is the cause of the will remaining alive in this? It comes from the love she has conceived for her own consolations <note>In Catherine’s theology, "consolations" are the pleasant emotional or spiritual feelings one gets during prayer.</note>, having made them her foundation. Some do this regarding visions and revelations, from which they draw great delight when they receive them, and when they do not receive them, they suffer. This is not a good principle, because they will often believe a vision is from God when it is actually from the Devil; for the Devil catches us with this hook, seeing us so ready to receive them. 

And even sometimes God will allow us many mental consolations—not so that we might place our primary affection there, but so that we might look to the affection of Him, the Giver, more than to the gift. Then, at another time, He will not give them, but will give another feeling: either of many battles, or darkness and sterility of mind. Because of this, the Soul comes to very great suffering, and it seems to her that she is deprived of God when she is deprived of that which she loves. God allows this to lift her out of imperfection and lead her to perfection—or to lift her away from the appetite for revelations and instead have her nourish herself at the <term>Table of Holy Desire</term> <note>Catherine’s famous metaphor for a state of being where one’s only "food" is doing God's will and seeking the salvation of others.</note>, in which she ought to make her every beginning.

## IV.
<margin><unclear>manuscript mark</unclear></margin>
Sometimes there are many who are deceived regarding penance. This happens when a <term>Creature</term> <note>A standard medieval term for any created human being.</note> places their primary affection on penance and attends more to killing the body than to killing their own will. In such a case, she ought to kill the will and merely mortify the body; yet she places so much love in [the physical act] that it seems she cannot have God without this penance. This foundation is not sufficient to build great edifices upon; indeed, it is very dangerous and harmful to the Soul. Therefore, one should not set penance as the foundation, but rather as the wall. Her beginning should be built upon the sweet affection of Charity and upon the intrinsic virtues of the Soul, which are never lost due to place or time—unless we wish it—and cannot be taken from us by any Creature. 

Penance should be taken up as an instrument and used to increase virtue, and not to <gloss>simply</gloss> mortify the body; it must not be the primary affection. Whoever does otherwise greatly deceives themselves. Indeed, a person should recognize that it is appropriate to perform penance at certain times, because it is not possible to follow it at all times as one began, since the vessel of the

physical penance. When the body is mortified and weakened at one time, it cannot do as much at another; when it is unable to perform as it once did, the soul suffers, and it seems to her that she is being rejected by God. The mind remains in darkness because that from which it seemed to receive light and consolation <note>In this context, light and consolation refer to the emotional "high" or sense of pride one might feel while successfully performing difficult fasts or vigils.</note> has been taken away. This happens to her because she made her foundation upon this external practice. Such people are prone to endure much toil but gain little fruit. They are prone to grumbling and to judgmental thoughts toward those who do not follow the same path of penance, because they would want to see everyone walking the same path they walk. They do not realize it, but it almost seems they wish to impose a law upon the <term>Holy Spirit</term> <note>The Third Person of the Trinity, viewed here as the flexible guide of the soul.</note>, who calls and guides us in diverse ways: some through penance, some through other means, some with little and some with much, according to the capacity of their nature; and some travel by the way of burning desire alone.

## V.
And these are those who make the great gain; they run along all illuminated, free, and without pain, because they have killed their own will. They do not pass judgment, but rather they rejoice to see such a diversity of ways among the <term>Servants of God</term>, because they see that in our Father's house there are many dwelling places <note>original: "manſioni" (referencing John 14:2)</note>, and that He has much to give. These people do not suffer over the loss of consolations; rather, they even enjoy the lack of them because of the <term>holy hatred</term> <note>A common term in Catherine's writings referring to a detachment from one's own selfish ego and physical comforts for the sake of God.</note> they have for themselves, reputing themselves worthy of the pain and unworthy of the fruit that follows the pain. They do not seek themselves for their own sake, but themselves for God; and they do not love God for their own pleasure, but for His goodness, for He is worthy of being loved by us. They love their neighbor because it is commanded, and they have seen by the light of living faith that God loves the neighbor ineffably; and therefore they love them. In this life they taste the <term>earnest-money</term> <note>original: "arra." A pledge or down-payment of what is to come.</note> of eternal life, because they have killed their will entirely—not halfway—in both spiritual and temporal things. Oh, dearest Sister, do not let it enter your mind that I despise physical penance; no, I even recommend it insofar as it is used as a tool, as has been said, but not as the primary object of affection. Otherwise, we would receive many great deceptions.

## VI.
We must, therefore, make a beginning of a knowledge of ourselves, and of God within us. All pure and generous, let us run to the <term>Table of the Most Holy Cross</term>, where we find the fire of divine Charity; and like hungry people at this table, let us take

<meta>This page continues Letter 360 from Catherine of Siena to Agnes of Montepulciano. Catherine is elaborating on the "Way of Truth," contrasting those who are obsessed with external penance with those who are grounded in the love of virtue and the "killing" of self-will.</meta>

...take the food of the honor of God and the <term>Salvation of Souls</term> <note>A central theme for Catherine, referring to the active pursuit of helping others reach heaven.</note>, filling ourselves with insults, mockery, and outrages, enduring even until death. In this way, we shall follow the doctrine of Christ Crucified, who is the Way, Truth, and Life <note>original: "Via, Verità, e Vita" (referencing John 14:6)</note>; and whoever walks through Him does not walk in darkness but reaches the light. 
<margin>John 14</margin>
And truly He is the Truth, for whoever follows His doctrine receives the light of grace; it takes away the darkness of self-love and ignorance, and he receives a light—that is, a supernatural light—with which light he has seen and known where it is necessary to make his beginning; and therefore he has made it, and has built the **City of the Soul**.

He has seen with great prudence that cause which hinders his perfection, and therefore he completely removes it from himself, and clings to and embraces that which will preserve and increase him in perfection. Expanding his heart and his affection in the fire of <term>Divine Charity</term> <note>In Catherine’s theology, "Carità" (Charity) is the supernatural love for God that overflows into love for neighbor.</note>, he does not think of himself; but thinks only how he may most please God by seeking His honor and the salvation of souls. And because he sees that he could not do this with a "living" will <note>Catherine uses the term "living will" to describe a person's ego or self-interest that has not yet been "mortified" or surrendered to God's will.</note>, he strives to kill and drown this will entirely, and to mortify the body, so much so that he seems to care for nothing except to clothe himself in the virtues.

Hence, if she <note>The text uses the feminine "ella" (she) because "the soul" (l'anima) is a feminine noun in Italian.</note> has consolation from God, or from creatures for God’s sake, she humbles herself, receiving it with thanksgiving and considering herself unworthy; and if she has tribulation, temptation, or darkness of mind, she receives them with patience and with love, knowing that whatever God permits to happen—whatever it may be—He gives it to her for love, to make her come to that perfect state for which she hungers. If she is removed from her penance—which she was doing to mortify the body—either through <term>Obedience</term> <note>Following the instructions of a spiritual director or superior, which Catherine valued above personal choice.</note> or because she is unable to perform it, she remains at peace and has no storm or bitterness in her mind; because she had not made her foundation upon that penance, but upon the love of virtue, and therefore she feels no distress.

Those who have made their beginning only in penance do exactly the opposite; because their will is "living" and not "dead," they experience intolerable pain when they are made to stop, or when by necessity they must leave it off—that is, when through natural frailty they cannot continue what they have begun, they fall into impatience with themselves and displeasure...

<summary>Catherine explains that true spiritual maturity involves "killing" the self-will and building one's foundation on virtue and Divine Charity rather than external physical penance. This allows the soul to remain at peace even when physical strength fails or when obedience requires one to stop their fasting or vigils.</summary>

...toward those who hinder them; and by wishing to reach perfection through their own efforts alone, they arrive at imperfection. Therefore, dearest Daughter, let us make our beginning and true foundation not in an imperfect thing, but in a perfect one—that is, in the true **knowledge of ourselves**, as has been said, with a desire for the virtues, which cannot be taken away from us. Let us nourish ourselves at the Table of holy and true desire, filling ourselves with the outrages of the humble Lamb <note>Catherine refers to Jesus as the "humble Lamb" who accepted insults and suffering during the Passion; she encourages Agnes to find spiritual satisfaction in enduring similar hardships.</note>, for in no other way could we weep with humble and continual prayers over the dead son of the human generation <note>A reference to the spiritual death of humanity due to sin.</note>, nor over the <term>Mystical Body</term> <note>The "Corpo mistico" refers to the Church as the collective body of all believers with Christ as the head.</note> of the Holy Church, which today we see in such great tribulation. Seeing that there is nothing better for working within ourselves and in others than making this sweet beginning, I said that I desired to see you make a true and real foundation, so that we may build upon true virtues. I say no more to you.

### VII.

Regarding what you sent word to me about, concerning going to the Holy Sepulcher <note>Agnes had apparently asked about making a pilgrimage to Jerusalem.</note>, it does not seem to me that it is the time to go there; rather, I believe it is more the sweet will of God that you remain steady and cry out continually with heartfelt sorrow in His presence, and with great bitterness at seeing Him so miserably offended—and especially by the **Heresy** that has been raised by wicked men to contaminate our Faith, saying that Pope Urban VI is not the true Pope. He is the true Supreme Pontiff and Vicar of Christ, and thus I confess in the sight of God and before all creatures. Bathe yourself in the Blood shed for us with such fire of love, and forgive me if I have spoken too presumptuously. Pray to God for <term>Christ on Earth</term> <note>Catherine’s favorite title for the Pope, emphasizing his role as Christ's representative.</note> and for me, that He may give me the grace to give my life for His sweet truth. Remain in the holy and sweet love of God. Sweet Jesus, Jesus Love.
