<meta>This page continues the commentary on Letter 361 by Saint Catherine of Siena. While the previous page provided the text of the letter itself, this page contains the scholarly annotations (Notes C and D) explaining the historical context of Catherine's advice regarding fasting and the "Holy Marys."</meta>

*In the City, it is customary to say "doing the Holy Marys." <note>original: "fare le Sante Marie." This refers to a specific devotional fast dedicated to the Virgin Mary.</note> This pious custom was born in Spain around the year 1249, and the great Virgin herself appeared to Ines, a poor shepherdess native to Cubas, a land in New Castile fifteen miles from Madrid. She revealed to her that it was pleasing to her that such a fast should be observed by her devotees, promising them copious treasures of Sacred Indulgences, and confirming her word with frequent apparitions and with* <margin>Chapter 1, Volume 1.</margin> *prodigious events, which can be read in various authors who have left a memory of this fact. In particular, see* <margin>page 100, Volume 2, part 3.</margin> *Father Antonio Dadda in the "Life of Sister Joan of the Cross,"* <margin>page 645.</margin> *and Monsignor Francesco Gonzaga in the history he wrote of his Seraphic Religion; <note>The "Seraphic Religion" is a traditional way of referring to the Franciscan Order, named after St. Francis of Assisi, the "Seraphic Father."</note> for in the place where the shepherdess Ines saw the Most Holy Mother, a temple and a monastery of Holy Virgins was raised under the Rule of the Third Order of Saint Francis.*

*( D ) **And do not drink only water on any day.** <note>Catherine is quoting back her own advice from the letter to Monna Agnes.</note> If the Saint used the harshest rigor toward herself, both regarding eating (which consisted only of herbs) and regarding drinking (using only water), she used no less Charity toward others by moderating their fervor, which might have led them to a too-rigorous abstinence.*

## Letter 363.

### In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary.

**D**earest daughter in sweet Christ Jesus, I Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious Blood with the desire to see you grow in a holy desire and in true patience, in such a way that you never forget the sweet will of God. Rather, may you know how to conform yourself with joy at all times that God gives you, and with joy drown yourself in the Blood of Christ Crucified, making there your rest and your every dwelling. In this glorious Blood you will receive light, because in the Blood darkness is consumed. You will receive in the Blood the life of grace; for in the Blood He took death away from us. And you will taste in the Blood the fruit of most burning Charity; for it was shed out of love, and love was also what held Him fastened and nailed to the Cross; for the nails would not have been sufficient if love had not held Him; but love held Him <note>This is a famous Catherinian theme: that the physical nails of the crucifixion were secondary to the "nails of love" that kept Christ on the Cross for the sake of humanity.</note>. Now, I want you to clothe yourself in this Love, and if you wish to clothe yourself in it, it is necessary for you to bathe in the Blood of Christ Crucified; and this is what I want you to do. Be diligent in holy prayer at its proper place and time when you can, for she <note>Catherine personifies Prayer as a "Mother."</note> is that Mother who nourishes the children of the virtues. I say no more to you. Remain in the holy and sweet love of God. Sweet Jesus, Jesus Love.

## Letter 365.

->In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary.<-

**D**earest daughter in sweet Christ Jesus, I Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious Blood with the desire to see you as a faithful servant to your Creator, constant and persevering in virtue, so that through this you may receive the abundance of grace, and in the lasting life we may enjoy the eternal vision of God, bound together in the sweet bond of Charity <note>Carità: In Catherine’s theology, this is the divine, selfless love that binds the soul to God and neighbor.</note>. But so that you may better grow and keep yourself in the affection of the virtues, I want you and Francesco <note>Francesco di Pippo, a Sienese tailor and devoted member of Catherine’s spiritual circle.</note> to hide yourselves in the Side <note>The wound in the side of the crucified Christ, which Catherine describes as a refuge where the soul can know God's love.</note> of Christ Crucified through holy desire. There, let the vessel of your heart be filled with His Blood, so that, as those in love and intoxicated by the Blood of Christ, you may taste the effect of His Charity; then the eternal Spouse will receive you and press you in His arms with great kindness and mercy.

<margin>A.</margin>
I am ready, my daughter, for the effect of your charity and for what you write to me; when I want you to come to me I do not answer you, but I tell you this much: that I will fulfill your desire and give refreshment to your soul, for when the hour has come I will send for you, and it will be soon by the grace of God. Comfort yourself in sweet Christ Jesus, and commend me closely to

<margin>B:</margin>
Bartolo <note>Bartolo di Canuolo, another follower of Catherine.</note> and Monna Orsa, and bless all the rest of the Family <note>The "Bella Brigata" or "Family," the group of disciples who surrounded Catherine.</note> for me, and comfort Francesco most closely. I say no more for now. Remain in the holy and sweet love of God. Sweet Jesus, Jesus love.

# To a Woman who was Gossiping.

->On the 20th day of October in Florence, 1378.<-

**I.** Regarding the light necessary for us to know the truth of God and the truth of <term>Creatures</term> <note>original: "Creature"; in Catherine’s theology, this refers to all created beings, especially human beings</note>, demonstrating what each of these truths consists of.
**II.** That the enlightened Soul judges everything to come from the hands of God, whether it be suffering or prosperity, and all for our own good.
**III.** How we must always judge our Neighbor for the best.
**IV.** She detests the blindness and pride of those who judge their Neighbor poorly.
**V.** She exhorts her not to imitate such people, but to strive for the acquisition of the true light, so that she may no longer judge her Neighbors poorly, nor be scandalized by them.

## Letter 368.

->In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary.<-

**I. D**earest Sister and Daughter in sweet Jesus Christ, I Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious Blood with the desire to see you with true and perfect light; for without light we cannot know the truth of God, nor the truth of Creatures; instead, we would fall into false and miserable judgment. Why? Because we would be deprived of light; for the Soul that is enlightened, and has removed <term>sensory passion</term> <note>original: "passione sensitiva"; the physical impulses and worldly emotions that cloud spiritual judgment</note> from itself, discerns and knows the truth, and therefore judges justly and with great discretion. What is this judgment which we must render and give to God? And what truth must we know in Him and in our Neighbor? I tell you: we must know this Truth seen not with the eye of the body, but with the eye of the <term>intellect</term> <note>original: "intelletto"; the faculty of the soul used for spiritual understanding</note>, containing within it the light of the most holy Faith: that God loves us inestimably, and for love He created us in His Image and

<summary>Catherine begins this letter by explaining that divine light is essential for understanding truth and avoiding the sin of judging others. She emphasizes that the soul must move past worldly passions to perceive God's love through the "eye of the intellect."</summary>
<keywords>Catherine of Siena, spiritual light, judgment, divine truth, sensory passion, intellect, Florence, 1378</keywords>

--- Page 795 ---
<meta>This page continues Letter 368 to an anonymous woman in Florence. It completes the discussion of Section I (knowing the truth through Christ) and covers the entirety of Section II (how an enlightened soul views prosperity and adversity).</meta>

[...in] His own likeness, so that we might receive and taste His supreme eternal Good. Who manifests to us that this is the truth? The Blood of the humble and immaculate Lamb <note>original: "Agnello"; a reference to Jesus Christ as the sacrificial Lamb of God</note> shed with such fire of love upon the wood of the most holy Cross.

### II.
Once the Soul has seen and known this Truth, it loves it; and with that love, it judges that whatever God gives and permits in this life to the <term>Creature</term> <note>original: "Creatura"; in Catherine's writings, this specifically refers to a human being as a created thing endowed with reason</note> who possesses reason, He permits it for our own good, so that we may be sanctified in Him. The soul judges justly with the light of discretion: if it is in prosperity, it recognizes that this is given by its Creator, not because of its own virtue, but through the infinite goodness of God. Therefore, through this knowledge, the Soul loves prosperity with an <term>ordered love</term> <note>original: "amore ordinato"; a theological concept where one loves God above all else, and loves worldly things only in relation to Him</note>, loving it for God’s sake and possessing it as something lent, and not as its own property—for these things are not its own. We realize this by the fact that sometimes we wish to hold onto them, yet they are taken from us; and not only material wealth, but the very life and health of Man, and every other thing—all pass away like the wind. No one can hold onto them as they wish, but only as much as it pleases Him who gives them.

This is the judgment of one who is enlightened in this sweet Truth; and if it is adversity and tribulation, they receive it humbly with true and holy patience. Such a person considers themselves worthy of the suffering and unworthy of the fruit <note>the spiritual reward or peace</note> that follows after the suffering, judging within themselves with humility that it comes to them because of their sins. Because they know that the supreme Judge is the rewarder of every good and the punisher of every evil, they consider it a great grace—and indeed it is—that God shows them such mercy; for the guilt, which deserves infinite punishment for having offended the infinite Good, is instead settled within a finite time through the giving of toil and tribulations. In whatever way He gives them to us, Eternal Truth gives them all either so that we may correct our defects, or to bring us to great perfection. In whatever way He gives them, we are certain that He gives them out of love and not out of hatred. This is what the Soul enlightened by sweet Truth sees and knows, and therefore it holds everything in due reverence; it judges justly the will of God and His providence within itself, for His providence provides for our every necessity, and His will desires nothing but our good.

<meta>This page continues Letter 368 by Catherine of Siena. It transitions from Section II, which discussed how the soul handles personal prosperity and adversity, into Section III, which explains how an enlightened soul should perceive and judge their neighbor. The text maintains its focus on the "light of truth" as the guiding principle for spiritual life.</meta>

### III.
Since the Soul has so sweetly known the truth in its Creator, and has so sweetly judged His mysteries as good, it wishes to hold this same truth and judgment toward its **Neighbor**; because charity for the neighbor flows from the charity of God. Therefore, this is the rule for those who fear Him: they will never wish to pass any judgment on any <term>Creature</term> <note>human being</note> except for good. Take care that even if one sees an evil that is clearly a fault of **mortal sin** <note>a grave sin that severs the soul's relationship with God's grace</note>, the soul does not take this as a matter for judgment, but rather carries it before God with a holy compassion, saying: "Today it is your turn, tomorrow it is mine, were it not for the **Supreme Goodness** that preserves me." 

I leave all judgment to the Supreme Judge, who must judge both the good and the wicked, and to the temporal Judge, who is placed there to uphold and execute justice for everyone according to what they deserve. The soul does not set itself up to judge based on the talk of other Creatures, nor by outward habits and actions, for it sees clearly that blessed **Christ** forbids this in the **Gospel**, saying: *Do not judge by appearances.* For if one loves the truth in their Neighbor with that same pure love they have for God—without regard for self—they judge the will of God in His Creatures holily, judging them for good and leaving the judgment of evil to God. 

Therefore, such a soul is not scandalized by the Mysteries of God nor by its Neighbor; its Charity, love, and reverence toward its Creator do not diminish because of any tribulation He might permit, nor toward the Creature because of any injury or temporal harm received. This is because the soul has judged holily and with truth that God permits these things to test the affection of charity in the Soul toward the one who causes the injury, and as a punishment for its own sin, saying: "Lord, You justly permit this to me; for even if I have not offended this Creature who injures me, I have offended You. Thus, for my own good, You have used them as an instrument to correct my faults." I tell you, dearest **Daughter**, that this Soul tastes **eternal life** in this life; because it judges everything in God and in its Neighbor with the light of truth.

### IV.
To this I invite you: that you always strive, while you live, to keep this upright way, so that you may be deprived of the supreme evil and reach the supreme eternal Good; because in the judgment by which we judge others, we ourselves shall be judged. Let us not act like the fools, who...

<summary>Catherine explains that a soul filled with God's love refuses to judge others, viewing even the faults of neighbors with compassion and seeing personal injuries as divine instruments for spiritual growth. She emphasizes that judging by outward appearances is forbidden by the Gospel and that living in this truth allows one to experience a foretaste of eternal life.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the text from Letter 368 by Catherine of Siena. It follows the contrast established on the previous page between a soul that judges through the "light of truth" and one that judges through the "blindness of self-love." The "Creature" referred to is the human soul.</meta>

...on the contrary to this, those who only wish to make themselves judges of the will of **Men**, not looking at how, nor in what manner, but as if blinded by their own passion, judging truth as a lie, and a lie as truth. Oh, how crooked is their path, for being blind they wish to judge the light; they wish to judge even the great **Mysteries of God**, and that which He works in His Servants, and their ways and customs in their own way. Oh **human pride**, and how is the <term>Creature</term> <note>a human being, as a created thing</note> not ashamed to want to take the office out of the hand of its **Creator**? For it belongs to the Creature to wait to be judged, and not to judge; but she does not know this because she is deprived of the **light of truth**, and therefore she lightly judges and condemns what she has heard or hears of her **Neighbor**, or what she never saw. 

Thus her **conscience** remains entangled, scandalized in God and in her Neighbor, deprived of the delight of **charity**. Every evil comes from this, and she becomes indiscreet <note>original: "indiscreta," meaning lacking in spiritual discernment or the ability to distinguish between good and evil</note>; her taste is spoiled, so that what is good tastes bad to her, and what is bad seems good to her. She comes to hate and dislike the Mysteries of God and the works of Creatures. Such a person deprives himself of the price of the Blood of **Christ Crucified**, strips himself of every good, and falls into every evil. He becomes ungrateful and unrecognizing of the benefits he has received and receives—which ingratitude dries up the fountain of **Piety** <note>original: "Pietà," referring here to the flow of God's mercy and the soul's devotion</note>. He becomes unbearable to himself, holding and loving inordinately, without God, the riches, delights, and statuses of the World; and he carries his **labors** with impatience, not attributing the cause of the labors to his own **sins**, but often placing the blame on him who is without fault. 

This seems clearly visible today in the World, and especially in your City <note>likely referring to Florence, which was experiencing significant political upheaval and conflict with the Papacy during Catherine's mission</note>, where the great **tribulations** and changes we have had—and are about to have—due to our faults and defects, we want to unload these burdens onto others. Like sick people, we judge a holy intention as evil and perverse, and the disordered or bad intention (which attends to nothing but **self-love**) as good. This is due to the deprivation of the light; but the stones fall back upon the one who throws them.

### V.
One must not act this way, sweetest Daughter, but rather by attributing [the fault] to ourselves and to our own defects, each one to themselves. By doing so, we will appease the wrath of God, and we will flee the evil...

<summary>Catherine warns against the pride of judging others, which stems from a lack of spiritual light and leads to ingratitude and a distorted perception of reality. She relates this spiritual blindness to the political unrest and "tribulations" currently facing the recipient's city.</summary>

# To a Woman, who is not named.

I. She desires to see her illuminated with the true light of Faith to know the eternal truth of God, and how it is manifested in the Blood of Jesus Christ.
II. She exhorts her to the virtue of patience, for which the aforementioned light is required, and she consoles her in the misfortune that befell her.

## Letter 369.

->In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary.<-

<margin>I.</margin> **D**earest Sister in Christ sweet Jesus, I Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in his precious Blood, with the desire to see you illuminated by the truth of God, because in no other way could you participate in the life of grace in this world; you would be in continual bitterness, and in the end you would receive eternal damnation; because being deprived of the light, you would be scandalized <note>original: "scandalizzeresti," meaning to take offense at God's actions or to stumble spiritually</note> in all his mysteries, judging that which he gives you out of love as being from hatred, and that which he gives you for life as being for death. And what truth must we know, dearest Sister? We must see that God loves us supremely, and out of love was moved to create us in his image and likeness to give us the enjoyment of his eternal vision. Who manifests this truth and this love to us? The Blood of the humble and immaculate Lamb; for since we were deprived of the vision of God by the sin of Adam and banished from eternal life, this sweet and loving Word <note>The "Word" refers to Jesus Christ, from the Latin "Verbum."</note> was sent from the Father to endure death to give us life, and to wash away our faults with his precious Blood; and he, like one in love, ran to the shameful death of the Cross to fulfill the obedience of the Father and our salvation. This truth is not hidden from us; the Blood manifests it to us; for if God had not created us for the end mentioned, and did not love us inestimably, he would not have <note>This sentence continues on the following page.</note>

<summary>Catherine begins a letter to an anonymous woman, emphasizing that the "light of faith" is necessary to understand that God's actions—even painful ones—stem from love rather than hatred. She points to the sacrifice of Christ (the "Blood") as the ultimate proof of this divine love and the means of human salvation.</summary>

...would have given so great a redeemer. Therefore, the soul illuminated by this truth immediately receives in the eye of her **intellect** <note>The "intellect" was considered the faculty of the soul that perceives truth, which then moves the "will" to love.</note> the light of the most **Holy Faith**, holding for certain that what God gives and permits in this life to his Creature, he gives for love, and so that this truth may be fulfilled in us; wherefore she is immediately made patient, so that she is troubled by nothing, but remains content with what is permitted to her by the divine goodness.

<margin>II.</margin> **II.** Bearing with true and holy patience sickness, the loss of wealth, of status, of relatives, and of friends; and not only does she bear them with patience, but she holds them in due reverence as things sent to her by her sweet **Creator** out of love and for her sanctification. And who is that madman and fool who could be troubled by his own good? Only the one who is deprived of the light, because he does not know the truth nor his own good. I desire, therefore, dearest **Sister**, that you open the eye of your **Intellect**, pulling up and uprooting every root of self-love <note>original: "amore proprio," a central concept in Catherine's writing, referring to a selfish attachment to one's own will or comfort that blocks divine love.</note> and tenderness for yourself, so that you may know this truth, and see that **God** is the supreme Physician, and knows, and is able, and wants to give us what we need and the medicine that is necessary for our infirmity; so that with a sweet, holy, and real patience you may carry the medicine that he has given you out of the singular love that he bears you. To this I invite you, sweetest **Sister**, so that through impatience you do not lose the fruit of your **labors**, but in this life may remain in perfect peace and tranquility, in accord with the sweet will of **God**, and be troubled by nothing except only the offenses committed against him and the harm to souls. Doing this, you will show that you are **illuminated** by the truth, and in the end you will receive infinite fruit from your labors. I have felt compassion for the misfortune that has occurred <note>The specific "caso avvenuto" (the event that happened) is not named, but it likely refers to the loss of a relative or social standing mentioned earlier.</note>, but if I see you in accord with the will of **God**, and drawing from it what you ought, I will rejoice in it together with you. I say no more. Remain in the holy and sweet love of **God**. **Jesus** sweet, **Jesus** love.

# To Lady Pavola of Siena, and to her Disciples, while she was at Fiesole.

I. She exhorts her to charity, and the love of God, showing how without it all the other virtues are dead.

## Letter 370.

And then the Soul becomes "ordered," because whatever she loves, she loves for God’s sake, and she loves nothing outside of Him; and thus she becomes "another Him" through desire, because no other will is found in her but God’s will. Therefore, do not be negligent, but always run, breaking your own wills.

# To the aforementioned Lady Paola in Fiesole.

I. Of the ineffable Mystery of the Incarnation of the Word, and of the Redemption explained with the likeness of the seed, the flower, and the fruit.
II. Of the desire which the Only-begotten Son of God had for the honor of the Father, and for the salvation of Men, and how this desire was also very great in His most Holy Mother.
III. She exhorts Paola and her Daughters to be grateful to the Virgin Mary, to whom they had offered and given themselves, and to imitate her in this holy desire, and how they may acquire it.
IV. She exhorts her not to fear the snares of the Demons, and to fight with the armor and the Knife of divine Charity.
V. That this Knife must be kept hidden in the knowledge of oneself, and what effects such knowledge produces in the Soul.
VI. She invites her to go with her to the Holy Sepulchre, and to give there her Blood and her life for Jesus Christ, advising them that the Pope had already sent a Bull <note>A formal papal document.</note> to the Provincial of the Preachers <note>The Dominican Order (Ordo Praedicatorum).</note>, and of the Minors <note>The Franciscan Order (Ordo Fratrum Minorum).</note>, and to Father Raymond <note>Raymond of Capua, Catherine’s confessor and biographer.</note> with orders to enroll all those who wished to go to the Holy Sepulchre and die for the Faith.

...yielding to no illusion of the Devil, nor to the word of any creature, but manfully <note>Catherine often used the adverb "manfully" (virilmente) to encourage spiritual courage and strength in both men and women.</note> run, taking up that sweet affection of Mary—that is, that you should always seek the honor of God and the salvation of souls; and so I pray you. **V.** And know that, if we do not wish to lose the armor with which we must defend ourselves, we must keep it hidden in the house of our soul through true knowledge of ourselves. For when the soul knows itself to be nothing <note>This refers to Catherine's central revelation: "I am He who is, and you are she who is not."</note>, but always acting from that thing which is not, it immediately becomes humbled before God and every creature for God’s sake. It recognizes every grace and every benefit as coming from Him; and it sees such goodness of God overflowing within itself that, out of love, it grows in such justice toward itself that it not only desires to take vengeance on its own faults, but desires that all creatures take vengeance upon it, and it judges every creature to be better than itself. # To certain Daughters from Siena .

**I.** She exhorts them to be faithful and persevering in divine service.
**II.** That holy desire grows through the love of God toward us.
**III.** She exhorts them to the acquisition of purity by fleeing vain conversations.
**IV.** That once the soul has acquired purity, it extends its love toward God for the benefit of the Neighbor, helping the poor and afflicted.

## Letter 372.

->**In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified,**<-
->**and of sweet Mary.**<-

**I. D**earest daughters in sweet Jesus Christ, I Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ <note>original: "serva, e schiava de' Servi di Gesù Cristo." purity of mind and body could not be maintained by having many social interactions with creatures, nor by placing our affection and love in them; nor in created things outside the will of God; nor with self-love and tenderness for our own body; but it is acquired with much <term>diligence: <note>original: "sollicitudine." ## Letter 373.

->In the Name of Jesus Christ Crucified, and of sweet Mary.<-

Dearest Daughter in sweet Jesus Christ, I Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious Blood with the desire to see you partake of the Blood of the Son of God; for without the Blood, you cannot have life. Who are those who partake of the Blood? Those who live with the holy and sweet fear of God. Whoever fears God would rather die than ever offend Him mortally.

Therefore, my daughter, I weep and grieve that you—created in the image and likeness of God and ransomed by His precious Blood—do not consider your own dignity nor the great price that was paid for you. You have become a servant and a slave to sin; you have taken the Devil as your master, and you serve him day and night. 

Consider that a master gives to his servant what he himself possesses; if you serve the Devil, you partake of what is his. And what does the Devil have, my daughter? Darkness, storms, bitterness, pain, torments, and scourges. | | |
|:---|:---|
| As it is said that he can constrain himself, he will want to make resistance. | As it is said *not* that he can constrain. |
| Which will being placed in love, the lie, and disordered. | <margin>Letter 224.</margin> Being placed in love of the **lie** <note>original: "bugìa." In Catherine's writing, the "lie" often refers to the false self-love or the deceptive nature of sin.</note>. |
| And do not delay to say tomorrow I will do. | <margin>Letter 226.</margin> And do not delay, and say tomorrow I will do. |
| We spend time, which is the dearest thing that we have, let us wake up now. | Which is the dearest thing that we have uselessly: let us wake up. |
| In this way you will well place the bridle, and he will not run off departing with the will of God. | <margin>Letter 228.</margin> In this way you will place the bridle on them, and it will not run off departing *from* the will of God. |
| She is the close Sister of Charity, and so much does this sweet Mother Charity love her. | <margin>Letter 230.</margin> She is the close *Daughter* of Charity, etc. |
| But there come to us our disordered ways. | <margin>Letter 232.</margin> But *forbid us* <note>original: "vietaci." A correction from "vienci" (comes to us).</note> our disordered ways. |
| And with delight to treat the hatred, the displeasure, which one's own **sensuality** <term>Sensuality: In medieval theology, this refers to the lower, physical nature of a human being as opposed to the higher, spiritual soul.</term> would want to conceive towards him. | <margin>Letter 234.</margin> With *love to draw out* the hatred, etc. |
| The height of the Deity descended to such lowliness, as much as is our vanity. | <margin>Letter 235.</margin> As much as is our *humanity*. |
| Now let us see what is that thing which takes it from us, and what the Soul does, which has this light in itself. | <margin>Letter 236.</margin> What is that thing that takes it from us, and what gives it to us. |
| Of these her virtues, one follows the other because love is not without hope; these are Columns. | <margin>Letter 243.</margin> Because love is not without faith, nor faith without hope. |
| He condemns even himself, and the will of God. He does not condemn the servants of the World. | <margin>Letter 249</margin> He condemns even himself, *seeing* the will of God who allows those people to molest him for his own good. He does not condemn, etc. |

| Consider that every perfection without any scandal or pain comes from this Holy and true judgment; likewise every pain, guilt, whispering, and ruin of infidelity towards the Servants of God [comes from the opposite]. | Every perfection without any scandal or pain will give you this Holy and true judgment; so on the contrary false judgment gives every pain, etc. |
| <margin>Letter 247.</margin> He who is not tied to the World, let him cut himself off from it. | He who is tied to the World, etc. |
| <margin>Letter 248.</margin> Wherefore if it is a wind of consolation, it moves with joy of Heart. | With lightness of Heart, etc. |
| In the time of Battles <note>In Catherine’s writing, "battles" usually refer to spiritual trials or temptations.</note> we seem to be infirm and to offend God. | To be rebels and to offend God. |
| Because if before his eye there was not anything. | To the eye of his intellect. |
| <margin>Letter 264.</margin> I write to you in his merciful Blood with a desire to find you as a lost sheep, every greatest desire to return [you] to the fold with your Companions but etc. | I write to you in his **precious** <note>original: "pretioso." The correction changes "pietoso" (merciful) to "pretioso" (precious), a standard descriptor for the Blood of Christ in Catherine's theology.</note> Blood with a desire to return you to the fold with your own. |
| And do not be so cruel for his salvation as to make an instance of one of your arrivals. | To make <unclear>part</unclear> of one of your arrivals. |
| <margin>Letter 267.</margin> These are the flesh with the disordered sensory desire. | With the disordered sensory delight. |

| <margin>Letter 276.</margin> We must with free will prepare to offer in the presence of God. | Present and offer. |
| <margin>Letter 284.</margin> But attend to one thing, that whoever acts against this Blood with those who persecute the Blood. | But attend to one thing, that whoever acts against this <unclear>rest</unclear> <note>original: "posa." This could refer to a state of spiritual peace or a specific pause in action.</note>, or holds with those who persecute the Blood. |

| In saying, we follow the defects of bad Pastors. | *We pursue the defects of bad Pastors.* | *Letter 286.* |
| And of the Children of every Creature. | *And of the little children, and of every Creature.* | |
| Also out of love He sought. | *Out of love He created us.* | *Letter 316.* |
| If they were not banished to the World. | *If they did not rejoice in the World.* <note>The correction changes "relegassen" (relegated/banished) to "rallegrassero" (rejoiced).</note> | *Letter 322.* |
| By doing any natural thing. | *Any manual thing.* | |
| Hope, which Man has in hatred, does the opposite. | *Which Man has in God.* <note>A crucial theological correction: the original transcription mistakenly used "odio" (hatred) instead of "Dio" (God).</note> | *Letter 335* |
| And more torn than any other Animal. | *And more foul than any other Animal.* | *Letter 343.* |
| May He make you go out of the ordered World. | *Out of the ordered way.* <note>original: "modo." This clarifies that the soul should follow an "ordered way" of life rather than leaving an "ordered world."</note> | *Letter 344.* |

| Also for love he sought. | *For love he created us.* <note>The correction changes "sought" (cercò) to "created" (creò), emphasizing Catherine's view of creation as an act of divine love.</note> | Letter 316. |
| If they were not relegated to the World. | *If they did not gladden you in the World.* <note>original: "rallegrassero" instead of "relegassero."</note> | Letter 322. |

| Makes you go out of the ordered World. | *Outside of the ordered manner.* <note>The scribe likely confused "mondo" (world) with "modo" (way/manner).</note> | Letter 344. |
| See you now in the World. | *You, an old woman by now.* <note>The word "vecchia" (old woman) was misread as "vegga" (see/look) or "mondo" (world). Catherine often referred to herself with humility as she aged.</note> | Letter 349. |
| Oh stability of mind. | *Oh sterility of mind.* | Letter 358. |
| Because she seeks the will of God, and the honor, and the salvation of Souls. | *Because she seeks the honor of God in the salvation of Souls.* | Letter 359. |
| That the Soul found itself in one, and in that be perfect in every way. | *And in that, let her strive to be perfect.* <note>The correction replaces a passive or confused state with the active "strive" (ingegni).</note> | Letter 361. |

**Spiritual self-love**, how it is recognized, 751, 756, and following; it is consumed by the love of God, 751 and following. <note>In St. Catherine’s theology, spiritual self-love is the tendency to seek one's own comfort or "spiritual sweetness" rather than seeking God’s will alone.</note>

**Sensory love**, how it must be restrained, 240, 241.

**Servile and filial love**, and the difference between them, 528, 529. <note>Servile love is the fear of punishment (like a slave), while filial love is the affection of a child for a parent.</note>

**Love** is acquired through love, 636.

**Love toward God** is demonstrated by means of our Neighbor, 78, 151, 174, and following, 447, 510; and is acquired through the same neighbor, 79; effects that it causes in the Soul, 238; from the love of God one passes to the love of one's Neighbor, 268; how this is practiced, 275; the sweetness that it brings to the Soul, 288; and the effects it causes there, 288 and following, 750 and following; how it is acquired, 294, 295, 755; and where, 707, 753; how it produces all virtues, 513; likened to fire, and how it increases, 522; how it must be demonstrated, 523; how different it is from the love of the World, 592, 593, 603 and following, 633 and following; it requires no intermediary whatsoever, 705.

**Andrea Cavalcabove**, Senator of Siena, 166 and following. <note>A prominent political figure in Siena during the 14th century who corresponded with St. Catherine.</note>

**Angevins** of the first lineage, 33. <note>The House of Anjou, a royal house of French origin that ruled parts of Italy, including Naples.</note>

**The Soul** likened to a Tree, 173; where it must be planted, ibid. <note>original: "ivi"; meaning "in the same place" or page</note> and following, and 635; what is required so that it may bear fruit, 636; the flowers it produces belong to God, and the fruits are ours, 635; similar to a City that has three Gates, 364; of these, only one is in our power, ibid.; through it, we are Masters of the City, 365; the guard of this Gate is Conscience, 365; with what weapons it must be defended, 787; these must be kept hidden, 787; how it disposes itself to receive graces from God, 431 and following; set on fire by the love of God, it is likened to a Burning Arrow, 433; where it catches fire, 434; it must love either God or the World, 446, 603; how foolish it is if it attaches itself to the World, 723; likened to a Field, 539; in which the will is the Worker, 540; fortified by the union of the divine Word to human nature, ibid.; fruits that it must produce, 541; the soul is the cause of its own evil, 569; its enemies are weak and cannot harm it if the soul does not wish it, 570; the harm it causes itself through sin, 577; it cannot be satisfied except by God, 640, 723; Bride of Christ, 398; what its clothing must be, 599; how jealous God is of the soul, 599; likened to a Garden, 732; illuminated by God, how it accepts trials and consolations, 775.

-> # ON THE HEAVENS <-

<margin>In Book 1 of *On the Heavens*.</margin>
It is certain that this entire universe and all its parts shall endure forever in terms of their substance. This is first proven concerning the heaven and the stars. For the heaven is the simplest body of the universe, which <term>Aristotle</term> calls the <term>fifth essence</term> <note>original: "quintam essentiam"; also known as aether, this was believed to be a celestial substance distinct from the four earthly elements</note>, without any contrariety <note>the conflict between opposing qualities like hot and cold which causes change</note> that might cause decay. For in the heaven there is no heat and no cold; there is no motion except circular motion, which has no contrary. Therefore, not only <term>Aristotle</term>, but also <term>Anaxagoras</term>, <term>Plato</term>, and other philosophers, as well as the Sacred Scriptures themselves, testify that the heaven and all the stars are eternal.

<margin>Book 2 of *On the Heavens*.</margin>
From this, it is also gathered that the heaven, regarding its substance, is not at all subject to change, even if it does not lack local motion <note>movement from one place to another</note>. Add to this that the heaven is not made of <term>Hyle</term> <note>a Greek term for "prime matter," the formless basic stuff of the physical world</note>, but of that divine matter which has potential only for local motion. And hence it is that the heaven is neither <term>heavy</term> nor <term>light</term>. For things that are <term>heavy</term> are carried toward the center; things that are <term>light</term> tend upward from the center. But the heaven, because it is a round body, moves around the center; neither toward the center nor away from the center. Therefore, the heaven is neither <term>heavy</term> nor <term>light</term>.

<margin>Book of *On the Heavens*.</margin>
<term>Aristotle</term> also proves the magnitude of the universe by the fact that there is only one world. For if there were many worlds, the heaven would be either <term>heavy</term> or <term>light</term>, which has already been shown to be impossible.

<margin>*Metaphysics*, Book 12.</margin>
Furthermore, if there were multiple worlds, there would also be multiple first movers, which is impossible. For it is necessary that the <term>first mover</term> <note>the "unmoved mover," the primary cause of all motion in the universe according to Aristotle</note> be one, as a unique and singularly one cause of all other motions.

B 3

<summary>This page outlines the Aristotelian argument for the eternal, immutable, and unique nature of the heavens. It argues that celestial bodies are composed of a "fifth essence" that lacks earthly weight and is governed by a single "first mover."</summary>
<keywords>Cosmology, Aristotle, Fifth Essence, Aether, First Mover, Eternity of the World, Hyle, Physics</keywords>
